**Fully Comprehensive Findings**

The research thread asks whether the effects of generative artificial intelligence on K-12 mathematics differ between classroom use and homework or home-based use, and to identify studies, pilot reports, or syntheses that specify setting, teacher mediation, dosage, student prompting behavior, curriculum alignment, and implementation conditions. The gathered materials contain a mix of K-12 mathematics-specific items, broader K-12 AI education syntheses, teacher perspective papers, design papers, and homework-oriented web pages. Several sources are directly relevant, while many others are adjacent or only indirectly informative.

A major synthesis source identified is a systematic review/meta-analysis on K-12 mathematics learning with AI: **“The Effectiveness of AI on K-12 Students’ Mathematics Learning: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis”** [2]. The raw search result confirmed the title and that it is a systematic review and meta-analysis, but only the title/metadata were returned in the search output. This is the most directly relevant synthesis to K-12 mathematics, though the search output did not provide setting-specific moderation details. Another broader synthesis is **“ChatGPT for good? On opportunities and challenges of large language models for education”** [1], which was returned with full text extracted from OpenAlex. The raw search output identified it as a broad review of large language models for education, not K-12 mathematics-specific, but relevant as background for how generative AI may be used in education generally.

The most directly relevant K-12 mathematics classroom study identified in the search outputs is **“Learning Quadratic Functions with ChatGPT: An Innovative Experience in High School Mathematics Education”** [14]. The ERIC entry states that it explores the possibility of using ChatGPT as a tutor, to support the teacher's work in creating solid didactic and adidactic situations in the mathematics classroom, employing qualitative analysis methodologies. The study was based on a didactic experiment carried out in a 10th-grade class in Portugal, involving 26 students who were obtained through purposive sampling. This source is important because it explicitly situates ChatGPT in the mathematics classroom and frames the tool as supporting the teacher’s work rather than replacing it. It also clearly specifies the classroom setting and a teacher-mediated implementation.

Another highly relevant classroom-oriented mathematics source is **“Evolving Techniques and Emerging Schemes: Prospective Teachers’ Transformation of ChatGPT”** [15]. The abstract says it used an instrumental approach (Drijvers et al., 2013) to investigate how artificial intelligence (AI) or large language models (LLMs), specifically ChatGPT 3.5, transitioned from an artifact into an instrument for four prospective secondary mathematics teachers through the development of schemes and techniques in using the AI to construct teaching materials, a lesson plan, student activities, and other instructional supports. This source is relevant because it specifies teacher use, teacher mediation, and classroom-oriented instructional design. It is not a student outcome study, but it directly informs implementation conditions and how ChatGPT is used by teachers in mathematics.

A further teacher-centered mathematics education source is **“How Utilizing Generative AI When Addressing Pedagogical and Mathematical Events Contributes to Mathematics Teacher Educators’ TPACK (Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge)”** [16]. The abstract states that the study examines the contribution that generative AI (ChatGPT) can make to the TPACK of mathematics teacher educators (MTEs) when addressing pedagogical and mathematical events. The study involved 15 experienced MTEs who were tasked with planning training sessions for elementary school teachers. The MTEs were asked to formulate pedagogical and mathematical prompts. This is relevant to teacher mediation and curriculum/lesson planning, though not directly to student learning outcomes. It provides evidence that generative AI is being used in teacher education around mathematics and instructional planning.

The search results also identified **“Collaborate with Generative AI to Improve Classroom Assessments”** [17]. The abstract says creating assessment questions aligned to standards is a time-consuming task for teachers, but large language models such as ChatGPT can help. The article describes a three-step process for using ChatGPT to create assessments: 1) Ask ChatGPT to break standards into measurable targets. 2) Determine how much time to spend on each target. 3) Ask ChatGPT to generate questions at different levels. This source is relevant to curriculum alignment and implementation conditions, especially in classroom practice. It is not mathematics-specific in the raw abstract, but it clearly addresses standards alignment and teacher-mediated use of generative AI for assessment design.

A teacher support and motivation source in K-12 is **“Teacher Support and Student Motivation to Learn with Artificial Intelligence (AI) Based Chatbot”** [18]. The abstract says that as AI advances technologically, it will inevitably bring many changes to classroom practices, and notes that research on AI in education reflects a weak connection to pedagogical perspectives or instructional approaches, particularly in K-12 education. It says AI technologies may benefit motivated and advanced students. Understanding the teacher's role of student motivation in mediating AI use is highlighted. This is directly relevant to teacher mediation and implementation conditions, though the raw search output did not include mathematics-specific details.

Another K-12 classroom design source is **“Designing for human-AI complementarity in K-12 education”** [19]. The abstract says recent work has explored how complementary strengths of humans and artificial intelligence (AI) systems might be productively combined, but successful forms of human-AI partnership have rarely been demonstrated in real-world settings. The paper presents the iterative design and evaluation of Lumilo, smart glasses that help teachers help their students in AI-supported classrooms by presenting real-time information to teachers. This is relevant to classroom implementation conditions and teacher mediation, though not specifically mathematics in the returned metadata.

Another classroom-oriented K-12 teacher design source is **“Learning design to support student-AI collaboration: perspectives of leading teachers for AI in education”** [20]. The abstract states that preparing students to collaborate with AI remains a challenging goal, that AI technologies are new to K-12 schools, and that there is a lack of studies that inform how to design learning when AI is introduced as a collaborative learning agent to classrooms. The study aimed to explore teachers’ perspectives on what curriculum design, student-AI interaction, and learning activities should look like. This is relevant to curriculum alignment and implementation conditions in classroom settings.

The search results also identified **“Supporting Self-Directed Learning and Self-Assessment Using TeacherGAIA, a Generative AI Chatbot Application: Learning Approaches and Prompt Engineering”** [21]. The abstract says self-directed learning and self-assessment require student responsibility over learning needs, goals, processes, and outcomes, but that student-led learning can be challenging in a classroom limited by one-to-many teacher-led instruction. The authors designed and prototyped a generative artificial intelligence chatbot application (GAIA), named TeacherGAIA, that can be used to support self-directed learning and self-assessment. This source is relevant to student prompting behavior and learning in a classroom context, although the returned metadata does not specify mathematics.

A directly relevant math-adjacent pilot/report source is **“Students’ Perceived Roles, Opportunities, and Challenges of a Generative AI-powered Teachable Agent: A Case of Middle School Math Class”** [22]. The abstract states that ongoing advancements in Generative AI (GenAI) have boosted the potential of applying long-standing learning-by-teaching practices in the form of a teachable agent (TA). The study explored middle school math class perceptions of the roles, opportunities, and challenges of a GenAI-powered teachable agent. This is relevant because it is explicitly a middle school math class, and the idea of a teachable agent is strongly linked to prompting behavior and student-AI interaction. The raw search result does not provide outcome sizes, dosage, or moderation by setting, but it does specify the setting and the tool type.

Related to that is **“Development of a generative AI-powered teachable agent for middle school mathematics learning: A design-based research study”** [23]. The abstract says this paper reports on a design-based research (DBR) study that aims to devise an artificial intelligence (AI)-powered teachable agent that supports secondary school students’ learning-by-teaching practices of mathematics learning content. The study is specifically mathematics-focused and explicitly labeled design-based research. It is relevant to implementation conditions, student prompting behavior, and how a generative AI-powered agent may be used in school settings. The raw metadata does not provide classroom/homework distinctions, dosage, or outcomes, but it is directly in the K-12 mathematics domain.

The abstract says that while generative artificial intelligence (AI) tools are gradually being integrated into educational practice, their actual usability in classroom settings remains insufficiently understood. This mixed-methods research was designed as a small-sample pilot study, offering preliminary insights to inform a future large-scale scientific evaluation. The review **“What Is the Impact of ChatGPT on Education? A Rapid Review of the Literature”** [47] was also identified. The abstract indicates that it aims to enrich understanding of ChatGPT’s capabilities across subject domains, how it can be used in education, and potential issues raised by researchers during the first three months of interest. This is relevant to the broader synthesis thread, though not specific to K-12 mathematics or setting.

The general AI-in-education review **“A Review of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in Education from 2010 to 2020”** [48] is a content analysis of studies aiming to disclose how artificial intelligence has been applied to the education sector and explore the potential research trends and challenges. It selected 100 papers including 63 empirical papers (74 studies) and 37 analytic papers. This is background rather than directly answering the setting question, but it supports broader contextualization.

Two additional broad sources from OpenAlex/ERIC are **“Artificial intelligence in education: Addressing ethical challenges in K-12 settings”** [49] and **“Artificial intelligence in higher education: the state of the field”** [50]. The K-12 ethics paper is relevant to implementation conditions, while the higher education review is not directly in scope but can support general methodological comparison. Both are useful only as broader context.

The search outputs did not yield strong direct evidence of setting moderating outcomes in K-12 mathematics between classroom and homework/home-based use. However, several sources suggest meaningful differences in how tools are used by setting. In classroom contexts, sources repeatedly frame GenAI as teacher-mediated, curriculum-aligned, or embedded in teacher planning and classroom interaction: [14], [15], [16], [17], [18], [19], [20], [23], [24], [28], [34], [44]. In homework/home-based contexts, sources emphasize self-learning, self-regulated learning, homework help, assignment completion, and parent/caregiver support: [25], [26], [31], [33], [36], [37], [38], [39], [40]. The raw literature gathered here therefore points to a likely difference in implementation conditions and use patterns, even though the search outputs did not provide a direct head-to-head experimental moderation analysis for K-12 mathematics classroom versus homework/home-based settings.

Setting-specific use patterns are visible in the raw excerpts:
- Classroom: teacher support, support for lesson planning, instructional reach, teacher authority, didactic/adidactic situations, classroom assessment generation, classroom settings, and teacher mediation [14], [15], [16], [17], [18], [19], [20], [24], [44].
- Homework/home-based: “homework preparation,” “self-learning,” “self-directed learning,” “students often use them for homework preparation, self-learning, etc.,” “students use AI especially for homework,” “students completing class assignments,” “afterschool,” “outside of the classroom,” “AI-mediated support for parental involvement,” and “AI homework help” [25], [26], [31], [33], [36], [37], [38], [39], [40].

Dosage information was largely absent in the raw search outputs. The closest implementation-condition details came from the small-sample pilot, design-based research, or classroom coding papers [14], [23], [24], [44]. These sources specify sample sizes or participant counts in some cases:
- 10th-grade class in Portugal, involving 26 students [14].
- 4 prospective secondary mathematics teachers [15].
- 15 experienced MTEs [16].
- small-sample pilot study [24].
- classroom codesign pilot [44].
- 15 K-12 teachers in a co-design workshop [19].
- 1,454 teachers in a mixed methods survey [51] (see source list below for citation).
However, no explicit dosage metrics (e.g., number of sessions, minutes, frequency of prompts) were surfaced in the search excerpts, and no head-to-head setting moderation statistics were returned.

Student prompting behavior was explicitly addressed or implied in several sources. Prompt engineering appears as a key feature in TeacherGAIA [21], the DoYouTrustAI tool [41], the teachable agent studies [22], [23], and the math-specific Chat-Mat™ suite [26]. The Google Scholar and ERIC snippets also show that prompt precision and refinement matter in generative AI use, especially for creating lesson plans, assessments, and math prompts [15], [17], [26], [34]. The teacher perspective paper [20] and AI literacy modules [42], [43] further suggest that prompting behavior and student-AI interaction are implementation conditions of interest.

Curriculum alignment is directly represented in several sources. The most explicit are [17], [28], [29], [34], [35], [36], [20], and [33]. For example:
- [17] describes using ChatGPT to break standards into measurable targets and generate aligned questions.
- [28] explicitly says the paper addresses the need for scalable and high-quality educational assessment tools and the significant challenges of ensuring factual accuracy and curriculum alignment.
- [29] mentions that the curriculum aligned with state standards.
- [34] mentions curriculum-aligned lesson planning in low-resource schools.
- [35] mentions SMS-based AI giving curriculum-aligned support.
- [36] mentions curriculum-aligned scaffolding to assist caregivers in math.
- [20] asks what curriculum design should look like when AI is introduced as a collaborative learning agent.
- [33] mentions curriculum-aligned interaction with AI tools.

Implementation conditions and teacher mediation are central throughout the classroom sources. The raw record shows that classroom deployment often includes:
- teacher authority preserved [44],
- teachers supporting students with real-time information [19],
- teacher work in lesson planning and assessment creation [15], [17],
- teacher support and student motivation [18],
- one-to-many teacher-led instruction as the baseline classroom problem [21],
- teacher help balanced with student freedom [33],
- teacher mediation of instructional roles [34],
- teacher work in creating didactic/adidactic situations [14].

Observationally, the literature gathered here suggests that classroom use tends to be more teacher-mediated and curriculum-oriented, while homework/home-based use tends to be more autonomous, self-regulated, and prompt-intensive. But the raw data gathered did not include a directly quoted causal moderation result showing that setting changes the effect size of generative AI on K-12 mathematics achievement. The strongest direct evidence is therefore descriptive rather than inferential.

The sources also include non-mathematics but relevant K-12 AI classroom/teacher literature from ERIC and arXiv, including teacher reactions to AI in an urban school district [51], ethical challenges in K-12 AI [49], and bibliometric analysis of GenAI in education [52]. These help frame implementation and policy but do not directly address K-12 mathematics classroom vs homework comparisons.

In sum, the gathered records identify multiple K-12 mathematics or K-12-relevant generative AI studies and syntheses that specify classroom or homework/home-based settings, teacher mediation, curriculum alignment, or prompting behavior. However, no returned source in the raw search results directly reports a formal moderation analysis comparing classroom versus homework/home-based effects in K-12 mathematics. The evidence instead suggests different implementation modes: classroom use is typically teacher-mediated and curriculum-aligned, while homework/home-based use is typically self-directed, self-regulated, or caregiver-supported [14]-[44].

**Fully Comprehensive Findings**

Relevant evidence on documented harms, misuse patterns, integrity problems, reliability concerns, hallucinations, incorrect feedback, overreliance, cheating, equity gaps, privacy concerns, safety issues, and usage restrictions/guardrails in generative AI for K-12 mathematics was identified in a mix of empirical studies, reports, reviews, opinion pieces, and practitioner guidance. Where possible, the findings below preserve wording and statistics verbatim and distinguish between empirically observed harms and anticipated or discussed risks.

1. A high-profile empirical study directly reported harms to learning in high school mathematics. The OpenAlex record for “Generative AI without guardrails can harm learning: Evidence from high school mathematics” [1] states that “Generative AI is poised to revolutionize how humans work, and has already demonstrated promise in significantly improving human productivity. A key question is how generative AI affects learning-namely, how humans acquire new skills as they perform tasks. Learning is critical to long-term productivity, especially since generative AI is fallible and users must check its outputs.” The Tavily ADS abstract for the same study [2] states: “While generative AI has been shown to enhance productivity, its influence on learning new skills remains unclear. Our research examines the impact of generative AI, specifically GPT-4, on student learning in math education. Through a large-scale field experiment in a high school, our study reveals that although AI-based tutoring improves performance during practice sessions, students relying on the technology may underperform when access to AI is subsequently removed, indicating reduced skill acquisition. However, we also find that carefully designed safeguards, especially asking the AI tutor to provide teacher-designed hints instead of giving away answers, can mitigate these negative effects. Our findings highlight the need for thoughtful integration of generative AI in educational settings to ensure that human learning is preserved.” The Tavily/PDF snippet [3] adds directly that “GPT-4 can harm educational outcomes.” The Tavily PMC snippet [4] provides additional detail that the study uses “the error rate in solutions generated by GPT Base in the assisted problems” and “interaction terms between the error rate of GPT Base and the treatment arm,” and that it examines “student performance and learning in the subsequent unassisted exam.” The Google Scholar result [5] for the same paper says: “However, we believe ChatGPT differs from prior technologies in two significant … , ChatGPT is highly unreliable and often provides incorrect responses. Our results suggest that students …” This study is the clearest direct empirical evidence found that AI can improve practice performance while harming later unassisted performance; the harms are not merely anticipated, and the authors explicitly state that safeguards can mitigate negative effects, especially teacher-designed hints rather than giving away answers. It is an RCT / field experiment in high school mathematics [1][2][4][5].

2. A closely related OpenAlex/SSRN record for “Generative AI Can Harm Learning” [6] states: “That is, access to GPT-4 can harm educational outcomes. These negative learning effects are largely mitigated by the safeguards included in GPT...” This appears to be the earlier or preprint version of the same line of work and reinforces the conclusion that harms are empirically observed and guardrails matter [6].

3. Another direct empirical study found that ChatGPT-generated help can produce learning gains equivalent to human tutor-authored help on mathematics skills. The OpenAlex record for “ChatGPT-generated help produces learning gains equivalent to human tutor-authored help on mathematics skills” [7] reports: “In this paper, we conduct an efficacy evaluation of ChatGPT-generated help using a 3 x 4 study design (N = 274) to compare the learning gains of ChatGPT to human tutor-authored help across four mathematics problem subject areas.” The record does not mention harms in the abstract, but it is relevant to the achievement-effects question because it suggests apparent positive effects are possible in a controlled setting [7]. No directly quoted harm, misuse, or guardrail language was returned in the raw abstract snippet for this record [7].

Although this is about essays rather than mathematics, it documents directly the concern that ChatGPT could be mistaken for student work and that empirical evidence on integrity was limited [8].

Overall, the strongest directly observed harms in K-12 mathematics from the gathered evidence are: 
- reduced learning / reduced skill acquisition after AI access is removed in high school math, despite improved practice performance [1][2][4][6];
- AI outputs being fallible / unreliable / often incorrect, requiring users to check outputs [1][5][28];
- overreliance on incorrect ChatGPT recommendations among high school seniors, not reduced by a short AI literacy intervention [63];
- the need for teacher-designed hints and other safeguards to mitigate harm [2][6];
- concerns that automatic solving can bypass interpretation, decision-making, and mathematical validation processes [58];
- explicit ethical concerns in K-12 including bias and privacy risks [60][64][73];
- cheating / academic integrity concerns and the ability to produce superficially compelling but possibly inaccurate answers [8][36][45][49][50][51][53][54][66][69][70].

In terms of whether harms qualify or nullify apparent achievement effects: the direct field experiment in high school mathematics shows that AI-based tutoring can improve performance during practice sessions but may underperform when access is removed, indicating that apparent achievement gains do not necessarily translate into durable learning gains [1][2][4][6]. The authors explicitly state that safeguards, especially teacher-designed hints instead of giving away answers, can mitigate the negative effects [2][6]. Thus, apparent achievement effects are not nullified in all settings, but they are qualified by the possibility of reduced skill acquisition and dependence on AI. The evidence also shows that some positive learning gains can be achieved under controlled conditions with ChatGPT-generated help equivalent to human tutor-authored help [7], but the raw findings do not show whether those gains persist without access or whether overreliance risks were present. Guardrails and usage restrictions appear repeatedly in the literature, especially teacher-in-the-loop designs, hint-based prompting, student training on accuracy/reliability, explicit anti-cheating guidance, and policies promoting responsible rather than shortcut use [2][6][27][37][44][64][65][70][72].

Certainly! Here's a foundational framing of generative AI in K-12 mathematics education, broken down by components:

### 1. Intervention
**Definition:** Generative AI in K-12 math education refers to the use of AI algorithms that can create and adapt educational content, provide personalized learning experiences, and support problem-solving and conceptual understanding in mathematics.

### 2. Tool Features
- **Content Generation:** Automatically creating math problems, quizzes, and explanations.
- **Adaptive Learning:** Tailoring difficulty and problem types to individual student needs.
- **Immediate Feedback:** Providing instant hints, corrections, and explanations.
- **Interactive Simulations:** Visual and interactive tools to explore math concepts.
- **Natural Language Processing:** Understanding and answering student queries in natural language.
- **Progress Tracking:** Monitoring student performance and adapting future content accordingly.

### 3. Outcomes
- Improved conceptual understanding of math topics.
- Increased student engagement and motivation.
- Enhanced problem-solving skills.
- Personalized learning paths leading to better individual performance.
- Immediate and targeted feedback reducing misconceptions.
- Development of higher-order thinking skills through exploration and reasoning.

### 4. Priority Student Groups
- Students struggling with foundational math concepts.
- Gifted students needing advanced challenges.
- English Language Learners (ELL) who benefit from language-adapted explanations.
- Students with special education needs requiring personalized pacing.
- Underrepresented or disadvantaged groups needing equitable access to quality resources.

### 5. Instructional Contexts
- Classroom settings with teacher facilitation.
- Remote or hybrid learning environments.
- After-school tutoring or intervention programs.
- Self-paced learning modules integrated into the curriculum.
- Collaborative group projects supported by AI tools.

### 6. Evidence
- Research studies showing improved test scores and concept retention.
- Case studies demonstrating increased student engagement.
- Data analytics from AI tools showing personalized learning gains.
- Teacher testimonials on ease of use and impact on instruction.
- Meta-analyses of adaptive learning technologies in STEM education.

A comprehensive review of the integration of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in K-12 mathematics education frameworks reveals several key insights:

**Effectiveness of AI in Mathematics Learning**

A systematic review and meta-analysis published in the *International Journal of Science and Mathematics Education* in April 2025 examined 21 studies on AI's impact on K-12 students' mathematics performance. The findings indicated a small overall effect size of 0.343 favoring AI, suggesting a generally positive impact of AI integration in mathematics classrooms. Notably, AI demonstrated a greater impact when utilized as intelligent tutoring systems and adaptive learning systems. ([eric.ed.gov](https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1461689&utm_source=openai))

**Teacher Perspectives and Acceptance**

An experimental study published in the *International Journal of Education in Mathematics, Science and Technology* in January 2026 investigated pre-service teachers' attitudes toward GenAI tools in assessment. The study found that engagement with differentiated GenAI tools led to notable changes in teachers' attitudes and acceptance levels, emphasizing the need for a nuanced approach to AI integration in education. ([files.eric.ed.gov](https://files.eric.ed.gov/fulltext/EJ1494399.pdf?utm_source=openai))

**Frameworks for AI Integration**

A report titled "Framework for AI-Powered Learning Environments," published by the National Center on Education and the Economy in 2024, discusses the evolving role of GenAI in education. The report emphasizes the importance of understanding how students should work with AI, highlighting the necessity for frameworks that guide effective AI integration in learning environments. ([eric.ed.gov](https://eric.ed.gov/?ff1=dtySince_2016&pg=8&q=artificial+AND+intelligence+AND+framework&utm_source=openai))

**Professional Knowledge for AI-Generated Lesson Planning**

A 2024 study titled "The Professional Knowledge Required for High-Quality AI-Generated Mathematics Lesson Planning" examines the expertise needed for mathematics teachers to effectively use GenAI in lesson planning. The study proposes a human-centered, iterative workflow model where GenAI-generated outputs are continuously refined through teachers' professional judgment, underscoring the indispensable role of teacher expertise in ensuring inclusive and instructionally meaningful materials. ([eric.ed.gov](https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED673901&utm_source=openai))

These studies collectively highlight the potential benefits of integrating GenAI into K-12 mathematics education, provided that educators possess the necessary professional knowledge to utilize these tools effectively. The development of comprehensive frameworks and ongoing professional development are crucial for the successful adoption of GenAI in educational settings.

To address K-12 math learning outcomes, here is an overview focusing on different instructional methods and tools including standard instruction, tutoring, worked examples, practice with feedback, educational software, intelligent tutoring systems, calculators, and online practice platforms, along with evidence from research comparing these approaches to baseline or no-generative AI conditions.

1. **Baseline and Standard Instruction**:
   - Baseline typically refers to traditional classroom teaching without additional support.
   - Standard instruction involves teacher-led lessons, textbooks, and regular classroom activities.
   - Research shows standard instruction produces varied outcomes depending on teacher quality, student engagement, and resources.

2. **Tutoring**:
   - One-on-one or small group tutoring has strong evidence supporting positive effects on math achievement.
   - Tutoring provides personalized support, immediate feedback, and adaptive pacing.
   - Studies indicate tutoring typically outperforms standard classroom instruction alone.

3. **Worked Examples**:
   - Worked examples guide students step-by-step through math problems, reducing cognitive load.
   - Research demonstrates that worked examples, especially when combined with practice, improve conceptual understanding and problem-solving skills.
   - Effective particularly for novices or struggling students.

4. **Practice with Feedback**:
   - Deliberate practice with immediate, corrective feedback is critical for skill acquisition.
   - Feedback helps correct errors, reinforce correct methods, and maintain motivation.
   - Studies show practice plus feedback is more effective than practice without feedback.

5. **Educational Software and Intelligent Tutoring Systems (ITS)**:
   - Educational software covers a range of tools from drill-and-practice programs to interactive lessons.
   - ITS are advanced systems using AI to provide personalized instruction, hints, and feedback.
   - Meta-analyses show ITS can produce learning gains comparable to or exceeding those from human tutoring in some contexts.
   - ITS benefits include scalability, consistency, and adaptability to student needs.

6. **Calculators**:
   - Calculators reduce computational load allowing focus on higher-level problem solving.
   - Studies suggest calculator use does not impair math learning and can support understanding when used appropriately.

7. **Online Practice Platforms**:
   - Platforms like Khan Academy, IXL, and others offer accessible math practice with instant feedback.
   - Research supports their effectiveness in supplementing instruction, providing differentiated practice, and increasing engagement.

**Comparison and Evidence Summary**:
- Tutoring outperforms standard instruction but is resource-intensive.
- Worked examples combined with practice and feedback outperform practice alone.
- ITS offer personalized, scalable tutoring-like support, with evidence indicating learning gains above baseline.
- Calculators and online practice platforms are effective supplements rather than replacements for instruction.
- Combining these approaches with quality instruction yields the best results.

Research comparing K-12 mathematics instruction methods—including standard instruction, worked examples, drill and practice, calculators, intelligent tutoring systems, and online practice platforms—has yielded valuable insights.

**Worked Examples and Self-Explanation:**
Integrating self-explanation with worked examples in intelligent tutoring systems (ITS) has been shown to enhance problem-solving skills and efficiency in algebra. A study involving middle school students demonstrated that guiding learners to select conceptually rich explanations during ITS sessions led to higher posttest scores, indicating improved conceptual and procedural understanding. ([files.eric.ed.gov](https://files.eric.ed.gov/fulltext/ED623402.pdf?utm_source=openai))

**Drill and Practice Systems:**
Early computer-assisted instruction (CAI) programs focused on drill and practice, supplementing traditional curricula. These systems provided repetitive exercises to reinforce skills, aiming to maintain high proficiency levels and master difficult exercises through daily interaction. While effective in skill reinforcement, their impact on conceptual understanding was limited. ([files.eric.ed.gov](https://files.eric.ed.gov/fulltext/ED030592.pdf?utm_source=openai))

**Intelligent Tutoring Systems (ITS):**
ITSs offer personalized instruction by adapting to individual student needs. For instance, the "I CAN Learn" program delivers interactive math lessons at a one-to-one student-to-computer ratio, allowing students to progress upon demonstrating mastery. This approach has been associated with improved mathematics achievement among high school students. ([eric.ed.gov](https://eric.ed.gov/default.aspx?ff1=subMathematics+Achievement&ff2=subAlgebra&ff3=subMathematics+Instruction&pg=5&q=funded%3Ay&utm_source=openai))

**Online Practice Platforms:**
Platforms like MathSpring provide personalized math content, remedial tutoring, and affective support. A randomized controlled trial involving fifth and sixth-grade students found that those using MathSpring outperformed peers on state assessments, highlighting the effectiveness of online practice platforms in enhancing mathematical outcomes. ([files.eric.ed.gov](https://files.eric.ed.gov/fulltext/ED674520.pdf?utm_source=openai))

**Calculator Use:**
The impact of calculator use in K-12 mathematics instruction varies. While calculators can aid in complex computations, excessive reliance may hinder the development of fundamental arithmetic skills. Balanced integration of calculators, alongside traditional methods, is recommended to support both procedural fluency and conceptual understanding.

In summary, integrating self-explanation with worked examples in ITSs appears particularly effective in enhancing algebra learning. Drill and practice systems are beneficial for skill reinforcement but may not significantly improve conceptual understanding. Online practice platforms offer personalized support, leading to better mathematical outcomes. Calculator use should be balanced to support skill development without hindering conceptual learning.

Generative AI tools are increasingly integrated into K-12 mathematics instruction, offering personalized learning experiences and immediate feedback. However, their effectiveness is influenced by several implementation conditions, including teacher mediation, prompt design, guardrails against incorrect outputs, curriculum alignment, limits on autonomous student use, interaction patterns, scaffolding, metacognitive prompts, and time on task.

**Teacher Mediation and Prompt Design**

Effective use of generative AI in math education requires active teacher involvement. Educators can guide students in formulating precise prompts, enhancing the quality of AI-generated responses. This process, known as prompt engineering, helps students develop critical thinking and problem-solving skills. For instance, a study on integrating generative AI into STEM education emphasizes the importance of prompt engineering to foster self-regulated learning and metacognitive reflection. ([link.springer.com](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s43031-025-00125-z?utm_source=openai))

**Guardrails Against Incorrect Outputs**

Without proper safeguards, generative AI tools may produce incorrect or misleading information. Research indicates that students might struggle to detect inaccuracies in AI-generated content, potentially undermining learning outcomes. Implementing guardrails, such as teacher oversight and AI-generated content verification, is crucial to ensure the reliability of AI-assisted learning. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12232635/?utm_source=openai))

**Curriculum Alignment and Limits on Autonomous Student Use**

Aligning AI-generated content with the existing curriculum ensures relevance and coherence in instruction. Establishing clear guidelines on the extent of autonomous student use of AI tools helps maintain a balance between AI assistance and independent learning. A framework suggests that, for middle school students, AI engagement should be limited to 60 minutes per day, with at least 80% of the work remaining student-driven. ([link.springer.com](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44436-025-00024-0?utm_source=openai))

**Interaction Patterns and Immediate Feedback**

Structured interaction patterns, such as setting specific time frames for problem-solving with AI tools, can enhance student engagement and focus. Providing immediate feedback through AI systems allows students to identify and correct errors promptly, reinforcing learning. Research on AI teachable agents in mathematics learning highlights the importance of time-boxed interactions to maintain student attention and task completion. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12635076/?utm_source=openai))

**Scaffolding and Metacognitive Prompts**

Scaffolding strategies, including step-by-step instructions and reflective prompts, support students in effectively using AI tools. Encouraging metacognitive reflection through AI-generated prompts helps students assess their understanding and learning processes. Studies on AI integration in education emphasize the role of scaffolding in developing critical thinking and metacognitive skills. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2666920X25001006?utm_source=openai))

**Time on Task**

Monitoring the duration of AI-assisted learning sessions is essential to prevent cognitive overload and ensure productive engagement. Implementing time limits and structured schedules can help maintain optimal learning conditions. A proposed framework recommends limiting AI use to 30 minutes per day for younger students, with a high percentage of independent work, to promote effective learning. ([link.springer.com](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44436-025-00024-0?utm_source=openai))

In summary, while generative AI tools offer promising avenues for enhancing K-12 math instruction, their success depends on thoughtful implementation strategies that address teacher mediation, prompt design, content accuracy, curriculum alignment, student autonomy, interaction patterns, scaffolding, metacognitive development, and time management.

Recent research has explored the integration of generative AI chatbots into K-12 mathematics education, focusing on prompt design, feedback mechanisms, and scaffolding strategies to enhance classroom learning.

A study published in the International Journal of Education in Mathematics, Science and Technology emphasizes the importance of process-centered approaches in AI-assisted education. It advocates for staged drafts, in-class checkpoints, and brief justifications to make authorship and decision pathways transparent. The study also recommends using multi-source evidence, including process artifacts and instructor judgment, rather than solely relying on AI-detection tools. To promote equity and access, the researchers advise providing institutionally vetted tools, accessibility features, and low-bandwidth or offline pathways to prevent widening existing gaps. In course design, generative AI should scaffold question generation, planning, formative feedback, and reflective synthesis, while reserving claim-evidence-reasoning, source evaluation, and final interpretations for learners. The research agenda should prioritize causal and longitudinal studies of learning and transfer, broadening representation to include faculty and students from diverse backgrounds. ([files.eric.ed.gov](https://files.eric.ed.gov/fulltext/EJ1494380.pdf?utm_source=openai))

Another study in the Asian Journal of Distance Education presents a co-design model for lesson planning that incorporates generative AI. Implemented with approximately 500 educators, including K-12 teachers, university faculty, instructional designers, and curriculum coordinators, the model demonstrated adaptability and effectiveness across diverse educational settings. Preliminary findings indicated that 85% of the lesson plans met satisfactory ratings, aligning with theoretical frameworks. However, challenges such as insufficient knowledge of the co-design model and lack of reference materials were noted, highlighting the need for comprehensive training and resources. ([files.eric.ed.gov](https://files.eric.ed.gov/fulltext/EJ1476270.pdf?utm_source=openai))

Additionally, a study published in the journal Computers & Education examined the effects of chatbot-assisted in-class debates on students' argumentation skills and task motivation. The research found that engaging students in debates with AI chatbots enhanced their argumentation abilities and increased motivation, suggesting that AI can serve as a valuable tool in developing critical thinking skills. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0360131523001392?utm_source=openai))

These studies collectively underscore the potential of generative AI chatbots to support K-12 mathematics education through effective prompt design, feedback mechanisms, and scaffolding strategies, provided that educators receive adequate training and resources to implement these technologies effectively.

--- SOURCE 2: How AI can improve tutor effectiveness | K-12 Dive ---
URL: https://www.k12dive.com/news/ai-tutor-effectiveness-stanford-university/728980/
Content: A Stanford University study of its AI tutor assistance tool revealed improved student performance and increased tutor capacity to support learning. Stanford University researchers found that an AI tutor assistance tool was able to improve student performance and increase tutors’ capacity to support learning with guided questions and additional support. * Using a generative artificial intelligence tool during in-person tutoring sessions increased the tutors’ capacity to guide students through complex math problems and led to improved student math performance, according to a study released Monday from Stanford University researchers. Students whose tutors used Tutor CoPilot were 4 percentage points more likely to progress through math tutoring session assessments successfully compared to students whose tutors did not have AI assistance, the study found. Students of lower-rated tutors who used the AI assistance increased their math proficiency up to 9 percentage points on average compared to students learning from lower-rated tutors without AI assistance. The study included 900 tutors and 1,800 elementary and secondary school students from a large school district in the South.

--- SOURCE 3: Kids who use ChatGPT as a study assistant do worse on tests ---
URL: https://hechingerreport.org/kids-chatgpt-worse-on-tests/
Content: Researchers at the University of Pennsylvania found that Turkish high school students who had access to ChatGPT while doing practice math problems did worse on a math test compared with students who didn’t have access to ChatGPT. Those with ChatGPT solved 48 percent more of the practice problems correctly, but they ultimately scored 17 percent worse on a test of the topic that the students were learning. The researchers titled their paper, “Generative AI Can Harm Learning,” to make clear to parents and educators that the current crop of freely available AI chatbots can “substantially inhibit learning.” Even a fine-tuned version of ChatGPT designed to mimic a tutor doesn’t necessarily help. The researchers believe the problem is that students are using the chatbot as a “crutch.” When they analyzed the questions that students typed into ChatGPT, students often simply asked for the answer. When students have access to ChatGPT, they might answer more problems correctly, but learn less.

--- SOURCE 4: What the research shows about generative AI in tutoring | Brookings ---
URL: https://www.brookings.edu/articles/what-the-research-shows-about-generative-ai-in-tutoring/
Content: Third, tutoring platforms enhanced by generative AI help to create psychologically safe learning environments where students feel comfortable seeking the academic help they need. Beyond supporting teacher development, these platforms can restructure how instructional time is used through models like flipped classrooms where students engage with introductory material at home via tutoring platforms enhanced by generative AI. While each tutoring platform outlined in Table 1 has its own particular affordances, all share a focus on pedagogically sound design, an approach that my new co-authored Brookings publication “A new direction for students in an AI world: Prosper, prepare, protect” has shown is critical for AI to deliver its promised learning benefits. The success of these tutoring platforms enhanced by generative AI is grounded in pedagogies that “teach, not tell”—employing Socratic approaches, asking questions that guide students to identify their own mistakes rather than providing direct answers, and breaking down complex issues to manage cognitive load and make learning more digestible.

--- SOURCE 5: AI Tutors: Hype or Hope for Education? ---
URL: https://www.educationnext.org/ai-tutors-hype-or-hope-for-education-forum/
Content: In Salman Khan’s new book, *Brave New Words: How AI Will Revolutionize Education (and Why That’s a Good Thing)* (Viking, 2024), the Khan Academy founder predicts that AI will transform education by providing every student with a virtual personalized tutor at an affordable cost. * A Harvard study found that students using a custom-designed AI chatbot tutor for a physics course showed approximately double the learning gains and significantly higher engagement compared to those in a traditional classroom. Researchers found that access to the AI tutors significantly improved math performance (by 48 percent to 127 percent) but subsequently harmed educational outcomes when access was removed (17 percent reduction), suggesting students used GPT-4 as a “crutch” instead of actually learning critical skills. While I am skeptical that we are about to undergo an AI-powered education revolution, I do believe that we should aggressively and widely experiment with all methods that may help students learn.

URL: https://www.newschools.org/blog/what-260-ideas-taught-us-about-genai-math-tutoring/
Content: This work unfolded against a backdrop of troubling NAEP math scores, growing educator interest in AI tutoring, and continued recognition of high-dosage tutoring as one of the most effective strategies for accelerating learning. At the same time, schools want to expand tutoring to reach more students in more settings, while leaders across sectors are making unprecedented investments in AI in education. The most promising ideas use AI to help tutors prepare more effectively, give teachers real-time insights to better support students, and make student learning more interactive and social. We backed solutions that keep people in the equation and use AI to make tutoring more scalable, effective, and human-centered. In the short term, success means students taking more ownership of their learning and tutors becoming more effective, supported by timely, accurate feedback. We’ll get better by collaborating with educators and students to test tools thoughtfully, learn what works, and improve along the way.

In the end, students using the supervised AI tutor performed slightly better than those who chatted online via text with human tutors — they were able to solve new kinds of problems on subsequent topics successfully 66.2% of the time, compared to 60.7% with human tutors. The new findings could encourage schools to use AI as a kind of “front line” tutor, with humans intervening when a student is “derailing the conversation, or they have such a persistent misconception that the AI can’t deal with it,” said Groot. “I still mostly think that entirely AI tutoring programs are biased towards students who want to do the work or are interested in learning,” Cohen said, “and it’s pretty easy to see that students who aren’t bought in or are frustrated are going to give up more readily with an AI tutor.”.

--- SOURCE 3: Generative AI use in K-12 education: a systematic review ---
URL: https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/education/articles/10.3389/feduc.2025.1647573/full
Content: Research has been conducted to understand what K-12 teachers think about and do with GenAI, such as ChatGPT ([Hays et al., 2024](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/education/articles/10.3389/feduc.2025.1647573/full#ref20)). Within the pre-service education context, which falls within the scope of this research as they are trained as future teachers, we excluded studies considering factors influencing their adoption of GenAI in teaching (e.g., [Hu et al., 2025](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/education/articles/10.3389/feduc.2025.1647573/full#ref22)). Papers that collected teachers’ perspectives after a ChatGPT training program, such as the integration of ChatGPT into primary schools ([Uğraş et al., 2024a](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/education/articles/10.3389/feduc.2025.1647573/full#ref52)), but did not report its implementation with students or effectiveness based on study evaluation, were not considered relevant for this study’s goals. [Jauhiainen and Guerra (2023)](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/education/articles/10.3389/feduc.2025.1647573/full#ref26) call for longitudinal studies on the topic, including research-based evidence about generative AI’s role and impacts on pupils’ learning outcomes, especially when learning material has been adapted with GenAI. With clear evidence from our review and researchers’ submissions (e.g., [Jauhiainen and Garagorry Guerra, 2024](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/education/articles/10.3389/feduc.2025.1647573/full#ref25)) of limited research experimenting with GenAI tools by teachers and students in school or out-of-school settings, there is a need for high-quality research and intervention studies along these lines.

--- SOURCE 4: Kids who use ChatGPT as a study assistant do worse on tests ---
URL: https://hechingerreport.org/kids-chatgpt-worse-on-tests/
Content: Researchers at the University of Pennsylvania found that Turkish high school students who had access to ChatGPT while doing practice math problems did worse on a math test compared with students who didn’t have access to ChatGPT. Those with ChatGPT solved 48 percent more of the practice problems correctly, but they ultimately scored 17 percent worse on a test of the topic that the students were learning. The researchers titled their paper, “Generative AI Can Harm Learning,” to make clear to parents and educators that the current crop of freely available AI chatbots can “substantially inhibit learning.” Even a fine-tuned version of ChatGPT designed to mimic a tutor doesn’t necessarily help. The researchers believe the problem is that students are using the chatbot as a “crutch.” When they analyzed the questions that students typed into ChatGPT, students often simply asked for the answer. When students have access to ChatGPT, they might answer more problems correctly, but learn less.

Content: ### Who the Research Focuses On. Most research on AI in education focuses on **students as users of AI tools**. The report reviews the current research, focusing specifically on studies that convincingly estimate causal impact, meaning studies that can tell us whether an AI tool changed outcomes for students or educators. After reviewing the full repository, we identified **only 20 high-quality causal studies** that rigorously examine how AI tools affect students or educators. **Figure 3**: Percentage of Research Repository and causal impact papers by the **user of the AI tool**. Across the causal studies reviewed, evidence suggests that **AI tools designed with pedagogical guardrails – such as tutoring systems that give hints or guide reasoning – show more promising outcomes than general-purpose chatbots that provide answers directly.**Learning science provides one way to interpret these findings. Early causal studies suggest that educator-facing AI tools may reduce time spent on tasks such as lesson preparation while maintaining instructional quality.

Educators and their students who use GenAI as a tutor, writing assistant, or brainstorming partner voice concerns about overdependence and losing their own skills, especially critical thinking (Simkute et al., 2025). A review of learning trends in computer science presents the conundrum of AI tools reducing students’ analytical thinking while learning to code at a time when knowing how to critically evaluate GenAI outputs is in itself a newly required competency (Prather et al., 2025). --- SOURCE 3: Research Notes: Two Emerging Strategies for Using AI in Tutoring ---
URL: https://www.future-ed.org/research-notes-two-emerging-strategies-for-using-ai-in-tutoring/
Content: Two new randomized controlled trials find that AI embedded in live, chat-based math tutoring can improve student academic outcomes, raising questions about the tradeoffs between cost and the value of personal connections provided by human tutors. One study, conducted by researchers from Google and Eedi Labs, evaluated LearnLM, a generative AI tutoring system that provides responses to students’ questions that are reviewed by a supervising human tutor. Within each tutoring session, students were randomly assigned to one of three conditions: chatting with a human tutor, chatting with LearnLM, or receiving static, pre-written hints from the Eedi Labs platform. In a study conducted between March and May 2024, 1,000 elementary school students were randomly assigned to chat-based sessions with either a human tutor alone or a human tutor using Tutor CoPilot. Research continues to demonstrate the positive impact of “sustained and strong” relationships between students and their tutors on student outcomes, prompting a fundamental question: can AI, on its own, replicate a human relationship? Content: Third, tutoring platforms enhanced by generative AI help to create psychologically safe learning environments where students feel comfortable seeking the academic help they need. Beyond supporting teacher development, these platforms can restructure how instructional time is used through models like flipped classrooms where students engage with introductory material at home via tutoring platforms enhanced by generative AI. While each tutoring platform outlined in Table 1 has its own particular affordances, all share a focus on pedagogically sound design, an approach that my new co-authored Brookings publication “A new direction for students in an AI world: Prosper, prepare, protect” has shown is critical for AI to deliver its promised learning benefits. The success of these tutoring platforms enhanced by generative AI is grounded in pedagogies that “teach, not tell”—employing Socratic approaches, asking questions that guide students to identify their own mistakes rather than providing direct answers, and breaking down complex issues to manage cognitive load and make learning more digestible.

A review of learning trends in computer science presents the conundrum of AI tools reducing students’ analytical thinking while learning to code at a time when knowing how to critically evaluate GenAI outputs is in itself a newly required competency (Prather et al., 2025). The new findings could encourage schools to use AI as a kind of “front line” tutor, with humans intervening when a student is “derailing the conversation, or they have such a persistent misconception that the AI can’t deal with it,” said Groot. “I still mostly think that entirely AI tutoring programs are biased towards students who want to do the work or are interested in learning,” Cohen said, “and it’s pretty easy to see that students who aren’t bought in or are frustrated are going to give up more readily with an AI tutor.”.

--- SOURCE 2: Generative AI use in K-12 education: a systematic review - Frontiers ---
URL: https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/education/articles/10.3389/feduc.2025.1647573/full
Content: Research has been conducted to understand what K-12 teachers think about and do with GenAI, such as ChatGPT ([Hays et al., 2024](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/education/articles/10.3389/feduc.2025.1647573/full#ref20)). Within the pre-service education context, which falls within the scope of this research as they are trained as future teachers, we excluded studies considering factors influencing their adoption of GenAI in teaching (e.g., [Hu et al., 2025](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/education/articles/10.3389/feduc.2025.1647573/full#ref22)). Papers that collected teachers’ perspectives after a ChatGPT training program, such as the integration of ChatGPT into primary schools ([Uğraş et al., 2024a](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/education/articles/10.3389/feduc.2025.1647573/full#ref52)), but did not report its implementation with students or effectiveness based on study evaluation, were not considered relevant for this study’s goals. [Jauhiainen and Guerra (2023)](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/education/articles/10.3389/feduc.2025.1647573/full#ref26) call for longitudinal studies on the topic, including research-based evidence about generative AI’s role and impacts on pupils’ learning outcomes, especially when learning material has been adapted with GenAI. With clear evidence from our review and researchers’ submissions (e.g., [Jauhiainen and Garagorry Guerra, 2024](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/education/articles/10.3389/feduc.2025.1647573/full#ref25)) of limited research experimenting with GenAI tools by teachers and students in school or out-of-school settings, there is a need for high-quality research and intervention studies along these lines.

Content: The reason for identifying ChatGPT as the focus of this special issue was mainly of practical nature: whilst studying resources and tools used by students for their learning of mathematics (in engineering and teacher education) in the researchers’ institutions (Pepin & Kock, 2021. study’s aim was to investigate the perspective of various stakeholders (e.g., students, educators) on the use of artificial intelligence in teaching mathematics, in particular after ChatGPT had been launched. By engaging in ongoing dialogues with students, ChatGPT not only answered their questions, but also encouraged deeper understanding through sequential questioning, which adapted to students’ evolving needs and helped to develop their communication abilities (e.g., Chiu et al., 2023a.Teacher support and student motivation to learn with artificial intelligence (AI) chatbot. Harvard Educational Review, 59(2), 217–222.")), we contend that the incorporation of AI technologies, with a particular focus on generative AI models such as ChatGPT, has been accompanied by a revolutionary atmosphere in the field of education, also in mathematics education, fundamentally altering the ways students engage with mathematical problem-solving.

URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12057034/
Content: This study integrates the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) and the Theory of Planned Behavior (TPB), incorporating a factor of AI awareness to explore the determinants of teachers’ usage behavior in employing Gen-AI for mathematics instruction. To effectively meet the research objective of identifying the key factors that significantly influence mathematics teachers’ usage behavior of Gen-AI tools in their teaching practices, we utilized smartPLS 4.0 software to examine the conceptual model in two areas: the measurement model and the structural model. First, by incorporating AI awareness as an external variable and adjusting the original models based on their strengths and weaknesses, this study extends the existing TAM and TPB models to explore the factors significantly influencing K-12 mathematics teachers’ use of Gen-AI in teaching activities. This study utilized the PLS-SEM method, drawing on an extended TAM and TPB model, to uncover the factors influencing K-12 mathematics teachers’ adoption of Gen-AI in their teaching practices.

--- SOURCE 7: Kids who use ChatGPT as a study assistant do worse on tests ---
URL: https://hechingerreport.org/kids-chatgpt-worse-on-tests/
Content: Researchers at the University of Pennsylvania found that Turkish high school students who had access to ChatGPT while doing practice math problems did worse on a math test compared with students who didn’t have access to ChatGPT. Those with ChatGPT solved 48 percent more of the practice problems correctly, but they ultimately scored 17 percent worse on a test of the topic that the students were learning. The researchers titled their paper, “Generative AI Can Harm Learning,” to make clear to parents and educators that the current crop of freely available AI chatbots can “substantially inhibit learning.” Even a fine-tuned version of ChatGPT designed to mimic a tutor doesn’t necessarily help. The researchers believe the problem is that students are using the chatbot as a “crutch.” When they analyzed the questions that students typed into ChatGPT, students often simply asked for the answer. When students have access to ChatGPT, they might answer more problems correctly, but learn less.

--- SOURCE 8: Stanford report questions AI impact in K-12 education ---
URL: https://www.edtechinnovationhub.com/news/stanford-report-finds-limited-evidence-behind-ai-impact-in-k-12-classrooms
Content: #### **New analysis from** **Stanford’s SCALE** **initiative highlights rapid growth in AI research, but finds only a small number of rigorous studies guiding real-world education decisions.**. **New analysis from** **Stanford’s SCALE** **initiative highlights rapid growth in** **AI** **research, but finds only a small number of rigorous studies guiding real-world education decisions.**. Stanford Graduate School of Education’s SCALE initiative has published a new review of artificial intelligence in K-12 education, finding that while AI tools are being adopted quickly across classrooms, there is still limited high-quality evidence on their actual impact on teaching and learning. The report, *The Evidence Base on AI in K-12: A 2026 Review*, analyzes more than 800 academic studies, now expanded to over 1,100 papers in its research repository, but identifies just 20 causal studies that rigorously measure how AI tools affect outcomes for students or educators. While student-focused research dominates, the report highlights early evidence that AI tools can support educators in specific areas.

## The intense debate over whether students should be able to use artificial intelligence in the classroom is intensifying as schools in the northern hemisphere prepare for a new term. In the UK experts who advise schools on technology say teachers need help and guidance to understand what is cheating and what isn’t. **Listen to Australian and world news, and follow trending topics with** **SBS News Podcasts****.**. *“I use it a lot for online homework, revision tools, so if I need any additional support and I don’t want to ask my teacher, or it’s something she can’t give me, it is available, like whenever I need it on, like AI programmes."*. *“I would say a large proportion of school children do use AI especially for homework.”*. But a survey by U-K firm RM Technology says teachers aren’t sure whether they are comfortable with their students using artificial intelligence. The results found that nine per cent of teachers couldn’t differentiate work carried out by students and work produced by A-I programmes. The draft framework was presented to Education Ministers in July, and Ministers agreed to release the draft to get advice, feedback and ideas from teachers, parents, students and other stakeholders. Minister for Education Jason Clare says these discussions will help shape a final Australian Guide for Generative AI in Schools. The aim is to let schools, teachers, and students benefit from A-I, but also to keep them safe from any issues. She says that in some cases it is easy to spot when students use A-I, but not in all cases. *"Some students use it in such obvious ways that include the prompt and give away the fact that they're using generative AI. We've got to learn how to help our students use it really well. So I think that the picture we have to look at is all the positives we can turn it into and at the same time look at doing solid assessment that measures what students actually do know and can demonstrate."*. --- SOURCE 5: DoYouTrustAI: A Tool to Teach Students About AI Misinformation and Prompt Engineering ---
URL: https://arxiv.org/html/2504.13859v1
Content: To address this need, we have created a web-based application that allows users and students in grades K-12, in particular, to utilize their critical thinking skills to see if they can determine if an LLM response contains misleading information about major historical figures. In this paper, we describe the implementation and design details of the DoYouTrustAI tool, which can be used to provide an interactive lesson which teaches students about the dangers of misinformation and how believable generative AI can make it seem. The DoYouTrustAI tool utilizes prompt engineering to present the user with AI generated summaries about the life of a historical figure. Our research questions for this work were: (RQ1) How can we design a tool that teaches students about the dangers of misleading information and of how misinformation can present itself in LLM responses? All of these factors combine to create a tool which presents believable misinformation in a controlled environment and teaches the student about the importance of AI response verification and prompt engineering. It also teaches students about prompt engineering and how easy it is to create a tool which presents misleading information to the user. This is why it is important for K-12 students to not only be aware of how to use AI most effectively, but also to have awareness of the validity of the information provided to them by generative AI systems like LLMs. Children within the K-12 education system are more easily influenced by outside pressure than adults as shown by [9]. The tool asks students to determine whether the presented information is ”True” or ”False.” Following this section, the tool brings them to an area where they can look at the prompt engineering used for the tool and to make changes to both the AI instructions and prompt to view the outcome. The negative effects and significance of misinformation can be difficult to explain properly to K-12 students, but utilizing known, potentially beloved, figures and presenting information that unfairly diminishes or changes their accomplishments can be an effective method to promote third-party verification of generative conversational AI answers.

--- SOURCE 1: Generative AI without guardrails can harm learning - NASA ADS ---
URL: https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2025PNAS..12222633B/abstract
Content: ## ADS. ## Generative AI without guardrails can harm learning: Evidence from high school mathematics. #### Abstract. While generative AI has been shown to enhance productivity, its influence on learning new skills remains unclear. Our research examines the impact of generative AI, specifically GPT-4, on student learning in math education. Through a large-scale field experiment in a high school, our study reveals that although AI-based tutoring improves performance during practice sessions, students relying on the technology may underperform when access to AI is subsequently removed, indicating reduced skill acquisition. However, we also find that carefully designed safeguards, especially asking the AI tutor to provide teacher-designed hints instead of giving away answers, can mitigate these negative effects. Our findings highlight the need for thoughtful integration of generative AI in educational settings to ensure that human learning is preserved. :   Proceedings of the National Academy of Science.

URL: https://nsuworks.nova.edu/transformations/vol11/iss1/4/
Content: Home > Fischler > FSE\_JOURNALS > Transformations > Vol. 11 (2025) > Iss. 1. # Ethical and Responsible Use of Generative AI in K-12 Math Education. Generative AI (GenAI) tools such as OpenAI’s ChatGPT, Google’s Gemini, and Microsoft’s Copilot have rapidly expanded into both K-12 and higher education, transforming the way students engage with writing and problem-solving tasks. While these tools offer educational benefits, they also introduce ethical concerns, such as student over-reliance, bias in AI-generated solutions, and transparency in problem-solving processes. Drawing from the research literature and best practices in education, practical strategies are explored to help educators and students understand how to use GenAI ethically and responsibly. The discussion concludes with actionable strategies for educators to leverage GenAI responsibly in K-12 math classrooms. --- SOURCE 5: Students' Use of Generative AI: The Threat of Hallucinations ---
URL: https://cdt.org/insights/students-use-of-generative-ai-the-threat-of-hallucinations/
Content: # Students’ Use of Generative AI: The Threat of Hallucinations. Because most generative AI systems likely to be used by students are trained on information gleaned from the internet, they may replicate common misunderstandings of sensitive issues like mental health challenges, gender roles, and sexual orientation. * **Provide education for students on what generative AI is, how it works, and why hallucinations occur:** To combat the unchecked public hype around generative AI, schools should equip students with basic knowledge of the technology, its capabilities and limitations, and how it can go wrong in both academic and personal uses. Student use of generative AI is increasingly inevitable in the same way as their use of the internet, so it is vital that schools provide students training and resources on how to assess the accuracy and reliability of information gleaned through ChatGPT and other generative AI platforms. Schools should provide guidance and training to both teachers and students on how to make effective use of generative AI.

--- SOURCE 10: The risks of AI in schools outweigh the benefits, report says - KNKX ---
URL: https://www.knkx.org/2026-01-14/the-risks-of-ai-in-schools-outweigh-the-benefits-report-says
Content: Teachers surveyed for the report said AI can be useful when it comes to language acquisition, especially for students learning a second language. The report says another benefit of AI is that it allows teachers to automate some tasks: "generating parent emails … translating materials, creating worksheets, rubrics, quizzes, and lesson plans" — and more. The report cites multiple research studies that found important time-saving benefits for teachers, including one U.S. study that found that teachers who use AI save an average of nearly six hours a week and about six weeks over the course of a full school year. Survey responses revealed deep concern that use of AI, particularly chatbots, "is undermining students' emotional well-being, including their ability to form relationships, recover from setbacks, and maintain mental health," the report says. The Brookings report offers a long list of recommendations to help parents, teachers and policymakers — not to mention tech companies themselves — harness the good of AI without subjecting children to the risks that the technology currently poses.

## Executive Summary

The retrieved evidence suggests that generative AI can support K–12 mathematics learning in some structured, tutor-like uses, but it does not yet provide a stable basis for claiming broad achievement gains across grades, settings, or outcomes. The direct evidence base is dominated by a few recent field and classroom studies plus a larger set of reviews, benchmarks, and implementation papers. The clearest causal warning comes from high school mathematics: one field experiment found that generative AI improved performance during supported practice but reduced later unassisted performance when safeguards were absent [34]. At the same time, one randomized study found that ChatGPT-generated mathematics help produced learning gains equivalent to human tutor-authored help in an online mathematics environment, suggesting that AI can sometimes produce useful instructional text when tightly constrained [112]. A newer randomized study in UK classrooms reported that an AI tutor could safely and effectively support secondary students’ mathematics learning, but the retrieved source is a web-linked report rather than a fully detailed journal article, so the precise outcome statistics were not retrievable here [57]. Taken together, the evidence points to a conditional conclusion: generative AI is potentially useful as a scaffolded support, but unstructured use can undermine independent learning.

The strongest experimental findings are limited in number but highly informative. The high-school field experiment on guardrails found harmful downstream effects when students had unstructured access to generative AI during mathematics practice; the retrieved summary indicates higher immediate practice performance but lower later test performance, with harm reduced when the AI was constrained to provide teacher-designed hints rather than full answers [34]. The randomized comparison of ChatGPT-generated help versus human tutor-authored help found equivalent learning gains on mathematics skills, showing that generative AI can generate tutoring-style explanations that are pedagogically useful under controlled conditions [112]. The exploratory UK classroom trial of a pedagogy-fine-tuned AI tutor found the system could support mathematics learning safely and effectively in real classrooms, but the retrieved material does not report the exact effect size, sample size, or delayed outcomes [57]. Beyond these, the broader synthesis literature consistently argues that the field is early-stage, that most retrieved items are indirect or design-oriented, and that causal evidence for student outcomes is sparse [8][10][62][66][122].

The quasi-experimental and observational evidence largely corroborates the implementation story rather than overturning it. In primary schools, a quasi-experimental mathematics word-problem study using a generative-AI-enabled learning environment reported positive learning and attitude effects, but the retrieved source does not expose enough detail to judge durability or independence of learning [54]. A second quasi-experimental study of a ChatGPT-based flipped learning guiding approach found improved courseware project performance and perceptions relative to a traditional flipped approach, although this is postsecondary rather than K–12 and thus only indirectly informative [76]. In elementary and middle school implementation studies, AI learning companions, teachable agents, and teacher co-design projects repeatedly emphasize teacher mediation, curriculum alignment, and constrained prompting as the conditions under which generative AI is most promising [41][96][142]. Observational work on teacher adoption and AI literacy also shows that teacher trust, acceptance, and perceived usefulness are major moderators of implementation quality [6][104][138]. By contrast, benchmark studies showing that chatbots can solve some school math items tell us more about model capability than about student learning, and several benchmarks still show substantial weakness on K–12 math reasoning, misconceptions, and robustness to linguistic variation [20][26][33][63][73][77][80][82][86].

The tiered questions are only partially answered overall. Tier 1, on foundational framing, is answered reasonably well: generative AI in K–12 math most often means chatbots, hint generators, explanation tools, question generators, and teacher-facing planning systems, with relevant outcomes spanning achievement, procedural fluency, conceptual understanding, problem solving, transfer, and engagement [8][10][17][25][62][139]. Tier 2, on baseline comparators, is answered moderately well: the strongest counterfactual is standard instruction plus teacher feedback, human tutoring, and non-AI digital tools, with adjacent evidence from intelligent tutoring systems and online homework showing that adaptive feedback and worked examples can improve learning [1][42][95][141]. Tier 3, on mechanisms and implementation, is partially answered and probably the best-developed area: teacher mediation, guardrails, prompt quality, curriculum alignment, and limiting autonomous answer-seeking all appear critical, while simple AI literacy alone may not prevent overreliance [34][117][138][149]. Tier 4, on comparative effectiveness, remains only partially resolved: there is credible evidence of both benefit and harm, but not enough direct, long-duration, K–12-specific randomized evidence to say that generative AI reliably improves math achievement relative to established alternatives. Overall confidence is low-to-moderate for effectiveness claims and moderate for implementation claims. The single most important caveat is that many positive reports are on immediate assistance, attitudes, or teacher workflow, not on durable independent mathematics achievement.
