finding.measure: Accuracy on MWPBENCH math word-problem benchmark (10 datasets spanning elementary to college level)

finding.finding_summary: The paper shows that MathScale is a scalable synthetic-data generation pipeline for producing large volumes of math instruction data with frontier LLMs. The authors generated 2 million question-answer pairs and note that the method scales effectively with dataset size, suggesting improved data-generation efficiency for model training rather than any classroom productivity outcome.
finding.measure: Size of generated dataset and scalability of the synthetic data-generation pipeline

paper_profiles.title: Automatic Generation of Question Hints for Mathematics Problems using Large Language Models in Educational Technology
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether large language models (LLMs) can generate pedagogically useful question-style hints for mathematics exercises, with an emphasis on secondary-level/high-school content. The authors focus on a practical intelligent tutoring system problem: how to produce hints that help students self-correct without simply revealing the answer, while respecting a cognitive-science-based pedagogical approach.

The study uses MIA Seconde, an educational remediation platform for French and mathematics in high school, and creates an experimental pipeline in which LLMs act both as students and as teachers. Student models (GPT-3.5-turbo, Llama-3-8B-Instruct, and Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3) solve four French math exercises at multiple temperature settings; GPT-4o and Llama-3-8B-Instruct then generate hints using several prompt types, including error-specific prompts and baseline prompts. The authors analyze error patterns, compare prompt effectiveness, and test whether hints improve answer revision accuracy. They find that higher temperature generally increases error frequency, that calculation-error prompts and a baseline prompt named BaselineTwo are most effective overall, and that hints can improve revision accuracy—especially for GPT-3.5-turbo. Interestingly, Llama-3-8B-Instruct often outperformed GPT-4o as the hint-generating teacher in this setup, though the authors caution that hint quality and pedagogical validity still need qualitative evaluation.

Overall, the paper provides early empirical evidence that LLMs can support math hint generation in an ITS-like workflow, but its findings are limited to simulated students, four exercises, and automated correctness checks rather than real learners. The authors frame the work as a proof of concept and highlight important risks and limitations, including misleading or insufficiently evaluated hints, model brittleness at higher temperatures, and the need for human expert review before deployment in authentic classrooms.

finding.finding_summary: Across four high-school-level math exercises, LLMs could sometimes self-correct after receiving hints, but performance depended strongly on the prompt, teacher model, student model, and temperature. For example, the best prompts (calculation-error prompt and BaselineTwo) often reduced revision error rates, and GPT-3.5-turbo showed a notable post-hint accuracy increase, while higher temperatures generally increased the number and diversity of initial errors.
finding.measure: Accuracy on solving and revising mathematics exercises; mean revision error rate by prompt; GPT-4o correctness verification of student responses
finding.study_size: 4 exercises; 40 initial simulations per exercise per temperature; 10 hint/revision repetitions per incorrect response per prompt

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that well-designed hints can support problem-solving, self-correction, and independent learning, which are durable skills relevant to mathematical reasoning. Empirically, the hint-generation setup improved simulated students’ response revision after errors, indicating potential support for metacognitive revision and problem-solving processes, though no direct measure of these constructs was reported.
finding.measure: Revision of incorrect responses after receiving hints; problem-solving success after hinting

finding.finding_summary: The study suggests that LLMs may reduce the manual effort required to generate math hints by automating the creation of pedagogically structured question hints. However, this was not directly measured as teacher workload or time savings; the evidence is indirect and based on the feasibility of automated hint generation in a proof-of-concept pipeline.
finding.measure: Feasibility of automated hint generation for math exercises

paper_profiles.title: Seeing the Big Picture: Evaluating Multimodal LLMs’ Ability to Interpret and Grade Handwritten Student Work
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of Educational Data Mining Conference
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can interpret and grade handwritten student mathematics work, with a focus on two distinct tasks: routine arithmetic with objective answers and more complex student-drawn mathematical illustrations. The authors frame the problem as one of learning analytics and teacher workload, arguing that handwritten work contains rich information about student thinking but is time-consuming to assess manually.

The study uses two experiments. Experiment A analyzes 288 handwritten arithmetic responses from Ghanaian middle school students working on fractions, percentages, and basic algebra. Experiment B evaluates 150 student-drawn mathematical illustrations from U.S. elementary students in the DrawEDU dataset. In both experiments, several frontier MLLMs (Claude 3.5, Claude 3.7, Gemini 2.5 Pro, GPT-4.1) are tested under consistent prompts; for the illustration task, the authors also test whether providing human-written descriptions of the images improves performance.

Results show a sharp contrast between task types. On routine arithmetic, Gemini 2.5 Pro reaches near-human performance (95% grading accuracy, LWK=0.90) on a balanced dataset of 288 responses. However, performance drops substantially for mathematical illustrations: with image only, accuracies are about 61-64% and kappa is low (0.15-0.38); with human descriptions, performance improves to about 72-75% accuracy and kappa around 0.43-0.47, still only moderate agreement. The authors conclude that current MLLMs may be useful for automating routine grading and triaging work, but they still struggle with visually complex, context-dependent student representations and lack the tacit pedagogical knowledge needed for reliable autonomous assessment.

finding.finding_summary: Across 288 handwritten middle-school arithmetic responses, the best-performing model (Gemini 2.5 Pro) achieved 95% grading accuracy with LWK=0.90, closely approaching human performance on objective math work. However, performance was lower for other models (77-84% accuracy) and dropped sharply on the more complex illustration task, indicating strong performance for routine numeracy but clear limitations for broader mathematical interpretation.
finding.measure: Accuracy, precision, recall, F1, and linear weighted kappa on grading handwritten arithmetic responses; image-based correctness judgments on mathematical illustrations
finding.study_size: n=288 for arithmetic; n=150 for illustrations

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that MLLMs could reduce teacher workload by automating routine grading of handwritten arithmetic work and pre-sorting more ambiguous student work for human review. This is supported indirectly by near-human grading performance on objective arithmetic tasks (95% accuracy for Gemini 2.5 Pro) and by the authors’ proposed use case of screening and triage rather than full automation.
finding.measure: Model grading accuracy and discussion of potential workflow use for grading/triage
finding.study_size: n=288 for arithmetic; n=150 for illustrations

finding.finding_summary: The authors conclude that MLLMs are promising for hybrid educational assessment systems but not yet reliable for autonomous deployment on complex student mathematical work. They recommend human-in-the-loop designs, transparency, and professional development, implying institutional adoption should be cautious and bounded by task type.
finding.measure: Feasibility of deployment based on accuracy and agreement metrics across two experiments

paper_profiles.title: FACET: Teacher-Centred LLM-Based Multi-Agent Systems—Towards Personalized Educational Worksheets
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the challenge of differentiating instruction in heterogeneous K-12 mathematics classrooms, where teachers must serve students with varying levels of mathematical proficiency and motivation. The authors argue that most existing AI personalization tools focus narrowly on performance and are oriented toward students rather than teachers, leaving a gap in teacher-facing support for creating context-sensitive classroom materials.

To address this, the paper introduces FACET, a teacher-centered, LLM-based multi-agent framework that simulates diverse learner profiles and generates personalized worksheets. The system uses separate learner, teacher, and evaluator agents to produce one-page mathematics worksheets aligned to grade 8 German curriculum content, with adaptations based on two learner dimensions: mathematical knowledge and intrinsic motivation. The evaluation combines automated agent-based scoring across ten iterations per learner profile with exploratory think-aloud feedback from five K-12 in-service mathematics teachers.

The results suggest that the framework can generate stable, reasonably high-quality worksheets that are perceived as suitable for different learner profiles. Automated ratings were consistently high for task suitability and clarity, and teacher feedback was generally positive, especially regarding structure and match to learner needs. Teachers also suggested improvements such as clearer scaffolding for lower-knowledge students, more narrative and everyday-life relevance for low-motivation students, and stronger curriculum specificity. The study concludes that multi-agent LLM systems may be promising for scalable teacher support, but it remains a feasibility study rather than evidence of impacts on student learning outcomes.

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds that FACET may reduce teacher workload by generating personalized worksheets and lowering prompting effort for non-expert users. In exploratory feedback from five K-12 in-service teachers, participants valued the tool’s ability to create differentiated tasks and noted that it could help keep a whole class on one topic while adjusting difficulty, thereby reducing manual preparation demands. No formal time-savings measure was reported.
finding.measure: Teacher feedback on perceived usefulness for worksheet generation, differentiation, and workload reduction
finding.study_size: n=5 teachers; 10 internal agent evaluations per worksheet profile

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that the system generated mathematics worksheets aligned to grade 8 curriculum tasks and adapted to learner profiles with high perceived suitability. Automated evaluations rated task suitability highly across four learner personas (e.g., M=4.78, SD=0.06 for agent-based evaluation; teacher ratings around M=5.05), but the study did not measure student achievement, test scores, or learning gains. The evidence is therefore about output quality and alignment, not direct effects on mathematics performance.
finding.measure: Worksheet quality and suitability for grade 8 mathematics tasks; alignment with learner profile
finding.study_size: n=5 teachers; 4 learner profiles; 10 iterations per profile
finding.std_deviation: SD=0.06 to 0.26 reported for agent ratings; teacher ranges reported instead of SD

finding.finding_summary: The framework explicitly incorporates intrinsic motivation and teachers judged the resulting worksheets favorably for supporting motivation, especially through personalization, reduced task load for low-motivation learners, and narrative/everyday-life framing. Teacher feedback suggested that these features could foster engagement and problem-solving motivation, but the study did not directly measure student motivation, persistence, or engagement outcomes.
finding.measure: Intrinsic motivation as a learner-profile dimension; teacher judgments of motivational support in generated worksheets

finding.finding_summary: The paper claims the worksheets were sequenced using Bloom’s taxonomy and included scaffolding, hints, and progression from simpler to more advanced tasks, which are intended to support reasoning and self-regulation. However, the study did not directly assess student metacognition, collaboration, or critical thinking; the evidence is limited to expert judgments about task design and appropriateness.
finding.measure: Didactical structure, scaffolding, and Bloom-aligned task sequencing in generated worksheets
finding.study_size: n=5 teachers; 10 internal iterations per profile
finding.std_deviation: SD=0.22 reported for didactical-structure agent ratings

finding.finding_summary: A smaller but still substantive focus of the paper is the development and feasibility of a teacher-facing AI authoring system for educational materials, rather than a student outcome. The paper shows that the system can produce classroom-ready worksheets and that teachers perceived them as suitable for heterogeneous classrooms, but it does not evaluate outcomes in a non-mathematics academic domain.
finding.measure: Feasibility and perceived quality of AI-generated worksheets as educational materials

paper_profiles.title: Automatic Large Language Models Creation of Interactive Learning Lessons
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether large language models can automatically generate scenario-based interactive lessons for training novice human tutors who teach middle school mathematics online. The authors focus on a tutor-training platform organized around the SMART framework and use retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) with GPT-4o to create lesson content for three tutoring topics: encouraging student independence, encouraging help-seeking behavior, and turning on cameras.

The main methodological question is whether decomposing the generation task into multiple prompted segments improves lesson quality compared with generating an entire lesson in one step. The authors compare one-, two-, three-, four-, and five-segment prompt strategies and have two experienced human coders rate the output using a rubric with 17 criteria. They also solicit structured feedback from two expert lesson designers to compare LLM-generated lessons with handcrafted lessons.

Results show that the three-segment approach produced the highest-rated lessons on average, suggesting that moderate task decomposition can improve coherence, alignment, and pedagogical quality. The generated lessons were praised for saving authoring time, producing varied scenarios, and avoiding obviously biased or offensive content, but they also showed important weaknesses, especially generic feedback, unclear learning-objective language, disjointed instruction, and unreliable citations. The study concludes that LLMs are promising for drafting tutor-training materials, but human review and refinement remain necessary, and the authors emphasize that their evidence is about lesson quality rather than student learning outcomes.

finding.finding_summary: Human lesson designers reported that LLM-assisted lesson generation substantially reduced the time and effort required to draft scenario sections and multiple-choice questions. In the comparison of prompt strategies, the three-segment approach achieved the highest average human rating (14.67) versus 10.67 for one-segment generation, indicating that moderate decomposition improved the efficiency/quality of content creation workflow rather than measuring student outcomes.
finding.measure: Human ratings of generated lesson quality; designer-reported time savings and drafting effort
finding.study_size: n=3 lessons generated per prompt strategy; n=2 lesson designers interviewed

finding.finding_summary: The paper focuses on generating lessons for novice tutors who teach middle school mathematics online, but it does not test student math achievement. The strongest evidence is indirect: the generated tutor-training lessons were judged to be structurally sound and pedagogically useful, with the three-segment approach receiving the highest average quality rating (14.67/?) across three middle-school math tutoring lessons.
finding.measure: Human rubric ratings of lesson quality for middle-school mathematics tutor training content

finding.finding_summary: The generated lessons aimed to support tutor competencies such as encouraging independence, help-seeking, and appropriate instructional reasoning, which are adjacent to metacognition and self-regulation. Human raters found strong alignment with learning objectives and useful examples, but also noted weak pedagogical grounding and unclear reasoning in some prompt configurations, especially one- and two-segment generation; the three-segment approach performed best on pedagogical grounding.
finding.measure: Human rubric codes including alignment with learning objectives, pedagogical grounding, clarity, and feedback quality

finding.finding_summary: The lessons were designed around tutoring behaviors that support student independence, help-seeking, relationship-building, and camera use, all of which relate to engagement and supportive interaction. Designers judged the LLM-generated scenarios to be realistic and generally useful, and they reported no biased or offensive content, but the paper did not measure student engagement or emotional outcomes directly.
finding.measure: Human evaluations of scenario realism, appropriateness, and bias/offensiveness; rubric feedback content
finding.study_size: n=3 lessons per prompt strategy; n=2 lesson designers

paper_profiles.title: A self-evolving multi-role collaborative framework with fine-grained difficulty guidance for innovative mathematical problem generation
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of automatic innovative mathematical problem generation (IMPG) with large language models, motivated by the need for scalable, high-quality high school math problems that are both correct and sufficiently novel. The authors argue that existing LLM-based problem generation systems tend to produce correct but unoriginal problems and that coarse difficulty control limits their usefulness for instruction and assessment.

To address this, the paper proposes a self-evolving multi-role collaborative framework built around a single fine-tuned LLM that alternates between generator and evaluator roles. The framework adds a fine-grained 16-bit difficulty encoding model, a data-driven association-guided path sampling algorithm (DAPS), and a closed-loop refinement process with apprentice and expert evaluation modes. The system is trained with continual pre-training, supervised fine-tuning on the HSM3K-CN high school math dataset, knowledge distillation from an expert model, and GRPO reinforcement learning.

The empirical setting is high school mathematics, specifically three core chapters: derivatives, sequences, and probability. The paper reports simulation tests on a 90-requirement benchmark (SIMU-90) and compares the proposed system against multiple open- and closed-source baseline LLMs using judge-model evaluations. The main conclusion is that the proposed method improves problem innovation and discrimination while maintaining high correctness, and that the expert-mode variant performs better than the apprentice-mode variant. However, this is a model-development paper rather than a student outcome study, so it does not provide evidence about effects on learner achievement.

finding.finding_summary: The proposed framework significantly improves the innovation and discrimination of generated high school mathematics problems compared with baseline models, while maintaining high correctness. The paper evaluates generation quality on SIMU-90 (n=90 requirement prompts) and reports higher overall scores for the proposed system than competing models, but it does not report a student achievement effect size because no learners were tested.
finding.measure: LLM-generated mathematics problem quality, including correctness, innovation, discrimination, and overall judge-model scores
finding.study_size: n=90 requirement prompts; 3,160 source problems in HSM3K-CN

paper_profiles.title: KwaiYiiMath: Technical Report
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This technical report presents KwaiYiiMath, a large language model for mathematical reasoning built by fine-tuning the KwaiYiiBase model with supervised fine-tuning (SFT), human preference alignment, reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF), and direct preference optimization (DPO). The authors focus on improving step-by-step math problem solving in English and Chinese, and on constructing high-quality training data with diverse reasoning paths and manually checked intermediate rationales.

The paper evaluates the model on three benchmarks: GSM8k, CMath, and an in-house Chinese primary-school math set called KMath (188 items). The report also studies robustness using a GSM8k adversarially modified set and a distractor-heavy CMath subset, and it includes fine-grained analyses by grade level, number of reasoning steps, number of digits, and number of distractors. The main findings are that KwaiYiiMath outperforms same-size open-source models and is close to GPT-4 on some elementary math benchmarks; the human-preference-aligned version improves slightly over the base model. Performance declines as problems become more complex, and distractors substantially reduce accuracy, indicating remaining robustness limitations.

finding.finding_summary: KwaiYiiMath improved mathematical reasoning performance relative to similarly sized open-source baselines on GSM8k, CMath, and KMath. The model reached 72.33% pass@1 on GSM8k, 85.33% on CMath, and 73.40% on KMath; the human-preference-aligned variant (KwaiYiiMath-HPA) rose slightly to 73.31%, 85.83%, and 74.47%, respectively. The paper does not report effect sizes or confidence intervals, but the gains are described as large versus same-size models and close to GPT-4 on some Chinese elementary-school benchmarks.
finding.measure: pass@1 accuracy on GSM8k, CMath, and KMath; fine-grained accuracy by grade, reasoning steps, digits, and distractors
finding.study_size: n=7,473 train / 1,319 test for GSM8k; CMath n=1.7k (960 downloadable); KMath n=188

finding.finding_summary: The report suggests improved multi-step reasoning capability, which is a durable skill closely tied to mathematical problem solving. Accuracy declined with greater reasoning complexity, but the model remained strong across elementary grades and did relatively well on tasks requiring more steps, indicating that the training approach improved stepwise reasoning performance rather than only final-answer recall.
finding.measure: accuracy as a function of number of reasoning steps and problem complexity measures

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT for Good? On Opportunities and Challenges of Large Language Models for Education
paper_profiles.population: All educational levels (primary, secondary, tertiary, professional development); not a study of a single sampled population
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This position paper examines the opportunities, limitations, and ethical challenges of large language models such as ChatGPT for education. Rather than testing an intervention, it synthesizes early examples of educational use and proposes a framework for how these models may support learning, teaching, assessment, and educational innovation. The paper is primarily concerned with how LLMs could be integrated responsibly into educational systems, while anticipating major risks such as bias, plagiarism, privacy/security concerns, overreliance, and difficulty distinguishing machine-generated from human-generated work.

The paper discusses use cases across student and teacher perspectives, including personalized practice, quiz generation, feedback, lesson planning, assessment support, tutoring, and content creation. It also reviews early studies and examples from adjacent areas such as conversational AI, automated feedback, and math word problem generation, but these are presented as illustrative prior work rather than a new empirical study conducted by the authors. The authors conclude that LLMs may be valuable educational tools if used with human oversight, critical thinking, fact-checking, and governance structures that address fairness, transparency, and sustainability.

Because the paper is a conceptual position paper, it does not report original experimental data, sample sizes, or effect sizes. Its contribution is mainly normative and descriptive: it identifies likely opportunities, summarizes early research directions, and recommends safeguards and implementation strategies for responsible adoption in education.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that LLMs can support reading and writing by generating summaries, explanations, prompts, syntactic corrections, and writing feedback, but it does not present original empirical evidence. It cites illustrative prior work on quiz generation and text support, but no sample sizes, effect sizes, or direct literacy outcomes are reported.
finding.measure: not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The paper states that LLMs may support mathematics learning by generating practice problems, step-by-step solutions, and math word problems for middle and high school students. However, this is presented as a prospective use case and literature overview rather than empirical evidence, so no measured math achievement results are reported.
finding.measure: not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests LLMs may improve engagement, curiosity, interaction, and participation, especially through conversational support and curiosity-prompting pedagogical agents. These claims are based on cited examples and conceptual reasoning, not original outcome data, so no quantitative estimates are reported.
finding.measure: not_reported

finding.finding_summary: A major focus of the paper is the potential for LLMs to affect critical thinking, problem-solving, collaboration, and fact-checking. The authors argue these systems can support such skills when used as a supplement, but they may also weaken them through overreliance and uncritical acceptance of generated text; no original effect estimates are reported.
finding.measure: not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The paper emphasizes substantial potential efficiency gains for teachers through automated assessment, feedback generation, quiz and exercise creation, lesson planning, and content adaptation. One cited example reports grading effort reductions of up to 85% in large courses using NLP-based feedback systems, but the paper itself does not report a new empirical study.
finding.measure: teacher grading effort; automated feedback and content generation workflows

finding.finding_summary: The paper foregrounds institutional issues including governance, privacy, copyright, fairness, sustainability, access, and policies for responsible adoption of LLMs in education. It argues that these systems could widen or narrow educational divides depending on deployment, but provides no original empirical institutional outcome data.
finding.measure: policy/governance considerations; access, privacy, bias, and sustainability risks

paper_profiles.title: The cognitive paradox of AI in education: between enhancement and erosion
paper_profiles.population: Not explicitly specified; discusses K-12 and higher education learners, with examples spanning high school and undergraduate contexts
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This opinion paper argues that artificial intelligence in education has a “cognitive paradox”: it can enhance learning through personalization, feedback, and efficiency, but it can also erode important cognitive skills if students over-rely on it. Using Cognitive Load Theory, Bloom’s Taxonomy, and Self-Determination Theory as interpretive lenses, the authors discuss how AI may reduce extraneous cognitive load and support lower-order learning, while also risking cognitive offloading, weaker retention, reduced autonomy, and diminished critical thinking.

The paper does not report a new empirical study; instead, it synthesizes examples from prior research and recent reports on AI tools such as ChatGPT, adaptive learning systems, and intelligent tutoring systems. It highlights evidence suggesting benefits in some contexts, such as improved performance on standardized tests and better fluency/idea generation, alongside risks such as lower concept understanding, reduced memory retention, and passivity when students accept AI-generated answers uncritically.

The discussion is broadly relevant to students, teachers, and policymakers implementing AI in blended learning environments. The authors recommend that AI be used as a supplement rather than a replacement for human instruction, with teacher guidance, reflection activities, AI-free practice, and fairness/transparency safeguards to preserve deep learning, metacognition, motivation, and equity.

finding.finding_summary: The paper cites secondary evidence that AI tutoring can raise standardized test performance in math-related learning contexts, including a reported 15% increase in scores for students using AI platforms compared with traditional instruction. However, it also notes that students using ChatGPT to practice solved 48% more problems but scored 17% lower on a concept-understanding test, suggesting gains in procedural performance may come with weaker conceptual learning.
finding.measure: Standardized test scores; problem-solving accuracy; concept-understanding test
finding.effect_size: 15% increase in scores; 48% more problems correct; 17% lower concept-understanding score

finding.finding_summary: The paper summarizes evidence that AI-based language tools, including speech recognition, chatbots, and virtual tutors, improved communicative competence and fluency. In the cited university context, more than 80% of respondents believed AI would be a major contributor to future language teaching, though the paper emphasizes that human interaction remained important for concept formation and engagement.
finding.measure: Communicative competence and fluency; respondent perceptions

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that AI can improve engagement and competence through personalized learning, but over-reliance may reduce autonomy, relatedness, and intrinsic motivation. It also cites prior work suggesting that excessive dependence on AI may lower motivation and engagement because students let AI do the thinking instead of actively solving problems.
finding.measure: Engagement; autonomy; relatedness; intrinsic motivation

finding.finding_summary: A central claim of the paper is that AI can support lower-order recall and some idea generation, but may weaken higher-order skills such as critical thinking, problem-solving, and independent reasoning when overused. The paper cites studies reporting lower memory retention with prolonged AI exposure and AI-related threats to critical thinking, and recommends reflection, AI-free practice, and source verification to preserve these skills.
finding.measure: Critical thinking; problem-solving; memory retention; divergent thinking

finding.finding_summary: The paper repeatedly notes that AI can reduce redundant work, personalize instruction, and increase efficiency in learning pathways. These claims are conceptual rather than newly tested in the paper, and no direct effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Learning efficiency; reduction of redundant work

finding.finding_summary: The paper discusses implementation and governance issues, including the need for needs analysis, teacher mediation, monitoring and feedback mechanisms, transparency, fairness-aware design, and diversified datasets to reduce algorithmic bias. Its conclusion emphasizes that AI policy and design should support equity and accessibility while preventing dependency and inequality.
finding.measure: Implementation guidance; fairness/bias considerations; monitoring and governance

paper_profiles.title: How Does ChatGPT Perform on the United States Medical Licensing Examination (USMLE)? The Implications of Large Language Models for Medical Education and Knowledge Assessment
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether ChatGPT can answer medical licensing exam questions at a level useful for medical education, and whether its responses are interpretable enough to support learning. The authors evaluated ChatGPT on four multiple-choice question sets spanning USMLE Step 1 and Step 2 content: AMBOSS questions and NBME free questions. They compared ChatGPT with GPT-3 and InstructGPT, and also examined whether adding an AMBOSS Attending Tip changed performance.

The study found that ChatGPT answered a substantial share of questions correctly, ranging from 42% to 64.4% depending on dataset, outperforming GPT-3 and InstructGPT overall. Performance was higher on NBME free questions than on AMBOSS questions, and on Step 1 than Step 2 in both datasets. Accuracy decreased significantly as AMBOSS difficulty increased for Step 1 without the tip (P=.01), suggesting sensitivity to question difficulty and some benefit from added context in certain settings.

Beyond accuracy, the paper reports that ChatGPT consistently produced logical explanations, used internal question information in nearly all responses, and used external information more often in correct than incorrect answers. The authors conclude that ChatGPT shows promise as an interactive educational tool or small-group learning adjunct, but they emphasize limitations of the study design, the closed and evolving nature of the model, and the need for further research on educational effectiveness rather than exam-answering performance alone.

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT demonstrated strong performance on medical knowledge question-answering tasks, achieving 44% (44/100) on AMBOSS-Step1, 42% (42/100) on AMBOSS-Step2, 64.4% (56/87) on NBME-Free-Step1, and 57.8% (59/102) on NBME-Free-Step2. The authors interpret the NBME-Free-Step1 result as roughly comparable to a passing threshold for a third-year medical student, and ChatGPT outperformed GPT-3 and InstructGPT across all four datasets.
finding.measure: Multiple-choice accuracy on USMLE Step 1/Step 2–style medical knowledge questions (AMBOSS and NBME free question sets)

finding.finding_summary: The paper evaluated narrative coherence and reasoning quality in ChatGPT responses, finding that 100% of outputs contained logical reasoning. Internal information from the question appeared in 96.8% (183/189) of all NBME responses, and external information was more common in correct than incorrect answers (NBME-Free-Step1: 92.9% vs 48.4%; NBME-Free-Step2: 89.8% vs 62.8%). These results suggest the model can support explanation, reasoning, and metacognitive-style discussion, though this was assessed descriptively rather than as a learner outcome.
finding.measure: Presence of logical reasoning, internal information, and external information in generated explanations

finding.finding_summary: The authors argue that ChatGPT could function as an on-demand adjunct tutor that helps learners quickly obtain explanations, context, and follow-up dialogue, potentially supporting independent study and reducing the need for immediate human feedback in some settings. However, this was not tested as a productivity or workload outcome; the evidence is inferential, based on the model’s dialogic responses and interpretability rather than a measured efficiency gain.
finding.measure: Descriptive evaluation of dialogic response quality and interpretability
finding.study_size: n=389 question responses; qualitative review on NBME subset

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests implications for medical education and knowledge assessment, proposing that ChatGPT may be useful as a virtual medical tutor and as a supplement to small-group or peer-learning environments. At the same time, the authors caution that performance varies by question set and difficulty, the model can generate incorrect answers, and its closed, updating nature limits educational reliability and generalizability.
finding.measure: Comparative performance and qualitative analysis of response usefulness for medical education

paper_profiles.title: Retrieval-augmented Generation to Improve Math Question-Answering: Trade-offs Between Groundedness and Human Preference
paper_profiles.venue: NeurIPS 2023 Workshop on Generative AI for Education (GAIED) / arXiv
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) can improve the quality of AI-generated conceptual math question answering for middle-school students, and whether increasing grounding in a textbook comes with trade-offs in human preference. The motivation is that math tutoring systems need responses that are both accurate and pedagogically useful, but large language models can hallucinate or give answers that are misaligned with the curriculum.

The authors build a RAG-based math QA system using OpenStax Prealgebra as the retrieval corpus and GPT-3.5 as the generator. They study three prompt-guidance conditions (none, low, high) plus an information-retrieval baseline, using 51 real student questions from Math Nation and evaluating generated responses with automated groundedness metrics, educator/designer preference rankings, groundedness judgments, and relevance annotations.

Results show that prompt guidance can increase groundedness, but the most grounded responses are not always the most preferred. Human evaluators preferred the low-guidance condition over both no guidance and high guidance, while the high-guidance condition was more clearly grounded in the source text. Retrieval relevance improved groundedness, but it did not meaningfully predict human preference. The authors conclude that math QA systems should balance faithfulness to educational materials with student-preferred response style, and they emphasize that better designs and evaluations are needed before such systems are deployed with students.

finding.finding_summary: The study does not measure student learning or achievement directly; instead, it evaluates the quality of AI-generated responses to middle-school math questions. Humans preferred retrieval-augmented responses when the prompt was lightly guided, but responses that were too strongly grounded in the textbook were less preferred, indicating a trade-off between groundedness and perceived usefulness for math QA.
finding.measure: Human preference rankings and groundedness judgments for generated responses to 51 middle-school math questions
finding.study_size: n=51 queries; n=9 educator/designer respondents; n=153 groundedness judgments

paper_profiles.title: VLM@school – Evaluation of AI image understanding on German middle school knowledge
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper introduces VLM@school, a benchmark for evaluating vision-language models (VLMs) on German middle-school curriculum material. The authors argue that many existing VLM benchmarks are overly English-centric, heavily multiple-choice, and too decontextualized, so they build a new dataset of 486 images and 2,038 open-ended questions across nine school-subject domains, with some adversarial questions designed to be unanswerable from the image alone.

The study evaluates 13 open-weight VLMs on these tasks, using an LLM-as-a-judge / panel-of-LLMs scoring scheme. The models are not interventions for learners; rather, they are the subject of evaluation. Performance is generally low: the best overall model reaches 43.26% accuracy, with especially weak results in math, music, and adversarial questions. The paper also analyzes error patterns, showing that models often fail at counting, map reading, following visual references, explaining diagrams, and refusing misleading questions.

The main conclusion is that middle-school-level visual reasoning in German remains challenging for current VLMs, even for large models that score well on public benchmarks such as MMMU. The authors find that benchmark performance does not transfer cleanly across languages or task formats, and that adversarial, open-ended, native-language questions expose substantial weaknesses. They suggest that future work should test English versions, compare with chain-of-thought reasoning, and further study why visual cues are less effective than textual hints for triggering correct answers.

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly evaluates VLM performance on middle-school mathematics items requiring counting, geometry, and basic calculations from images. The best overall model on the math subset reached only 34.09% accuracy (Qwen2.5VL 32B), while several models were far lower (e.g. Ovis2 4B at 9.09%), indicating substantial difficulty with visually grounded numeracy tasks.
finding.measure: Accuracy on math questions (open-ended benchmark items involving area, circumference, counting, coordinate reading, and formula identification)
finding.study_size: n=308 math questions (part of 2,038 total questions)

finding.finding_summary: The benchmark includes physics and biology tasks that require interpreting diagrams, extracting values, and explaining scientific relationships from images. Performance is moderate to low: the best physics score reported is 47.65% (Qwen2.5VL 32B) and the paper notes frequent failures on explanation-based items such as why stars become red giants or why adding a resistor changes bulb brightness.
finding.measure: Accuracy on physics and biology questions involving diagrams, tables, and explanation of scientific phenomena
finding.study_size: n=234 physics questions and n=169 biology questions

finding.finding_summary: The study substantively examines performance across non-STEM school subjects including arts, history, music, religion, geography, and sports. Results are generally weak and highly domain-dependent; for example, best scores are around 54% in history/religion, while music is especially poor (best around 31%), and adversarial religious questions are answered correctly only rarely.
finding.measure: Accuracy on subject-specific open-ended questions across arts, geography, history, music, religion, and sports
finding.study_size: arts n=286; geography n=251; history n=264; music n=166; religion n=206; sports n=154

finding.finding_summary: Although not framed as a learner study, the paper directly assesses VLM abilities related to visual reasoning, multi-step inference, and recognizing when a question is unanswerable. The authors report that models often guess instead of abstaining and struggle with adversarial prompts, reverse lookup, and cross-modal reasoning, indicating weak performance on these durable-skill-like reasoning tasks.
finding.measure: Accuracy on adversarial questions and other reasoning-intensive benchmark items
finding.study_size: n= adversarial subset within 2,038 total questions; exact adversarial n not fully reported in the excerpt

finding.finding_summary: The paper’s evaluation pipeline relies on automated judging because open-ended questions are too numerous for manual scoring, and it discusses limitations of LLM-as-a-judge as an efficiency tradeoff. However, this is methodological rather than an educational efficiency intervention; the main operational finding is that scalable evaluation required a jury-of-LLMs approach and additional case-by-case scoring hints.
finding.measure: Feasibility of automated scoring for >2,000 open-ended answers using LLM judges

paper_profiles.title: Improving Student Learning with Hybrid Human-AI Tutoring: A Three-Study Quasi-Experimental Investigation
paper_profiles.venue: The 14th Learning Analytics and Knowledge Conference (LAK ’24)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether hybrid human-AI tutoring can improve middle school mathematics learning compared with using math software alone or with other supports. The central problem is that many low-income and historically underserved students have limited access to high-dosage human tutoring, while fully automated software often does not provide enough relational or motivational support to sustain engagement.

Across three urban, low-income middle school settings, the authors evaluated a hybrid tutoring model in which students used adaptive math software while remote tutors provided motivational, relational, and content support. The implementations varied by site: one site compared software-only, software plus math teacher support, and software plus math teacher plus tutor support; a second site compared pre-tutoring software use with a short tutoring period; and a third site examined changes in tutor-to-student ratio and dashboard support over time. The study used learning-process measures such as time on task, questions answered, skills proficient, lessons passed, and workspaces completed.

The main conclusion is that hybrid human-AI tutoring improved engagement and intermediate learning outcomes relative to software-only conditions, especially for students with lower baseline achievement. The tutoring added benefits beyond math teacher support in some analyses, and more intensive tutor support or better tutor allocation appeared to increase productivity. However, the study did not directly measure standardized test score gains; instead, it inferred potential achievement implications from prior correlations between software usage and test performance. The authors conclude that hybrid tutoring is promising for low-income middle school math settings, but stronger evidence from randomized trials and better dashboard-guided targeting is still needed.

finding.finding_summary: Across three quasi-experimental site studies, hybrid human-AI tutoring improved math learning-process outcomes relative to software-only conditions. In Site 1, adding math teacher support and then remote tutoring significantly increased time spent, questions answered, and skills proficient; for example, tutoring had a positive effect on time spent (β=0.202, 95% CI [0.057, 0.347], p=0.006, over n=125 students), and skills proficient was also higher in late spring than software-only. In Site 2, tutoring increased lessons passed per week (β=0.244, 95% CI [0.106, 0.381], n=385), and in Site 3, increasing tutor access from 1:8 to 1:4 raised MATHia workspaces completed by 0.36 per hour (95% CI [0.02, 0.70], n=75).
finding.measure: Math software learning-process measures: time spent, questions answered, skills proficient, lessons passed, workspaces completed per hour

finding.finding_summary: The study found that hybrid human-AI tutoring increased student engagement with math software, which is a social-emotional/engagement outcome central to the paper’s mechanism. In Site 2, average weekly time on task increased from 24 minutes before tutoring to 33 minutes during tutoring, and the authors interpret this as improved engagement; in Site 1, time spent also increased significantly under tutoring. The paper frames these changes as evidence that human support helps sustain motivation and participation among low-income middle school students.
finding.measure: Engagement/time on task, participation with math software
finding.effect_size: β=0.202 for time spent in Site 1; pre/post increase from 24 to 33 minutes in Site 2
finding.confidence_interval: [0.057, 0.347] for Site 1 tutoring effect; not_reported for pre/post change

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that hybrid human-AI tutoring increased the productivity of software use and suggests a more efficient allocation of tutor time, especially when tutor access improved. In Site 3, moving from a tutor-to-student ratio of 1:8 to 1:4 increased student progress to an additional 0.36 workspaces completed per hour (95% CI [0.02, 0.70]), and the authors argue that dashboard-guided tutoring could reduce unnecessary interruptions for already-engaged students. The discussion also emphasizes a substantially lower marginal cost than traditional high-dosage tutoring, around $700 per student annually.
finding.measure: Workspaces completed per hour; tutor-to-student ratio; marginal cost per student

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that hybrid human-AI tutoring has promise for scalable, lower-cost support in under-resourced school systems, with implications for educational equity and tutoring access. It reports average marginal costs below $750 per student per year and frames the model as a potentially scalable alternative to expensive human-only tutoring, while noting that better dashboards and further trials are needed before broad adoption. This is an institutional-level implication rather than a directly measured policy outcome.
finding.measure: Annual marginal cost per student; scalability/implementation feasibility

paper_profiles.title: Beyond Final Answers: Evaluating Large Language Models for Math Tutoring
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether large language models (LLMs) are ready to function as math tutors, not just as problem solvers. The authors argue that benchmark performance on final answers is insufficient for tutoring contexts, where step-by-step scaffolding, feedback, and correctness throughout the dialogue matter. They therefore evaluate several ChatGPT-family models on college algebra tasks drawn from an existing intelligent tutoring system (Apprentice Tutors).

The study uses two complementary methods. First, the authors generate 22 algebra problem types from the intelligent tutor, create 110 problem-answer pairs, and test GPT-3.5 Turbo, GPT-4, GPT-4o, o1-mini, and o1-preview on final-answer correctness. Second, they have human evaluators interact with the same models as if they were students seeking help, then rate the resulting tutoring dialogues for pedagogical quality and complete correctness using a rubric and independent review.

Results show that LLMs can often solve algebra problems and provide seemingly strong tutoring support, but they still make substantial errors. In the tutor-based benchmark, overall final-answer accuracy was 85.5%, with GPT-4o performing best at 97.3%. In the interactive tutoring condition, 90% of dialogues were judged high-quality by reviewers, but only 56.6% were entirely correct, indicating that many conversations contained at least one mistake. The authors conclude that LLMs are not yet suitable as standalone math tutors without human oversight or additional correctness mechanisms, though they may be useful for generating hints, alternative explanations, and positive reinforcement when integrated with intelligent tutoring systems.

finding.finding_summary: Across 110 college algebra problem-answer pairs, the LLMs achieved an overall final-answer accuracy of 85.5%, with GPT-4o the best at 97.3% and GPT-4 the worst at 74.5% in the tutor-based benchmark. In the interactive tutoring condition on 150 dialogues (30 problems x 5 models), final-answer accuracy averaged 88.6%, but only 56.6% of dialogues were entirely correct, showing that mathematically correct final answers often co-occurred with errors in intermediate steps or tutoring guidance.
finding.measure: Final-answer accuracy on college algebra problems; correctness of tutoring dialogues (all responses correct vs. any error)
finding.study_size: n=110 problem-answer pairs; n=150 tutoring dialogues

finding.finding_summary: The interactive tutoring review identified positive reinforcement and encouraging feedback as recurring strengths of the LLMs. Reviewers noted 7 instances of motivational or supportive language, suggesting the models can contribute to persistence and engagement even when mathematical accuracy is imperfect.
finding.measure: Qualitative coding of tutoring dialogues for encouragement and reinforcement

finding.finding_summary: The paper evaluates whether LLMs support step-by-step reasoning, scaffolding, and problem-solving strategies, which are central to durable skills in tutoring contexts. Reviewers found that 90% of dialogues were high-quality pedagogically, but only 56.6% were fully correct, and several dialogues overemphasized final answers rather than helping students understand intermediate steps. This suggests LLMs can model strategies and hints, but their support for robust metacognition and reasoning is inconsistent.
finding.measure: Rubric-based quality ratings and qualitative thematic analysis of tutoring dialogues

finding.finding_summary: A secondary implication of the study is that LLMs may improve instructional efficiency by generating hints, alternative explanations, and feedback without requiring full human tutoring. The authors explicitly suggest that LLMs could support intelligent tutoring systems in tasks such as hint generation and question generation, although the paper does not directly measure time savings or teacher workload.
finding.measure: Qualitative assessment of tutor support capabilities and potential integration with ITS
finding.study_size: n=150 tutoring dialogues; n=110 benchmark items

paper_profiles.title: Combining Large Language Models with Tutoring System Intelligence: A Case Study in Caregiver Homework Support
paper_profiles.venue: LAK 2025 (The 15th International Learning Analytics and Knowledge Conference)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how large language models (LLMs) can be combined with intelligent tutoring system (ITS) data and tutoring principles to support caregivers who help children with math homework. The authors argue that caregivers often want to help but lack the instructional knowledge to do so effectively, and that hybrid tutoring scenarios could benefit from conversational support that is both pedagogically sound and tailored to the student’s current problem-solving context.

The intervention is the Caregiver Conversational Support Tool (CCST), built into a middle-school equation-solving tutor (Lynnette). CCST uses real-time tutoring-system data such as correctness, hint use, current equation state, and next-step solution paths to generate caregiver message recommendations with Llama 3, using prompt engineering that combines few-shot examples with tutoring best practices and instructional intelligence from the ITS. The study first reports prompt-engineering experiments across seven rounds, then a prototyping study with ten middle-school caregivers (four in person, six remote) who interacted with the tool during simulated homework support sessions.

Findings from the qualitative evaluation suggest that incorporating tutoring-system context makes the LLM’s advice more specific, more pedagogically appropriate, and less prone to incorrect math guidance than prompts with limited context. Caregivers valued recommendations that focused on content-level support and self-explanation prompts more than purely motivational messages, because these better matched their homework-help needs and helped them understand students’ thinking. The study concludes that LLMs can support hybrid tutoring when grounded in ITS data and tutoring principles, but that message length, tone, and latency remain important design constraints.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that integrating real-time problem-solving context from the tutoring system into LLM prompts improved the specificity and pedagogical appropriateness of caregiver math-support messages for equation solving. In the qualitative evaluation with ten middle-school caregivers, the system was judged to provide more contextually relevant guidance for math homework, though no student learning or achievement outcome was experimentally measured.
finding.measure: Quality and relevance of LLM-generated math-support recommendations during equation-solving tutoring; caregiver judgments of usefulness for math homework support

finding.finding_summary: Caregivers preferred prompts that asked students to self-explain and describe their thought process, indicating support for metacognition and explanatory reasoning. In the qualitative study, five caregivers explicitly favored messages that elicited student reasoning, because these helped them identify knowledge gaps and understand how the child was solving equations.
finding.measure: Caregiver preferences for metacognitive/self-explanation message recommendations

finding.finding_summary: The tool’s motivational and praise-oriented messages were appreciated by some caregivers, but many preferred content-focused support and viewed motivational messaging as less useful or less aligned with their tutoring style. Caregivers also commented on tone, with some finding messages encouraging and others finding them artificial, suggesting mixed acceptability rather than a uniformly positive social-emotional effect.
finding.measure: Caregiver perceptions of motivational support, praise, and message tone

paper_profiles.title: Novice Learner and Expert Tutor: Evaluating Math Reasoning Abilities of Large Language Models with Misconceptions
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether large language models (LLMs) can do more than solve grade-school math problems correctly: specifically, whether they can mimic a novice learner making a mistake for a known misconception, and whether they can act like an expert tutor by identifying the misconception behind an incorrect answer. The motivation is educational, because robust student simulation and misconception diagnosis are important for intelligent tutoring systems and other AI-supported learning tools.

The authors evaluate GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 on an Eedi dataset of multiple-choice grade-school mathematics questions paired with expert-curated student misconceptions. First, they test standard question answering and show that both models can answer the questions very well, especially with explanations (e.g., GPT-4 reaches 94.8% accuracy with explanation prompting). They then ask the models to intentionally produce misconception-based wrong answers and to infer misconceptions from wrong answers. Performance drops substantially in both tasks: GPT-4 reaches only 61.7% accuracy in the novice-learner setting under zero-shot prompting with explanations, improves to 67.9% with few-shot examples of the same misconception, and reaches 91.9% in the expert-tutor setting when given only four misconception candidates but falls to 39.8% as the candidate set grows to 100. The paper concludes that although LLMs are strong at solving math problems, they are much weaker at controlled error generation and large-scale misconception diagnosis, indicating limitations for tutoring applications that depend on reliable student modeling.

finding.finding_summary: LLMs performed very well on standard grade-school math question answering, but substantially worse when asked to behave like a novice learner or an expert tutor grounded in misconceptions. GPT-4 achieved 0.948 accuracy on direct question answering with explanation prompting (vs. 0.774 without explanation), but only 0.617 accuracy in the novice-learner task under zero-shot prompting with explanations and 0.679 with few-shot same-misconception examples; in the expert-tutor task, GPT-4 reached 0.919 accuracy with 4 misconception options but dropped to 0.398 when the option set grew to 100.
finding.measure: Accuracy on grade-school multiple-choice math questions; accuracy on misconception-based wrong-answer generation; accuracy on misconception identification
finding.std_deviation: 0.005-0.031 (reported across four random trials, depending on condition)

paper_profiles.title: Evaluating the Design Features of an Intelligent Tutoring System for Advanced Mathematics Learning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper evaluates two design features in Xiaomai, an intelligent tutoring system for advanced mathematics: the use of free-response questions with automatic feedback and a metacognitive error-reflection prompt when students make mistakes. The authors ask whether these features improve learning outcomes and in-system practice performance compared with more conventional multiple-choice practice and with no reflection.

The study was conducted with 120 Chinese university students taking advanced mathematics, randomly assigned to a 2x2 factorial design: multiple-choice vs. free-response and reflection vs. no reflection. Students completed a pretest, 40 minutes of practice on three knowledge components in Xiaomai, and a posttest. The main finding was that multiple-choice practice outperformed free-response practice on practice performance and on posttest learning gains, while reflection on errors did not produce significant benefits for either learning outcomes or practice performance.

The authors report that multiple-choice conditions had higher practice scores, more attempts, and higher posttest scores than free-response conditions, though the item-format effect on posttest was only marginal after controlling for pretest scores. Error reflection showed no significant main effect, and a median-split analysis suggested that prior knowledge did not moderate the reflection effect. The paper concludes that the current implementation of free-response items and error-reflection prompts in Xiaomai does not improve effectiveness and may need redesign, such as better support for free-response evaluation and richer feedback on misconceptions.

finding.finding_summary: Students in the multiple-choice conditions achieved better mathematics learning outcomes than students in the free-response conditions. After controlling for pretest scores, posttest performance was higher for multiple-choice practice (estimated marginal mean = 9.21) than free-response practice (7.94), with the item-format effect marginally significant (F(1,115)=3.72, p=0.06). The study used n=120 undergraduate students and reported larger pretest-to-posttest gains for the multiple-choice groups than for the free-response groups, though no exact effect size was provided for the ANCOVA comparison.
finding.measure: Advanced mathematics pretest and posttest scores (number of correct answers)

finding.finding_summary: The error-reflection feature did not improve learning outcomes, practice performance, or the pretest-to-posttest gain. Reflection had no significant main effect on posttest scores (F(1,115)=0.07, p=0.79), on number of attempts during practice (t(118)=0.47, p=0.64), on correctness (p=0.81), or on time per item (p=0.70). The study with n=120 thus found no evidence that the metacognitive reflection prompt enhanced students' self-monitoring or learning in this implementation.
finding.measure: Reflection condition effects on posttest scores, practice attempts, correctness, and time per item

paper_profiles.title: Educators’ Perceptions of Large Language Models as Tutors: Comparing Human and AI Tutors in a Blind Text-only Setting
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether large language model (LLM) tutors can match or outperform human tutors on key tutoring qualities when judged in a blind, text-only setting. Rather than measuring student learning gains, the authors focus on latent tutoring characteristics that may contribute to learning: engagement, empathy, scaffolding, and conciseness.

The study uses paired dialog snippets from grade-school math word problem tutoring conversations. On the human side, dialogs come from MathDial, where annotators with teaching experience interacted with an AI-simulated student; on the AI side, dialogs come from MWPTutor, an LLM-based tutoring system with guardrails to improve correctness. Thirty-five educators/teachers on Prolific compared 210 paired conversations in a randomized blind pairwise preference task, each truncated to the first five turns. The paper reports that human annotators generally preferred the LLM tutor on all four metrics, with statistically significant advantages for conciseness, empathy, and scaffolding, while engagement was not statistically significant. The authors conclude that LLMs can perform well in text-only tutoring roles and may reduce teacher workload, but they also note clear limitations: the study is restricted to one math problem domain, one LLM tutor, and a non-naturalistic text-only setting, so the results should not be interpreted as evidence of student learning gains or broad classroom effectiveness.

finding.finding_summary: The paper does not measure student achievement or math learning gains directly. Instead, it compares human and LLM tutoring dialogs on grade-school math word problems and finds that educators generally judged the LLM tutor (MWPTutor) as better on tutoring qualities relevant to math support, especially scaffolding and conciseness, with significant advantages on scaffolding (t=3.16, p<0.001) and conciseness (t=3.65, p<0.001), but no significant advantage for engagement (t=1.32, p=0.09).
finding.measure: Educator blind pairwise judgments of tutoring dialogs for grade-school math word problems on conciseness, engagement, empathy, and scaffolding

finding.finding_summary: Educators perceived the LLM tutor as stronger than the human tutor on empathy, and also generally more engaging, though engagement was not statistically significant. For empathy, the human rating table reports a mean score of 0.65 with SD 2.81 and a significant t-score of 3.36 (p<0.001), indicating a clear preference for MWPTutor on this social-emotional tutoring dimension.
finding.measure: Blind educator ratings of engagement and empathy in tutoring conversations

finding.finding_summary: The study frames scaffolding as a key tutoring quality related to helping students reason through problems independently rather than receiving direct answers. Educators rated the LLM tutor as better at scaffolding than the human tutor, with a significant difference (t=3.16, p<0.001; mean score 0.55, SD 2.51), suggesting stronger support for guided problem solving in the judged dialogs.
finding.measure: Blind educator ratings of scaffolding quality in tutoring dialogs

finding.finding_summary: Conciseness is treated as a proxy for making progress without unnecessary back-and-forth, which the authors connect to tutor efficiency and reducing frustration. Educators preferred the LLM tutor on conciseness with the strongest reported advantage in the paper (t=3.65, p<0.001; mean score 0.55, SD 2.19), and the discussion explicitly argues that delegating repetitive tutoring to LLMs could reduce teacher load.
finding.measure: Blind educator ratings of conciseness of tutoring dialogs

paper_profiles.title: Interactive, Intelligent Tutoring for Auxiliary Constructions in Geometry Proofs
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a specific and difficult part of K-12 geometry proof learning: how students discover auxiliary constructions such as added lines or points that make a proof possible. The authors argue that existing geometry theorem provers and intelligent tutoring systems either do not support auxiliary constructions or generate proofs in ways that are not transparent to students, limiting their educational value.

To address this, the paper introduces AGPT (Advanced Geometry Proof Tutor), an interactive geometry tutor that builds on the automated prover iGeoTutor. AGPT parses uploaded geometry figures, infers constraints, and then tutors students through a two-phase process: first selecting the correct template shape and then manually constructing the needed auxiliary elements. The system deliberately reveals only limited hints, uses backtracking when students get off track, and is designed to teach the reasoning process behind the prover rather than simply present answers.

The paper reports a pilot study with 78 ninth-grade students from a local high school. Students were divided into three groups: human tutor, iGeoTutor alone, and AGPT. All groups improved from pre-test to post-test, but when partial credit for correct auxiliary constructions was included, AGPT produced significantly better gains than iGeoTutor and performed comparably to a human tutor. The authors conclude that interactive tutoring built on an AI solver can help students learn auxiliary constructions more effectively than a non-interactive solver alone, though some students became frustrated and the support could be richer.

finding.finding_summary: In a pilot study with 78 ninth-grade students (n=26 per group), AGPT helped students learn auxiliary constructions in geometry proof problems more effectively than the non-interactive geometry theorem prover iGeoTutor. When partial credit for correctly identified auxiliary constructions was included, the ANOVA on improvement scores showed a significant difference among groups, and Tukey post hoc tests found AGPT significantly better than iGeoTutor while not significantly different from the human tutor.
finding.measure: Geometry proof test performance; number of correctly solved problems and partial-credit scores for correct auxiliary constructions

finding.finding_summary: The study reports that AGPT’s feedback and interactive process generally helped students persist through a difficult task, but some students experienced frustration and gave up after seven attempts. The authors observed that 21 students solved at least one problem and noted both successful independent constructions and cases where students relied on feedback, suggesting both productive engagement and occasional frustration.
finding.measure: Observed student interaction history, number of attempts, redirections, and reports of frustration during tutoring sessions

finding.finding_summary: AGPT was designed to teach students a systematic approach to template matching and construction-based reasoning in geometry proofs. The interaction logs show that many students engaged in multiple attempts and redirections, and the authors interpret the process as helping students think through problems more thoughtfully; 8 students found solutions different from AGPT’s reference solution, indicating independent problem solving.
finding.measure: Template selection and construction behavior, number of attempts/redirections, ability to derive correct auxiliary constructions or alternative solutions

finding.finding_summary: AGPT automated geometry-figure recognition, constraint synthesis, and interactive guidance, reducing the manual burden of geometry tutoring compared with traditional instruction. However, the paper does not report formal time savings or workload effect sizes; the evidence is mainly descriptive, centered on how the system streamlines problem setup and tutoring interactions.
finding.measure: System automation of figure parsing, constraint extraction, and tutoring workflow

paper_profiles.title: Effective and Scalable Math Support: Experimental Evidence on the Impact of an AI-Math Tutor in Ghana
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper evaluates whether access to an AI-powered math tutor, Rori, improves math learning for students in Ghana. The central question is whether a scalable, low-cost, WhatsApp-based conversational tutor can provide learning gains beyond regular classroom instruction in a low-resource context where access to human tutoring and internet-connected computers is limited.

The intervention was implemented in 11 Rising Academies schools in Ghana. Schools were randomly assigned to treatment or control. Students in grades 3-9 in the treatment group received two 30-minute sessions per week with Rori during study hall, for about eight months, while the control group continued normal math instruction without access to Rori. The assessment used the same 35-item math test at baseline and endline, covering numeracy and algebra skills aligned to the Global Proficiency Framework.

Results showed that students with access to Rori had substantially larger math growth scores than controls. The treatment group improved from a mean of 20.29 to 25.42, compared with 20.20 to 22.32 in the control group, yielding an effect size of d = 0.36 and p < 0.001. The authors interpret this as a moderate-to-large educational effect, potentially equivalent to about a year of learning, and argue that such chat-based AI tutoring could be a cost-effective and operationally scalable support for learning in LMIC school systems. The paper also notes limitations, including possible ceiling effects for older students, attrition, and the need for replication over multiple years and in other settings.

finding.finding_summary: Students assigned to the AI math tutor showed substantially higher math growth than controls over about 8 months. The treatment group (n=237 at endline) improved by 5.13 points versus 2.12 points for controls (n=241), a difference of 3.01 points that was statistically significant (p < 0.001) and corresponded to Cohen's d = 0.36.
finding.measure: Math assessment scores / growth scores on a 35-item test covering numeracy and algebra skills
finding.std_deviation: Control growth SD=6.30; Treatment growth SD=7.03

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that the intervention is highly scalable and operationally efficient because it uses basic mobile phones, WhatsApp, and low-bandwidth data, with an estimated marginal annual cost of about $5 per student. Teachers did not need to provide additional instructional time or extensive training, and the program was integrated into existing study hall periods.
finding.measure: Estimated implementation cost, infrastructure requirements, and instructional staffing/training burden

finding.finding_summary: The authors conclude that the intervention has potential relevance for education systems in low- and middle-income countries because it can be implemented on widely available mobile devices and may help address learning gaps at scale. The paper frames Rori as a potentially policy-relevant model for cost-effective supplementary instruction in under-resourced school systems.
finding.measure: Scalability and policy relevance discussion; implementation across 11 schools in Ghana

paper_profiles.title: AI tutoring can safely and effectively support students: An exploratory RCT in UK classrooms
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether a generative AI tutor can safely and effectively support secondary school students in mathematics, especially when compared with standard static hints and with human tutoring. The authors position the study as an exploratory in-classroom test of LearnLM, a pedagogy-fine-tuned generative model, integrated into the Eedi mathematics platform used in UK secondary schools.

The trial recruited N=165 students in Years 9 and 10 (ages 13–15) across five UK secondary schools. Students were randomized either to static, pre-written hints or to interactive tutoring; in the tutoring condition, each session was further randomized to a human tutor alone or to a supervised LearnLM session, where expert tutors reviewed every AI-generated message before it reached the student. The model was prompted to use concise Socratic dialogue and had access to the student’s incorrect answer and misconception context.

Results indicate that supervised LearnLM was a reliable source of pedagogical guidance: tutors approved about 74.4%–76.4% of drafted messages with zero or minimal edits, and audit review found zero harmful/risky content and only five factual errors out of 3,617 messages. For immediate learning outcomes, LearnLM performed about as well as human tutors and better than static hints: 93.0% of students corrected their mistake on the second attempt with LearnLM versus 91.2% with human tutors and 65.4% with static hints. On misconception resolution, LearnLM again matched human tutoring (95.4% vs. 94.9%) and outperformed hints (86.8%).

The most notable result was on near-term transfer to a new topic: students supported by LearnLM were more likely to answer the first question in the next unit correctly (66.2%) than students with human tutors alone (60.7%), a difference of 5.5 percentage points (95% credible interval: -1.4 to +12.4). The authors interpret this as promising evidence that supervised genAI tutoring may support durable learning at scale, while also noting risks such as over-persistence in Socratic questioning, the need for human judgment around pacing and emotional nuance, and limited evidence for generalization beyond mathematics.

finding.finding_summary: In an exploratory RCT with N=165 Year 9–10 students across five UK secondary schools, supervised LearnLM tutoring was at least as effective as human tutoring for mathematics learning and outperformed static hints. For immediate remediation, 93.0% of students with LearnLM answered the second attempt correctly versus 91.2% with human tutors and 65.4% with static hints; for misconception resolution, LearnLM reached 95.4% versus 94.9% for human tutors and 86.8% for hints. For transfer to the next topic, LearnLM improved success to 66.2% versus 60.7% with human tutors alone, a 5.5 percentage-point advantage (95% credible interval [-1.4, +12.4]).
finding.measure: Performance on Eedi mathematics study-unit outcomes: second-attempt correctness, misconception resolution within the unit, and correctness on the first question of the next unit
finding.effect_size: 5.5 percentage points for knowledge transfer vs human tutors alone; other comparisons not_reported
finding.confidence_interval: [-1.4, +12.4] for transfer vs human tutors alone

finding.finding_summary: The paper treats knowledge transfer to a new mathematics topic as the key durable learning outcome. Supervised LearnLM increased the probability of answering the first question in the next unit correctly to 66.2%, compared with 60.7% for human tutors alone and 56.2% for static hints, suggesting better transfer beyond immediate correction. The reported 5.5 percentage-point advantage over human tutoring was estimated with a 95% credible interval of [-1.4, +12.4].
finding.measure: Knowledge transfer to the next study unit (first question of the following topic sequence)
finding.effect_size: 5.5 percentage points vs human tutors alone

finding.finding_summary: Student survey feedback suggested that interactive tutoring was experienced positively. Students who received interactive tutoring rated helpfulness at 3.9 out of 5, compared with 3.6 for static hints, with a posterior probability of 74.9% that tutoring was better. The paper also reports tutor observations that LearnLM’s Socratic style sometimes risked frustrating students, indicating a tradeoff between productive struggle and maintaining engagement.
finding.measure: Post-trial student helpfulness ratings; qualitative observations of engagement/frustration during tutoring
finding.study_size: n=27 student survey responses; qualitative interviews with n=5 tutors
finding.confidence_interval: [3.1, 4.7] for interactive tutoring helpfulness; [2.9, 4.2] for static hints

finding.finding_summary: The study provides qualitative and survey evidence that supervised LearnLM improved tutoring workflow and perceived scalability. In post-trial surveys, 82.4% of tutors selected 'supporting multiple students at the same time' as LearnLM’s most useful feature, and interview data indicated tutors felt the process was more fluid and efficient.
