However, the authors note the RCT design did not allow a rigorous throughput estimate during the trial, so efficiency evidence is suggestive rather than causal.
finding.measure: Tutor survey responses and interview themes about workload, supervision, and ability to support multiple students

paper_profiles.title: Leveraging LLMs to Assess Tutor Moves in Real-Life Dialogues: A Feasibility Study
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This feasibility study asks whether large language models can reliably identify and evaluate specific tutor moves in authentic tutoring conversations. The motivation is practical: researchers and practitioners want scalable ways to study which tutoring behaviors are associated with better learning, but manual coding of transcripts is time-consuming and difficult. The paper focuses on two tutoring skills that are commonly linked to effective math tutoring: delivering process-focused praise and responding appropriately when students make math errors.

The authors analyze 50 randomly selected audio transcripts from remote math tutoring sessions in which college students tutored middle school students. They compare several LLMs (GPT-4, GPT-4o, GPT-4-turbo, Gemini 1.5 Pro, and LearnLM) against human expert annotations using prompt-engineered tasks for both a filter stage (detect whether the relevant situation occurred) and an evaluation stage (judge whether the tutor move met best-practice criteria). The approach includes iterative prompt refinement, few-shot examples, chain-of-thought prompting, prompt chaining, and self-consistency/majority voting.

Results show that the models were highly accurate at identifying whether praise occurred and whether a math error occurred, and they were also reasonably aligned with human judgments when evaluating the quality of the tutor response. Reported accuracies were 94-98% for praise detection and 82-88% for error detection, with evaluation-stage accuracies of 83-89% for praise quality and 73-77% for error responses. The paper concludes that LLMs can support scalable assessment of tutoring moves in realistic settings, while also noting limitations such as missing video/chat context, challenges in speaker identification, and the need for further validation before broader use.

finding.finding_summary: The study finds that LLMs can efficiently and reliably automate a tutoring transcript coding task that would otherwise require expert human review. Across 50 transcripts, GPT-4, GPT-4o, GPT-4-turbo, Gemini 1.5 Pro, and LearnLM achieved high accuracy for detecting tutor praise (94-98%) and student math errors (82-88%), and their evaluation of tutor response quality aligned with human judgments at 83-89% for praise and 73-77% for error responses.
finding.measure: Accuracy of LLM-based filter and evaluation prompts on transcript coding tasks compared with human expert annotations
finding.confidence_interval: 95% bootstrap CIs reported for model accuracies: praise filter 94-100%, error filter 70-96%, praise evaluation 75-95%, error evaluation 62-87% (varies by model)

finding.finding_summary: Although the paper does not test student learning outcomes directly, it substantively studies tutoring behaviors in middle school mathematics contexts. The study shows that LLMs can identify and judge math tutoring moves related to process-focused praise and responses to student math errors, with detection accuracies above chance and strong agreement with human coders.
finding.measure: Classification accuracy for tutor praise and math-error response coding in math tutoring transcripts
finding.confidence_interval: 95% bootstrap CIs reported for accuracies; no learning effect size reported

paper_profiles.title: Designing AI Peers for Collaborative Mathematical Problem Solving with Middle School Students: A Participatory Design Study
paper_profiles.venue: CHI '26 Proceedings of the 2026 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how middle school students perceive and want AI to function as a peer during collaborative mathematical problem solving, rather than as a tutor. The authors argue that most prior AI-in-education work has emphasized one-to-one tutoring and evaluative support, while much less is known about AI designed to participate inside small-group classroom collaboration.

To study this question, the researchers ran a five-day participatory design summer camp with 24 rising grades 6-8 students. Students completed human-only collaborative math tasks and then worked with a sandboxed AI peer technology probe built around two LLM-based agents, before co-designing their ideal AI peer through posters, reflections, interviews, and preference surveys. The camp focused on middle-school mathematics tasks aligned to grade-level standards, including ratio/proportional reasoning, expressions and equations, and early functions/geometry.

The study found that students wanted an AI peer that was scaffold-first, deferential, and controllable: it should offer hints, checks, and concept refreshers before giving full answers, and should speak only when students want it to. Students preferred a friendly expert tone rather than exaggerated persona styling, and they valued co-agency, emotional attunement, and peer-like collaboration over rigid instructional behavior. The paper also surfaces tradeoffs: AI peers reduced perceived time pressure, but increased physical/operational burden and reduced social cohesion and perceived coordination. Overall, the findings provide design guidance for AI peers in middle school mathematics CPS, emphasizing that correctness alone is insufficient for acceptable classroom collaboration support.

finding.finding_summary: The study did not test learning gains on math achievement, but it directly examined students' experiences with AI-supported collaborative mathematics problem solving on grade-aligned tasks. Students valued mathematical hints, checks, concept refreshers, and explanations, but rejected AI behavior that felt like it was doing the math for them or providing conflicting solution paths without clear clarification.
finding.measure: Collaborative mathematical problem-solving tasks; qualitative judgments about math help and AI peer behavior

finding.finding_summary: Students reported that AI peers reduced temporal pressure but also lowered affective engagement and failed to provide emotional support when they felt confused or frustrated. Qualitatively, students said they wanted encouragement, acknowledgment, and attunement, and noted that lack of emotional responsiveness could lead to self-blame or reduced trust.
finding.measure: NASA-TLX frustration-related experience; interview/reflection themes about emotional attunement and trust
finding.study_size: n=22 for paired survey analyses; n=18 interview participants
finding.effect_size: Temporal demand d=1.15; physical demand d=1.14; ATGS d=0.94; GIT d=0.81 (all paired comparisons reported)
finding.std_deviation: Temporal demand SDs 4.38 vs 4.13; physical demand SDs 4.65 vs 2.41; ATGS SDs 1.81 vs 2.05; GIT SDs 1.58 vs 1.52

finding.finding_summary: This paper centrally studies collaboration and co-agency in mathematical group work, showing that students wanted AI peers to support joint reasoning rather than take over. Qualitatively, students criticized didactic, repetitive, or nonresponsive AI moves as violating peer norms and breaking collaboration; they preferred AI that negotiated methods, asked questions, and preserved shared problem solving.
finding.measure: GEQ group integration/task and social cohesion; interview and reflection themes on co-agency, collaboration, and peer norms
finding.study_size: n=22 for paired survey analyses; n=18 interview participants; N=24 enrolled
finding.effect_size: GIT d=0.81; ATGS d=0.94; temporal demand d=1.15 and physical demand d=1.14 as related collaboration tradeoffs
finding.std_deviation: GIT SDs 1.58 vs 1.52; ATGS SDs 1.81 vs 2.05

finding.finding_summary: AI peers made collaborative math tasks feel faster by reducing temporal demand, but they also increased the physical/operational burden of using a text-based interface. In paired-samples comparisons across human-only versus AI-peer CPS, temporal demand decreased significantly (M=5.67, SD=4.38 vs M=9.62, SD=4.13, d=1.15), while physical demand increased significantly (M=8.48, SD=4.65 vs M=4.90, SD=2.41, d=1.14).
finding.measure: NASA-TLX temporal demand and physical demand
finding.effect_size: Temporal demand d=1.15; physical demand d=1.14
finding.std_deviation: Temporal demand SDs 4.38 vs 4.13; physical demand SDs 4.65 vs 2.41

finding.finding_summary: The paper also involved students in AI literacy and design activities, including card-sorting around when AI should or should not be used and co-design of AI peer personas and behaviors. Students developed more nuanced judgments about AI's role in learning, including concerns about authority, transparency, and appropriate use, but the study did not measure academic outcomes in this domain.
finding.measure: AI card-sort, poster design artifacts, preference survey, and reflections

paper_profiles.title: A Benchmark for Math Misconceptions: Bridging Gaps in Middle School Algebra with AI-Supported Instruction
paper_profiles.population: Middle School (grades 4-8, especially grades 6-10 in educator feedback)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the challenge of helping educators identify students’ algebra misconceptions and common errors, especially in middle school, where misconceptions can hinder later mathematical learning. The authors argue that current AI systems and large language models (LLMs) are not yet reliable enough for classroom use without topic-specific structure and educator input, and they aim to bridge research-based misconceptions with practical AI-supported instruction.

The paper introduces a benchmark dataset of 55 algebra misconceptions/common errors with 220 diagnostic examples, synthesized from 145 peer-reviewed and scholarly sources. The benchmark is designed for middle school algebra topics spanning number sense, operations, ratios and proportional thinking, functions, variables, equations, and inequalities. The authors then evaluate GPT-4 Turbo using in-context learning in two repeated random subsampling experiments: one with test examples drawn from the full dataset and one with test examples constrained within topic. Topic-constrained testing improved performance substantially, and incorporating expert educator relabeling further increased apparent accuracy.

A second component is educator feedback: five middle school math teachers reviewed misconception clarity, occurrence in classrooms, and potential uses of the dataset with AI. Most teachers reported that the misconceptions were familiar in their classrooms, and four of five were interested in using the benchmark with AI to diagnose misconceptions or train teachers. The paper concludes that topic-constrained evaluation and educator expertise are important for useful AI-assisted misconception diagnosis, while also noting limitations such as the absence of multimodal capability for diagram-dependent items and the need for more diverse, student-tested validation.

finding.finding_summary: The paper’s central empirical result is that GPT-4 Turbo can diagnose middle school algebra misconceptions with moderate to strong accuracy when supported by topic-constrained examples and educator feedback. In Experiment 1, precision and recall were 0.526 and 0.529 across 5,500 iterations; in Experiment 2, topic-constrained testing improved to 0.753 precision and 0.748 recall across 1,100 iterations, and educator relabeling raised apparent accuracy to 83.91% in the topic-constrained setting.
finding.measure: Misconception classification performance on algebra question/answer pairs (precision, recall, and expert-adjusted accuracy)
finding.study_size: n=220 diagnostic examples; 5,500 iterations in Experiment 1; 1,100 iterations in Experiment 2

finding.finding_summary: The benchmark is positioned as a tool to reduce teacher burden in diagnosing student misconceptions and to support more efficient instructional response. Five educators reported interest in using the dataset with AI for diagnosis or teacher training, suggesting potential productivity benefits, but the paper does not directly measure workload reduction or time savings.
finding.measure: Teacher-reported perceived utility of AI-supported misconception diagnosis and training

finding.finding_summary: The study finds that the benchmark is relevant to classroom practice and may help align AI tools with educator needs in underserved contexts. Four of five teachers reported teaching in underserved settings, most said the misconceptions were common in their classrooms, and several suggested broader applications such as diagnostic tests, chatbots, and teacher training, indicating possible institutional value for K-12 math support systems.
finding.measure: Educator survey/interview responses on relevance, classroom occurrence, and intended use of the benchmark

paper_profiles.title: Aligning Tutor Discourse Supporting Rigorous Thinking with Tutee Content Mastery for Predicting Math Achievement
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether human tutor discourse and students’ individual practice performance in an intelligent tutoring system (ITS) jointly predict math achievement for 9th-grade students. The authors focus on whether specific tutor talk moves—especially those aligned with accountable talk and rigorous thinking—interact with students’ proximal mastery on the MATHia ITS to explain external math assessment scores and changes in those scores over time.

The study uses data from 1,080 9th-grade students in a large urban Midwestern district receiving high-dosage small-group tutoring during the 2022–23 school year. Students alternated between human-tutor sessions and independent work in Carnegie Learning’s MATHia ITS; tutorials were audio/video recorded and tutors’ talk moves were automatically labeled with a RoBERTa-based classifier. The authors built interpretable decision trees extracted from random forest classifiers to predict assessment outcomes from six tutor talk-move features and five ITS performance features, using nested cross-validation and multiple score thresholds.

Results show that the combined model outperformed models using only talk moves or only ITS metrics. The extracted decision tree from combined features achieved AUC=0.79 on the whole dataset for predicting assessment scores (and AUC=0.77 for predicting score changes), compared with lower AUCs for tutor talk moves alone and ITS alone. The strongest pattern was an interaction: Press for Reasoning was more predictive for students with higher ITS mastery, whereas Revoicing was more predictive for students with lower ITS mastery. The authors emphasize that these findings are correlational rather than causal and suggest future work on temporal ordering, efficiency, and additional student covariates.

finding.finding_summary: The combined model using tutor talk moves plus MATHia ITS metrics best predicted math assessment performance, achieving AUC=0.79 on the whole dataset and 5-fold test AUC=0.77 for changes in scores. The strongest interpretable pattern was that Press for Reasoning predicted higher assessment scores for students with higher ITS mastery, while Revoicing predicted higher scores for students with lower ITS mastery.
finding.measure: External math skills assessment scores and changes in consecutive assessment scores
finding.study_size: n=1080 students; 4124 assessment rounds (4012 rounds for change-score analysis)

paper_profiles.title: Efficient RL for optimizing conversation level outcomes with an LLM-based tutor
paper_profiles.population: Middle School (Grade 6); broader K-12 math tutoring context
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how to optimize an LLM-based math tutor for conversation-level success rather than turn-by-turn preference optimization. The authors argue that standard RLHF and prompt-based tutoring often optimize local responses, such as directly answering a student, even when the better pedagogical strategy is to ask questions, diagnose understanding, and keep the student working toward solving the problem independently.

To address this, the paper proposes a lightweight offline RL framework that compresses dialogue history into a 25-dimensional latent student state and trains a policy over four high-level tutor actions: instruct, encourage, refocus, and ask a question. The system uses Claude 3 Sonnet both as a synthetic tutor/student generator and as an evaluator for student state, action labels, and simulated outcomes. Training is performed on 3,000 synthetic sixth-grade math tutoring dialogues, with an additional 2,500 optimism-guided augmented dialogues; performance is measured in a simulated student environment by the student’s success rate at solving the target problem within 20 turns.

The main result is that RL-based policies, especially Conservative Q-learning trained on augmented data, outperform prompt engineering and behavioral cloning on the simulated math tutoring task. The paper reports higher average student success rates for the augmented-data policy, while also noting that data augmentation increases coverage and success in the synthetic corpus. However, the authors also find that the approach does not generalize well to new math problems from GSM8K, and they emphasize a key limitation: all evaluations rely on LLM-simulated students rather than real learners. Overall, the paper is best read as a methods paper showing how long-horizon optimization could improve LLM tutoring behavior, not as evidence from a real classroom intervention.

finding.finding_summary: In simulated sixth-grade math tutoring, the RL-optimized tutor improved the student’s probability of solving the target problem within the dialogue window. The paper reports that CQL trained on augmented data (D+) achieved the highest average success rate across 300 conversation samples, outperforming prompt engineering, behavioral cloning, and fitted Q-iteration in the simulator.
finding.measure: Student problem-solving success rate within maximum dialogue length (binary solve/not solve per conversation)
finding.study_size: n=300 conversation samples per tutor evaluation; training data D=3,000 dialogues, D+=5,500 dialogues
finding.confidence_interval: 95% CI shown in figure; numeric interval not reported in text

paper_profiles.title: V-MATH: An Agentic Approach to the Vietnamese National High School Graduation Mathematics Exams
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper presents V-MATH, an autonomous agentic AI framework designed to support Vietnamese high school students preparing for the National High School Graduation Mathematics Exam (NHSGME) and to help teachers generate exam-aligned materials. The system combines three agents: one for creative question generation aligned to the Ministry of Education’s specification matrix, one for step-by-step solving and explanation, and one for personalized learning-path customization based on student performance.

The work is situated in the Vietnamese upper-secondary exam-preparation context, where students face a high-stakes, standardized mathematics test spanning algebra-analysis, geometry-measurement, and statistics-probability across recognition, comprehension, and application levels. The paper also introduces a large structured dataset of 500 official exam sets extracted from 220 PDF sources, and evaluates the framework against strong general-purpose and math-specialized LLMs on exact-match accuracy, section-wise accuracy, set-level accuracy, explanation quality, and memory ablations.

Results indicate that V-MATH performs very strongly on exam-solving benchmarks: it reports 100% average exact-match accuracy on the VNHSGE benchmark across 2019–2023, section-wise accuracies of 98.1%/93.8%/88.4% on held-out NHSGME exams, and better set-level accuracy than comparison models. The memory-augmented retrieval component improves harder-item accuracy and step completeness with a small latency cost. The personalized-learning agent is reported to increase student scores by 11.8 points and reduce repeated skill errors, while the generation agent produces matrix-compliant, teacher-rated novel questions. The paper concludes that the framework is promising for scalable exam preparation and teacher support, though the evidence is preliminary and largely system-evaluation based rather than a controlled student outcome study.

finding.finding_summary: V-MATH substantially improved mathematics problem-solving performance on Vietnamese high-school exam tasks. On the VNHSGE benchmark (250 questions across 2019–2023), the system reports 100% exact-match accuracy on all years, compared with 87.6% for o1-preview and 86.4% for GPT-4 Omni. On 50 held-out NHSGME exams, it achieved 98.1% accuracy on Part I, 93.8% on Part II, 88.4% on Part III, and 92.1% item accuracy with 64% set-level accuracy.
finding.measure: Exact-match accuracy; section-wise accuracy; item accuracy; set-level exam accuracy
finding.study_size: n=250 VNHSGE questions; n=50 held-out NHSGME exams

finding.finding_summary: The personalized learning agent is reported to improve engagement and learning persistence-related indicators, though these are system-level evaluation metrics rather than a controlled learner study. Table 4 reports an engagement score of 0.76 for Agent 3, along with a +11.8 point pre/post score gain and a 43% reduction in repeated skill errors, suggesting better sustained practice and self-regulated study support.
finding.measure: Engagement score; pre/post score gain; repeated skill-error reduction

finding.finding_summary: The paper claims that V-MATH supports step-by-step reasoning, explanation quality, and personalized study-path decisions, all of which are adjacent to durable skills such as metacognition and problem decomposition. The solver agent achieved 82.1% step completeness and 4.5/5 explanation quality, while the personalized agent used error analysis to map mistakes to skill gaps and recommend targeted practice.
finding.measure: Step completeness; explanation quality; path effectiveness

finding.finding_summary: The system reduced teacher workload and improved content-generation efficiency by automating exam creation, answer generation, and report production. The generation agent reached 96.7% matrix compliance with a teacher rating of 4.6/5 and low novelty overlap (7.8%), and the paper explicitly states that the framework reduces manual workload by generating compliant exam questions and building question banks.
finding.measure: Teacher-rated question quality; matrix compliance; novelty overlap; latency; workload reduction claims

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that V-MATH could support scalable, equitable exam preparation aligned with national standards and improve institutional exam-material production. Evidence is indirect and based on dataset construction plus system benchmarking, including creation of a 500-exam NHSGME dataset from 220 official PDFs and alignment to the 2025 MOET specification matrix.
finding.measure: Dataset construction; exam-format alignment; institutional usability claims

paper_profiles.title: Stepwise Verification and Remediation of Student Reasoning Errors with Large Language Model Tutors
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a key problem in LLM-based dialog tutoring: large language models often generate incorrect or hallucinated tutoring responses because they must simultaneously judge a student’s solution, identify the error, choose a pedagogical strategy, and generate feedback in one pass. The authors argue that this is especially risky in mathematics tutoring, where identifying the exact first reasoning error is crucial for giving targeted, actionable help without giving away the solution.

To address this, they propose a verify-then-generate architecture for math dialog tutoring. First, a verifier checks whether a student’s multi-step solution is correct and, if not, identifies the first error using one of three approaches: classification-based stepwise verification, free-form error description, or step alignment between student and reference solutions. The verifier output is then fed into a response generation model so the tutor can produce more targeted feedback. They build a dataset of 1,002 teacher-annotated student solutions from K-12 math word-problem dialogs derived from MathDial/GSM8K-style problems, and evaluate prompted and fine-tuned LLMs plus human teacher judgments.

The main findings are that verification is itself difficult even for strong LLMs, especially without a reference solution, but adding a reference solution and/or fine-tuning improves performance. More importantly, conditioning tutor responses on the verifier output improves targetedness, correctness, and actionability, with free-form error descriptions performing best overall. The paper concludes that modular verification can reduce hallucinations and make AI tutors more pedagogically useful, though the work is limited to multi-step math problem solving and uses teacher-centered evaluation rather than direct student learning outcomes.

finding.finding_summary: The paper does not test student achievement directly, but it shows that verify-then-generate tutoring outputs are more accurate and more targeted in multi-step math problem solving than direct generation. In human evaluation on 40 conversations, the Error Description variant improved targetedness, correctness, and actionability relative to the baseline (e.g., GPT-3.5 baseline: 30.0/37.5/30.0 vs Error Description: 57.5/62.5/45.0 for targeted/correct/actionable), suggesting better math tutoring feedback quality.
finding.measure: Teacher-rated quality of math tutoring responses; automatic text generation metrics (sBLEU, KF1, BF1) on math dialog responses
finding.study_size: n=1,002 annotated solutions for verification; n=40 conversations for human evaluation

paper_profiles.title: MATHDIAL: A Dialogue Tutoring Dataset with Rich Pedagogical Properties Grounded in Math Reasoning Problems
paper_profiles.population: Elementary (Grade school; roughly sixth grade math word problems)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the lack of high-quality datasets for training and evaluating dialogue tutoring systems in mathematics. The authors argue that current tutoring corpora are too small, low-quality, or lack pedagogical grounding, which limits progress on AI tutors that can scaffold student thinking rather than simply solve problems or reveal answers.

To address this, the paper introduces MATHDIAL, a semi-synthetic dataset of 2,861 one-to-one tutoring dialogues (14,197 utterances) grounded in GSM8k math word problems. The collection pipeline pairs expert human teachers with an LLM that simulates student confusions and uses annotated teacher moves such as Focus, Probing, and Telling. Teachers were recruited from Prolific and the dialogues were designed around grade-school multi-step math reasoning problems, with the simulated student intended to resemble a sixth grader.

The paper evaluates the dataset descriptively and uses it to fine-tune several language models for tutor response generation, comparing them to prompted large models such as ChatGPT. The main findings are that fine-tuned smaller open-source models can outperform much larger prompted models on automatic metrics and human judgments of correctness and equitable tutoring, and can achieve similar interactive student-solving success with less direct telling. The authors also find that models still struggle with generalization to unseen problems, and that longer multi-step problems remain harder. Overall, the paper is primarily a dataset and modeling paper, not a student outcome study, but it provides evidence that pedagogically grounded data can improve AI tutoring behavior.

finding.finding_summary: The paper shows that a semi-synthetic collection pipeline can produce a much larger tutoring corpus than prior public datasets, with 2,861 dialogues and 14,197 utterances. The authors argue that this reduces a key bottleneck for developing dialogue tutors and enables scalable dataset creation without recording real tutoring sessions.
finding.measure: Dataset size / corpus scalability and completeness

finding.finding_summary: The paper centers on tutoring moves that support scaffolding, reasoning, and student exploration, and it reports that expert teachers frequently used Focus and Probing moves rather than direct telling. In human evaluation, the collected dialogues were rated as more equitable when they preserved room for student thinking and problem solving, indicating pedagogically stronger tutor behavior.
finding.measure: Teacher move taxonomy; human ratings of equitable tutoring
finding.study_size: n=50 responses per model in human evaluation; 102 utterances in a move-agreement sample; 2,861 dialogues in corpus

finding.finding_summary: The dataset and models are grounded in grade-school multi-step math word problems, and the interactive evaluation measures whether the student reaches the correct answer. Finetuned Flan-T5780M achieved 30% Success@5 and 39% Success@10 with <1% and 4% Telling@5/@10, respectively, compared with ChatGPT's 29% Success@5 and 53% Success@10 but much higher telling (16% and 32%).
finding.measure: Interactive problem-solving success on math word problems (Success@k); tutor response quality on GSM8k-based tutoring dialogues
finding.study_size: n=2,861 dialogues; interactive tutoring evaluation on sampled problems

finding.finding_summary: The paper discusses student engagement and frustration as relevant to tutoring quality, and uses equitable tutoring as a criterion that emphasizes giving students room to explore rather than immediately revealing answers. In the interactive evaluation, the finetuned tutor reduced telling relative to ChatGPT, which the authors interpret as better support for sustained engagement in problem solving.
finding.measure: Equitable tutoring ratings; telling rate in interactive tutoring
finding.study_size: n=50 responses per model in human evaluation; interactive tutoring simulation

paper_profiles.title: Brilla AI: AI Contestant for the National Science and Maths Quiz
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper presents Brilla AI, an end-to-end real-time AI system built to participate in Ghana’s National Science and Maths Quiz (NSMQ), with the broader goal of demonstrating how AI could support science learning in low-resource African contexts. The motivation is educational access: the authors argue that teacher shortages and limited learning support in Sub-Saharan Africa create a need for AI-assisted tutoring and question answering tools that can understand Ghanaian-accented speech and respond in a locally appropriate accent.

Technically, the system combines four modules: speech-to-text using Whisper, question extraction using a fine-tuned BERT classifier, question answering using both extractive and generative approaches (including Mistral-7B and Falcon-7B), and text-to-speech using a fine-tuned VITS model. The system was evaluated on archived NSMQ riddles from 2019 and 2020, with human contestant performance used as a benchmark, and then deployed live in the 2023 NSMQ Grand Finale for the Riddles round.

The paper reports that the generative QA approach outperformed the extractive approach on the riddles benchmark, though it remained below GPT-3.5 and far below human students. In live deployment, Brilla AI correctly answered 1 of 4 riddles before the human teams, but performance was limited by transcription errors, missed clue detection, and latency from sequential processing. The authors conclude that the prototype is promising as a foundation for science tutoring and educational support, but that better ASR, more robust clue segmentation, lower-latency orchestration, and improved QA are needed before practical classroom use.

finding.finding_summary: The system was evaluated on science-and-math quiz riddles, with QA accuracy measured on 316 archived riddles (2019 n=156; 2020 n=160) and in a live NSMQ deployment. In offline all-clues evaluation, Mistral achieved EM 38.46% (2019) and 27.5% (2020), outperforming extractive QA but underperforming GPT-3.5 (40.38%/33.75%) and students (76.3%/75%). In live deployment, Brilla AI answered 1 of 4 riddles correctly (25% EM) but was hampered by speech recognition errors and late/incorrect answer attempts.
finding.measure: Exact Match (EM) and Fuzzy Match (FM) accuracy on NSMQ science and math riddles; live quiz performance
finding.study_size: n=316 riddles (2019-2020 benchmark); live deployment with 4 riddles

finding.finding_summary: Mathematics was one of the subject areas included in the NSMQ riddles, but the paper does not report separate math-only results. The combined science-and-math QA benchmark shows moderate model performance relative to humans: Mistral reached EM 38.46% in 2019 and 27.5% in 2020 on the full riddle set, while students reached 76.3% and 75%. The results suggest the system can sometimes solve mathematics-related quiz questions, but the evidence is not disaggregated enough to isolate a math-specific effect.
finding.measure: EM and FM accuracy on mixed science/mathematics riddles

finding.finding_summary: The paper primarily evaluates the efficiency of real-time AI components for live quiz deployment, including speech-to-text latency, QA turnaround, and text-to-speech latency. Whisper Medium (English) was selected as a tradeoff model with WER 31.61% and latency 0.94 seconds; TTS models showed mean latencies around 1.05-1.28 seconds; and the authors report that the sequential pipeline introduced bottlenecks and visible lag during the live event. Overall, the system demonstrates feasible real-time operation, but with clear efficiency limitations that affected deployment quality.
finding.measure: Latency, word error rate, and pipeline processing speed

finding.finding_summary: The paper frames Brilla AI as a response to teacher shortages and limited learning support in Sub-Saharan Africa, arguing that AI could augment scarce educators and support one-on-one tutoring at scale. While the work does not test policy or institutional interventions directly, it reports a live public deployment in the NSMQ Grand Finale and positions the system as a potential foundation for broader educational access and infrastructure in low-resource contexts.
finding.measure: Live deployment milestone; conceptual institutional implications for AI tutoring access

paper_profiles.title: Systematic review of research on artificial intelligence applications in higher education – where are the educators?
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a systematic review of artificial intelligence applications in higher education published between 2007 and 2018. The authors ask how the field developed over time, how AI in higher education is conceptualized, what ethical challenges and risks are discussed, and what kinds of AI applications have been studied across the student life cycle.

The review screened 2,656 records and included 146 peer-reviewed journal articles. Most studies were quantitative and came from computer science and STEM fields; only a small minority explicitly defined AI or critically reflected on risks such as privacy and cost. The applications were grouped into profiling and prediction, intelligent tutoring systems, assessment and evaluation, and adaptive systems/personalization. Across the reviewed studies, AI tools often showed promising classification or prediction performance and generally positive preliminary results in tutoring, assessment, and adaptive learning, but the review emphasizes that evidence is mostly short-term, often descriptive, and rarely grounded in educational theory.

The paper’s main conclusion is that research on AI in higher education has been driven more by technical than educational perspectives, with relatively little involvement from educators and limited attention to ethics, governance, and pedagogy. It argues that stronger interdisciplinary work is needed, especially studies that examine how AI affects teaching, learning, and institutional practice in realistic settings over longer periods. Because this is a review of higher education research, it does not provide direct K-12 mathematics learning evidence, but it does summarize adjacent evidence on intelligent tutoring systems and related AI tools.

finding.finding_summary: Across the reviewed higher-education studies, AI applications were repeatedly framed as improving efficiency by automating prediction, grading, feedback, and student support tasks. The review reports that machine learning models often outperformed logistic regression in classification accuracy, and that automated essay scoring could reach high agreement with human raters (e.g., 94.6%–98.2%), suggesting potential reductions in staff time and cost.
finding.measure: Prediction accuracy; automated grading agreement with human raters; reported efficiency/cost implications
finding.study_size: n=146 included studies; individual primary studies vary

finding.finding_summary: A substantial portion of the reviewed literature addressed institutional uses of AI, especially profiling and prediction for admissions, dropout/retention, course scheduling, and student services. The review concludes that these systems can support administrative decision-making and early warning functions, but notes that such work is concentrated in technical disciplines and rarely includes educational or ethical critique.
finding.measure: Admissions prediction, dropout/retention prediction, institutional decision support, student-service applications
finding.study_size: n=146 included studies; institutional-level subset summarized in review

finding.finding_summary: Several reviewed studies used AI to predict or support engagement, motivation, academic self-regulation, and retention-related behaviors. The review describes generally positive preliminary results for engagement monitoring and early intervention systems, but also notes at least one negative case where the type of tutoring support was less suitable for advanced learners, indicating that effects depend on learner fit and context.
finding.measure: Engagement, motivation, retention-risk indicators, self-regulation-related behaviors
finding.study_size: n=146 included studies; individual primary studies vary

finding.finding_summary: The review includes several studies on AI-supported collaboration, feedback, and learner modeling that relate to collaboration, metacognition, and problem solving. It reports mostly positive preliminary findings for collaborative-learning support and intelligent tutoring, but also highlights limitations such as short-term pilots, novelty effects, and inconsistent fit to learner level, so the evidence for durable-skill gains is suggestive rather than conclusive.
finding.measure: Collaborative learning behavior; problem-solving support; learner modeling; feedback processes
finding.study_size: n=146 included studies; individual primary studies vary

finding.finding_summary: The review finds broad use of AI for non-mathematics academic tasks such as assessment, evaluation, personalized content recommendation, and tutoring across higher education subjects. It reports that many systems performed well on task-specific measures, including automated grading agreement and prediction accuracy, but the evidence base is fragmented across disciplines and rarely includes long-term outcome data.
finding.measure: Automated grading, feedback quality, personalized content delivery, academic performance prediction
finding.study_size: n=146 included studies; individual primary studies vary

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT for Good? On Opportunities and Challenges of Large Language Models for Education
paper_profiles.population: All education levels (primary, secondary, tertiary, and professional development); no specific study population
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a position paper that surveys the emerging landscape of large language models (LLMs), especially ChatGPT, for education. It asks what opportunities and challenges LLMs create for learners and teachers, and it synthesizes early examples of use across content generation, tutoring, feedback, assessment, and educational design. The paper is not an experiment or review of a bounded intervention; rather, it provides a conceptual overview of potential educational uses and risks, drawing on a small number of illustrative studies.

The paper argues that LLMs could support personalized practice, feedback, quiz and question generation, explanation, and dialogue across multiple levels of schooling, including primary, secondary, higher education, and teacher workflows. It also emphasizes that the technology is brittle and can produce biased, inaccurate, copyright-sensitive, privacy-sensitive, and overreliance-inducing outputs, so teachers and institutions must provide human oversight, critical thinking instruction, and governance. The authors recommend responsible, ethical, and pedagogically grounded integration, but they do not present original outcome data or direct causal evidence on K-12 learning.

For mathematics specifically, the paper mentions that LLMs can generate math word problems and support problem solving, but this is framed as a prospective opportunity rather than empirical evidence. The paper’s main contribution is thus a high-level synthesis of benefits, risks, and mitigation strategies for educational deployment of LLMs, not a study of learning gains.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that LLMs may reduce teacher workload by automating or assisting with lesson planning, quiz and question generation, feedback, grading support, and other preparation tasks. Reported claims are illustrative rather than experimental; for example, the paper cites prior work suggesting grading effort could be reduced by up to 85% in large courses, but this position paper itself does not provide original empirical estimates.
finding.measure: Teacher workload, grading effort, and content-generation efficiency

finding.finding_summary: The paper emphasizes institutional-level opportunities and risks, including policy needs for responsible AI adoption, privacy and security compliance, copyright, bias mitigation, integrity, sustainability, and fair access. It concludes that LLM adoption in education requires governance, human oversight, and institutional strategies, but it does not test policy interventions or report outcome data.
finding.measure: Governance, privacy, fairness, integrity, and adoption considerations

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests that LLMs may support critical thinking, problem-solving, creativity, and collaboration when used as a supplement to instruction, but it also warns that overreliance on model-generated answers may weaken these same skills. No original study is reported; the discussion is conceptual and based on the authors’ synthesis of risks and opportunities.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, problem-solving, creativity, and collaboration

finding.finding_summary: The paper states that LLMs may increase student engagement, interaction, curiosity, and willingness to ask questions, and it cites early examples such as GPT-3-based pedagogical agents for curiosity-prompting. However, this paper does not report original experimental effects on engagement or motivation; the evidence is discussed qualitatively.
finding.measure: Engagement, curiosity, interaction, and participation

finding.finding_summary: Mathematics is mentioned as one subject area where LLMs could generate practice problems and math word problems and provide step-by-step explanations to support problem solving. The paper does not present direct K-12 math learning outcome data, effect sizes, or comparative evidence against standard instruction or other supports.
finding.measure: Math word problems, practice problems, and problem-solving support

paper_profiles.title: How Does ChatGPT Perform on the United States Medical Licensing Examination (USMLE)? The Implications of Large Language Models for Medical Education and Knowledge Assessment
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper evaluates whether ChatGPT can answer USMLE-style multiple-choice questions accurately and provide interpretable reasoning. The authors tested the model on four text-only question sets spanning Step 1 and Step 2 content: two AMBOSS-derived sets and two NBME free-question sets. They also compared ChatGPT with GPT-3 and InstructGPT, and qualitatively coded responses for logical reasoning, use of information from the question, and use of external knowledge.

Across the four datasets, ChatGPT achieved accuracies ranging from 42% to 64.4%, outperforming InstructGPT by 8.15 percentage points on average and GPT-3 by a larger margin. Performance was higher on NBME than AMBOSS items and higher on Step 1 than Step 2 items; within AMBOSS Step 1, accuracy decreased significantly as question difficulty increased (P=.01). The authors also found that ChatGPT always provided a logical explanation, used internal question information in nearly all responses, and used external information more often in correct than incorrect answers, suggesting that correctness was associated with richer contextual integration.

The study frames ChatGPT as a possible interactive medical education tool rather than as a tested instructional intervention. The paper does not measure learner outcomes, and it does not study K-12 settings or mathematics learning. Its main contribution is benchmarking a generative AI model on medical knowledge assessment tasks and discussing potential educational uses such as tutoring, small-group support, and reflective learning, while noting risks and limitations related to accuracy, prompt dependence, and model updates.

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT showed substantial performance on medical knowledge question-answering tasks, with accuracies of 44% (44/100) on AMBOSS-Step1, 42% (42/100) on AMBOSS-Step2, 64.4% (56/87) on NBME-Free-Step1, and 57.8% (59/102) on NBME-Free-Step2. The model outperformed InstructGPT by 8.15 percentage points on average and GPT-3 performed near random chance; accuracy also declined with increasing AMBOSS Step 1 difficulty (P=.01).
finding.measure: Multiple-choice medical knowledge accuracy on AMBOSS and NBME USMLE-style question sets

paper_profiles.title: Generative AI
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This Catchword article is a conceptual and agenda-setting paper on generative AI, aimed at the information systems and business engineering research community rather than reporting a primary empirical study. It defines generative AI, distinguishes model-, system-, and application-level perspectives, and explains how modern systems such as LLMs, diffusion models, GANs, and RLHF-based conversational agents work. The paper also situates generative AI in socio-technical systems, emphasizing human-AI co-creation, hybrid intelligence, and the need for appropriate theories of interaction.

The article further reviews major limitations and risks of current generative AI systems, including incorrect outputs and hallucinations, bias and fairness problems, copyright violation, and environmental costs. It argues that these issues are likely to persist across applications and thus require both technical and organizational mitigation. The paper does not test an educational intervention or analyze student outcomes directly; instead, it uses education as one of several application areas to illustrate future research opportunities.

In its education discussion, the paper notes that conversational agents may change assessment practices, enable digital teaching assistants, and support creation of supplemental teaching materials. It emphasizes the need for governance frameworks that help learners use generative AI appropriately and verify outputs. The article’s contribution is therefore conceptual and normative: it frames generative AI as a transformative technology with important opportunities and risks, while calling for rigorous future research, including in education.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that generative AI will reshape educational assessment, teaching support, and governance, but it provides no empirical estimate. In education specifically, it anticipates shifts toward digital teaching assistants, supplemental teaching materials, and new policies for appropriate use and verification of outputs; these are presented as future implications rather than observed effects.
finding.measure: not_reported

paper_profiles.title: The cognitive paradox of AI in education: between enhancement and erosion
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This opinion paper argues that artificial intelligence in education has a paradoxical effect: it can enhance learning through personalization, efficiency, and scalability, but it can also erode cognition through over-reliance and cognitive offloading. Using Cognitive Load Theory, Bloom’s Taxonomy, and Self-Determination Theory as organizing frameworks, the authors discuss how AI may support lower-order learning, reduce extraneous load, and improve access to practice and feedback, while potentially weakening retention, critical thinking, autonomy, and motivation.

The paper is not an empirical study of a new intervention. Instead, it synthesizes prior literature and selectively cites examples of AI-based tutoring, ChatGPT-related learning studies, and broader AI-in-education work across undergraduate, vocational, and language-learning contexts. The main conclusion is that AI should complement, not replace, human instruction: effective implementation should preserve active cognitive effort, encourage reflection and source verification, and maintain teacher guidance and human interaction. The article also highlights risks such as algorithmic bias, dependency, reduced intrinsic motivation, and possible declines in higher-order thinking if AI is used as a substitute for thinking rather than a support for it.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that generative AI may improve some lower-order cognitive outcomes but can also undermine durable skills such as critical thinking, independent reasoning, and higher-order thinking through cognitive offloading. It cites prior studies and examples suggesting that AI-supported learners may become more passive and less able to verify sources or sustain effortful problem-solving, although the paper itself does not report a new experiment or effect size.
finding.measure: critical thinking, problem-solving, higher-order thinking, source verification, independent reasoning

finding.finding_summary: The paper claims AI can increase competence through personalization but may also reduce autonomy, relatedness, and intrinsic motivation if students become overly dependent on AI. It cites concerns that over-reliance on AI may lower engagement and motivation, but these are conceptual claims supported by secondary references rather than direct empirical estimates in this paper.
finding.measure: motivation, autonomy, engagement, relatedness

finding.finding_summary: The article discusses AI-supported learning more broadly across educational domains, including adaptive learning, tutoring, memory retention, and procedural performance, but without focusing on a specific academic subject outcome in a primary study. It uses cited examples to suggest AI can improve access and performance on some tasks while risking shallow learning and reduced conceptual understanding.
finding.measure: memory retention, procedural performance, conceptual understanding

paper_profiles.title: Sparks of Artificial General Intelligence: Early experiments with GPT-4
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a qualitative demonstration and critique of an early, text-only version of GPT-4. The authors ask whether GPT-4 exhibits signs of broad intelligence by presenting it with novel prompts across many domains, including language, coding, mathematics, vision, common-sense reasoning, tool use, and social understanding. The approach is intentionally exploratory rather than experimental: the authors generate bespoke tasks to probe capabilities and limitations, compare GPT-4 informally with ChatGPT, and emphasize both striking successes and clear failure modes.

The mathematics-related material is not an educational intervention study. Instead, the paper showcases GPT-4’s performance on mathematical conversation, elementary proof generation, and benchmark-style problem solving, often contrasted with ChatGPT. The examples suggest that GPT-4 can solve some high-school-level math problems, produce elegant proofs, and outperform earlier models on prompt following and reasoning, but it still makes basic arithmetic errors and lacks robust planning. The paper also discusses hallucinations, bias, and other risks, arguing that GPT-4 is a significant step toward more general intelligence but still incomplete and not reliably human-like.

Because the paper is about model capability demonstration rather than K-12 instruction, it does not provide evidence on student learning outcomes, teacher implementation, dosage, grade-level moderators, or classroom settings. Its relevance to K-12 mathematics is indirect only, via examples that the model can answer some math prompts at a level comparable to or above human performance in isolated tasks.

finding.finding_summary: In illustrative, non-experimental examples, early GPT-4 successfully solved a high-school-level math problem and produced a correct proof-style response for the infinitude of primes. The paper also reports that GPT-4 was considerably stronger than ChatGPT on the showcased math prompts, but these are anecdotal demonstrations rather than measured instructional outcomes.
finding.measure: Accuracy/quality on ad hoc mathematical reasoning prompts and examples

paper_profiles.title: Combining Large Language Models with Tutoring System Intelligence: A Case Study in Caregiver Homework Support
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses how large language models (LLMs) can be combined with intelligent tutoring system (ITS) data to support caregivers who help children with online math homework. The authors argue that caregivers often want to help but lack the instructional knowledge needed for modern curricula, and that generative AI could potentially provide timely, context-aware conversational support during homework support sessions.

The study introduces the Caregiver Conversational Support Tool (CCST), which integrates the Lynnette equation-solving ITS with a Llama 3 8B Instruct model. The system uses real-time tutoring context such as correctness, hint use, the current equation, and recommended next steps to generate chat-message suggestions for caregivers. The paper reports iterative prompt-engineering experiments and a prototyping study with 10 middle-school caregivers in which participants interacted with the tool during simulated homework support sessions.

Findings suggest that the LLM generated better recommendations when grounded in tutoring-system context and few-shot examples of effective tutoring practices. Caregivers preferred content-level help over motivational messaging, especially prompts that encouraged student self-explanation and revealed thinking processes. Participants also found the recommendations useful for identifying mistakes and supporting metacognition, but they noted tradeoffs including message length, occasional inauthentic tone, and latency of about 25 seconds. The paper is primarily a design and feasibility study, not a learning-outcomes evaluation, so it does not provide causal evidence that the tool improves math achievement.

finding.finding_summary: This paper does not evaluate student math learning gains or compare outcomes against standard instruction, no support, or alternative tutoring supports. Instead, it presents a design/prototyping case study showing that context-grounded LLM prompts can generate math-help messages aligned with equation-solving steps, correctness, and hint use for middle-school homework support (n=10 caregivers).
finding.measure: not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The main observed benefit was that caregivers preferred LLM-generated messages that prompted student self-explanation and reflection, which the authors interpret as supporting metacognition. In the prototyping study with 10 middle-school caregivers, five explicitly preferred messages that asked students to explain their reasoning, and the paper argues these prompts may help caregivers elicit deeper understanding during math practice.
finding.measure: Caregiver preference / qualitative feedback on metacognitive prompting and self-explanation support

finding.finding_summary: The system was designed to reduce the burden on caregivers by generating three context-sensitive message recommendations in real time, and participants generally found the number of suggestions adequate. However, six of nine caregivers found the messages too long, two of six found generation somewhat slow, and the authors report average latency of about 25 seconds, indicating usability tradeoffs that could limit efficiency in live homework support.
finding.measure: Caregiver reports of message length, adequacy, and latency; system response time

finding.finding_summary: Caregivers valued some motivational and encouraging language, but their preferences leaned strongly toward content-level support rather than purely motivational messages. The authors report that 6 caregivers preferred direct math guidance, 2 found both types useful, and 1 preferred to provide motivation independently; several caregivers also appreciated the positive tone when it felt authentic and not harsh.
finding.measure: Qualitative caregiver preferences regarding motivational support, tone, and encouragement

paper_profiles.title: Elementary School Students’ and Teachers’ Perceptions Towards Creative Mathematical Writing with Generative AI
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how elementary school students and teachers perceived a generative AI-supported creative mathematical writing activity. The authors were motivated by the promise of GenAI to scaffold mathematical storytelling while also recognizing classroom-level risks such as overreliance, reduced human feedback, and inappropriate or overly polished AI outputs.

The study implemented a GenAI-powered tool in six 5th-grade classrooms across two U.S. schools with 79 students and 6 teachers. Students engaged in a three-step process—Ask, Represent, Transform—where they analyzed math story prompts, visually represented ideas, and co-created/corrected math stories with GPT-4 and DALL·E 3. Data came from student focus groups, teacher interviews, open-ended surveys, and classroom observations, and were analyzed thematically.

The findings are qualitative rather than outcome-based: participants reported that GenAI could support creativity, mathematical understanding, AI literacy, interest, curiosity, and ownership of learning. At the same time, they identified important challenges, including weak critical evaluation of AI outputs, difficulty generating coherent prompts/stories, insufficient feedback and adaptivity, reduced opportunities for independent work, limited social interaction, and accessibility barriers such as lack of speech-to-text. The paper concludes that GenAI can be pedagogically promising in mathematics, but only when intentionally designed to preserve student agency, teacher feedback, social learning, and room for productive imperfection.

finding.finding_summary: Participants perceived the GenAI-supported creative mathematical writing activity as helping students understand math problems, represent mathematical ideas, and uncover misconceptions. However, the paper reports no direct achievement data or causal effect sizes; the evidence is qualitative and based on interviews, open-ended surveys, and observations from 79 fifth-grade students and 6 teachers.
finding.measure: Perceived mathematical understanding, problem comprehension, and knowledge representation from interviews, open-ended surveys, and classroom observations

finding.finding_summary: Students and teachers described the GenAI activity as making math more interesting, enjoyable, and curiosity-provoking, while also increasing students’ sense of ownership over learning. These are perceived motivational benefits rather than measured outcomes, and no effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Perceived interest, curiosity, enjoyment, and ownership of learning

finding.finding_summary: The study suggests GenAI-supported math writing may foster creativity, flexible thinking, and prompt-engineering/AI-literacy practices, but it also highlights weaknesses in students’ critical evaluation of AI-generated content and challenges in formulating coherent prompts. No quantitative performance outcomes or effect sizes were reported.
finding.measure: Perceived divergent/convergent thinking, originality, flexibility, prompt engineering, and critical evaluation of AI output

finding.finding_summary: The paper focuses on mathematical creative writing, with participants reporting that GenAI helped them draft, revise, and expand story-based mathematical writing. It also surfaces literacy-related risks, including overreliance on AI-generated text and limited opportunities for students to independently produce and improve their own writing.
finding.measure: Perceived creative writing support, drafting/revision, and originality in math-story composition

paper_profiles.title: AI tutoring can safely and effectively support students: An exploratory RCT in UK classrooms
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether a generative AI tutor can safely and effectively support secondary students’ mathematics learning in real classrooms. The authors position one-to-one tutoring as highly effective but hard to scale, and test whether LearnLM—a pedagogy-fine-tuned generative AI model—can provide tutoring support comparable to human tutors while preserving safety and instructional quality.

The exploratory RCT was conducted over seven weeks in five UK secondary schools with 165 students in Years 9 and 10 (ages 13–15) using the Eedi mathematics platform. Students were randomized either to receive static, pre-written hints or interactive tutoring; students in the tutoring arm were then randomized session-by-session to a human tutor alone or a human tutor supervising LearnLM. The supervised AI tutor was reviewed by expert tutors before messages reached students.

The main finding is that supervised LearnLM was at least as effective as human tutoring on immediate learning outcomes and somewhat better on transfer to a novel topic. LearnLM messages were approved with minimal or no edits in 74.4% of cases, with only five factual errors and no harmful content identified in the audited corpus of 3,617 drafted messages. Compared with static hints, interactive tutoring substantially improved mistake remediation and misconception resolution; compared with human tutoring alone, LearnLM produced higher transfer on the next unit’s first question (66.2% vs. 60.7%, a 5.5 percentage-point advantage, 95% credible interval [−1.4, +12.4]). The paper also reports qualitative evidence that tutors valued the model’s Socratic questioning but often had to adjust pacing and tone to avoid frustration, highlighting the importance of human supervision.

finding.finding_summary: This exploratory RCT found that interactive tutoring improved mathematics learning relative to static hints, and that supervised LearnLM performed at least as well as human tutoring on immediate correction and misconception resolution. On near-term transfer, students tutored by LearnLM were more likely to solve the first question of the next unit correctly (66.2% vs. 60.7% for human tutoring), a 5.5 percentage-point advantage with a 95% credible interval of [−1.4, +12.4].
finding.measure: Correctness on mathematics platform outcomes: second attempt at same question (mistake remediation), any post-intervention question within the unit (misconception resolution), and first question of the next unit (knowledge transfer)
finding.effect_size: 5.5 percentage-point advantage for LearnLM over human tutoring on transfer; static hints vs tutoring differences reported as outcome rates rather than standardized effect sizes
finding.confidence_interval: [−1.4%, +12.4%] for LearnLM vs human tutoring on transfer; [88.5%, 93.6%] human tutoring and [90.4%, 95.3%] LearnLM on second attempt; [92.6%, 96.8%] human tutoring and [93.1%, 97.1%] LearnLM on misconception resolution

finding.finding_summary: Student-reported helpfulness favored interactive tutoring over static hints, suggesting a more positive learning experience, though the difference was modest and uncertain. In post-trial surveys, students who received interactive tutoring rated helpfulness at 3.9/5 versus 3.6/5 for static hints, with a posterior probability of advantage of 74.9%.
finding.measure: Student survey ratings of helpfulness of support received

finding.finding_summary: The study suggests AI supervision may improve tutoring efficiency and capacity, but this was supported mainly by tutor reports and informal simulation rather than a rigorous throughput experiment. Tutors reported that LearnLM made their work feel more fluid and efficient, and 82.4% selected “supporting multiple students at the same time” as the most useful feature; the paper also reports an informal post-trial scalability simulation indicating higher simultaneous conversation volume with LearnLM.
finding.measure: Tutor survey responses and qualitative interview evidence about multitasking/throughput; informal scalability simulation
finding.study_size: n=17 tutors surveyed; n=5 interviewed; informal simulation sample not_reported

paper_profiles.title: Automated Feedback in Math Education: A Comparative Analysis of LLMs for Open-Ended Responses
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether large language models can improve automated scoring and feedback generation for open-ended middle-school mathematics responses. The authors compare three systems: a fine-tuned Mistral-based model (GOAT), an existing SBERT-Canberra similarity model, and GPT-4 used zero-shot with a grading rubric. The task is not to test student learning directly, but to evaluate how accurately models match teacher-assigned scores and how teachers judge the quality of model-generated feedback.

The study uses data from an online learning platform containing 50 open-response math problems, each with 100 student answers, teacher scores, and teacher-written feedback. The models are evaluated on a 4,000-example training split and 1,000-example test split, with two teachers also rating 100 sampled feedback instances for accuracy, relevance, motivation, and preference. GOAT performs best on scoring metrics, while GPT-4 is preferred for feedback quality.

Overall, the paper finds that fine-tuning an LLM on teacher-scored student work can improve automated scoring relative to a prior retrieval-based method, but general-purpose GPT-4 produces feedback that teachers judge as more accurate, more relevant, less demotivating, and more preferred. The paper also highlights limitations in teacher feedback quality and subjectivity in judging motivational language, suggesting that training data quality and rater perspective materially affect outcomes. Because the paper evaluates model performance rather than student learning gains, it provides indirect evidence relevant to math learning support and teacher workload, not direct causal evidence of K-12 achievement effects.

finding.finding_summary: On the scoring task for middle-school open-ended math responses, the fine-tuned GOAT model matched teacher scores better than SBERT-Canberra and GPT-4. GOAT achieved AUC=0.697, RMSE=1.119, and Cohen’s kappa=0.422 on 1,000 test responses (trained on 4,000 examples), compared with SBERT’s AUC=0.662, RMSE=1.364, kappa=0.362 and GPT-4’s AUC=0.639, RMSE=1.16, kappa=0.266.
finding.measure: Agreement with teacher-assigned scores on open-ended math responses (AUC, RMSE, Cohen’s kappa)
finding.study_size: n=1000 test responses (from 50 problems; 4000 training entries)

finding.finding_summary: The paper frames automated scoring and feedback as a way to reduce teacher grading burden, and the results suggest that both GOAT and GPT-4 can generate usable feedback for middle-school math responses. Two experienced teacher raters judged GPT-4 feedback most often preferred (77.5%), with GOAT preferred 12% and SBERT 12%, indicating potential for teacher-facing drafting support even though the paper does not measure actual time savings.
finding.measure: Teacher judgments of feedback accuracy, relevance, motivation, and overall preference
finding.study_size: n=100 sampled feedback instances rated by 2 teachers

finding.finding_summary: The feedback evaluation included motivational tone, showing that GPT-4 was least demotivating and slightly most motivating. Consensus ratings found GPT-4 motivating in 52% of cases, GOAT in 48%, and SBERT in 46%, while demotivating feedback was rare for GPT-4 (1%) compared with GOAT (5%) and SBERT (11%).
finding.measure: Teacher ratings of feedback motivation and demotivation
finding.study_size: n=100 sampled feedback instances rated by 2 teachers

paper_profiles.title: Promises and challenges of generative artificial intelligence for human learning
paper_profiles.population: Not applicable (perspective paper; no direct study population)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This perspective paper examines the promises, challenges, and research needs surrounding generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in human learning. Rather than testing a specific intervention, it synthesizes prior literature to argue that GenAI may support learning by scaling personalized tutoring, generating learning resources, providing feedback, and enabling more authentic assessments, while also introducing risks such as hallucinations, privacy concerns, inequities, and assessment disruption.

The paper is not an empirical study of K–12 learners or any other single population; instead, it draws on examples across educational settings, including some references to mathematics tutoring and K–12 assessment implications. Its core contribution is conceptual: it proposes that effective use of GenAI in education requires AI literacy, evidence-based decision-making, and stronger methodological rigor in research. The authors conclude that GenAI should augment rather than replace human learning processes, and they call for rigorous longitudinal and controlled studies to determine its actual effects on cognition, metacognition, creativity, and educational outcomes.

Because the article is primarily a perspective and does not report original quantitative results, it provides no direct effect estimates for student outcomes. The paper is therefore most useful as a theoretical and agenda-setting source for understanding how GenAI may shape learning, teaching, and assessment, rather than as evidence of efficacy for a specific educational tool.

paper_profiles.title: Reflection on whether Chat GPT should be banned by academia from the perspective of education and teaching
paper_profiles.population: K-12 and higher education (discussed broadly; not an empirical sample)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is an opinion essay that argues against a blanket academic ban on ChatGPT while acknowledging serious risks related to academic integrity, privacy, bias, and over-reliance. The author frames ChatGPT as part of a broader wave of generative AI and discusses its potential to reshape teaching, learning, assessment, and educational governance.

Rather than reporting original empirical research, the article synthesizes existing commentary and examples to make a normative case for regulated integration of ChatGPT into education. It contends that AI tools can support learning efficiency, personalized tutoring, teacher workload reduction, and educational digital transformation, but should be used with clear rules to protect academic honesty and preserve human critical thinking.

The paper discusses K-12 schooling, higher education, and the broader education system, with particular attention to classroom use, assessment redesign, and policy responses in various regions and universities. Its main conclusion is that schools should not simply ban ChatGPT; instead, they should adapt curricula, assessment, and regulations so that AI use is transparent, responsible, and aligned with educational goals.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that ChatGPT can reduce workload and improve efficiency for educators and researchers by automating drafting, literature review support, and other routine text tasks. However, this is a conceptual claim rather than an empirically tested effect; no sample size or effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Perceived teacher/researcher workload and task efficiency

finding.finding_summary: The author repeatedly states that over-reliance on ChatGPT may weaken students' independent thinking, critical thinking, judgment, exploration, and summarization skills, while appropriately used AI may support higher-order thinking and creativity. These claims are presented as a theoretical argument grounded in prior commentary, not original outcome data.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, independent thinking, judgment, and related cognitive skills

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that institutions should regulate rather than ban ChatGPT, and that AI will drive broader educational reform, assessment redesign, and digital transformation. The discussion is normative and policy-oriented, with examples of school and university restrictions, but it does not report empirical institutional outcome data.
finding.measure: Policy and governance responses to generative AI in education

paper_profiles.title: Artificial intelligence in higher education: the state of the field
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks what the research field on artificial intelligence in higher education has looked like from 2016 through 2022, with a focus on where the studies were conducted, who produced them, what student populations and disciplines were studied, and how AI was used in higher education settings. The authors use PRISMA-guided systematic review methods to identify and code 138 peer-reviewed journal articles, drawing on both deductive and grounded qualitative coding.

The review is not an intervention study of a single AI tool; instead, it synthesizes the state of the field across countries, departments, student levels, subject domains, intended users, and AI use-cases. The sample was dominated by undergraduate studies, with students as the primary intended users, and language learning, computer science, and engineering as the most common domains. The paper finds a marked increase in publications in 2021–2022, a shift in publication leadership from the U.S. toward China, and a growing role for education-affiliated researchers.

In terms of applications, five major AI use-cases emerged: assessment/evaluation, predicting, AI assistants, intelligent tutoring systems, and managing student learning. The review concludes that higher education AI research has largely focused on traditional uses such as grading, prediction, tutoring, and learning analytics, while more exploratory or transformative uses remain underdeveloped. Because it is a descriptive systematic review, it does not report a pooled effect size or causal impact on learning outcomes.

finding.finding_summary: The review reports substantial use of AI for writing, reading, and vocabulary acquisition in higher education, especially within language learning contexts, but it does not evaluate a single intervention effect. It notes that AI was often used for automated feedback and assessment of writing and related literacy tasks across the 138 included studies, with no pooled effect size reported.
finding.measure: Writing, reading, and vocabulary-related outcomes in higher education language learning studies

finding.finding_summary: Mathematics appears in the review primarily through examples of AI assistants and tutoring in college mathematics courses, but the paper does not synthesize a direct achievement effect for mathematics. The review describes AI uses such as volition support and adaptive help in online mathematics learning, without reporting a causal estimate.
finding.measure: Mathematics course learning/performance and support behaviors

finding.finding_summary: Several included studies used AI to address student emotions, persistence, engagement, and self-regulation, especially through feedback, assistance, and emotional analysis. The review characterizes these uses as supportive of students' motivation and persistence, but it does not aggregate effect sizes or provide a pooled estimate of impact.
finding.measure: Student emotions, persistence, engagement, self-regulation, and effort regulation

finding.finding_summary: The review identifies AI applications that support higher-order thinking, collaborative reflection, and metacognitive or self-regulated learning processes. These are described as beneficial applications of AI in higher education, but the paper is descriptive and does not report a meta-analytic effect size.
finding.measure: Higher-order thinking, reflection, collaboration, metacognition/self-regulated learning

finding.finding_summary: Operational efficiency is a central focus of the review, especially through assessment/evaluation, automatic grading, automated test generation, learning analytics, and instructional design tools. The paper reports that automatic assessment was the most common use within assessment/evaluation (26 studies) and that AI can reduce instructor grading time and support management of student learning, but it does not provide a pooled effect size.
finding.measure: Instructor grading time, automated assessment/evaluation, test generation, learning analytics, instructional management
finding.study_size: n=138 studies (systematic review); 26 studies in automatic assessment; 19 studies in managing student learning

finding.finding_summary: The review finds that AI is increasingly used for institutional functions such as predicting dropout risk, admissions, curriculum sequencing, and quality assurance systems. These applications suggest institutional and governance relevance, but the paper remains descriptive and reports no pooled impact estimate.
finding.measure: Dropout prediction, admissions, curriculum sequencing, quality assurance, and institutional data use

paper_profiles.title: Revolutionizing education with AI: Exploring the transformative potential of ChatGPT
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This article is a narrative review of artificial intelligence in education, with particular emphasis on chatbots and ChatGPT. The paper asks what AI technologies can do for teaching and learning, what risks and ethical issues they introduce, and how they might be responsibly integrated into educational settings.
