finding.finding_summary: The paper evaluates LLM performance on elementary arithmetic word problems and finds that some model families perform better on GSM8k than on the newly created GSM1k, with accuracy drops of up to 8 percentage points on GSM1k. At the same time, frontier models show minimal signs of overfitting and all models still generalize to novel math problems, indicating mixed evidence: real arithmetic reasoning is present, but benchmark scores are inflated for some models by contamination or memorization.
finding.measure: Accuracy on grade-school arithmetic word-problem benchmarks (GSM8k vs. GSM1k)

paper_profiles.title: Ensembling Large Language Models to Characterize Affective Dynamics in Student–AI Tutor Dialogues
paper_profiles.venue: 2025 13th International Conference on Affective Computing and Intelligent Interaction Workshops and Demos (ACIIW)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the underexplored question of how students feel while interacting with an LLM-based tutor, arguing that educational evaluations of generative AI have focused too narrowly on cognitive outcomes such as test scores. The authors develop an ensemble framework that uses three frontier LLMs (Gemini, GPT-4o mini, and Claude 3.5 Sonnet) to automatically annotate student–tutor dialogue turns with valence, arousal, learning-helpfulness, and discrete emotion labels.

The study analyzes 16,986 conversational turns from 261 undergraduates using PyTutor, a GPT-4o–based Socratic coding tutor deployed across two semesters at MIT, Georgia State University, and Quinsigamond Community College. The paper does not evaluate learning gains or compare tutoring conditions; instead, it characterizes affective patterns and temporal transitions in naturalistic usage. The main findings are that student affect is generally mildly positive with moderate arousal, but confusion and curiosity are common and frustration still appears in a meaningful minority of turns.

Using a first-order Markov model over valence tertiles, the authors find that emotional states are short-lived but not random: positive states are the most stable, neutral states are least stable, and negative affect often resolves directly into positive affect rather than lingering or moving first to neutral. The paper concludes that LLM tutors may need affect-aware scaffolding to support students when frustration or confusion emerges, but it offers descriptive evidence only and explicitly notes the lack of human-annotated gold labels for validation.

finding.finding_summary: Across 16,986 student turns from 261 undergraduates, the ensemble-fused affect scores show mildly positive valence (median v=5, IQR 4–5), moderate arousal (median a=5, IQR 5–6), and above-neutral learning-helpfulness (median ℓ=6, IQR 5–6). At the same time, confusion (22.15% of turns) and frustration (8.62%) remain common, indicating that students experience both supportive and challenging emotions during AI tutoring.
finding.measure: Turn-level ensemble-fused valence, arousal, learning-helpfulness ratings and discrete emotion labels

finding.finding_summary: The paper focuses on affective dynamics during problem solving, including confusion, curiosity, frustration, and emotional recovery, which are closely tied to persistence, self-regulation, and metacognitive engagement. The authors report that neutral moments often function as turning points toward positive affect (Pneu→pos=0.38 vs. Pneu→neg=0.33), and that negative affect frequently rebounds directly to positive (Pneg→pos=0.29), suggesting dynamic regulation rather than sustained breakdown.
finding.measure: Markov transition matrix over valence tertiles; emotional state persistence and transitions within sessions
finding.study_size: n=261 learners; transitions computed over student turns

finding.finding_summary: The tutoring context is introductory Python/computing, so the paper substantively studies affect during computing problem solving rather than performance on a standardized academic outcome. The authors find that students commonly experience confusion alongside curiosity during code-debugging interactions, but they do not report achievement scores or direct learning gains; instead, learning-helpfulness ratings are generally above neutral (median ℓ=6).
finding.measure: Learning-helpfulness ratings and emotion labels during introductory Python/computing tutoring dialogues

paper_profiles.title: Improving Student Learning with Hybrid Human-AI Tutoring: A Three-Study Quasi-Experimental Investigation
paper_profiles.venue: The 14th Learning Analytics and Knowledge Conference (LAK ’24)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether a hybrid human-AI tutoring model can improve math learning for middle school students in low-income urban settings. The core problem is that high-dosage human tutoring is effective but expensive and difficult to scale, while AI tutoring systems can provide adaptive practice but may not keep students engaged without human support.

Across three quasi-experimental studies in three U.S. middle schools, the authors compare math software use alone with versions that add either a math teacher, remote human tutors, or both, and in one site also use a tutor-facing dashboard. The software platforms differed by site (IXL, i-Ready, and MATHia), but the common intervention was a hybrid model in which tutors supplemented AI-guided math practice during the school day. The samples were drawn from urban, predominantly low-income student populations, including 125 seventh graders in Pennsylvania, 385 seventh graders in California, and 75 male students in a Pennsylvania charter school.

The main findings are that hybrid human-AI tutoring increased student engagement with the software and improved intermediate learning outcomes such as time on task, questions answered, skills proficient, lessons passed, and workspace completion rates. Effects were strongest for students with lower baseline performance: lower-pretest students or students below grade level benefited more than higher-performing peers. The paper does not report new standardized achievement-test effects; instead, it argues that the observed gains in software usage and lesson completion are promising early indicators that could translate into later achievement gains. Overall, the authors conclude that hybrid human-AI tutoring is a scalable and potentially cost-effective approach for supporting math learning, especially for students with the greatest need.

finding.finding_summary: Across three quasi-experimental site studies, hybrid human-AI tutoring improved math learning process outcomes relative to software-only conditions. In Site 1 (n=125), the tutoring condition increased skills proficient and time spent; the mixed-effects model showed a positive effect on time spent (β=0.202, 95% CI [0.057, 0.347], p=0.006) and significant gains in skills proficient, with stronger effects for lower-pretest students. In Site 2 (n=385), students completed more lessons during the 3-week tutoring period than during the prior 25 active weeks, and the effect was larger for students below grade level (β=0.243, 95% CI [0.106, 0.381], p<0.001; interaction β=-0.0526, p=0.000217). In Site 3 (n=75), moving from a 1:8 to a 1:4 tutor-student ratio increased MATHia progress by 0.36 workspaces completed per hour (95% CI [0.02, 0.70], p=0.03).
finding.measure: Math software learning process and progress measures: IXL time spent, questions answered, skills proficient; i-Ready lessons passed per week; MATHia workspaces completed per hour

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that hybrid human-AI tutoring increased student engagement and usage of math software, which the authors treat as an intermediate learning-process outcome closely tied to motivation and persistence. In Site 2, average weekly time on task increased from 24 minutes before tutoring to 33 minutes during tutoring, and in Site 1 the tutoring condition significantly increased time spent and questions answered. However, the study does not use direct survey measures of motivation or self-regulation, so the evidence is indirect and based on behavioral engagement measures.
finding.measure: Time spent on task, questions answered, and software usage/progress logs
finding.effect_size: β=0.202 for time spent in Site 1; 24 to 33 minutes/week in Site 2

finding.finding_summary: The intervention improved the efficiency of student progress through the math software and was explicitly framed as a scalable, lower-cost tutoring model. Site 3 showed that reducing the tutor-student ratio from about 1:8 to 1:4 increased the rate of MATHia progress by 0.36 workspaces completed per hour, suggesting more efficient tutoring-supported software use. The authors also report an estimated annual marginal cost of about $700 per student, substantially below typical high-dosage tutoring costs, but this is presented as a descriptive cost estimate rather than a formal cost-effectiveness analysis.
finding.measure: Workspaces completed per hour; tutor-student ratio; estimated marginal cost per student
finding.effect_size: 0.36 workspaces/hour; cost approx. $700 per student annually

paper_profiles.title: E-EVAL: A Comprehensive Chinese K-12 Education Evaluation Benchmark for Large Language Models
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper introduces E-EVAL, a new benchmark for evaluating large language models (LLMs) on Chinese K-12 educational content. The authors argue that existing benchmarks do not adequately cover the full span of primary, middle, and high school subjects in China, especially elementary education, and they therefore curate 4,351 multiple-choice questions across 23 subjects drawn from regional homework, practice materials, and mock exams.

The benchmark is used to compare 15 open-source and proprietary LLMs under zero-shot, few-shot-answer-only, and few-shot-chain-of-thought prompting. The study is not an intervention study with students; it is a model evaluation of LLM performance on subject-specific K-12 questions. Results show that Chinese-dominant models outperform English-dominant models overall, but most models struggle with science subjects and especially mathematics. The paper also reports that few-shot prompting helps modestly overall, while chain-of-thought prompting helps science subjects more than arts subjects but can reduce average performance.

The authors further observe that models sometimes perform worse on primary-school questions than on middle-school questions, suggesting that mastering higher-level knowledge does not guarantee mastery of simpler knowledge. Overall, the paper positions E-EVAL as an evaluation resource for tracking LLM progress in Chinese K-12 education rather than as evidence of educational effectiveness on learners.

finding.finding_summary: The benchmark reports that almost all evaluated LLMs performed poorly on mathematics compared with arts subjects. For example, the best model (Qwen-72B-Chat) achieved 84.0% on science overall and 89.3% on primary-level items, but the paper emphasizes persistent weaknesses in complex mathematics, and even top models failed on a simple primary-school time-comparison question.
finding.measure: Multiple-choice accuracy on mathematics items within the E-EVAL benchmark
finding.study_size: n=4351 total questions; mathematics items are part of the 10 science subjects (subject-level counts reported, but exact math-only total not separately stated in the excerpt)

finding.finding_summary: Models performed substantially better on science when using chain-of-thought prompting than on arts subjects, indicating that structured reasoning helped on science items. However, overall science performance remained below arts performance, and the paper notes that CoT was especially beneficial for challenging science subjects such as mathematics.
finding.measure: Multiple-choice accuracy on science subjects (physics, chemistry, biology, mathematics, and primary science) across zero-shot, few-shot-ao, and few-shot-cot prompting

finding.finding_summary: Across the full benchmark, models generally performed better on arts subjects than on science subjects, with Chinese-dominant models outperforming English-dominant models overall. For instance, Qwen-72B-Chat reached 92.5% on arts versus 84.0% on science, and the paper reports that performance varies by subject area, level, and prompting strategy.
finding.measure: Accuracy across K-12 subject categories, especially arts vs. science and primary/middle/high school levels

finding.finding_summary: The paper uses reasoning-oriented prompting analyses to assess whether models can perform step-by-step reasoning, but the evidence is indirect because the benchmark is still multiple-choice accuracy rather than a direct test of human durable skills. The authors conclude that chain-of-thought can help structured reasoning on science problems, while it can hurt performance overall and on arts items, showing that reasoning benefits are task-dependent.
finding.measure: Accuracy under zero-shot, few-shot-answer-only, and few-shot-chain-of-thought prompting
finding.study_size: n=15 models evaluated on n=4351 benchmark questions

finding.finding_summary: E-EVAL is presented as infrastructure for benchmarking and tracking LLM progress in Chinese K-12 education, with a public leaderboard and a held-out test set to reduce contamination. The paper argues that this benchmark can support future research, model development, and more accurate assessment of LLMs for educational deployment in China.
finding.measure: Benchmark construction and public evaluation infrastructure (leaderboard, hidden test set, data sourcing and curation process)

paper_profiles.title: GPT takes the SAT: Tracing changes in Test Difficulty and Students’ Math Performance
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether SAT Math has become more or less difficult over time and whether observed changes in student SAT Math scores reflect changes in student mathematical performance or changes in the exam itself. The authors argue that inter-temporal comparisons of SAT scores are confounded by changing test difficulty, format changes, and policy changes such as the removal of negative marking and the move to a 1600-point scale.

To address this, the paper introduces a novel “Transformed Control” approach: GPT-4 Turbo is used as a benchmark control group that repeatedly takes sampled SAT Math exams from 2008 to 2023. The model’s year-to-year score changes are treated as a proxy for changes in exam difficulty, while differences between GPT-4 and high school student scores are interpreted as changes in student performance relative to that baseline. The analysis uses bootstrapped exam samples, score concordance tables, linear interpolation, and a Bayesian comparison of means, with national, state-aggregated, and Massachusetts district-level data.

The paper concludes that SAT Math became less difficult over time, with an estimated 71-point decline in rigor from 2008 to 2023. At the same time, student performance declined by an estimated 36 points, yielding a 107-point divergence between student scores and the GPT-4 benchmark. Heterogeneity analyses suggest especially large declines for White students, male students, and, to a lesser extent, Black and Asian students. The authors interpret these patterns as consistent with broader educational and social mechanisms such as test-optional policies, increased screen time, grade inflation, and worsening adolescent mental health.

finding.finding_summary: Using SAT Math score data from 2008 to 2023, the authors estimate that student math performance declined over time relative to a GPT-4 Turbo benchmark that serves as a transformed control. They report a 36-point decline in student performance from 2008 to 2023 and a 107-point divergence between students and the GPT-4 baseline, with statistically significant differences in later years.
finding.measure: SAT Math scaled scores / Average Difference in Scores (ADS) relative to baseline 2008
finding.study_size: national annual averages (2008-2023), state-aggregated averages, and 228 Massachusetts school districts; exact analytic n not reported
finding.effect_size: 36-point decline in student performance; 107-point divergence; 71-point drop in exam rigor

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that SAT Math has become less rigorous over time and that this shift may affect the test’s usefulness in college admissions and institutional sorting. It reports a 71-point decline in SAT Math rigor from 2008 to 2023, suggesting that standardized testing practices and admissions relevance may need reevaluation.
finding.measure: GPT-4-based transformed control estimates of SAT Math difficulty over time; admissions relevance discussion
finding.study_size: 2008-2023 SAT exam archive; exact n not reported

paper_profiles.title: Enhancing Large Language Model Efficiency via Symbolic Compression: A Formal Approach Towards Interpretability
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of token inefficiency and limited interpretability in large language models, especially for code generation and logical reasoning. The authors propose a formal symbolic-compression framework that combines combinatory logic, information-theoretic encoding, context-aware inference, and parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) to reduce redundant token generation while preserving semantic meaning.

The study is framed as an engineering and theoretical contribution rather than a direct educational intervention. Although the author affiliation includes a middle school, the paper’s experiments are conducted on standard software-engineering benchmarks (HumanEval and MBPP), not K–12 learners or classrooms. The proposed method is evaluated against standard prompting and grammar constraints, reporting a 78.3% token compression rate, interpretability improvements, and slightly faster inference time.

Overall, the paper concludes that symbolic compression can improve efficiency and logical traceability in LLM-generated code without increasing computational overhead. It suggests possible future applications in mathematical proof generation and complex logical reasoning, but it does not present evidence on student learning, mathematics achievement, or any K–12 educational outcome.

finding.finding_summary: The proposed symbolic compression framework substantially improved token efficiency in code-generation benchmarks. On HumanEval and MBPP, it achieved a 78.3% compression rate and reduced inference time to 0.9x relative to the standard method, compared with 0% compression for standard prompting and 41% for grammar constraints.
finding.measure: Token compression rate; inference time (relative multiple)

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports improved logical traceability and interpretability, which is relevant to reasoning-oriented durable skills. The proposed method scored 4.2/5 on an expert interpretability rating, versus 2.8 for standard prompting and 3.1 for grammar constraints, and the authors report a 58% improvement in error-localization efficiency.
finding.measure: Expert interpretability rating; error-localization efficiency

paper_profiles.title: Mathematical Capabilities of ChatGPT
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper evaluates the mathematical capabilities of early ChatGPT versions (9-Jan-2023 and 30-Jan-2023) and GPT-4 using a newly created benchmark, GHOSTS, plus a smaller miniGHOSTS subset. The authors argue that existing natural-language math benchmarks were too narrow and mostly elementary, so they designed prompts spanning several dimensions of mathematical work: factual recall, proof completion, proof-based reasoning, symbolic integration, undergraduate/graduate exercises, olympiad-style problems, and search-engine-like retrieval of mathematical definitions and theorems.

The study uses 709 prompts in GHOSTS and 170 prompts in miniGHOSTS, with human experts manually rating responses on a 1–5 scale and assigning error/warning codes. The dataset includes undergraduate- and graduate-level textbook exercises, math.stackexchange excerpts, MATH problems, integration problems, and handcrafted prompts aimed at testing how useful the models might be as assistants to mathematicians. The evaluation is descriptive and benchmark-oriented rather than experimental, and it does not involve K–12 learners or instruction.

The main conclusion is that ChatGPT is inconsistent and generally below graduate-student level on advanced mathematics, though it can be useful for factual lookup and some simpler tasks. GPT-4 performs better than ChatGPT, especially on undergraduate-level material, but still fails on many graduate-level and proof-heavy tasks. The paper emphasizes that GPT-4 can sometimes act as a useful mathematical search engine or knowledge-base interface, but it is not reliable for consistently solving advanced mathematical problems.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports mixed mathematical performance across 709 GHOSTS prompts and 170 miniGHOSTS prompts. ChatGPT averaged 3.20 (SD=1.23) on the 9-Jan version and 3.29 (SD=1.28) on the 30-Jan version, while GPT-4 averaged 4.15 (SD=1.12) on miniGHOSTS. The models did better on factual recall and some undergraduate-level tasks, but performed poorly on proof-based, olympiad-style, and graduate-level questions; the authors conclude the systems remain below graduate-student level overall.
finding.measure: Human-rated accuracy/quality on mathematics prompts (1–5 rating scale) across proof, computation, retrieval, and problem-solving tasks
finding.study_size: n=709 prompts (GHOSTS); n=170 prompts (miniGHOSTS); 1636 human ratings

finding.finding_summary: The benchmark includes proof completion, theorem proof, and problem-solving tasks that require reasoning, gap filling, and cross-domain thinking, which are closely related to durable skills such as critical thinking and metacognition. Performance was strong only on some gap-filling or factual tasks, but weak on proof-heavy and olympiad-style reasoning, indicating inconsistent higher-order reasoning rather than robust transferable skill use.
finding.measure: Human ratings on proof completion, theorem proof, and olympiad-style reasoning prompts
finding.study_size: n=709 prompts (subset of GHOSTS tasks spanning reasoning-oriented subdatasets)

finding.finding_summary: The authors find that ChatGPT can function as a mathematical assistant for querying facts, acting like a search engine or knowledge base interface, and may speed up lookup tasks in mathematicians’ workflows. This is a productivity-oriented benefit, though it is limited to factual retrieval and simple assistance rather than reliable problem solving.
finding.measure: Qualitative assessment of usefulness as a mathematical assistant / search engine / knowledge base interface

paper_profiles.title: Confucius3-Math: A Lightweight High-Performance Reasoning LLM for Chinese K-12 Mathematics Learning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper presents Confucius3-Math, a 14B-parameter open-source reasoning large language model designed specifically for Chinese K–12 mathematics learning. The paper addresses the problem that general-purpose reasoning LLMs, while strong on broad math benchmarks, often underperform on K–12 math tasks and are too costly to deploy widely in educational settings.

The authors describe a post-training pipeline built primarily on reinforcement learning, using a combination of open-source math datasets and proprietary Chinese K–12 math problems drawn from their business operations. They also introduce three training innovations: Targeted Entropy Regularization, Policy-Specific Hardness Weighting, and Recent Sample Recovery, all intended to stabilize RL, improve sample efficiency, and boost reasoning performance. The work is framed as a model-development and evaluation report rather than an educational intervention study.

Evaluation is conducted on internal and public math benchmarks, including CK12-MATH, GAOKAO-Bench (Math), MathBench (K12), CMATH, MATH500, AIME24, and AIME25. Confucius3-Math is reported to outperform several strong baselines, including DeepSeek-R1 on the internal CK12-MATH benchmark by 3.5 points and to show large gains over its base model across all benchmarks. The paper also emphasizes deployment efficiency, reporting lower inference cost and higher throughput than DeepSeek-R1, but it does not measure student learning outcomes, classroom use, or causal effects on learners.

finding.finding_summary: Confucius3-Math achieved strong performance on multiple math benchmarks relevant to Chinese K-12 education. On the internal CK12-MATH benchmark (n=500), it scored 96.24%, outperforming DeepSeek-R1 by 3.5 points and its base model DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-14B by 13.38 points; it also posted large gains on AIME25 (+26.98 over the base model).
finding.measure: Accuracy / pass@1 on Chinese K-12 and competition mathematics benchmarks (CK12-MATH, GAOKAO-Bench Math, MathBench K12, CMATH, MATH500, AIME24, AIME25)
finding.study_size: n=500 for CK12-MATH; other benchmark sizes not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The model was designed and evaluated for deployment efficiency, with a major emphasis on low-cost inference and high throughput. The paper reports a peak total throughput of 31,994 tokens/s on H800 hardware and states this is a 15.8× speedup over DeepSeek-R1; it also reports low inference cost of $0.15 per million tokens under full load.
finding.measure: Inference throughput (tokens/s) and estimated inference cost

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that a low-cost, open-source, high-performing K-12 math LLM could help broaden access to educational AI and reduce inequities associated with expensive model access. However, these are projected system-level implications rather than empirically tested institutional outcomes; no causal evaluation of policy, adoption, or equity effects is reported.
finding.measure: Projected accessibility, openness, and cost implications of model deployment

paper_profiles.title: Using Large Language Models to Assess Tutors’ Performance in Reacting to Students Making Math Errors
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of Machine Learning Research (AAAI 2024 Workshop AI4ED)
paper_profiles.population: Middle School (6th-8th grade) students; college student tutors
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether large language models can reliably evaluate human tutors’ performance when tutors respond to middle school students who make math errors. The authors focus on a specific tutoring skill taught in a scenario-based lesson, “Reacting to Errors,” which emphasizes responding to mistakes in a process-focused, motivating, indirect, immediate, and accurate way rather than directly pointing out errors.

To test this, the authors first used GPT-4 to generate synthetic tutoring dialogues and calibrate human annotation of five response criteria. They then evaluated 50 real-world tutoring dialogues from remote online tutoring sessions involving college-student tutors working with 6th-8th grade students from two schools. GPT-3.5-Turbo and GPT-4 were prompted to score each dialogue on whether the student made an error and whether the tutor met each of the five criteria.

Results show both models were reasonably good at judging tutor responses, especially the immediate and accurate criteria, but both struggled to determine when a student had actually made an error. GPT-4 performed slightly better than GPT-3.5-Turbo across criteria and was more willing to infer student uncertainty as an error. The paper concludes that GPT-3.5-Turbo may be sufficiently cost-effective for scalable dialogue assessment, but the models are not yet reliable enough to stand alone for evaluating tutoring skill or learning transfer after training.

finding.finding_summary: The study found that GPT-3.5-Turbo and GPT-4 can assess tutor responses to student math errors with useful accuracy, suggesting potential for automating tutor evaluation. On 50 real-life tutoring dialogues, GPT-4 achieved F1 scores of 0.64, 0.73, 0.63, 0.93, and 0.95 for process-focused, motivating, indirect, immediate, and accurate criteria, respectively, while GPT-3.5-Turbo achieved 0.55, 0.72, 0.61, 0.80, and 0.80.
finding.measure: Precision, recall, and F1 scores for automated scoring of tutor dialogue criteria; dialogue classification accuracy for whether a student made an error
finding.std_deviation: SD=45.9 words per synthetic dialogue; SD=2.7 utterances per synthetic dialogue

paper_profiles.title: Elementary Math Word Problem Generation using Large Language Models
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of automatically generating elementary mathematics word problems (MWPs) with large language models (LLMs). The authors argue that manually creating grade-appropriate MWPs is time-consuming, and that prior generation systems often require extra inputs such as seeds or equations and do not reliably control grade level, question type, solvability, or diversity.

To address this, the authors build an MWP generation system that takes only three inputs: the number of problems, grade, and question type. They compare open-source LLMs (Llama-2, Mistral, Zephyr), test multiple prompt patterns, tune decoding parameters for diversity, and then improve outputs with QLoRA fine-tuning, few-shot prompting, preference optimization (DPO/KTO/CPO), and a secondary LLM used to filter unsolvable problems. They also create two datasets: a 4K curriculum-aligned MWP dataset with grade and section labels (Mathwizards), and a 1005-item preference dataset with accepted/rejected examples for selected grade-section combinations.

The evaluation combines human annotation and LLM-based judging (G-Eval), with 312 MWPs used for correlation analysis and 8,561 questions reviewed during the broader evaluation. Results show that the best system improves solvability, grammatical quality, and diversity, but still struggles to consistently satisfy grade and section requirements. The authors conclude that generative AI can produce high-quality elementary MWPs, but curriculum alignment remains the main challenge, motivating future work on retrieval-augmented generation and curriculum-aware prompting.

finding.finding_summary: The system generated math word problems intended for elementary grades, and human/LLM evaluation showed strong surface quality and solvability but persistent weakness in grade and section alignment. The best configuration improved average evaluation accuracy to 92.66% (5-shot fine-tuned Llama-2) and further to 92.28% after solvability filtering, but the paper does not report downstream student achievement or learning gains.
finding.measure: Quality of generated math word problems; solvability, realism, grade relevance, section relevance, diversity (Self-BLEU, Jaccard)
finding.study_size: n=312 for correlation study; 8,561 questions reviewed overall; 4K Mathwizards corpus created

paper_profiles.title: EZYer: A simulacrum of high school with generative agent
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper presents EZYer, a generative-agent system designed to support high school mathematics instruction by automatically producing teaching materials, LaTeX Beamer courseware, in-class interaction scripts, and summarized notes. The authors frame EZYer as addressing common limitations of current educational tools, including incomplete service, weak interactivity, poor quality control, and difficulty generating mathematically formatted instructional content.

The system has three main components: a Teacher Module that turns uploaded text or textbook content into structured math teaching materials and exercises, a Student Module that simulates classroom dialogue through five roles (Teacher, Assistant, Top Student, Struggling Student, and Note Taker), and a Controller that filters content and checks quality before output. The evaluation is not a learner-outcome study; instead, the paper assesses 100 generated Beamer files and 100 Notes files using five large language models as judges across five dimensions: content accuracy, knowledge coverage, usability, formatting correctness, and visual design/appeal.

Results show consistently high ratings for the generated outputs, especially for content accuracy and knowledge coverage. The authors report average scores around 4.74 for Beamer and 4.70 for Notes on those dimensions, with somewhat lower scores for usability and visual design. The paper concludes that EZYer has promising application potential for high school mathematics teaching, but it also acknowledges limitations such as restricted subject scope, generation latency, and the absence of human evaluation.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that EZYer-generated Beamer courseware and notes were judged to be high quality for high school mathematics content. Across 100 generated Beamer documents and 100 Notes documents, five LLM evaluators gave high average scores for content accuracy and knowledge coverage, with mean scores of 4.74 for Beamer and 4.70 for Notes on these dimensions, suggesting the system can generate mathematically relevant instructional materials.
finding.measure: LLM-rated quality of generated high school mathematics Beamer files and Notes across content accuracy and knowledge coverage
finding.study_size: n=100 Beamer files; n=100 Notes files

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT for Good? On Opportunities and Challenges of Large Language Models for Education
paper_profiles.population: All education levels (including elementary, secondary, tertiary, and professional development); not a primary K-12 empirical sample
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This position paper examines the potential opportunities and risks of large language models, especially ChatGPT, for education. Rather than testing a specific intervention, it synthesizes early applications and conceptual arguments about how LLMs could support learning, teaching, assessment, and educational innovation, while also identifying major concerns such as bias, plagiarism, overreliance, privacy, sustainability, and unequal access.

The paper discusses use cases for learners and teachers across schooling levels, including elementary, secondary, university, and professional learning. Examples include generating practice questions, quizzes, feedback, summaries, tutoring dialogue, lesson-planning support, and automated assessment. The authors emphasize that LLMs may improve personalization, engagement, and efficiency, but only if used with strong human oversight, critical thinking safeguards, and clear institutional policies.

Because this is a position paper rather than an empirical study, it does not report primary outcome data or effect sizes. Its main contribution is a framework of opportunities, risks, and mitigation strategies for responsible educational use of LLMs, including the need for further research before broad adoption in classrooms.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that large language models can reduce teacher workload and increase efficiency in assessment, lesson planning, and content creation. It cites examples such as semi-automated grading, generation of quizzes, exercises, summaries, and feedback, but reports no original empirical effect estimates.
finding.measure: Conceptual discussion of teacher workload, grading efficiency, and automated content generation

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests LLMs could support critical thinking, problem-solving, collaboration, and metacognitive activities when used appropriately, but also warns that overreliance may weaken these same skills. No direct empirical measurement is reported; the claims are theoretical and based on cited examples.
finding.measure: Conceptual discussion of critical thinking, problem-solving, and collaboration

finding.finding_summary: The authors describe LLMs as potentially improving student engagement, curiosity, and participation, including through curiosity-prompting and conversational support. However, the paper does not present original outcome data; the claims are framed as opportunities and supported by cited prior work.
finding.measure: Conceptual discussion of engagement, curiosity, and participation

finding.finding_summary: A central focus of the paper is the institutional and policy implications of deploying LLMs in education, including bias, privacy, copyright, sustainability, fair access, and the need for governance and human oversight. The paper does not evaluate policy outcomes empirically, but it strongly centers system-level implications and mitigation strategies.
finding.measure: Conceptual discussion of governance, policy, privacy, fairness, and institutional implementation

paper_profiles.title: Using Large Language Models to Assess Tutors’ Performance in Reacting to Students Making Math Errors
paper_profiles.venue: AAAI 2024 Workshop AI4ED / Proceedings of Machine Learning Research
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether large language models can accurately evaluate human tutors’ responses when students make math errors. The motivation is practical: expert human coding of tutor moves is slow and costly, so the authors explore whether GPT-3.5-Turbo and GPT-4 can score tutoring dialogue on five pedagogical criteria associated with effective error response: process-focused, motivating, indirect, immediate, and accurate.

The study analyzes 50 real-life remote tutoring dialogues involving college-student tutors and middle school students in grades 6–8. Two human annotators first coded the dialogues, and the LLMs were then prompted to score the same transcripts. The paper reports that both models performed reasonably well on easier criteria like immediate and accurate, but were weaker on process-focused and indirect responses. GPT-4 slightly outperformed GPT-3.5-Turbo overall, but both models struggled to reliably determine whether a student had actually made an error; GPT-4 in particular tended to infer errors from uncertainty more often than human raters.

The authors conclude that LLMs may be useful as scalable assistants for tutor assessment, especially for straightforward scoring tasks, but are not yet sufficient as stand-alone evaluators of nuanced tutoring behavior. They also note important limitations: a small sample of dialogues, fragmented real-world transcripts, and the need to test whether improvements in tutor scoring can support learning transfer after tutor training.

finding.finding_summary: Using GPT-3.5-Turbo and GPT-4 to score tutor dialogue was presented as a scalable alternative to time-consuming human evaluation. Both models achieved relatively strong performance on some criteria, especially immediate and accurate (GPT-3.5-Turbo F1=0.80 for both; GPT-4 F1=0.93 and 0.95), suggesting potential efficiency gains for tutor assessment workflows.
finding.measure: LLM scoring accuracy / F1 on tutor-response criteria compared with human graders

finding.finding_summary: The paper is centered on math tutoring dialogues and on identifying student math errors, but it does not measure student learning outcomes directly. It evaluates whether LLMs can judge tutor responses to math mistakes; performance was decent on criteria tied to math tutoring quality, but the models struggled to detect when a student actually made an error, with GPT-3.5-Turbo correctly identifying no-error dialogues 54% of the time and GPT-4 63% of the time.
finding.measure: Error detection and criterion scoring in math tutoring transcripts
finding.std_deviation: SD=45.9 words per dialogue; SD=2.7 utterances per dialogue

finding.finding_summary: A central construct in the paper is tutor- and student-level response to errors, including indirectness, process focus, and guidance toward self-correction, which are metacognitive/strategic skills rather than direct achievement outcomes. The LLMs showed moderate-to-strong agreement with human raters on several of these nuanced criteria, especially immediate and accurate scoring, but weaker performance on process-focused and indirect criteria.
finding.measure: Scoring of pedagogical criteria associated with self-correction and guided problem solving

finding.finding_summary: The tutoring criteria assessed include motivating language, effort praise, and avoiding discouraging feedback, which are closely related to student persistence and confidence. GPT-3.5-Turbo achieved F1=0.72 and GPT-4 achieved F1=0.73 on the motivating criterion, indicating fairly good detection of this affective tutoring move, though the study does not measure student motivation directly.
finding.measure: Motivating-feedback classification in tutoring dialogue

paper_profiles.title: GPT-4 as a Homework Tutor can Improve Student Engagement and Learning Outcomes
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether GPT-4 can replace or augment traditional homework in a real high-school setting while improving both learning and student experience. The authors argue that homework is most effective when students receive timely feedback and follow-up questions, and they propose a prompting strategy that turns GPT-4 into an interactive homework tutor with minimal teacher preparation.

The intervention was tested in a randomized controlled trial in four classes at an Italian technical institute. Students in the treatment group completed weekly English homework through GPT-4 chats, while control students completed the teacher’s usual homework. The study included 75 students across third- and fifth-year classes, with pre/post tests, weekly questionnaires, and final surveys used to measure learning and engagement.

The main findings are mixed but generally positive. Overall learning gains favored the treatment group modestly, with a small non-significant overall effect (d=0.251, p=0.314), and a larger marginally significant gain in the third-year cohort (d=0.603, p=0.087) but essentially no effect in the fifth-year cohort (d=-0.004, p=0.991). Students in the treatment condition also reported higher engagement and more positive homework experiences, and most said they wanted to keep using the tutor. The authors report very low observed hallucination/error rates and no evidence that benefits were limited to stronger students; they conclude that GPT-4 homework tutoring can improve engagement and may improve learning under some conditions, though the academic gains were modest in this short intervention.

finding.finding_summary: The intervention was evaluated on English-learning outcomes, with the main reported academic gain being improved grammar performance. Across all students, the learning gain difference favored the GPT-4 group modestly (Cohen’s d=0.251, p=0.314), and the third-year cohort showed a larger marginally significant benefit (d=0.603, p=0.087) on pre/post test scores. The fifth-year cohort showed essentially no difference (d=-0.004, p=0.991).
finding.measure: Pre-test and post-test multiple-choice English test scores; grammar learning gain
finding.effect_size: d=0.251 overall; d=0.603 third year; d=-0.004 fifth year

finding.finding_summary: Students in the GPT-4 condition reported better homework experiences and higher engagement. Weekly questionnaire ratings were higher for interestingness (d=0.593, p=0.011) and level of resources/support (d=0.586, p=0.015), while usefulness (d=0.356, p=0.125) and comprehensiveness (d=0.281, p=0.234) were not statistically significant. In the final survey, 32/35 treatment respondents said the tutor helped them, and 32/35 wanted to continue using it.
finding.measure: Weekly and final questionnaire ratings of interestingness, usefulness, comprehensiveness, perceived support/resources, and willingness to continue using the tutor
finding.study_size: n=75 total; questionnaire subsamples varied (e.g., 35 treatment respondents in final survey)
finding.effect_size: d=0.593 interestingness; d=0.586 level_of_resources; d=0.356 usefulness; d=0.281 comprehensiveness

finding.finding_summary: The system was designed to reduce teacher preparation burden by turning ordinary homework into an interactive GPT-4 tutoring workflow with minimal extra content preparation. The paper reports that the teacher initially faced a learning curve but, in post-study feedback, believed the workflow would reduce workload somewhat in the long term; however, this outcome was not directly measured with a formal workload instrument. The strongest evidence is descriptive rather than experimental.
finding.measure: Teacher post-study feedback about workload; implementation requirements for homework preparation

paper_profiles.title: Tutor CoPilot: A Human-AI Approach for Scaling Real-Time Expertise
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether a generative-AI system can improve live K-12 tutoring by giving novice tutors real-time, expert-like guidance. The core problem is that tutoring quality depends heavily on instructional expertise, but high-quality training and coaching are expensive and hard to scale, especially in under-resourced settings.

The authors introduce Tutor CoPilot, a human-AI system embedded in a virtual tutoring platform. When activated, it uses de-identified live chat context, lesson topic, and a selected pedagogical strategy to generate suggestions for tutors, with the goal of helping them respond more effectively in the moment. The system is built on a prior method (Bridge) that distills expert educator reasoning from think-aloud data into language-model prompts.

The study is a preregistered randomized controlled trial involving about 900 tutors and 1,800 K-12 students from historically under-served communities in a large southern U.S. school district. The tutoring context was in-school, virtual math tutoring for grades 3-8, delivered through FEV Tutor. Tutors were randomly assigned to either have access to Tutor CoPilot or to tutor as usual.

The main finding is that access to Tutor CoPilot improved proximal math learning outcomes: students in the treatment group were 4 percentage points more likely to pass exit tickets than control students (62% to 66%, p<0.01). Benefits were larger for students assigned to lower-rated or less-experienced tutors, with improvements of up to 9 percentage points. The system also shifted tutor behavior toward more high-quality instructional strategies and away from answer-giving, suggesting a mechanism for the learning gains. However, the paper reports no statistically significant improvement on end-of-year math test scores, likely because the intervention was short and student exposure was limited.

finding.finding_summary: In a preregistered RCT with 4,136 tutoring sessions involving 1,800 K-12 students and 900 tutors (initial assignment), students whose tutors had access to Tutor CoPilot were 4 percentage points more likely to pass their math exit tickets than control students (62% to 66%, p<0.01). The authors also report a smaller positive effect on exit-ticket attempts (2 p.p., p<0.1) and conditional passing (3 p.p., p<0.01), but no statistically significant improvement on end-of-year math test scores is reported in the paper.
finding.measure: Math tutoring exit-ticket pass rate; exit-ticket attempt rate; conditional exit-ticket pass rate; end-of-year math test scores
finding.study_size: n=4136 sessions (1,800 students; 900 tutors initially assigned)
finding.effect_size: 4 percentage points (exit-ticket pass rate); 2 p.p. attempt; 3 p.p. conditional pass

finding.finding_summary: The treatment had no significant effects on student self-report survey outcomes, but the direction of several measures was slightly positive. On 5-point survey items about tutor caring, confidence in learning math, and preference for understanding over memorization, treatment effects ranged from -0.004 to 0.03 and were not statistically significant (n=1,931 to 1,952 survey responses).
finding.measure: Student post-session survey responses (e.g., tutor caring, confidence in learning math, preference for understanding over memorization)

finding.finding_summary: Tutor CoPilot was associated with more efficient and higher-quality tutoring language. Using classifiers over 550,000+ messages, the authors found treatment tutors were significantly more likely to use strategies that fostered understanding, such as prompting explanation and asking guiding questions, and less likely to give away answers or rely on generic encouragement. The paper also estimates the system cost at about $20 per tutor annually based on study usage.
finding.measure: Tutor chat language / pedagogical strategy usage; estimated annual cost per tutor
finding.study_size: n=550,000+ messages; 2,000+ uses of Tutor CoPilot
finding.effect_size: about 2 standard deviations more frequent log-odds for some high-quality strategies; $20 per tutor annually

finding.finding_summary: The paper provides evidence that Tutor CoPilot improved strategy use linked to deeper learning and comprehension, which the authors frame as fostering critical thinking and student understanding. Specifically, treatment tutors were more likely to prompt students to explain their reasoning and ask questions to guide thinking, while control tutors were more likely to give away the answer or solution strategy (F1 for strategy classifiers ranged from 0.65 to 0.90).
finding.measure: Classified pedagogical strategies in tutor-student dialogue (e.g., prompt explanation, ask guiding questions, give away answer)
finding.study_size: n=550,000+ messages; 3,000 labeled messages for classifier training
finding.effect_size: approximately 2 standard deviations more frequent log-odds for key high-quality strategies

paper_profiles.title: Combining Large Language Models with Tutoring System Intelligence: A Case Study in Caregiver Homework Support
paper_profiles.venue: LAK 2025 (The 15th International Learning Analytics and Knowledge Conference)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how a large language model (Llama 3) can be combined with the instructional intelligence of an intelligent tutoring system to generate conversational recommendations for caregivers supporting middle-school students during math homework. The authors developed the Caregiver Conversational Support Tool (CCST), which uses live tutoring-system context such as correctness, hint use, prior chat messages, and suggested next steps to generate personalized message recommendations for caregivers.

The study has two main parts. First, the authors conducted prompt engineering experiments to see how different prompt designs affected the quality and contextual relevance of generated caregiver messages. They found that prompts combining tutoring best practices with real-time problem-solving context produced the most desirable recommendations, especially when the LLM was given examples of effective tutoring dialogue and explicit guidance on how to use tutoring-system data.

Second, they ran a qualitative prototyping study with ten middle-school caregivers recruited through a university summer program and related outreach channels. Caregivers used the CCST in simulated homework-support sessions and then participated in semi-structured interviews and annotation activities. The findings showed that caregivers preferred content-level instructional support over motivational support, especially messages that prompted students to explain their thinking and reveal metacognitive processes. They also valued contextualization based on student errors and hint use, though they wanted shorter, faster, and more natural-sounding messages.

Overall, the paper concludes that LLMs can be made more useful for hybrid tutoring if they are grounded in tutoring-system data and pedagogical guidance, but that the current evidence is design-oriented and perceptual rather than outcome-based. The study contributes a prototype and qualitative insights about caregiver needs rather than direct measures of student learning.

finding.finding_summary: Caregivers reported that the system was most valuable when it prompted students to explain their thinking and self-explain during equation solving, which they viewed as helping them understand their child’s reasoning and locate mistakes. In the qualitative sample of ten caregivers (n=10), these metacognitive prompts were preferred over purely motivational messages, but the study did not report quantitative learning gains.
finding.measure: Caregiver interview and annotation feedback on message recommendations that prompted metacognition/self-explanation

finding.finding_summary: The paper focuses on math equation-solving support in a middle-school intelligent tutoring system and shows that context-aware LLM prompts could generate more relevant instructional recommendations for algebra practice. Evidence is qualitative: caregivers valued messages tied to equations, hint use, error status, and suggested next steps, but no student math achievement outcome was measured.
finding.measure: Qualitative evaluation of LLM-generated support for equation-solving practice in an ITS

finding.finding_summary: Caregivers preferred some motivational and encouraging messages, and the paper reports that the system’s supportive tone was often viewed as positive and reassuring, though several caregivers found such messages less useful than content-level help. The study did not quantify changes in engagement or motivation, but it suggests that carefully worded encouragement may support confidence during homework help.
finding.measure: Caregiver perceptions of motivational versus content-level support; tone/encouragement feedback

finding.finding_summary: The study reports that the CCST could generate recommendations in real time, but latency was a concern: average message generation was about 25 seconds, and some caregivers felt the system was too slow for live homework support. At the same time, others judged the output fast enough and usable, so the operational result was mixed rather than uniformly positive.
finding.measure: Caregiver feedback on latency and responsiveness of generated message recommendations

paper_profiles.title: Elementary School Students’ and Teachers’ Perceptions Towards Creative Mathematical Writing with Generative AI
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how elementary students and teachers perceived a generative AI-powered platform for creative mathematical writing. The authors are interested in whether AI can support young learners in generating and revising math stories, understanding math concepts, and engaging more deeply and creatively with mathematics, while also identifying classroom-level challenges and design implications.

The study implemented a GenAI-based learning tool built with GPT-4 and DALL·E 3 in six fifth-grade classrooms across two U.S. schools. Students worked through a structured three-step routine: Ask (analyze a math story), Represent (visually model ideas), and Transform (co-create and revise a culturally relevant math story with AI). Data came from focus-group interviews with 10 students, interviews with all six teachers, open-ended survey responses, and classroom observation notes, and were analyzed through inductive and deductive thematic analysis.

Findings were organized into six themes. Perceived benefits included supporting creativity in math, strengthening mathematical understanding, promoting AI literacy, and improving affective outcomes such as interest, curiosity, and ownership. Perceived challenges included weak student critical evaluation of AI output, limited student competence in generating coherent prompts/stories, AI being perceived as "too perfect," lack of pedagogical feedback, reduced autonomy, weak social connection, and limited communication modes. The paper is qualitative and does not report causal achievement effects; its main contribution is design and implementation insight for GenAI-supported math learning in elementary classrooms.

finding.finding_summary: Students and teachers perceived that GenAI-supported creative mathematical writing helped students understand math problems, represent mathematical ideas visually, and uncover misconceptions. At the same time, some students struggled to formulate coherent math stories and align their ideas with the system’s expectations, so the reported outcome was beneficial but not uniformly positive.
finding.measure: Student and teacher perceptions from interviews, open-ended surveys, and classroom observations about mathematical understanding, problem representation, and misconception detection

finding.finding_summary: The paper found that GenAI-supported mathematical creative writing was perceived to improve students’ writing-related creativity, including divergent thinking, original story creation, and revising AI-generated drafts into more coherent stories. Because the evidence is qualitative, no standardized writing outcome or effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Perceptions of creative writing quality, originality, and revision processes in math-story writing tasks

finding.finding_summary: Participants perceived that working with GenAI made math more interesting, enjoyable, and curiosity-provoking, and increased students’ sense of ownership over their learning. Thematic evidence suggests stronger engagement and motivation, but the study did not report quantitative attitudinal measures.
finding.measure: Perceived interest, curiosity, enjoyment, and ownership of learning from interviews and survey responses

finding.finding_summary: The study reported that GenAI-supported writing promoted AI literacy and prompt-engineering skills, including iterative prompting, evaluating AI strengths and weaknesses, and refining requests. It also suggested some gains in flexible and convergent thinking, but these were based on perceptions rather than direct performance measures.
finding.measure: Perceptions of prompt engineering, AI literacy, divergent/convergent thinking, and flexible thinking

paper_profiles.title: Confucius3-Math: A Lightweight High-Performance Reasoning LLM for Chinese K-12 Mathematics Learning
paper_profiles.population: K-12 (Chinese primary, middle, and high school; benchmarks and internal user queries)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper presents Confucius3-Math, a 14B-parameter open-source reasoning language model designed specifically for Chinese K-12 mathematics. The authors’ goal is not to test a classroom intervention, but to develop a low-cost, high-accuracy math model that can serve students and educators in real educational settings. They argue that existing strong reasoning LLMs are often too expensive, too large for practical deployment, or not sufficiently aligned to Chinese K-12 math tasks.

The paper describes the model-development pipeline in detail, including data curation from open-source math corpora and proprietary K-12 math questions, a three-stage pure reinforcement-learning training process, reward modeling, and several algorithmic modifications such as Targeted Entropy Regularization, Policy-Specific Hardness Weighting, and Recent Sample Recovery. The reported evaluation focuses on benchmark accuracy on Chinese K-12 math datasets (CK12-MATH, GAOKAO-Bench Math, MathBench K12, CMATH) and competition-style datasets (MATH500, AIME24, AIME25), plus deployment throughput and training cost.

The main conclusion is that Confucius3-Math achieves strong benchmark performance relative to several open models, including its own base model and DeepSeek-R1, while also being much cheaper to train and deploy. However, the paper does not report a randomized, quasi-experimental, or classroom study of student learning outcomes; the evidence is model-performance benchmarking rather than direct evidence of effects on K-12 learners. As a result, it supports feasibility and technical performance claims, but not durable achievement impacts in students.

finding.finding_summary: Confucius3-Math outperformed the comparison models on the paper’s K-12 math benchmarks. On CK12-MATH (n=500 internal user-query problems), it reached 96.24% accuracy, exceeding DeepSeek-R1 by 3.50 points and its base model by 13.38 points; it also improved on GAOKAO-Bench (Math), MathBench (K12), and CMATH, with gains up to 26.98 points on AIME25 versus the base model.
finding.measure: Accuracy on Chinese K-12 mathematics benchmarks and competition-style math benchmarks (CK12-MATH, GAOKAO-Bench Math, MathBench K12, CMATH, MATH500, AIME24, AIME25)
finding.study_size: n=500 for CK12-MATH; other benchmark sizes not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports substantially better deployment efficiency and lower cost than DeepSeek-R1. Confucius3-Math achieved up to 31,994 tokens/s total throughput at QPS=4 on H800 hardware, described as a 15.8× speedup over DeepSeek-R1, and could run on a single RTX 4090D where DeepSeek-R1 could not. Training cost was reported as $26K for 13,109 GPU hours.
finding.measure: Inference throughput (tokens/s) and training cost

paper_profiles.title: Integration of AI in STEM Education – Addressing Ethical Challenges in K-12 Settings
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the ethical, pedagogical, and implementation challenges of integrating artificial intelligence into K-12 STEM education. Rather than testing a specific AI intervention, it synthesizes recent literature to examine how AI tools such as intelligent tutoring systems, automated assessment, predictive analytics, and surveillance technologies may affect learning, equity, privacy, and teacher practice.

The paper uses a critical conceptual review and synthesis of scholarship from 2016-2025, alongside policy and framework documents. It argues that AI in K-12 STEM has potential benefits for personalization, feedback, and efficiency, but that these benefits are constrained by algorithmic bias, privacy risks, limited transparency, and unequal access. The authors propose a three-phased implementation roadmap and a tiered professional development model grounded in TPACK and critical algorithmic literacy to support responsible AI adoption.

The paper is not an empirical evaluation of student learning outcomes; instead, it offers an equity-centered conceptual framework for AI integration in STEM classrooms. Its main conclusion is that AI should be introduced gradually, with strong teacher preparation, bias auditing, low-resource adaptation strategies, and policy alignment to ensure that AI supports rather than undermines human-centered, equitable education.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that AI integration in K-12 STEM could improve personalization, feedback, and operational efficiency, but it may also amplify inequities, privacy violations, and opaque decision-making. It proposes a phased roadmap and governance safeguards (e.g., mandatory bias audits, student data governance, policy alignment) rather than reporting new outcome data.
finding.measure: conceptual synthesis of policy, governance, and implementation issues

finding.finding_summary: The paper consistently frames AI tools such as automated assessment and intelligent tutoring systems as potentially reducing teacher workload through immediate feedback, scalable scoring, and targeted intervention support. No new empirical estimate is reported; the claim is based on literature synthesis and illustrative references.
finding.measure: teacher workload, assessment efficiency, scalability of feedback

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests AI ethics activities and project-based learning can strengthen critical thinking, ethical reasoning, and digital citizenship, but it also warns that over-reliance on AI may narrow problem-solving and limit creative thinking. These claims are synthesized from prior studies and examples rather than newly measured in this paper.
finding.measure: critical thinking, ethical reasoning, digital citizenship, problem-solving

paper_profiles.title: 3DG: A Framework for Using Generative AI for Handling Sparse Learner Performance Data From Intelligent Tutoring Systems
paper_profiles.venue: LAK'24: International Workshop on Generative AI for Learning Analytics (GenAI-LA)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of sparse learner performance data in intelligent tutoring systems (ITSs), where missing or limited attempts and question responses can weaken learner modeling and knowledge tracing. The authors propose 3DG (3-Dimensional tensor for Densification and Generation), a framework that first imputes missing performance values using tensor factorization and then augments data using generative models.

The study is evaluated on a dataset from the AutoTutor ITS reading-comprehension lessons developed for the Center for the Study of Adult Literacy (CSAL), involving 118 adult participants. The paper compares GAN- and GPT-4-based simulation approaches for generating learner-performance data after clustering learners into learning-pattern groups using K-means++ and fitting power-law learning curves. Results suggest that tensor completion can effectively densify sparse performance tensors, and that GAN produces more reliable simulated distributions than GPT-4 in this setting.

Overall, the paper is primarily a methodological/technical contribution to educational data simulation rather than a student-outcome evaluation. It does not test a classroom intervention on learning gains or other educational outcomes; instead, it focuses on improving the quality and scalability of learner-performance data for downstream ITS modeling and personalized instruction research. The empirical comparisons are limited to properties of the generated data and tensor-completion behavior.

finding.finding_summary: The framework was designed to improve the efficiency of handling sparse learner-performance data in ITSs by imputing missing values and generating scalable synthetic samples. On the CSAL AutoTutor dataset (n=118), tensor completion reduced sparsity from 80%–85% missingness to a denser tensor, and the authors report that GAN-based simulation produced more reliable synthetic distributions than GPT-4 for this data-setting.
finding.measure: Tensor completion / data densification quality; simulated-data reliability and distributional fit

paper_profiles.title: Tinkering in Primary School: From Episode to Science Practice
paper_profiles.venue: The Primary School as a Playful Space
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This chapter examines whether and how tinkering can be integrated into primary school classrooms as a constructionist practice that supports science learning. The authors are interested in a broader pedagogical problem: open-ended tinkering is engaging and generative, but teachers often struggle to connect it to curricular objectives and to handle the scientific questions that emerge from students’ exploration.

The paper presents the TIDE model (Tinkering, Ideas generation, Disciplinary connection, Exploration), developed to help teachers bridge open exploration with structured classroom learning. The main implementation, Oﬃcina della Luce, ran from September 2021 to September 2022 in four primary schools in Bologna, involving 13 classrooms, 24 teachers, and approximately 300 students. Teachers received professional development, access to a digital resource library, and documentation tools including fishbowl discussions; the project was later compressed because of pandemic disruptions.

The evidence base is primarily qualitative and descriptive, drawing on questionnaires completed by 20 teachers, coded teacher responses, and analysis of fishbowl documentation. The authors conclude that tinkering can strongly re-engage students who are often less successful in conventional school settings, while also revealing vulnerabilities among some high-achieving students. At the same time, the study finds that teachers frequently feel unprepared to follow up on authentic scientific questions and often choose humanities or expressive follow-up activities rather than disciplinary science work. The chapter argues that future iterations of TIDE should include stronger disciplinary support and better longitudinal documentation of student learning.

finding.finding_summary: Tinkering reliably surfaced authentic scientific questions and supported classroom inquiry, especially around light and color, but teachers often could not fully develop those questions into disciplinary science lessons. In the fishbowl example, students generated a substantial question about producing white light with filters, but the teacher reported feeling unable to answer it and left it unresolved; the authors conclude that future implementations need stronger disciplinary support.
finding.measure: Teacher-reported observations from questionnaires and fishbowl documentation; emergence and follow-through of student scientific questions
finding.study_size: n=20 teachers (questionnaire); 1 documented fishbowl protocol; approximately 300 students in the broader project

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that tinkering increased student engagement, participation, enthusiasm, and willingness to collaborate, especially for students typically seen as disengaged or difficult in conventional instruction. In the questionnaire, 70% of teachers reported unexpected or partially expected behavior, noting high motivation, sustained attention, and stronger peer interaction during the workshops.
finding.measure: Teacher questionnaire responses about engagement, participation, motivation, and classroom behavior

finding.finding_summary: The chapter suggests that tinkering fostered collaboration, self-reflection, process focus, and problem solving, with teachers noting that students learned to manage frustration and work more effectively in pairs or groups. Some aligned students became more relaxed about mistakes and more focused on reasoning, indicating gains in collaboration and perseverance rather than immediate content mastery.
finding.measure: Teacher descriptions coded into themes for aligned and non-aligned students; questionnaire responses

paper_profiles.title: What is essential is visible to the eye: Saliency in primary school ranking and its effect on academic achievements
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper studies whether students’ relative rank in primary school affects later academic achievement, and whether the effect comes from ranks that are visible to students versus ranks that are not. The authors focus on a key identification problem in rank research: class rank is typically correlated with underlying ability, so apparent rank effects may partly reflect ability peer effects rather than saliency or self-perception.

Using administrative panel data on several hundred thousand Italian public-school students, the paper constructs two rank measures in grade 5: a visible rank from teacher-assigned class grades that students see, and an invisible rank from standardized test scores that are not reported to students. The main empirical strategy includes student fixed effects and flexible controls for prior achievement and class distribution features, and it uses the invisible rank as a placebo. The authors also use a companion cohort to show that standard rank specifications remain correlated with earlier test scores, motivating their alternative approach.

The findings suggest that visible rank has a substantial positive association with later performance, while invisible rank becomes small and insignificant once the full controls are included. Being at the top rather than the bottom of the primary-school class ranking is associated with gains of about 8.5 percentile points in middle-school standardized test scores and 7.7 percentile points in high school scores. The paper concludes that saliency and perceived rank matter, that standard rank specifications may understate the effect, and that the quality of the peer/class environment has a much larger effect than rank itself.

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds that a higher visible class rank in grade 5 is associated with improved later math-related achievement as measured by national standardized test percentiles. In the main specification, ranking at the top rather than the bottom of the primary-school class distribution predicts a gain of 8.5 percentile points in grade 8 and 7.7 percentile points in grade 10; the invisible rank is near zero and not significant once full controls are included.
finding.measure: National standardized test scores in math and Italian, reported as percentile achievement in grades 8 and 10
finding.study_size: n=387,614 combined across the two main cohorts (205,123 in 2018 cohort; 182,491 in 2019 cohort)

finding.finding_summary: The study’s main outcome is later academic achievement on national standardized tests, combining Italian and math, with the effect estimated for visible versus invisible rank. The visible rank has a sizeable positive association with subsequent achievement, while the invisible rank is essentially null after controls; the top-versus-bottom visible rank contrast corresponds to about 8.5 percentile points in grade 8 and 7.7 percentile points in grade 10.
finding.measure: National standardized test achievement percentiles in grades 8 and 10 (Italian and math)
finding.study_size: n=387,614 combined across the two main cohorts

finding.finding_summary: Using the 2018 student questionnaire, the authors find that a higher visible rank improves students’ perceptions of school, self-esteem, perceived recognition by peers, and interest in subjects studied. These questionnaire results are interpreted as evidence that the rank effect operates through psychological/perception channels rather than through the invisible ability rank.
finding.measure: Student questionnaire responses on a six-point Likert scale about self-esteem, school perception, peer recognition, and subject interest

finding.finding_summary: The paper shows that class quality, defined via class value-added, has a much larger association with later achievement than class rank. A one-standard-deviation increase in class quality is associated with gains of 13.0 percentile points in middle school and 13.3 in high school, compared with only 2.2 and 1.9 percentile-point gains from a one-standard-deviation increase in rank; the authors also argue that standard rank specifications understate the rank effect because of omitted-variable bias and saliency mismatch.
finding.measure: Class value-added / class quality and later national standardized test scores
finding.study_size: n=387,614 combined across the two main cohorts

paper_profiles.title: VLM@school – Evaluation of AI image understanding on German middle school knowledge
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper presents VLM@school, a new benchmark for evaluating vision-language models (VLMs) on German middle-school-level content. The authors argue that existing multimodal benchmarks are often English-only, heavily multiple-choice, and too decontextualized, so they construct a more realistic dataset drawn from German school textbooks and related educational materials across nine domains, including mathematics, physics, biology, history, arts, music, religion, geography, and sports.

The benchmark contains 486 images and 2,038 open-ended questions, including some deliberately adversarial questions that cannot be answered from the image alone. The paper evaluates 13 open-weight VLMs using an automated jury-of-models scoring approach. Results show that even the best model reaches under 45% overall accuracy, with particularly weak performance on math, music, and adversarial items. The authors conclude that middle-school tasks in German remain challenging for current VLMs and that performance on public benchmarks such as MMMU does not reliably predict performance on this more realistic educational benchmark.

The study is not an instructional intervention or learner-outcome evaluation; it is a model benchmark study focused on image understanding and reasoning. Its educational relevance lies in identifying how well current AI systems can handle middle-school academic content when visual interpretation and subject knowledge must be combined. The paper suggests that language, question design, and the need to say 'I don't know' substantially affect model performance, and it highlights the limits of current systems in open-ended multimodal educational contexts.

finding.finding_summary: The benchmark includes 308 math questions based on middle-school geometry and related calculations. The best model achieved only about 34.09% on math (Qwen2.5VL 32B), while other models were lower, and the authors note that the best scores for math were only around 34% overall. This indicates that current VLMs perform poorly on visually grounded middle-school mathematics tasks in German.
finding.measure: Accuracy on open-ended middle-school math questions
finding.study_size: n=308 math questions (486 images total; 13 VLMs evaluated)

finding.finding_summary: The dataset includes biology and physics questions that require visual interpretation plus domain reasoning, and the models often struggled when explanation or inference was required. For example, best performance in biology and physics remained modest, and the paper reports that models frequently failed on explanation-based physics items and on identifying biology terms from diagrams. Overall, the results indicate weak scientific-reasoning performance relative to the benchmark demands.
finding.measure: Accuracy on biology and physics open-ended questions
finding.study_size: n=169 biology questions; n=234 physics questions (486 images total; 13 VLMs evaluated)

finding.finding_summary: The benchmark substantively covers non-math, non-science school subjects including arts, history, music, religion, geography, and sports. Performance varied widely by domain: best scores were about 54% in history and religion, but only about 31% in music, with substantial difficulty also in geography and sports. This suggests uneven and often weak performance on broader school-subject knowledge tasks.
finding.measure: Accuracy across arts, geography, history, music, religion, and sports questions
finding.study_size: n=286 arts; n=251 geography; n=264 history; n=166 music; n=206 religion; n=154 sports questions

finding.finding_summary: The paper emphasizes that models often fail at tasks requiring combined visual reasoning, background knowledge, counting, reverse lookup, and following arrows or legends—abilities related to higher-order reasoning rather than rote recognition. The authors interpret these failures as evidence that current VLMs do not reliably perform the kind of integrated reasoning needed for such open-ended school tasks.
finding.measure: Accuracy on reasoning-heavy open-ended benchmark items requiring integrated visual and textual inference
finding.study_size: n=2038 questions total; reasoning-centered analyses reported qualitatively

paper_profiles.title: Implementing a Chatbot Solution for Learning Management Systems
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This preprint describes the design and implementation of an educational chatbot intended to be integrated into a learning management system, specifically Blackboard. The authors frame the work as an exploration of how chatbot technology and machine learning tools can be combined with web scraping and browser scripting to create a virtual teaching assistant for students.
