The solution uses the ChatterBot Python library for conversational responses, PySide2 for the GUI, Selenium/Beautiful Soup for web scraping, and Tampermonkey to embed the chatbot into Blackboard without altering the platform source code. The study is situated in a higher-education context, using a local Blackboard test instance provided by the institution's IT department. The chatbot was able to run and interact with users, but the authors report substantial limitations in training quality, integration constraints, and Blackboard security that prevented full use of course content scraping.

The paper's main conclusion is that integrating an AI chatbot into an LMS is technically plausible, but the prototype remained limited and required much more training and better data pipelines to be practically useful. No student learning experiment, classroom deployment, or outcome evaluation was conducted; the paper is primarily a systems/implementation report with discussion of potential educational uses rather than an effectiveness study.

paper_profiles.title: PB-LLM: Partially Binarized Large Language Models
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether large language models (LLMs) can be compressed to extremely low bit-widths through network binarization while retaining useful language reasoning performance. The central problem is that standard binarization methods collapse on LLMs, so the authors propose Partially-Binarized LLM (PB-LLM), which preserves a small fraction of salient weights in higher precision and binarizes the rest.

The paper develops both post-training quantization (PTQ) and quantization-aware training (QAT) versions of PB-LLM. For PTQ, the authors adapt GPTQ-style layerwise reconstruction to the partially binarized setting; for QAT, they freeze salient weights and derive an analytic optimal scaling factor for binary weights. Experiments are conducted on pretrained OPT-1.3B and LLaMA-7B models using language modeling perplexity and zero-shot common-sense reasoning benchmarks such as BoolQ, PIQA, HellaSwag, WinoGrande, ARC-E, ARC-C, and OpenBookQA.

The main conclusion is that naive binarization methods perform worse than random guessing on these LLM benchmarks, while PB-LLM substantially improves low-bit performance. In particular, preserving salient weights and using the proposed scaling strategy recovers much of the lost performance, and PB-LLM with QAT converges much faster than prior LLM QAT approaches. This is a model-compression study for adult-oriented NLP systems, not an educational intervention study, and it contains no K–12 student outcome evidence.

paper_profiles.title: Elucidating STEM Concepts through Generative AI: A Multi-modal Exploration of Analogical Reasoning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper presents a generative-AI educational prototype that uses a large language model (GPT-4) together with text-to-image generation to create analogies, storyboards, and animated videos for explaining STEM concepts. The authors frame the work around the challenge of helping learners understand abstract STEM ideas, especially through multimodal representations that combine verbal and visual explanations.

The system takes a STEM concept as input, generates three analogies, lets the user select one, then turns it into a four-scene storyboard and an animated video. The paper reports preliminary content-generation trials rather than a full learner experiment: the authors evaluate whether the tool can produce usable analogies and visuals for concepts in mathematics, physics, and programming, and they note limitations in visual completeness and dynamic depiction.

No participant-based learning-outcome study is reported in this paper. Instead, the authors explicitly state that an empirical between-subject study with learner participants is planned for future work, so the paper’s conclusions are mainly about feasibility and design potential, not demonstrated educational effectiveness.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that the system could reduce educator workload by generating analogies, storyboards, and videos for STEM instruction, but this is presented as a design implication rather than a measured outcome. No quantitative productivity or time-savings data are reported; the paper only provides preliminary evidence that the prototype can generate instructional content across incremental steps.
finding.measure: content generation feasibility / perceived pedagogical efficiency

finding.finding_summary: The paper is substantively focused on explaining STEM concepts, including physics and programming examples, through analogical reasoning and multimodal representations. However, it does not report learner outcome data; instead, it describes prototype generation performance and notes that some analogies were partially incomplete or hard to render dynamically (e.g., water pressure/current and electric voltage/current).
finding.measure: prototype-generated analogies and visual storyboards for STEM concepts

paper_profiles.title: A Multimedia Adaptive Tutoring System for Mathematics that Addresses Cognition, Metacognition and Affect
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper presents the Wayang Outpost/MathSpring mathematics tutoring system and synthesizes several years of design-based development and empirical evaluations. The central question is how an intelligent tutoring system can simultaneously support cognition, metacognition, and affect in K-12 mathematics learning, particularly for students who struggle with math and need individualized support on standardized-test-style problems.

The system combines multiple components: adaptive problem selection, multimedia worked examples and hints, math fluency training, open student models, progress reports, and affective learning companions. The paper reports results from multiple classroom and controlled studies with middle and high school students in Massachusetts, including comparisons against control conditions and analyses of pre/post test gains, MAP growth, and MCAS performance. Reported findings suggest positive effects on mathematics learning and engagement-related outcomes, with stronger gains in some conditions and subgroups, such as the combination of Wayang with math facts retrieval training and tailored algebra-focused use in eighth grade.

The paper is best understood as a design-and-evaluation article that brings together quantitative intervention findings and system-description evidence rather than a single standalone experiment. It concludes that adaptive tutoring can improve short-term learning and some longer-term standardized test outcomes, while also supporting student self-regulation and affect through carefully designed scaffolds and teacher-facing reporting tools.

finding.finding_summary: Across multiple classroom and controlled studies, Wayang Outpost/MathSpring was associated with improved mathematics performance. In the 2012 study of 198 seventh- and eighth-grade students, 7th graders in the Wayang condition showed a near-significant gain on MCAS scores compared with control (Mean Wayang=244.82, Mean Control=239.50; F(1,93)=2.2, p=0.14), and 8th graders had significantly more students in the proficient/advanced category (Chi Square(92,1), p=0.05). The paper also reports a significant MAP growth difference in patterns/algebra (Cohen’s d=0.38) and a larger 8th-grade algebra/patterns gain (d=0.77).
finding.measure: MCAS mathematics scores; MAP patterns and algebra growth; pre/post math tests
finding.study_size: n=198 for the 2012 classroom study; n=250 for the MFR + Wayang randomized study

finding.finding_summary: The paper explicitly targets engagement, motivation, and affect, arguing that these are central outcomes of the system. It reports that affective companions, progress reports, and effort-based tutoring were designed to reduce disengagement and support perseverance; in the broader set of evaluations, students using Wayang were described as showing improved engagement and more positive learning experience, though many affect results are reported descriptively rather than with a single pooled effect size. In the SPP experiment, the intended manipulation had limited uptake because students were rarely bored, so total SPP use did not differ reliably between conditions.
finding.measure: Student gaming/engagement logs; self-reported emotions; affect detector outputs; use of student progress pages

finding.finding_summary: The system was designed to improve metacognition, self-regulation, help-seeking, and reflection through open student models and progress pages. The paper reports that these features are intended to support students in monitoring progress, setting goals, choosing to continue/review/challenge themselves, and improving self-regulation; however, the empirical evidence presented for these metacognitive interventions is mixed and sometimes indirect, with the clearest quantitative result being on math achievement rather than a direct metacognitive test score. The SPP study found that students were seldom bored, so the prompted intervention did not produce a reliable usage difference.
finding.measure: Student progress page usage; choice behavior; self-reported emotion; inferred metacognitive behaviors

finding.finding_summary: The teacher tools were described as providing immediate, fine-grained reports on student mastery, effort, engagement, and problem-level difficulty, enabling teachers to identify struggling students and skills in real time. The paper emphasizes that this reduced the burden of diagnosing needs and supported classroom instruction, but it does not report a formal efficiency metric such as time saved or workload reduction.
finding.measure: Teacher report utility and real-time student performance dashboards

paper_profiles.title: Elementary School Students’ and Teachers’ Perceptions Towards Creative Mathematical Writing with Generative AI
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how elementary school students and teachers perceive a generative AI-powered learning activity for creative mathematical writing. The authors focus on whether GenAI can support students in generating, revising, and personalizing math stories while also helping teachers understand classroom opportunities and challenges.

The study was conducted in six fifth-grade classrooms across two U.S. schools with 79 students and six teachers. Students used a researcher-developed system that supported an Ask–Represent–Transform process: first analyzing a math story, then representing ideas visually, and finally co-creating a culturally relevant math story with GPT-4 and DALL·E 3. The paper uses semi-structured student focus groups, one-on-one teacher interviews, open-ended survey responses, and classroom observations, analyzed through thematic analysis.

Findings were organized into six themes. Perceived benefits included fostering creativity in math, improving mathematical understanding, promoting AI literacy, and strengthening affective outcomes such as interest, curiosity, and ownership. Challenges centered on students’ difficulty critically evaluating AI outputs, limited opportunities for independent work and peer interaction, insufficient formative feedback, and accessibility concerns such as lack of speech-to-text. The paper concludes that GenAI can support mathematical creative writing, but its educational value depends on thoughtful pedagogical design rather than simply high-performing AI output.

finding.finding_summary: Students and teachers perceived that the GenAI-supported creative math writing task improved mathematical understanding, including breaking down problems, representing ideas, and uncovering misconceptions. The study is qualitative, so it does not report test-score gains, but participants consistently described stronger engagement with fraction concepts and problem structure across the 79 fifth-grade students in six classrooms.
finding.measure: Perceived mathematical understanding; problem breakdown; mathematical knowledge representation; misconception identification from interviews, surveys, and observations

finding.finding_summary: Participants reported improved interest, curiosity, enjoyment, and ownership during the GenAI-supported math writing activities. Students described math as fun and motivating, and teachers noted increased attention and responsibility for learning in the 79-student classroom implementation.
finding.measure: Perceived interest, curiosity, enjoyment, and ownership of learning from interviews, open-ended surveys, and observations

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that the activity promoted creativity, flexible and divergent thinking, prompt engineering, and evaluation of AI strengths and weaknesses. Students experimented with prompts, revised inputs, and reflected on how AI works, suggesting gains in metacognitive and critical-thinking-related skills rather than measured achievement outcomes.
finding.measure: Perceived creativity, divergent/convergent thinking, prompt engineering, and evaluation of AI outputs from interviews and classroom observations

finding.finding_summary: The study centered on creative writing in mathematics and found that GenAI helped students draft, revise, and elaborate stories. Students and teachers said the system supported original story creation, richer detail, and more coherent writing, but the paper does not report standardized writing scores.
finding.measure: Perceived creative writing quality, story development, and revision support in math writing tasks

paper_profiles.title: Combining Large Language Models with Tutoring System Intelligence: A Case Study in Caregiver Homework Support
paper_profiles.venue: LAK 2025 (The 15th International Learning Analytics and Knowledge Conference)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses how large language models (LLMs) can be combined with intelligent tutoring system (ITS) data to support caregivers who help children with math homework. The authors argue that caregivers often want to help but lack the content knowledge and tutoring strategies needed to provide effective support, especially in modern curricula and online homework contexts.

The intervention studied is the Caregiver Conversational Support Tool (CCST), a prototype embedded in a middle-school equation-solving tutor (Lynnette). CCST uses problem-solving context from the tutor—such as current equation, correctness, hint use, prior chat, and next viable steps—plus tutoring-practice examples to prompt Llama 3 to generate personalized caregiver chat recommendations. The study includes prompt-engineering experiments and a prototyping evaluation with ten middle school caregivers in workshop and remote interview settings.

The main findings are qualitative rather than achievement-based. The authors found that the LLM produced more contextually relevant and pedagogically appropriate recommendations when tutoring-system context and example-based prompting were included. Caregivers especially valued content-level guidance and self-explanation prompts, while motivational prompts were seen as less useful by many participants. The paper concludes that merging ITS intelligence with LLMs can improve the relevance of caregiver support in hybrid tutoring, but that better message brevity, tone, and latency are needed for practical use.

finding.finding_summary: This paper does not evaluate student math achievement or learning gains. Instead, it studies whether an LLM-based caregiver support tool can generate contextually relevant math-help messages for middle school equation-solving, and reports qualitative caregiver feedback from n=10 participants. No effect size, confidence interval, or achievement outcome is reported.
finding.measure: Qualitative caregiver perceptions of LLM-generated math-support messages during equation-solving homework support

finding.finding_summary: Caregivers reported that the system’s messages could support student motivation and engagement when phrased as encouragement or praise, although many caregivers preferred content-focused help over motivational support. This was assessed through qualitative interviews and workshop feedback with n=10 caregivers; no quantitative effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Caregiver perceptions of motivational/praise-oriented message recommendations

finding.finding_summary: A major qualitative finding was that caregivers preferred prompts that elicit student self-explanation and metacognition, because these messages helped them better understand student thinking and identify misconceptions. The evidence comes from thematic analysis of interviews with n=10 caregivers; no quantitative effect size, CI, or SD is reported.
finding.measure: Caregiver preferences for self-explanation and metacognitive chat recommendations

paper_profiles.title: Students' Perceived Roles, Opportunities, and Challenges of a Generative AI-powered Teachable Agent: A Case of Middle School Math Class
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how middle school students perceive a generative AI-powered teachable agent (TA) in an authentic math classroom. The central question is not whether the system improves test scores, but how students interpret the TA’s roles, benefits, and challenges when learning math through a learning-by-teaching interaction.

The authors studied a GenAI-based chatbot-like TA built with GPT-4-Turbo and retrieval augmented generation, designed to simulate a less knowledgeable peer that students teach. The system was used in a 6th-grade rates-and-ratio unit over two class periods in a public laboratory middle school in the southeastern United States. Data came from classroom observations, open-ended surveys, and focus-group interviews with 108 students (with 14 interviewed), and the analysis used thematic coding.

Findings show that students viewed the TA as a learning companion, learning facilitator, and collaborative problem-solver. They also reported opportunities such as a more student-centered climate, greater autonomy, stronger cognitive/social/emotional capacities, improved math knowledge and application, more enjoyment and motivation, interdisciplinary connections, and more positive attitudes toward AI. Reported barriers included weak problem presentation, surface-level questioning, poor support for different learning styles, disorganized sequencing, limited socio-emotional and pedagogical abilities, technical issues, interface problems, and a need for teacher facilitation. Because the study is qualitative, it does not provide achievement effect sizes, but it suggests design implications for GenAI-powered TAs in K–12 mathematics.

finding.finding_summary: Students reported that teaching and interacting with the GenAI-powered TA helped improve their understanding of rate and ratio concepts, their ability to explain math ideas in multiple ways, and their application of knowledge to new contexts. These claims were based on observations, open-ended surveys, and interviews with 108 sixth-grade students; no standardized achievement test or effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Students’ self-reported math understanding, application of knowledge, and qualitative classroom observations/interviews about rate and ratio learning

finding.finding_summary: Students described increased enjoyment of math, stronger intrinsic motivation, and higher self-efficacy when learning with the TA. The study also reports more engagement and eagerness to continue using the system, but these are qualitative perceptions rather than measured test-based outcomes.
finding.measure: Student perceptions of enjoyment, motivation, engagement, and self-efficacy from surveys, interviews, and observations

finding.finding_summary: Students reported improvements in cognitive and social capacities, including reasoning, self-explanation, communication, perspective-taking, and collaborative problem-solving. The paper also frames the TA as promoting metacognition and deeper thinking, but all evidence is qualitative and no quantitative skill gains were reported.
finding.measure: Qualitative reports of reasoning, metacognition, communication, perspective-taking, and collaboration

finding.finding_summary: Students reported that learning with the GenAI-powered TA fostered interdisciplinary learning, especially connecting computer science with mathematics. This finding was based on student comments and classroom observations rather than a direct subject-matter assessment.
finding.measure: Student perceptions of interdisciplinary learning (math + computer science)

finding.finding_summary: Students reported developing more positive attitudes toward AI and greater awareness of how AI works while using the TA. The paper treats this as an educational outcome relevant to AI literacy, but it is measured qualitatively through observations, interviews, and open-ended survey responses.
finding.measure: Student perceptions of AI attitudes and AI literacy

paper_profiles.title: Improving Student Learning with Hybrid Human-AI Tutoring: A Three-Study Quasi-Experimental Investigation
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether a hybrid human-AI tutoring model can improve middle school math learning opportunities and intermediate achievement-related outcomes for historically underserved students. The core question is whether combining adaptive math software with human tutor support increases student engagement and progress more than software alone, and whether effects differ by baseline ability.

Across three quasi-experimental studies in urban, low-income middle schools, the authors evaluated different implementations of hybrid tutoring during the regular school day. Site 1 compared software-only support to software plus a math teacher and then software plus teacher plus remote tutors; Site 2 compared weeks of i-Ready use before and during a short tutoring period; Site 3 examined changes in MATHia progress when tutor-to-student ratios improved and a dashboard was introduced. The samples were 125 students in Pennsylvania, 385 students in California, and 75 students in a Pennsylvania charter school, with over 90% low-income participation across sites.

The study found positive effects on engagement and software-based learning process measures. In Site 1, hybrid tutoring increased time spent, questions answered, and skills proficient relative to software only, with the additional tutoring effect on time spent showing 0.202 standardized units and a stronger benefit for lower pretest students. In Site 2, tutoring increased weekly i-Ready time from 24 to 33 minutes and raised lesson completion, especially for students below grade level; in Site 3, moving from about 1:8 to 1:4 tutor-student ratios increased MATHia progress by 0.36 workspaces per hour. The authors conclude that hybrid human-AI tutoring can improve engagement and intermediate learning outcomes, especially for lower-performing students, but they do not directly measure external standardized test gains in this paper.

finding.finding_summary: Across three quasi-experimental site studies in middle school math, hybrid human-AI tutoring improved multiple math process outcomes relative to software-only or lower-support conditions. In Site 1 (n=125), the tutoring condition increased time spent (β=0.202, 95% CI [0.057, 0.347]) and was associated with higher questions answered and skills proficient; in Site 2 (n=385), tutoring increased weekly i-Ready time from 24 to 33 minutes and lesson completion; in Site 3 (n=75), improving tutor access from about 1:8 to 1:4 increased MATHia progress by 0.36 workspaces per hour (95% CI [0.02, 0.70]).
finding.measure: Math software process outcomes and learning progress: time spent, questions answered, skills proficient, lessons passed, workspaces completed per hour

finding.finding_summary: The paper treats engagement, usage, and participation as central intermediate outcomes and reports consistent gains under hybrid tutoring. In Site 1, time spent and questions answered increased significantly in the tutoring conditions; in Site 2, weekly time-on-task rose from 24 to 33 minutes during tutoring; and in Site 3, students completed more workspaces per hour when tutor support increased. The authors interpret these as improved engagement with the learning software and more productive participation.
finding.measure: Time on task / time spent, questions answered, engagement with math software, participation
finding.effect_size: Site 1 time spent β=0.202; Site 3 progress +0.36 workspaces/hour; Site 2 24 to 33 minutes/week

finding.finding_summary: The intervention is framed partly as a scalable tutoring model that can increase tutor leverage and support more students per tutor. The paper reports that the hybrid model operated at roughly $700 per student annually and that increasing tutor-to-student ratios from about 1:8 to 1:4 improved productivity in Site 3, where students completed 0.36 more MATHia workspaces per hour (95% CI [0.02, 0.70]). These results suggest improved tutoring efficiency and lower marginal cost compared with traditional high-dosage tutoring.
finding.measure: Tutor-student ratio, workspaces completed per hour, annual marginal cost per student
finding.study_size: n=75; cost estimate across three sites

paper_profiles.title: Generative AI alone may not be enough: Evaluating AI Support for Learning Mathematical Proof
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper evaluates whether an LLM-powered tutoring system, LLM-Tutor, can improve learning in an introductory discrete mathematics course, with a particular focus on proof-writing. The study asks whether the system improves homework and exam performance, changes time spent on coursework, and how students with different self-efficacy levels use the tool.

LLM-Tutor combined two generative-AI supports: a proof-review tutor that gave real-time, highlighted feedback on students’ LaTeX proofs, and a chatbot for math questions. The authors deployed the system in a university discrete math course and randomly assigned students to experimental and control groups, with 155 participants in the analysis and interview follow-up with 19 students. Quantitatively, the tool improved homework scores after introduction but did not significantly improve exam performance or reported time spent. Regression and mediation analyses showed chatbot use was negatively associated with Midterm 3 scores, especially for lower-self-efficacy students, while proof-review usage showed no benefit on Midterm 3 but was linked to better final exam performance in the mediation model. Qualitative interviews suggested students valued accessibility and immediate feedback, but also worried about over-reliance and limitations in conceptual support.

Overall, the paper concludes that generative AI alone is not enough for comprehensive mathematics learning support: the chatbot feature may encourage unhelpful dependence, whereas the structured proof-review component appears more promising when paired with learning-sciences-informed design. The authors argue for hybrid systems that complement, rather than replace, human support and traditional course resources.

finding.finding_summary: In this randomized classroom study of an introductory discrete mathematics course (n=155 recruited; analyses often reported on n=146-148 due to attrition), LLM-Tutor significantly improved homework performance but did not improve exam performance overall. Homework scores after introduction were higher for the experimental group (M=99.64, SD=8.03) than the control group (M=96.55, SD=11.66), t(146)=2.19, p=.030; however, there were no statistically significant differences on midterm or final exam scores.
finding.measure: Homework grades and exam scores (midterms and final exam) in discrete mathematics proof-writing assignments
finding.study_size: n=155 recruited; 148/146 in reported analyses depending on comparison
finding.std_deviation: HW experimental SD=8.03; HW control SD=11.66

finding.finding_summary: The study found that self-efficacy was positively associated with exam performance, and qualitative interviews suggested many students felt more confident or less hopeless when using LLM-Tutor. At the same time, some students reported no confidence change, and chatbot reliance was associated with lower performance among lower-self-efficacy students, indicating a mixed relationship between the tool and socio-emotional outcomes.
finding.measure: Self-efficacy survey, interview reports of confidence/motivation, and related mediation/correlation analyses
finding.study_size: n=155 total; self-efficacy survey analyzed among survey respondents; interviews n=19

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly examines problem-solving support, proof-writing process quality, and self-regulated use of AI feedback. Interview data showed students often used the system as a 'sanity check' or to clarify proof steps, but some worried about over-reliance and reduced independent problem-solving. The quantitative results also suggest different usage patterns mattered: chatbot use was negatively associated with exam outcomes, while proof-review use was not helpful on Midterm 3 and only appeared beneficial for the final exam through mediation.
finding.measure: Interview themes about independent problem-solving and proof-writing; usage-frequency correlations and mediation models

finding.finding_summary: The study examined whether LLM-Tutor changed perceived time spent on coursework. Survey results showed no significant differences in time spent between groups either before or after LLM-Tutor access (e.g., before use: Control M=11.81 hours, SD=3.98; Experimental M=12.07 hours, SD=4.71, t=0.26, p=0.79; after use: Control M=7.55 hours, SD=2.85; Experimental M=7.68 hours, SD=3.06, t=0.20, p=0.83).
finding.measure: Self-reported weekly time spent on assignments and textbook reading
finding.study_size: n=41 experimental respondents and n=40 control respondents with matched survey responses
finding.std_deviation: Before use: 3.98 vs 4.71; after use: 2.85 vs 3.06

finding.finding_summary: Although the paper is centered on mathematics, it also specifically studies students' understanding of proof-writing as an academic task beyond routine numeracy. Interviews indicated many students felt LLM-Tutor helped them better understand complex concepts and proof techniques, but a smaller group reported little or no improvement and preferred lecture notes or TA office hours.
finding.measure: Interview reports of understanding proof-writing concepts and strategies

paper_profiles.title: AI tutoring can safely and effectively support students: An exploratory RCT in UK classrooms
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether a generative AI tutor can safely and effectively support secondary school students in mathematics classrooms. The authors address a practical scaling problem in one-to-one tutoring: it is highly effective but expensive and difficult to provide widely. They test whether LearnLM, a pedagogically fine-tuned generative AI model, can help deliver tutoring support with quality comparable to human tutors.

The study was conducted in five UK secondary schools with N=165 Year 9 and 10 students (ages 13–15) using the Eedi mathematics platform. Students were randomly assigned either to static, pre-written hints or to interactive tutoring; students receiving tutoring were further randomized to human tutors or to LearnLM supervised by human tutors who could approve, edit, or rewrite each AI-generated message. The trial measured immediate mistake remediation, misconception resolution, and knowledge transfer to the next topic, and also audited message safety and tutor/student experiences.

The main findings are that supervised LearnLM tutoring was safe, with tutors approving most drafted messages and identifying no harmful content in the reviewed corpus. In learning outcomes, LearnLM performed at least as well as human tutoring on immediate remediation and misconception resolution, and it outperformed human tutoring on a durable transfer measure: students tutored by LearnLM were 66.2% successful on the first question of the next unit versus 60.7% for human-tutor sessions, a 5.5 percentage-point advantage. The authors conclude that pedagogically supervised genAI tutoring may be a promising way to scale individualized mathematics support, while noting that longer-term effects still need study.

finding.finding_summary: This exploratory RCT found that supervised LearnLM tutoring improved students' mathematics learning outcomes, especially knowledge transfer to new topics. On the durable outcome measure, students tutored by LearnLM were 66.2% successful on the first question of the next unit versus 60.7% for students tutored by human tutors, a difference of 5.5 percentage points [–1.4, +12.4].
finding.measure: Performance on Eedi mathematics platform study units, including mistake remediation, misconception resolution, and knowledge transfer to the next unit
finding.confidence_interval: [–1.4%, +12.4%] for the LearnLM vs human-tutor difference on knowledge transfer

finding.finding_summary: The paper includes student and tutor experience data indicating that interactive tutoring was viewed favorably and that students rated the helpfulness of tutoring slightly higher than static hints. In post-trial surveys, students receiving interactive tutoring rated helpfulness at 3.9 [3.1, 4.7] out of 5 versus 3.6 [2.9, 4.2] for static hints, suggesting improved perceived engagement/support rather than a direct psychosocial intervention effect.
finding.measure: Post-trial student helpfulness ratings and qualitative interview/survey feedback
finding.study_size: n=27 student survey responses; n=17 tutor survey responses; n=5 tutor interviews
finding.confidence_interval: Posterior probability of advantage for tutoring: 74.9%

finding.finding_summary: The study reports that LearnLM made tutors' work feel more fluid and efficient, with tutors able to support multiple students at the same time. In post-trial surveys, 82.4% of tutors selected 'supporting multiple students at the same time' as LearnLM's most useful feature, and tutor comfort with AI rose from 3.4 [2.9, 4.0] to 3.9 [3.3, 4.4] out of 5 (posterior probability of increase: 90.0%).
finding.measure: Tutor surveys and interviews on workload, comfort with AI, and perceived efficiency
finding.confidence_interval: Tutor comfort with AI increased from 3.4 [2.9, 4.0] to 3.9 [3.3, 4.4]

finding.finding_summary: Although the primary academic focus is mathematics, the paper also frames knowledge transfer as a durable skill-adjacent outcome involving transfer of learning to new problems and topics. LearnLM improved transfer to a novel topic relative to human tutoring by 5.5 percentage points, with students answering the first question of the next unit correctly at 66.2% versus 60.7% for human-tutor sessions.
finding.measure: Knowledge transfer to the next study unit in the same mathematics sequence

paper_profiles.title: MathVC: An LLM-Simulated Multi-Persona Virtual Classroom for Collaborative Mathematical Problem Solving
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses whether large language models can be used to simulate multiple peer classmates in a mathematics collaborative problem-solving environment, with the goal of supporting middle school students’ mathematical discussion when real peer-group conditions are unavailable or uneven. The authors argue that collaborative problem solving is central to mathematics learning but is often difficult to sustain in classrooms because of limited time, class size, and imbalanced participation.

To explore this, the authors designed MathVC, a multi-persona LLM-simulated virtual classroom in which one student collaborates with two virtual peers during math problem solving. The system uses a meta-planning module to manage discussion stages (shared understanding, team organization, planning, execution, and validation) and a persona simulation module that injects mathematical misconceptions into one peer and assigns advanced knowledge to another. The implementation uses GPT-4o and a web-based interface.

The study evaluated MathVC with 14 U.S. middle school students (grades 6–8, plus one advanced student below grade 6) through approximately 60-minute sessions that included onboarding, problem solving, a semi-structured interview, and an exit survey. The researchers collected chat logs, survey responses, and interview data, then used descriptive statistics and thematic analysis. Students generally reported positive experiences, including constructive interaction, shared understanding, and improved engagement, motivation, and confidence, although some noted that the virtual peers sometimes sounded too formal or adult-like.

Overall, the paper concludes that multi-persona LLM simulations can create a plausible collaborative problem-solving setting for middle school mathematics and may support students’ socio-emotional engagement and perceived collaboration. The evidence is primarily exploratory and qualitative, with self-reported positive attitudes rather than direct achievement gains or durable learning outcomes.

finding.finding_summary: Students reported that MathVC increased engagement, motivation, persistence, and confidence during mathematical problem solving. In exit survey responses (n=14), students agreed that they interacted constructively with simulated classmates (Mean=4.36/5) and could work effectively in the virtual environment (Mean=4.21/5), and interview data indicated the system reduced cognitive burden and supported motivation through immediate scaffolding and diverse perspectives.
finding.measure: Exit survey Likert responses; semi-structured interview themes on engagement, motivation, confidence, and persistence

finding.finding_summary: The paper substantively examines collaborative problem solving and related metacognitive behaviors. Students reported that they could plan steps, understand how their own and classmates’ actions contributed to solution progress, and reach shared understanding; exit survey ratings were high for planning/contribution (Mean=4.36/5 and Mean=4.29/5), and interviews described collaborative reasoning, critique, and articulation of thinking.
finding.measure: Exit survey items on planning/contribution and shared solution; chat logs and interview themes on collaborative problem solving and metacognition

finding.finding_summary: The system was used for collaborative mathematics problem solving, and students reported that they could understand the math problem and work effectively with the virtual classroom. However, the paper does not report standardized achievement gains, post-tests, or effect sizes for math learning; evidence is limited to perceived problem-solving support and successful completion of tasks in-session.
finding.measure: Math problem-solving tasks in MathVC; exit survey item on understanding the math problem and working effectively

paper_profiles.title: Personality-aware Student Simulation for Conversational Intelligent Tutoring Systems
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of how to simulate realistic student behavior for conversational intelligent tutoring systems (ITSs), especially when the goal is to test whether large language models (LLMs) can generate student-like responses that reflect both language ability and personality. The authors argue that current conversational ITS evaluation often focuses on post-learning outcomes and does not adequately model student heterogeneity or personality-related dialogue behavior.

To tackle this, they propose a personality-aware student simulation framework for tutoring conversations, built around a refined version of the Big Five personality model adapted to tutoring contexts (BF-TC). They also add a multi-aspect validation framework that checks whether generated dialogues match the intended student personality, language ability, and teacher scaffolding behaviors. The concrete case study is primary-school language learning through an image-description task, where a teacher and a simulated student interact in a dialogue to practice descriptive language.

The experiments compare several LLMs (Zephyr-7B-beta, Vicuna-13B-v1.5, GPT-3.5, GPT-4) on their ability to follow personality and language-ability instructions, and then analyze whether teacher scaffolding changes in response to simulated student profiles. Results show that GPT-4 is the strongest simulator, with better adherence to BF-TC traits and language-ability labels than the smaller open models. The paper concludes that LLM-based simulation can generate diverse tutoring conversations and that teachers/agents adapt scaffolding strategies according to student ability and personality, supporting the value of personalized conversational tutoring systems.

finding.finding_summary: The paper does not test student learning gains; instead, it evaluates whether simulated primary-school learners can produce language outputs consistent with specified ability levels. Across 500 generated dialogues, GPT-4 achieved the strongest language-ability classification consistency (precision=0.831, recall=0.715, F1=0.741), and high-ability simulations produced more complete, grammatical sentences than low-ability simulations.
finding.measure: Dialogue-level language ability labeling; conversational response quality in an image-description tutoring task

finding.finding_summary: The study finds that personality-aware simulation changes affective and engagement-related dialogue behaviors in ways aligned with the intended traits. For example, low extraversion and high neuroticism were associated with hesitation and worry, while high extraversion produced more talkative and engaging student responses; GPT-4 showed the best overall BF-TC categorization consistency (averaged F1=0.802).
finding.measure: Dialogue-level BF-TC personality categorization; response patterns indicating engagement, hesitation, and anxiety
finding.study_size: 500 generated tutoring dialogues (BF-TC validation set also included 50 human-annotated dialogues)

finding.finding_summary: The paper evaluates whether personality-aware student simulation influences pedagogical interaction and scaffolding, which is relevant to adaptive communication and dialogic participation rather than achievement. GPT-4-based tutoring conversations showed clear adaptation of scaffolding strategies to student characteristics, and the authors report that low openness, conscientiousness, and extraversion elicited more hints, while neuroticism shifted teacher scaffolding patterns, especially for lower-ability students.
finding.measure: Utterance-level scaffolding categorization and correlation analysis between student traits/ability and teacher scaffolding types

paper_profiles.title: Sticky Help, Bounded Effects: Session-by-Session Analytics of Teacher Interventions in K-12 Classrooms
paper_profiles.venue: LAK 2026: 16th International Learning Analytics and Knowledge Conference
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how teachers decide whom to help during technology-supported K–12 mathematics classwork and whether those help visits have benefits that extend beyond the current session. The authors focus on a practical orchestration problem in blended classrooms: teachers have limited in-the-moment attention, and learning analytics tools may help them allocate support more equitably and effectively.

The study uses a mixed-methods design. First, the authors interviewed nine middle-school math teachers to identify the factors teachers say they use when deciding whom to help, what kinds of support they provide, and how they think about fairness and classroom coverage. Teachers emphasized current engagement state, especially idle behavior and struggle, plus prior help history, peer support, and contextual cues. These interviews informed the quantitative analysis.

For the log analysis, the authors analyzed 1,437,055 MATHia transactions from 339 students across 14 math classes in 10 U.S. K–12 schools. They used mixed-effects logistic regression, cross-lagged panel models, and additive factor modeling to study whether prior help history predicts later teacher help, whether help changes later disengagement, and whether help predicts later skill acquisition. The results show that help is ‘sticky’: students who were helped once were more likely to be helped again, and idle behavior also influenced teacher attention. However, help did not predict later learning gains across sessions, even though help and learning were positively associated within sessions.

Overall, the paper concludes that teacher help in ITS-supported math classrooms is temporally bounded: it is associated with immediate learning and support during a session, but those benefits do not clearly carry over to later sessions. The authors argue that analytics dashboards should surface visit distributions, under-visited students, and repeated revisits to help teachers make more deliberate and equitable allocation decisions.

finding.finding_summary: Teacher help did not significantly predict the number of new knowledge components (KCs) acquired in the next session. In the cross-lagged panel analysis, prior help had no significant effect on later skill acquisition (b_K = 0.04, z = 0.64, p = .52) across AFM-based mastery indicators derived from 425,285 first attempts and 827 KCs.
finding.measure: AFM-based new KC acquisition / predicted mastery threshold (>80%) across sessions

finding.finding_summary: Help was associated with immediate within-session learning and occurred more often when students were idle, but these effects were largely session-bound. Prior idle behavior predicted later idle behavior (c1 = 0.12, z = 5.21, p < .001), while help did not reduce later idle behavior (d1 = -0.05, z = -1.45, p = .147), suggesting limited sustained impact on engagement across sessions.
finding.measure: Idle behavior / disengagement states; teacher help visits
finding.effect_size: help → idle: b = -0.05; idle → help: b = -0.10; idle stability: c1 = 0.12

finding.finding_summary: The paper does not evaluate a productivity intervention directly, but it does quantify help allocation patterns relevant to orchestration efficiency. Teacher help was concentrated and ‘sticky’ across sessions, with prior help predicting additional help (OR = 1.32, 95% CI [1.19, 1.46]) and a high concentration of visits across students (Gini = 0.641), implying analytics could improve how limited teacher attention is distributed.
finding.measure: Likelihood of receiving teacher help; concentration of help across students

paper_profiles.title: Investigating student perceptions of creativity and generative ai in computational physics
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how students conceptualize creativity and how those conceptions connect to their perceptions of generative AI (gen-AI) in an upper-division computational physics course. The authors situate the study in the growing use of gen-AI in education and in physics education research, then use the Four C Model of creativity to interpret student responses.

The study draws on narrative essay responses from six physics majors enrolled in an upper-division computational physics sequence (PH 366) at Oregon State University. Students responded to prompts about gen-AI, creativity, intuition, and the relationship between creativity and gen-AI. The authors coded responses iteratively using expanded definitions of the Four C Model, especially mini-c and little-c creativity, to capture how students described personal learning, problem solving, and social sharing of work.

The main finding is that students mostly framed creativity in mini-c and little-c terms: creativity was tied to individual learning, novel approaches, and, in some cases, collaboration and sharing with classmates. Students generally viewed gen-AI as a useful support for brainstorming, outlining, code checking, and other learning tasks, but they were skeptical of its originality, accuracy, and creativity. The paper concludes that students can use gen-AI in ways that support learning while still recognizing its limitations, and suggests further research on how students prompt and trust gen-AI in computational physics.

finding.finding_summary: The study found that students associated creativity with problem solving, thinking outside the box, and collaboration, which the authors interpret as mini-c and little-c creativity. In the qualitative essays (n=6), students described using gen-AI for brainstorming, outlining, revising, and code checking, but they also expressed skepticism about its originality and reliability, indicating both support for and concern about its role in creative thinking and collaboration.
finding.measure: Narrative essay responses about creativity, intuition, and gen-AI use; Four C Model coding

finding.finding_summary: In an upper-division computational physics context, students reported using gen-AI as a learning resource for tasks such as brainstorming ideas, outlining work, clarifying sentence structure, and reviewing code. The paper does not measure achievement, but it does show that gen-AI was perceived as helpful for learning-related tasks while also being viewed as producing unoriginal or unreliable outputs.
finding.measure: Student perceptions and self-reported uses of gen-AI in computational physics coursework

paper_profiles.title: Novice Learner and Expert Tutor: Evaluating Math Reasoning Abilities of Large Language Models with Misconceptions
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks a methodological question about whether large language models (LLMs) can be evaluated not only on answering mathematics questions correctly, but also on producing specific incorrect answers that align with known student misconceptions, and on identifying the misconception behind a wrong answer. The authors frame this as a “novice learner” task (generate a misconception-consistent error) and an “expert tutor” task (infer the misconception from an error), arguing that these capabilities are relevant to educational uses such as intelligent tutoring systems.

The study uses a grade-school multiple-choice math dataset from Eedi that includes expert-curated misconceptions for incorrect choices. After preprocessing, the dataset contains 213 questions, 482 answer choices, and 319 misconceptions. The authors test GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 under several prompting strategies, including zero-shot and few-shot setups, and report accuracy across repeated trials. LLMs perform very well at standard correct-answer math solving (e.g., GPT-4 reaches 94.8% with explanation prompting), but substantially worse when asked to emulate a novice learner with a specific misconception (GPT-4: 61.7% zero-shot with explanation; 67.9% few-shot with same-misconception examples) or to identify misconceptions as an expert tutor; performance decreases as the number of candidate misconceptions increases.

The main conclusion is that current LLMs can solve the underlying math problems accurately, but are much weaker at controlled error generation and misconception identification. The paper suggests this gap limits their ability to faithfully model student thinking and highlights opportunities for improving student-simulation and tutoring-oriented capabilities. Because the work is an evaluation study on model behavior rather than a student-intervention trial, it does not provide evidence of learning gains for children; its educational relevance is primarily to AI tutoring and diagnostic assessment.

finding.finding_summary: The paper evaluates LLM performance on grade-school mathematics tasks from an Eedi multiple-choice dataset (213 questions, 482 choices, 319 misconceptions). GPT-4 performs strongly on standard correct-answer solving (94.8% with explanation prompting; Table 1), but much worse when asked to answer incorrectly in a misconception-specific way (61.7% zero-shot with explanation; 67.9% few-shot with same-misconception examples; Table 2) and when identifying misconceptions, with accuracy dropping as the number of candidate misconceptions increases to 100 (GPT-4 average 39.8% as reported in Figure 2).
finding.measure: Accuracy on grade-school math question answering; accuracy on misconception-specific incorrect-answer generation; accuracy on misconception identification
finding.std_deviation: GPT-4 standard deviation reported across 4 trials: ±0.009 to ±0.027 for some conditions; GPT-3.5 ±0.010 to ±0.031 depending on condition

paper_profiles.title: Leveraging Affect Transfer Learning for Behavior Prediction in an Intelligent Tutoring System
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the 2021 IEEE International Conference on Automatic Face & Gesture Recognition (FG 2021)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of predicting student problem-solving outcomes from video in an intelligent tutoring system (ITS). The motivation is that if an ITS can anticipate whether a learner is likely to skip, solve, guess, or need hints, the system may be able to intervene earlier with hints or encouragement and potentially improve learning outcomes.

The authors propose ATL-BP (Affect Transfer Learning for Behavior Prediction), a video-based model that transfers a facial affect representation learned from the AffectNet emotion dataset to student behavior prediction. The model combines an affect embedding, traditional facial analysis features (action units, gaze, head pose from OpenFace), and a two-layer LSTM to model temporal information in webcam video of students solving math problems in MathSpring. They also compare against a version without transfer learning and one using VGG-Face embeddings, and they test user-personalized fine-tuning on the initial portion of a student’s data.

The main datasets are MathSpringSP+ (54 students, 68 sessions, 2,749 math-problem video segments) and a separate children’s dataset collected with the same protocol (51 K-12 students, 968 segments). Results show that the proposed model improves outcome prediction over prior work, especially with user personalization: on MathSpringSP+ with leave-users-out and personalization, ATL-BP with affect embedding reaches mean F-score 0.308 and accuracy 55.1%, compared with 0.206 and 43.8% for the prior method. On the children dataset, finetuning with child-face affect datasets further improves performance to mean F-score 0.278 and accuracy 45.2%.

finding.finding_summary: The paper evaluates an ITS-related classifier for math-problem outcome prediction, not math achievement directly. On MathSpringSP+, the proposed ATL-BP model with affect embedding improved 7-class problem-outcome prediction to accuracy 60.2% and mean F-score 0.330 versus 46.2% accuracy and 0.228 F-score for the prior method (n=54 students, 2,749 problem samples). With leave-users-out personalization, performance further improved to 55.1% accuracy and 0.308 F-score versus 43.8% and 0.206 for the prior method.
finding.measure: 7-class math problem outcome prediction accuracy and mean F-score on MathSpring/MathSpringSP+

finding.finding_summary: The model is explicitly motivated by affect-sensitive tutoring and uses facial affect features to predict student behavior from video, which is a direct proxy for engagement/emotion-related states during problem solving. On the children dataset (n=51 K-12 students, 968 samples), finetuning with children’s affect embeddings improved prediction to 45.2% accuracy and 0.278 mean F-score versus 32.0% and 0.202 for the prior method, suggesting better detection of affect-linked behavioral states relevant to intervention timing.
finding.measure: Behavior/outcome prediction from facial affect, gaze, head pose, and gesture signals during math tutoring

paper_profiles.title: FineMath: A Fine-Grained Mathematical Evaluation Benchmark for Chinese Large Language Models
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper introduces FineMath, a fine-grained benchmark for evaluating the mathematical reasoning abilities of Chinese large language models (LLMs) on elementary-school mathematics word problems. The authors aim to move beyond coarse accuracy scores by organizing 1,584 problems into 17 math word-problem categories and three difficulty levels based on the number of reasoning steps required.

The benchmark was created by collecting questions from textbooks, workbooks, and the internet, then filtering, standardizing, and manually annotating them. The paper also transforms the items into multiple-choice form for automatic scoring and analyzes how prompting and evaluation format affect results. No instructional intervention or student learning study is conducted; instead, the paper evaluates GPT-4, GPT-3.5-Turbo, and several Chinese LLMs on benchmark performance, as well as contamination risk from overlapping training data.

The main conclusion is that current LLMs still have substantial room for improvement on elementary mathematics reasoning, especially as reasoning step count increases. GPT-4 performs best overall, while some smaller or less instruction-tuned models perform poorly. The authors also find that prompt wording and whether tasks are answered by generation versus option prediction can materially change measured accuracy, and that data contamination can inflate scores for some models.

finding.finding_summary: FineMath is an evaluation benchmark, not a student-outcome intervention study, but it directly measures mathematical reasoning performance on elementary-school math word problems. Across 1,584 items, GPT-4 achieved 0.7266 overall accuracy, GPT-3.5-Turbo 0.6206, and other Chinese LLMs ranged lower; performance declined as reasoning steps increased (e.g., GPT-4 from 0.83 on level-1 to 0.62 on level-3 under Prompt 0).
finding.measure: Accuracy on elementary-school math word problems across 17 categories and three reasoning-step levels

paper_profiles.title: Embracing AI in Education: Understanding the Surge in Large Language Model Use by Secondary Students
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how middle and high school students in the United States are using large language models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT for schoolwork. The authors are motivated by the rapid spread of generative AI in education and the lack of large-scale evidence on secondary students’ real-world usage patterns, especially across grades and socioeconomic contexts.

To address this, the authors conducted a survey of 306 students in grades 6–12 from 43 U.S. states. The survey asked about frequency of LLM use, subjects in which students used LLMs, perceived usefulness, school policy strictness, ethical concerns, and demographic differences such as state technological development, school type, and paid-versus-free access to models. No instructional intervention or outcome test was administered; the paper is descriptive and correlational.

The main finding is that LLM use is widespread: 71% of respondents had used an LLM at least once and 9% used one daily, with usage remaining fairly consistent across grades 7–12. Students reported using LLMs across subjects, including math (28% reported math use), but opinions were mixed because of hallucinations and incorrect answers. The authors conclude that LLM adoption is already common in secondary education and that access differs by region, school type, and paid access, raising equity concerns and motivating proposals for student-adapted models, AI tutors, and AI classrooms.

finding.finding_summary: The survey found that 28% of students reported using LLMs for math assignments, and 43% of LLM users said they found them useful for math and STEM questions. However, students also reported that LLMs sometimes produced incorrect answers and lacked rigorous reasoning, so the paper does not show durable achievement gains in math—only usage and perceived usefulness.
finding.measure: Self-reported LLM use for math assignments; perceived usefulness for math/STEM questions

finding.finding_summary: Students reported using LLMs across multiple school subjects, including language arts, history, foreign languages, and math. The strongest usage signal was in writing-oriented tasks, with 57% of LLM users reporting that the tools were useful for writing text; students also noted occasional hallucinations in history and factual contexts.
finding.measure: Self-reported subject areas for LLM use; perceived usefulness for writing text

finding.finding_summary: The paper captures students’ perceptions that LLMs may help simplify complex topics, but it also reports concerns that reliance on such tools could reduce fundamental skills and that LLMs sometimes answer inaccurately. These responses suggest mixed perceived effects on critical thinking and related durable skills, but no direct skill assessment was conducted.
finding.measure: Open-ended survey responses about academic performance and LLM helpfulness

finding.finding_summary: The study found widespread LLM use despite school restrictions: students rated school policy strictness at an average of 3.48/5, while their average ethical-concern rating was 2.83/5. The paper also identified disparities in access, with 80.2% usage in the five most technologically advanced states versus 64.3% elsewhere, and 76.7% usage among private-school students versus 71.3% in public schools.
finding.measure: Self-reported school policy strictness, ethical concern, and LLM usage rates by state technology index and school type

paper_profiles.title: Chat-Based Support Alone May Not Be Enough: Comparing Conversational and Embedded LLM Feedback for Mathematical Proof Learning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether an LLM-based tutoring system can improve learning in an undergraduate discrete mathematics course, with a specific focus on proof writing. The authors ask whether earlier access to GPTutor is associated with better homework and exam performance, and whether different forms of LLM support relate differently to student reliance and outcomes.

GPTutor combines two supports: a conversational chatbot for math questions and a structured proof-review tool that gives localized feedback on students’ written proof attempts. In an IRB-approved classroom deployment at a large US research university, 155 consenting students were randomly assigned to early vs. delayed access in a staggered-access design; 148 students were included in the main analyses. The study uses homework scores, midterm exam scores, interaction logs, a baseline self-efficacy survey, and coded chatbot session behaviors to compare the two tools.

Results show that earlier access to GPTutor was associated with higher homework performance during the period when only the experimental group had access (B = 2.71, 95% CI [0.32, 5.09], β = 0.23), but this advantage did not transfer to Midterm 2 or Midterm 3 scores. Lower self-efficacy and lower prior performance predicted greater use of both tools. However, only chatbot use was negatively associated with subsequent Midterm 3 performance (B = -0.030, p = .014), while proof-review use showed no independent association.

The paper further finds that answer-seeking and escalation behaviors in chatbot sessions are associated with lower Midterm 3 performance, even after accounting for prior achievement in some models. The authors conclude that conversational LLM support may be a marker of difficulty and potential overreliance risk, whereas structured feedback anchored in students’ own work appears less likely to relate to poorer outcomes. Overall, the study argues that interface design matters: chat alone may not be enough for durable proof-learning gains, and work-anchored feedback may be a more promising direction.

finding.finding_summary: Earlier access to GPTutor was associated with higher homework performance during the interval when only the experimental group had access, with a mixed-effects regression estimate of B = 2.71 (SE = 1.22), 95% CI [0.32, 5.09], p = .026, standardized β = 0.23, based on the HW5-HW6 interval. However, this advantage did not transfer to exam performance: Midterm 2 and Midterm 3 differences by condition were not statistically significant after controlling for Midterm 1.
finding.measure: Homework scores (HW5-HW6) and midterm exam scores (Midterm 2, Midterm 3) in discrete mathematics proof learning

finding.finding_summary: Lower baseline self-efficacy was associated with greater use of both GPTutor components: chatbot usage (r = -0.34, β = -27.70, p < .001) and proof-review usage (r = -0.30, β = -4.30, p < .001). In the mediation model, lower self-efficacy also predicted higher chatbot use (B = -20.52, p = .004) and proof-review use (B = -3.59, p = .006), suggesting that students with lower confidence relied more heavily on the system.
finding.measure: Baseline mathematics self-efficacy survey and GPTutor usage frequency

finding.finding_summary: Chatbot reliance was negatively associated with later exam performance beyond prior achievement and self-efficacy. In the multiple regression predicting Midterm 3, chatbot usage remained a significant negative predictor (B = -0.030, SE = 0.012, p = .014), while proof-review usage was not significant (B = 0.048, p = .480). Session-level labels also showed that students who ever exhibited answer-seeking intent scored lower on Midterm 3 (Δ = 8.1 points, |d| = 0.55), and those who escalated after pedagogical responses also scored lower (Δ = 9.1 points, |d| = 0.62).
finding.measure: Chatbot usage frequency, answer-seeking/escalation session labels, and Midterm 3 performance
finding.confidence_interval: [2.9, 17.4] for non-user vs answer-seeking comparison; other CI not_reported

finding.finding_summary: Proof-review usage was not independently associated with Midterm 3 performance after controlling for baseline self-efficacy and prior performance (B = 0.048, SE = 0.067, p = .480). In the mediation model, the proof-review pathway was also not significant (indirect effect = -0.24, 95% CI [-0.72, 0.12]), suggesting no detectable association between structured feedback use and later exam performance in this dataset.
finding.measure: Proof-review usage frequency and Midterm 3 score

paper_profiles.title: Take Out Your Calculators: Estimating the Real Difficulty of Question Items with LLM Student Simulations
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether large language models can simulate student responses well enough to estimate the difficulty of K–12 mathematics items. The motivation is practical: standardized test item difficulty is usually established through expensive human pilot studies, so the authors explore whether open-source LLMs can serve as a lower-cost screening tool for assessment development.

The study uses 631 NAEP multiple-choice math items from grades 4, 8, and 12. The authors compare several prompting strategies and model families, including direct difficulty prediction from text, direct prediction of percent-correct, and simulated student-response generation followed by Item Response Theory (IRT) estimation. They also vary classroom size, student identifiers, and demographic-style first names to see whether these factors improve alignment with real NAEP item statistics.

Results show that direct text-based and direct percent-correct prompting are weak, but simulated student responses correlate moderately to strongly with real item performance, with the best reported correlations reaching 0.75, 0.76, and 0.82 for grades 4, 8, and 12, respectively. Diverse-name prompts and larger simulated classrooms improve performance, and an ensemble of top models performs especially well. The paper concludes that LLM-based student simulation may be a useful preliminary tool for item screening, though it is not a substitute for human piloting and still struggles to model distractor choice and some content areas such as algebra.

finding.finding_summary: Simulated student responses from open-source LLMs aligned moderately to strongly with real NAEP mathematics item performance across grades 4, 8, and 12. Using a classroom size of 300, the best simulations reached Pearson correlations of r=0.69 (Grade 4), 0.61 (Grade 8), and 0.74 (Grade 12) for Gemma-2-9B, while weighted ensembles of top models reached r=0.75, 0.76, and 0.82 across the three grades. The resulting IRT-estimated difficulties also discriminated easy vs. hard items well, with AUC values reported in the 0.78–0.90 range for Gemma models.
finding.measure: NAEP multiple-choice math item percent-correct rates and IRT-estimated item difficulty alignment with expert difficulty labels / real-world item statistics

paper_profiles.title: Investigating the Effectiveness of ChatGPT in Mathematical Reasoning and Problem Solving: Evidence from the Vietnamese National High School Graduation Examination
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper evaluates ChatGPT’s ability to solve high-school mathematics multiple-choice questions from the Vietnamese National High School Graduation Examination (VNHSGE) across 2019–2023. The authors assembled a dataset of 250 questions spanning four cognitive levels (knowledge, comprehension, application, high application) and ten math topic areas, then prompted ChatGPT to answer each item and compared its responses against the official keys.

The study asks whether a generative AI chatbot can reliably handle high-stakes high-school math problems and where its strengths and weaknesses lie by topic and difficulty. ChatGPT performed best on low-difficulty items, with 83% accuracy on knowledge-level questions and only 10% on high-application questions; overall average performance was 147/250 correct (58.8%), with year-level scores ranging from 5.2 to 6.6 on a 10-point scale. Performance was especially weak on items requiring graph interpretation or more advanced spatial/calculus reasoning, and stronger on arithmetic progression, geometric progression, and exponential/logarithmic functions.

The paper also compares ChatGPT’s performance to Vietnamese students and to other exams (SAT Math, AP Statistics, GRE Quantitative, AMC 10/12, AP Calculus BC) using figures and reported benchmark numbers. The authors conclude that ChatGPT has potential as a supportive teaching tool for mathematics but is currently limited by difficulty handling higher-order problems and visual/graphical information. Because the paper is a benchmark-style capability assessment rather than an educational intervention study, it provides indirect evidence about generative AI in K-12 mathematics rather than classroom implementation evidence.

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT answered 147 of 250 Vietnamese national high-school math exam questions correctly overall (58.8%). Performance was much higher on knowledge-level items (85/103 correct, 83%) than on higher-order items, where accuracy fell to 62% for comprehension, 27% for application, and 10% for high-application questions. The study also reports topic-level accuracy ranging from 0% to 100% depending on topic and year.
finding.measure: Accuracy on multiple-choice mathematics exam questions; year-level math score on a 0-10 scale

paper_profiles.title: AI to the rescue: Exploring the potential of ChatGPT as a teacher ally for workload relief and burnout prevention
paper_profiles.venue: Research and Practice in Technology Enhanced Learning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper explores whether generative AI, specifically ChatGPT, can serve as a teacher assistant to reduce workload and help prevent burnout. The authors ground the study in a literature review on teacher burnout and non-teaching work, arguing that lesson planning and content development are major contributors to workload stress, then test ChatGPT on prompt-based lesson-plan generation for English, science, and math.

The empirical component does not involve students or classroom implementation. Instead, the researchers generate and iteratively revise lesson plans for secondary-level classes, including a Grade 8 math lesson on square roots and cube roots, and evaluate the outputs against the 5Es instructional model. They also test differentiation and content-development prompts. The study concludes that ChatGPT can produce useful first-draft lesson plans and supporting materials, but only with careful, specific prompting and human review; initial outputs were often incomplete or weak, and the tool is positioned as an assistive aid rather than a replacement for teacher expertise.

For the K-12 context, the paper is best understood as an exploratory, prompt-based analysis of ChatGPT's potential to reduce teacher planning workload in secondary schooling, not as a student-impact study. It provides indirect evidence relevant to operational efficiency and teacher support, while explicitly noting limitations in ecological validity and generalizability to real classrooms. The math-specific content is limited to lesson-planning examples rather than measured student mathematics outcomes.

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT showed potential to reduce teacher workload by rapidly generating lesson plans and supplementary materials for secondary classes, including a Grade 8 math lesson on square roots and cube roots. The authors report that the tool could produce usable drafts, but only after multiple specific prompts and human refinement; no student-level outcomes were measured.
finding.measure: Quality of ChatGPT-generated lesson plans evaluated against the 5Es instructional model; teacher workload implications inferred from prompt-based lesson planning tasks

paper_profiles.title: Pre-service teachers and ChatGPT in multistrategy problem-solving: Implications for mathematics teaching in primary schools
paper_profiles.venue: International Electronic Journal of Mathematics Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how ChatGPT compares with pre-service primary school teachers (PSTs) in solving a single mathematical word problem using multiple problem-solving strategies. The study is situated in teacher education rather than a K-12 classroom trial: 58 final-year PSTs from an Australian university solved the same problem individually as part of coursework, and ChatGPT 3.5 was prompted to solve it in several ways tailored to a primary-school context.

The main focus is not student learning but the kinds of strategies used and whether the solutions were correct and appropriate for primary-school teaching. PSTs produced a range of approaches, most commonly guess-check-refine, diagrams, tables, and some algebraic methods; their solutions were mostly correct, though some strategies were judged not developmentally appropriate for children. ChatGPT sometimes produced correct answers, especially with algebraic prompts, but often failed when asked to use non-algebraic strategies such as guessing, manipulatives, counting, or visual representations, and it occasionally misinterpreted its own table-based reasoning. The author concludes that ChatGPT may be useful in teacher education for discussing multiple strategies, but its outputs must be verified and contextualized for primary mathematics instruction.

finding.finding_summary: This study directly examined mathematical problem-solving performance on a single word problem. Among 58 pre-service teachers, most solutions were correct, and ChatGPT achieved correct answers mainly when using algebraic prompts (5/5 correct trials), but it was often incorrect for other strategies such as guess-check, counting by twos, manipulatives, and most visual approaches.
finding.measure: Accuracy of solutions to a mathematical word problem; problem-solving strategies used
finding.study_size: n=58 PSTs; ChatGPT trialed 5 times per prompt across 4 prompts

paper_profiles.title: MathChat: Converse to Tackle Challenging Math Problems with LLM Agents
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper presents MathChat, a conversational framework for solving difficult math word problems with large language models (LLMs) and tool use. The system pairs an LLM agent with a user-proxy agent that extracts Python code, executes it, and feeds results back to the model, enabling iterative multi-turn problem solving. The authors also introduce a prompt that combines strategy selection, step-by-step reasoning, and tool use.

The evaluation is conducted on level-5 problems from the MATH benchmark, which the authors describe as primarily challenging high-school competition mathematics. They compare MathChat against zero-shot vanilla prompting, Program of Thoughts prompting, and Program Synthesis prompting, using GPT-4 across six MATH categories (with Geometry removed). MathChat achieves the highest overall accuracy (44.71% vs. 37.67% for PoT, 39.60% for PS, and 28.69% for vanilla), with especially notable gains in Algebra.

The study is an empirical benchmark of LLM math-solving performance, not a K-12 classroom intervention. It provides indirect evidence relevant to advanced secondary mathematics because the test set is drawn from high-school competition problems, but it does not involve students, teachers, or learning outcomes in authentic educational settings. The paper also includes failure analysis showing that many errors arise from planning failures, execution mistakes, and technical issues in tool use.

finding.finding_summary: On 1,192 level-5 MATH test problems (six categories, Geometry excluded), MathChat achieved 44.71% accuracy overall, outperforming Program of Thoughts (37.67%), Program Synthesis (39.60%), and vanilla prompting (28.69%). The largest gain was in Algebra (59.93% vs. 42.67% PoT and 43.32% PS), indicating that conversational tool use improved performance on difficult high-school-level mathematics problems.
finding.measure: Problem-solving accuracy on MATH level-5 problems

paper_profiles.title: Evaluating large language models in analysing classroom dialogue
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether a generative AI model, GPT-4, can accurately and efficiently analyze classroom dialogue for educational research and teaching diagnosis. The motivation is methodological: traditional qualitative coding of lesson transcripts is slow, labor-intensive, and subject to coder variability.

The authors collected classroom video and transcript data from two junior high school classes in Beijing, one mathematics and one Chinese language, spanning six lessons per subject. They created a customized GPT-4 workflow using retrieval-augmented generation and prompt engineering based on a classroom dialogue coding scheme, then compared GPT-4’s codes with human expert annotations.

The study does not test student learning outcomes or an instructional intervention in mathematics; rather, it evaluates AI-assisted qualitative analysis. GPT-4 substantially reduced coding time and showed high agreement with human coders on most dialogue categories, but performance was uneven for more context-dependent codes such as coordination/synthesis categories. The authors conclude that LLMs have strong promise for scalable classroom dialogue analysis, while noting the need for broader validation across subjects, ages, and settings.

finding.finding_summary: GPT-4 dramatically improved the efficiency of classroom dialogue coding compared with manual annotation. For one math lesson (82 dialogue turns; 41 min 29 s), manual coding took about 150 minutes while ChatGPT/GPT-4-based coding took about 5 minutes, a roughly 30× time-saving factor. Across the dataset, the authors report that total AI-assisted analysis of the classroom dialogue corpus did not exceed one hour.
