finding.measure: Time to code classroom dialogue transcripts; coding efficiency
finding.study_size: n=12 lessons total (6 math, 6 Chinese); time comparison reported on one math lesson with 82 dialogue turns

finding.finding_summary: The paper substantively evaluates GPT-4’s ability to reproduce human qualitative coding of classroom dialogue, which is a research task tied to analytical reasoning and interpretation. Inter-coder agreement between human coders and GPT-4 was high overall, with reported agreement above 90% in both math (90.37%, 576 turns) and Chinese (90.91%, 348 turns) lessons, although some higher-order categories showed much weaker agreement.
finding.measure: Agreement and Cohen’s kappa for dialogue coding categories
finding.study_size: Math: 6 lessons, 576 dialogue turns; Chinese: 6 lessons, 348 dialogue turns

paper_profiles.title: Retrieval-augmented Generation to Improve Math Question-Answering: Trade-offs Between Groundedness and Human Preference
paper_profiles.venue: NeurIPS 2023 Workshop on Generative AI for Education (GAIED)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) can improve the quality of generative AI responses for middle-school math question answering, and whether increasing groundedness in a textbook comes at a cost in human preference. The authors built a RAG system using OpenAI GPT-3.5-turbo and an OpenStax Prealgebra textbook as the retrieval corpus, then varied prompt guidance across conditions to test how much the model’s responses reflected the retrieved source material.

The paper includes three small studies. Study 1 compares groundedness metrics across prompt conditions on 51 real student math questions from the Math Nation platform. Study 2 surveys 9 educators/education technology designers who ranked responses for the same questions under none, low, and high guidance prompts and rated groundedness. Study 3 examines whether the relevance of the retrieved document predicts groundedness and preference. The main finding is that RAG can increase perceived groundedness, but the most preferred responses were those with low guidance rather than the most heavily grounded responses; too much textual grounding could reduce response quality or conversational usefulness.

This is not a student learning study and does not measure math achievement. It is an early systems-and-preference evaluation of generative AI for conceptual middle-school math QA, intended to inform future classroom deployment. The authors explicitly note that future work should test actual middle-school students and learning outcomes.

finding.finding_summary: The paper evaluates generative math QA responses for middle-school algebra and geometry questions, but it measures response groundedness and human preference rather than student math learning. Across 51 real student queries, low-guidance RAG responses were preferred over both no-guidance and high-guidance responses, while high guidance produced the most grounded responses (mean groundedness 0.90 vs 0.59 low and 0.52 none).
finding.measure: Human preference rankings and groundedness judgments of generated math QA responses

finding.finding_summary: The paper frames RAG as a way to support scalable conceptual math tutoring by automating parts of the tutoring process and making responses more closely aligned with vetted materials. However, it does not directly measure time savings, teacher workload, or production efficiency; the evidence is limited to feasibility and preference outcomes in a prototype system.
finding.measure: Prototype RAG system feasibility and survey-based response quality judgments

paper_profiles.title: Tareas matemáticas abiertas como respuesta didáctica a la inteligencia artificial generativa en contextos post-IA
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses how school mathematics might be redesigned in so-called post-AI contexts, where generative AI tools are widely available and many conventional tasks can be completed automatically. The central concern is not whether AI can solve mathematics problems, but how task design and classroom regulation can preserve students’ mathematical thinking, decision-making, and validation processes.

The paper reports on a classroom experience in secondary education in which open mathematical tasks were implemented alongside a didactic regulation device called COMPAS. COMPAS structures classroom work into phases of understanding the situation, organizing assumptions and data, mathematical modeling, producing and exploring results, analyzing and validating, and sharing/synthesizing. The intervention is framed as a response to generative AI: rather than banning AI or using it uncritically, the teacher uses open-ended tasks that require interpretation, assumption-making, and validation before any AI-supported calculation can be meaningfully used.

Using a qualitative, descriptive-interpretive approach, the study analyzes student written work, classroom interactions, and teacher-observer notes. The classroom context is a secondary mathematics course in regular sessions, with the paper focusing on the forms of mathematical work that emerge when students engage with open tasks under explicit didactic regulation.

The main conclusion is that open tasks, when coupled with explicit regulation, can preserve students’ epistemic control over mathematical activity even in the presence of generative AI. The paper argues that AI becomes a subordinate resource for exploration or checking rather than a replacement for mathematical reasoning, and that tensions between AI outputs and student models can productively prompt revision, discussion, and validation. The paper is conceptual/interpretive rather than outcome-oriented and does not report quantitative effects.

finding.finding_summary: The study reports that, in a secondary classroom experience using open mathematical tasks with the COMPAS regulation device, students maintained epistemic control over mathematical activity even with generative AI available. Students were observed formulating assumptions, building models, and validating results rather than simply accepting AI-generated answers; however, no quantitative effect sizes or inferential statistics were reported.
finding.measure: Student mathematical work, modeling and validation practices, classroom interactions, written productions

finding.finding_summary: The paper describes positive effects on mathematical agency, decision-making, argumentation, and critical validation. Students were reported to take an active role in negotiating assumptions, comparing models, and questioning the plausibility of AI outputs, indicating strengthened metacognitive and critical-thinking behaviors within the classroom task environment.
finding.measure: Observed agency, argumentation, decision-making, and validation during task resolution

finding.finding_summary: The classroom experience is described as sustaining active participation and engagement in mathematical work by preventing premature task closure and encouraging discussion. The paper does not measure motivation or persistence with a formal instrument, but it reports that students remained involved in the task through iterative discussion and validation.
finding.measure: Observed participation and engagement in classroom task work

paper_profiles.title: Designing AI Peers for Collaborative Mathematical Problem Solving with Middle School Students: A Participatory Design Study
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the 2026 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI ’26)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how middle school students perceive and want to interact with generative AI when it is framed not as a tutor, but as a peer in collaborative mathematical problem solving. The authors note that most GenAI-in-education work has focused on one-on-one tutoring, while far less is known about AI designed to participate as a student teammate in small-group math work.

To explore this question, the researchers ran a five-day summer camp with 24 rising grades 6–8 students. Students first completed human-only mathematics collaborative problem solving tasks and then interacted with two AI peers in a web-based technology probe powered by GPT-4o; they also engaged in participatory design activities, poster creation, surveys, interviews, and reflection sessions. The math tasks focused on grade-aligned middle-school topics including ratio and proportional reasoning, expressions and equations, and early functions/geometry.

The study found that students preferred AI peers that provided scaffold-first help, such as hints, checks, concept refreshers, and follow-up practice, rather than direct answers. Students also wanted strong user control over when the AI spoke, how much it said, and what type of help it gave. Quantitatively, AI-peer sessions reduced perceived temporal demand on NASA-TLX but increased physical demand and lowered some group-climate scores, suggesting a tradeoff between faster progress and higher operational/collaboration burden. Qualitatively, students rejected overly teacher-like or repetitive AI behavior and emphasized that an acceptable AI peer should support co-agency, listen, and show emotional attunement during struggle.

Overall, the paper is best understood as a participatory design and formative evaluation study, not an efficacy trial. Its main contribution is a youth-grounded set of design requirements for future GenAI peers in middle-school mathematics collaborative learning, along with an exploratory prototype and descriptive evidence about how students react to such systems.

finding.finding_summary: The study directly centered on middle-school mathematics collaborative problem solving tasks aligned to grade 6-8 standards (ratio and proportional reasoning, expressions and equations, early functions/geometry), but it did not test learning gains. Instead, it showed that students preferred AI help that scaffolded mathematical reasoning with hints, checks, and concept refreshers rather than direct answers.
finding.measure: Performance and experience during grade-aligned mathematics CPS tasks; student preferences for math-help behaviors

finding.finding_summary: Students reported lower temporal demand with AI peers but also described emotional friction, reduced warmth, and frustration when the AI acted in a teacher-like or repetitive way. The paper argues that students valued encouragement, acknowledgment, and emotional scaffolding during moments of uncertainty, even more than perfect correctness.
finding.measure: NASA-TLX subscales; interview and reflection themes about frustration, trust, and emotional support
finding.study_size: n=22 paired survey comparisons; n=18 interviews; n=5 whole-class reflection sessions
finding.effect_size: d=1.15 (temporal demand reduction); d=1.14 (physical demand increase); d=0.94 (ATGS decrease); d=0.81 (GIT decrease)
finding.std_deviation: Temporal demand SDs: 4.38 (AI) vs 4.13 (human); Physical demand SDs: 4.65 (AI) vs 2.41 (human); ATGS SDs: 1.81 (AI) vs 2.05 (human); GIT SDs: 1.58 (AI) vs 1.52 (human)

finding.finding_summary: The paper substantively examined collaboration, co-agency, and coordination in small-group mathematics CPS. Students preferred AI peers that listened, negotiated methods, and supported joint sensemaking; they rejected AI behavior that felt repetitive, overly directive, or nonresponsive. Quantitatively, group integration-task scores were lower with AI peers, indicating weaker perceived coordination.
finding.measure: Group Environment Questionnaire (GEQ), especially Group Integration-Task and Attractions to Group-Social; qualitative accounts of collaboration and co-agency
finding.study_size: n=22 paired survey comparisons; n=18 interviews; n=5 whole-class reflection sessions
finding.effect_size: d=0.81 (lower GIT with AI peers); d=0.94 (lower ATGS with AI peers)
finding.std_deviation: GIT SDs: 1.58 (AI) vs 1.52 (human); ATGS SDs: 1.81 (AI) vs 2.05 (human)

paper_profiles.title: E-EVAL: A Comprehensive Chinese K-12 Education Evaluation Benchmark for Large Language Models
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper introduces E-EVAL, a Chinese K-12 evaluation benchmark for large language models (LLMs). The authors argue that existing LLM benchmarks do not adequately cover Chinese primary, middle, and high school content, especially elementary-level material, and they therefore construct a 4,351-item multiple-choice benchmark spanning 23 subjects, including mathematics, science, language arts, and humanities.

The paper is not an intervention study in classrooms; rather, it evaluates multiple open-source and proprietary LLMs on the benchmark using zero-shot, five-shot answer-only, and five-shot chain-of-thought prompting. The benchmark questions were drawn from homework, practice materials, and mock exams, with manual processing for formulas and multiple rounds of quality checks. For mathematics specifically, the benchmark contains primary, middle, and high school math questions, but the paper only reports model accuracy on these items and does not study student learning, instructional implementation, or educational outcomes.

The main findings are that Chinese-dominant LLMs generally outperform English-dominant models on Chinese K-12 tasks, but performance remains relatively weak on mathematics and other science subjects compared with arts subjects. Few-shot prompting modestly improves performance for most models, while chain-of-thought prompting tends to help science subjects more than arts overall but lowers average performance across the benchmark. The paper concludes that LLMs still struggle with basic elementary math and that stronger educational benchmarks are needed for Chinese K-12 evaluation.

finding.finding_summary: The benchmark includes primary, middle, and high school mathematics items (e.g., n=102 primary math, n=172 middle school math, n=251 high school math). Across models, math/science performance was substantially lower than arts, and the paper reports that LLMs especially struggled with simple primary-school math; for example, top models incorrectly answered a basic time-conversion problem that required choosing the shortest duration. Chain-of-thought prompting improved performance for science subjects, including mathematics, relative to few-shot answer-only in many cases, but overall math remained a weak area.
finding.measure: Multiple-choice accuracy on K-12 mathematics benchmark items
finding.study_size: n=525 math items total (102 primary, 172 middle, 251 high)

finding.finding_summary: The science portion of E-EVAL includes mathematics, physics, chemistry, biology, and primary science. Models generally performed worse on science than arts, but chain-of-thought prompting was reported to help complex science subjects more than few-shot answer-only prompting. The paper emphasizes that structured reasoning supports science problem solving, though overall science accuracy remained below arts accuracy.
finding.measure: Multiple-choice accuracy on E-EVAL science subjects

finding.finding_summary: The paper evaluates model performance across non-math/non-science K-12 subjects such as Chinese, English, politics, history, and geography. Across all tested models, arts subjects were easier than science subjects, and few-shot prompting improved arts performance more than science performance. The benchmark itself is positioned as a broad academic evaluation tool rather than a learning intervention.
finding.measure: Multiple-choice accuracy on K-12 arts/humanities subjects

finding.finding_summary: The paper does not directly measure durable skills in learners, but it does examine whether chain-of-thought prompting improves model reasoning. The authors report that chain-of-thought lowered average accuracy overall while helping structured science problems more than arts problems, suggesting that explicit stepwise reasoning is beneficial only in some contexts.
finding.measure: Prompt-conditioned model accuracy as a proxy for reasoning performance

paper_profiles.title: Should There be a Teacher In-the-Loop? A Study of Generative AI Personalized Tasks Middle School
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether generative AI can support teacher-created personalized mathematics tasks in a middle school setting, and whether teachers should remain “in the loop” when using the tool. The authors focus on teachers using ChatGPT/GPT-4o to modify existing Illustrative Mathematics problems so that they connect to students’ interests, especially popular culture references, while preserving mathematical coherence and realism.

Seven 7th-grade mathematics teachers from six U.S. schools participated. After training, they used ChatGPT to create 143 personalized versions of IM problems across two units: proportional relationships/percentages and expressions/equations/inequalities. Their interactions were logged and coded, and 521 students (512 in the analytic sample) completed the resulting assignments in ASSISTments. Student ratings and open-ended feedback were collected for subsets of problems, allowing the authors to analyze prompting patterns, perceived problem quality, and teacher efficiency over time.

The study finds that teachers typically needed multiple prompts per problem, with an average of 3.2 prompts and about 246 seconds per problem to produce a personalized task. Prompts often focused on adjusting grain size, realism, age-appropriateness, and specific student interests. Students generally preferred fine-grained, specific references, but they did not strongly attend to deeper realism issues. Importantly, using 3–5 prompts was associated with slightly higher student ratings of interestingness and closeness to interests (about 0.24 points on a 5-point scale), but teachers did not become more time-efficient from Unit 4 to Unit 6; in fact, they used more prompts and more time in the second unit, even as student ratings improved.

finding.finding_summary: The study directly examines teacher-generated personalized math problems and their perceived mathematical quality/coherence, but it does not measure student achievement. Teachers reported that mathematical clarity issues were relatively rare (16 prompt instances), and when 3–5 prompts were used to create a problem, student ratings of the problem being interesting and close to their interests were higher by about 0.24 points on a 5-point scale (B=0.240, SE=0.085, p=0.0073).
finding.measure: Teacher prompting/coding of math clarity and student ratings of problem interestingness/closeness to interests
finding.study_size: n=143 problems; n=521 students (512 analytic sample)
finding.std_deviation: SD=2.6 prompts/problem; SD=165.7 seconds/problem; student rating SDs reported for unit means

finding.finding_summary: The paper’s student-facing outcomes are primarily about interest and perceived relevance. Students more often described personalized tasks as interesting when they matched a preferred topic or specific reference, and ratings of interestingness increased modestly when teachers used 3–5 prompts to refine the task. Average interestingness ratings were 2.46/5 overall, with higher ratings in Unit 6 (2.56) than Unit 4 (2.27).
finding.measure: Student self-report ratings of interestingness and closeness to interests; open-ended feedback about interest
finding.study_size: n=454 responses to interest item; n=449 responses to closeness item; n=521 students
finding.effect_size: B=0.33 for unit effect on ratings; B=0.240 for 3–5 prompts vs. other prompt counts
finding.std_deviation: Overall interestingness SD=1.24; closeness SD=1.28; Unit 4 interestingness SD=1.17; Unit 6 interestingness SD=1.26

finding.finding_summary: The study directly measures teacher time and prompting effort while using ChatGPT to personalize math tasks. Teachers averaged 3.2 prompts per problem and 246 seconds per problem (about 4 minutes), and efficiency did not improve over time; in fact, Unit 6 took significantly longer than Unit 4 (286 vs. 204 seconds per problem) and required more prompts (4.6 vs. 3.2). The authors conclude that the process was not particularly time efficient, even after teacher reflection and iteration.
finding.measure: Time to pose each problem; number of prompts per problem; unit-to-unit change in prompt count and time
finding.effect_size: B=1.26 more prompts per problem in Unit 6; B=70.4 seconds more per problem in Unit 6
finding.std_deviation: SD=2.6 prompts/problem; SD=165.7 seconds/problem; Unit 4 SD=153 seconds; Unit 6 SD=169 seconds

finding.finding_summary: The paper infers some teacher learning and refinement in prompting practice, but this is not measured as a durable skill outcome with a validated instrument. Teachers appeared to improve in crafting more interesting problems over time and used reflective iteration, yet they also required more prompts and more time in the second unit, indicating that development in prompting fluency was uneven.
finding.measure: Teacher prompting moves, reflection-based iteration, and change from Unit 4 to Unit 6

paper_profiles.title: Elementary School Students’ and Teachers’ Perceptions Towards Creative Mathematical Writing with Generative AI
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how elementary school students and teachers perceived a GenAI-powered tool designed to support creative mathematical writing. The authors are interested in whether and how generative AI can help young learners create math stories, represent mathematical ideas, and revise AI-generated drafts in a classroom setting.

The study was conducted in six elementary classrooms with 79 fifth-grade students and six teachers across two U.S. schools. Students used a three-step workflow—Ask, Represent, Transform—to engage with math stories, visual representations, and GenAI-assisted story generation using GPT-4 and DALL·E 3. Data came from student focus groups, teacher interviews, open-ended survey responses, and classroom observation notes, and were analyzed thematically.

The main findings were qualitative rather than outcome-based: participants saw GenAI as supporting creativity, mathematical understanding, AI literacy, interest, curiosity, and ownership of learning. At the same time, they identified challenges such as weak critical evaluation of AI output, insufficient feedback and adaptivity, reduced autonomy, limited social interaction, and accessibility gaps. Overall, the paper argues that GenAI may be promising for mathematical creative writing in elementary classrooms, but it needs stronger pedagogical design and classroom integration to support learning rather than simply generating polished text.

finding.finding_summary: Participants reported that GenAI-supported creative mathematical writing helped students understand math problems, represent mathematical ideas, and surface misconceptions, but also created challenges when students struggled to formulate coherent stories and math ideas aligned with the system. This was based on qualitative evidence from 79 fifth-grade students and 6 teachers, with no numerical effect size reported.
finding.measure: Student and teacher perceptions of mathematical understanding, mathematical knowledge representation, and misconception detection during creative math writing activities

finding.finding_summary: Students and teachers perceived the GenAI activity as increasing interest, curiosity, enjoyment, and ownership of learning. The paper reports that students found math more fun and engaging and felt more responsible for their work as authors of math stories, but no quantitative effect sizes were reported.
finding.measure: Perceived interest, curiosity, enjoyment, and ownership of learning from interviews, survey responses, and observation notes

finding.finding_summary: The study found that GenAI-supported math writing was perceived to foster creativity, flexible thinking, prompt engineering, and evaluation of AI strengths and weaknesses. Students described iterating on prompts and revising stories, suggesting gains in divergent and convergent thinking, but the evidence is qualitative and no effect sizes were reported.
finding.measure: Perceived creativity, flexible thinking, prompt engineering, and critical evaluation of AI output

finding.finding_summary: The GenAI tool was perceived to support creative mathematical writing itself, including story generation, original creation, and use of culturally relevant narratives. Students and teachers reported that AI drafts, images, and prompts helped them produce more interesting math stories, but the paper did not report any quantitative writing scores.
finding.measure: Perceptions of creative mathematical writing performance and story creation quality

paper_profiles.title: A Benchmark for Math Misconceptions: Bridging Gaps in Middle School Algebra with AI-Supported Instruction
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper develops and evaluates an algebra misconception benchmark intended for AI-supported educational systems. The authors compile 55 middle-school-algebra-related misconceptions and common errors from 145 prior sources, yielding 220 diagnostic examples, and frame the resource as a bridge between math education research and large language model (LLM) applications.

The paper then uses GPT-4-turbo in two in-context learning experiments to diagnose misconceptions from labeled question-answer pairs. In the first experiment, examples were sampled across the whole dataset; in the second, sampling was constrained within topic. Performance improved from precision/recall of 0.526/0.529 to 0.753/0.748, and expert relabeling of some “errors” as acceptable matches raised the second experiment’s apparent accuracy to 83.91%.

The paper also includes feedback from five middle-school math educators (four interviewed) who rated sample misconceptions as clear and commonly encountered. The educators generally expressed interest in using the benchmark with AI to diagnose misconceptions or support teacher learning, but the study does not test classroom student outcomes, instructional impact, or real-world deployment effects. It is best characterized as a benchmark-building and model-evaluation paper with a small educator feedback component, not an intervention study.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that GPT-4-turbo could diagnose middle-school algebra misconceptions with moderate-to-strong accuracy on a benchmark of 55 misconceptions and 220 diagnostic examples. Performance was 0.526 precision / 0.529 recall in the unrestricted condition (5,500 iterations) and improved to 0.753 precision / 0.748 recall when test items were constrained by topic (1,100 iterations); expert relabeling of some ambiguous cases raised the apparent accuracy to 83.91% in the topic-constrained condition.
finding.measure: Precision and recall for misconception classification on labeled algebra question-answer pairs
finding.study_size: n=220 examples; model evaluations across 5,500 iterations (Experiment 1) and 1,100 iterations (Experiment 2)

finding.finding_summary: The study suggests the benchmark could help educators and AI systems diagnose student misconceptions more efficiently, and four of five surveyed teachers said they were interested in using it for diagnosis or teacher training. However, this is preference/feasibility evidence rather than a measured productivity outcome, and the paper does not report time savings or workload metrics.
finding.measure: Teacher survey/interview responses about potential usefulness for diagnosis and teaching support

finding.finding_summary: Educators reported that the benchmark could support diagnosing students’ thinking and understanding misconceptions, which the authors frame as useful for insight into underlying reasoning. The paper does not directly measure student metacognition or critical thinking, but the central task concerns classification of misconceptions and reasoning patterns in student work.
finding.measure: Human expert judgments about misconception clarity and interpretability

paper_profiles.title: CMATH: Can Your Language Model Pass Chinese Elementary School Math Test?
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether popular large language models (LLMs) can solve Chinese elementary-school math word problems and how their performance varies by grade, problem complexity, and distracting information. To support this, the authors introduce CMATH, a dataset of 1.7k elementary-level Chinese math word problems drawn from real workbooks and exams, each annotated with grade, answer, number of reasoning steps, and number of digits.

The study evaluates several commercial and open-source LLMs in a zero-shot setting, including GPT-4, ChatGPT, and multiple Chinese-language models. The main result is that GPT-4 is the only model that achieves at least 60% accuracy across all six elementary grades; ChatGPT performs well through grade 4 but declines on grades 5–6, and the remaining models perform substantially worse. Accuracy decreases with higher grade level, more reasoning steps, and greater arithmetic complexity, and models other than GPT-4 are also vulnerable to added distractor information.

The paper is not an intervention study in a classroom or field setting; rather, it is a benchmark/evaluation paper on model capability. It provides direct empirical evidence about generative AI performance on K-12 mathematics tasks, but no student learning outcomes or educational implementation outcomes are measured. The conclusions are therefore about model robustness and benchmark performance, not instructional effectiveness.

finding.finding_summary: Across 1.7k Chinese elementary-school math word problems, model performance varied substantially by grade and complexity. GPT-4 was the only model to exceed 60% accuracy across all six grades, while ChatGPT succeeded through grades 1–4 and other models largely failed; accuracy also declined as reasoning steps and digit complexity increased. The distractor dataset (n=60 original items, with 1–5 distractors per item) showed that non-GPT-4 models were readily misled by irrelevant information.
finding.measure: Accuracy on elementary-school math word problems; robustness under distractor-augmented problems

paper_profiles.title: Evaluation Report on Large Language Models Solving High School Mathematics Questions
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This report evaluates how well multiple large language models (LLMs) can solve high school mathematics exam questions. The authors use selected mathematics items from Chinese college entrance examination papers spanning 2019–2023, then query at least eight LLMs via API and compare their outputs using several custom metrics, including accuracy, response time, logical reasoning, guidance sensitivity, and creativity.

The paper is not a classroom intervention or student study; it is a benchmark-style model evaluation using exam questions as test items. Question types include multiple-choice, fill-in-the-blank, and comprehensive problems, and the authors further stratify items by difficulty. They also test prompting variants (e.g., “mathematician,” “college entrance student,” “math teacher”) and multi-solution prompts to examine how guidance changes performance.

Overall, the report concludes that different LLMs trade off among speed, accuracy, reasoning, and creativity. Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and ERNIE-Speed-128K are described as strongest on accuracy for comprehensive and multi-solution items, gemma-2-9b-it and Meta-Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct are often fastest on some item types, and GLM-4-Flash is portrayed as strong in creativity and guidance but slower. Because the paper evaluates model outputs rather than learner outcomes, it provides indirect evidence about generative AI’s potential for mathematics problem solving in high school contexts rather than evidence of instructional effectiveness.

finding.finding_summary: The paper benchmarked eight LLMs on high school mathematics exam questions from 2019–2023, including multiple-choice, fill-in-the-blank, and comprehensive items. Performance varied substantially by model and task: for single-solution accuracy, ERNIE-Speed-128K and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct were best on comprehensive questions (0.950 and 0.850, respectively), while multi-solution accuracy was highest for Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (0.64) and ERNIE-Speed-128K (0.63).
finding.measure: Accuracy on high school mathematics exam questions; response time; logical reasoning; multi-solution richness/complexity

finding.finding_summary: The report explicitly evaluated logical reasoning and creativity-related dimensions of the models’ outputs, which are closer to durable skills than academic achievement. Logical scores ranged from 0.28 (Meta-Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct) to 0.42 (Hunyuan-lite), and creativity-related complexity scores ranged from 33 (Yi-34B) to 68 (GLM-4-Flash), indicating notable between-model differences in reasoning and solution diversity.
finding.measure: Logical reasoning score, guidance attempts/success rate, creativity/solution complexity, solution richness

finding.finding_summary: A major focus of the paper is response time, treated as an operational efficiency measure. In single-solution scenarios, gemma-2-9b-it and Meta-Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct were often fastest on easier items, while Yi-34B and GLM-4-Flash were slower; in multi-solution scenarios, Spark-lite was reported as fastest (688 s total) and GLM-4-Flash slowest (7400 s total).
finding.measure: Model response time on math questions, including 95th-percentile timing and total time in multi-solution settings

finding.finding_summary: The paper also evaluates LLMs as general question-answering systems on high school science-style exam items as described in the abstract, but the substantive analyses presented are overwhelmingly mathematics-focused. Because the evidence is not about a non-math academic domain in a direct way, this is only a weak ancillary outcome and should be used cautiously.
finding.measure: Question-answer performance on exam items

paper_profiles.title: Investigating the Effectiveness of ChatGPT in Mathematical Reasoning and Problem Solving: Evidence from the Vietnamese National High School Graduation Examination
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper evaluates ChatGPT’s ability to solve Vietnamese high school mathematics multiple-choice questions from the National High School Graduation Examination (2019–2023). The authors assembled a dataset of 250 questions spanning four Bloom’s-taxonomy difficulty levels (knowledge, comprehension, application, high application) and ten math topics, then prompted ChatGPT to answer each item in a standardized format and compared responses against the official answer keys.

The study is not an intervention trial with students; it is a benchmark-style assessment of a generative AI model’s performance on exam questions. ChatGPT achieved substantially better accuracy on easier items than on harder ones, with reported overall scores ranging from 5.2 to 6.6 out of 10 across years and an average of 5.88/10 (147/250 correct). Accuracy was highest at the knowledge level (83%) and lowest at the high-application level (10%), and performance varied notably by topic, with difficulties especially around derivative/application items and questions requiring graphical interpretation.

The paper also compares ChatGPT’s scores with Vietnamese students’ exam score distributions and with other math exams reported by OpenAI (SAT Math, AP Statistics, GRE Quantitative, AMC 10/12, AP Calculus BC). The authors conclude that ChatGPT has promise as a supportive math tool but still has major limitations in handling harder reasoning tasks and visual/graphical information.

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT showed strong performance on easier mathematics items but weak performance on harder reasoning items. Across 250 VNHSGE multiple-choice questions (n=250), it answered 147 correctly overall (58.8%), with accuracy of 83% on knowledge-level questions, 62% on comprehension, 27% on application, and 10% on high-application items. Topic-level performance also varied widely, and the authors note particular difficulty with derivative/application items and questions requiring graphical interpretation.
finding.measure: Accuracy on Vietnamese high school mathematics multiple-choice exam questions; topic- and difficulty-level correctness rates

paper_profiles.title: AMO-Bench: Large Language Models Still Struggle in High School Math Competitions
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper introduces AMO-Bench, a new benchmark for evaluating large language models (LLMs) on advanced mathematical reasoning at the level of high school mathematics competitions and above. The benchmark contains 50 human-crafted, original problems spanning algebraic equations and inequalities, functions and sequences, geometry, number theory, and combinatorics. The authors emphasize that the benchmark is designed to avoid contamination from prior contest problems, to meet IMO-level difficulty standards, and to support automatic grading through final-answer-only responses.

The paper is not an intervention study in a K-12 classroom; instead, it evaluates 26 LLMs on benchmark problems, using repeated sampling (32 runs per model) and reporting AVG@32 accuracy. The main result is that even the strongest model achieves only 52.4% accuracy on AMO-Bench, with most models below 40%. The authors also report that higher test-time compute generally improves performance and that pass@k increases meaningfully with larger k, suggesting remaining headroom for reasoning improvements.

In the context of K-12 mathematics, the paper is best understood as a benchmark and model-evaluation study rather than direct evidence of AI use in classrooms. It provides near-adjacent evidence about generative AI capability on high-school-level mathematics tasks, but it does not test student learning, teacher use, or instructional impact.

finding.finding_summary: Across 26 LLMs evaluated on 50 Olympiad-level math problems, performance was generally low: most models scored below 40% accuracy, and the best model (GPT-5-Thinking High) reached 52.4% AVG@32. The paper also shows that performance improves with more test-time compute, with pass@32 exceeding 70% for some top-tier models and near-linear gains as output length increases.
finding.measure: Benchmark accuracy on AMO-Bench (AVG@32), pass@k, and output-token scaling on advanced math problems
finding.study_size: n=26 models; 50 problems; 32 samples per model

paper_profiles.title: Students' Perceived Roles, Opportunities, and Challenges of a Generative AI-powered Teachable Agent: A Case of Middle School Math Class
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how middle school students perceive a generative AI-powered teachable agent (TA) used in a real 6th-grade mathematics classroom. The study is motivated by the idea that generative AI could strengthen the long-standing learning-by-teaching approach by making the TA more conversational, personalized, and responsive than earlier teachable agents.

The intervention was an in-class GenAI-powered TA built with GPT-4-Turbo and retrieval-augmented generation, designed for rate-and-ratio math practice. Students in six 6th-grade classes at a public laboratory middle school interacted with the TA during two class periods (47-50 minutes each) and completed eight math problems. Data came from classroom observations, open-ended surveys, and focus-group interviews with 14 selected students, yielding a thematic analysis of students' perceived roles, opportunities, and challenges.

Students described the TA as a learning companion, facilitator, and collaborative problem-solver. They also reported that the experience supported a more student-centered climate, autonomy, cognitive/social/emotional capacities, subject-matter knowledge, intrinsic motivation, and positive attitudes toward AI. At the same time, students identified several barriers, including weak problem presentation, overly surface-level questions, limited accommodation of learning styles, technical glitches, lack of multimodal interaction, weak interoperability, and the need for stronger teacher facilitation. The paper concludes that GenAI may expand the possibilities of teachable agents in K-12 math, but effective instructional design, better interaction quality, and human teacher support remain essential.

finding.finding_summary: In this qualitative classroom study (n=108 sixth-grade students; 14 interviewed), students reported that the GenAI-powered teachable agent helped them better understand rate-and-ratio concepts and apply math knowledge in new contexts. Students said that explaining answers to the TA made basic concepts, models, and formulas clearer, but they also noted that the TA sometimes presented problems in ways that were confusing or insufficiently scaffolded.
finding.measure: Students' perceived math learning, understanding of rate-and-ratio concepts, and application of knowledge; qualitative interview, survey, and observation data

finding.finding_summary: Students reported stronger enjoyment, intrinsic motivation, and self-efficacy when using the GenAI-powered TA. They described the experience as fun and engaging, said it made math feel less dry, and noted increased confidence and energy to persist after errors or frustration.
finding.measure: Students' perceived joy of math, intrinsic motivation, self-efficacy, and engagement; qualitative interview, survey, and observation data

finding.finding_summary: Students perceived gains in cognitive and social capacities, including logical reasoning, reflection, communication, perspective-taking, and collaborative problem-solving. The TA's follow-up prompts such as asking students to elaborate were said to deepen reasoning and encourage students to explain their thinking more clearly.
finding.measure: Students' perceived critical thinking, metacognition, communication, and collaboration; qualitative interview, survey, and observation data

paper_profiles.title: Can ChatGPT pass the Vietnamese National High School Graduation Examination?
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether ChatGPT can solve the Vietnamese National High School Graduation Examination (VNHSGE) well enough to “pass” the exam. The study uses the VNHSGE evaluation dataset, which includes multiple-choice questions across subjects such as mathematics, literature, English, physics, chemistry, biology, history, geography, and civic education, along with literature essays. ChatGPT was prompted in zero-shot mode and its responses were graded against human-verified answer keys.

The intervention is not an educational intervention in the classroom; it is a benchmark-style evaluation of a generative AI model (ChatGPT/GPT-3.5) on high-school exam questions. The authors compare ChatGPT’s scores by subject and year (2019–2023) and also compare them with Vietnamese student score distributions for 2019–2022. They report that ChatGPT’s average subject scores ranged from 4.8 to 7.92, with mathematics around 5.88 and English around 7.92, and conclude that the model would pass the exam under their scoring calculation.

Because the paper is a direct performance evaluation of a generative model on standardized high-school test items rather than a study of student learning, its relevance is mainly to assessment validity and AI capability in education. It provides direct evidence that ChatGPT can answer some Vietnamese high-school exam questions at a passing level, but it does not test classroom use, learning gains, or instructional effectiveness. The paper also notes limitations such as poor handling of some subjects and the lack of image/chart understanding, especially relevant for geography.

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT answered the mathematics portion of the VNHSGE at a passing level, with reported scores ranging from 5.2 to 6.6 across 2019–2023 and an average mathematics score of 5.88. The authors conclude that this level is sufficient to pass the exam, though performance was generally below most Vietnamese students in the comparison analysis.
finding.measure: VNHSGE mathematics score (10-point scale)

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT’s performance varied substantially across non-mathematics subjects on the VNHSGE, with strong results in English and weaker results in chemistry, history, geography, and civic education. Reported average scores across subjects ranged from 4.8 in chemistry to 7.92 in English, and the authors state that ChatGPT passed the overall exam using their scoring formula.
finding.measure: VNHSGE subject scores across literature, English, physics, chemistry, biology, history, geography, and civic education

finding.finding_summary: The paper indirectly addresses higher-order reasoning demands through exam performance, especially in subjects the authors describe as requiring analytical and problem-solving skills. However, this is not a direct measurement of critical thinking or metacognition; the closest empirical evidence is ChatGPT’s subject-specific exam scores, which were weaker in areas like chemistry and civic education and stronger in more text-based subjects.
finding.measure: VNHSGE performance on exam items requiring analytical/problem-solving skills

paper_profiles.title: MathOdyssey: Benchmarking Mathematical Problem-Solving Skills in Large Language Models Using Odyssey Math Data
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper introduces MathOdyssey, a new benchmark dataset for evaluating large language models (LLMs) on mathematical problem solving. The dataset contains 387 expert-crafted problems spanning Olympiad-level, high school, and university-level mathematics, with answer formats including true/false, multiple-choice, and open-answer items. The authors describe the dataset construction, human review process, topic coverage, and evaluation prompts used for grading model responses.

The study benchmarks several open- and closed-source LLMs, including GPT-4 Turbo, GPT-4, GPT-3.5 Turbo, Gemini 1.5 Pro, Claude 3 Opus, Llama-3-70B, and DBRX-Instruct, using chain-of-thought prompting. Results show that models perform well on routine high-school tasks but struggle substantially with Olympiad-level and more complex university-level problems. The paper concludes that while open-source models are narrowing the gap with earlier proprietary models, significant weaknesses remain on the most difficult mathematics questions.

This is not a study of K-12 generative AI instruction or classroom implementation. It is a model-evaluation benchmark paper about LLM mathematical capability, with direct evidence limited to benchmark accuracy on non-student model outputs. For the requested K-12 generative-AI-in-mathematics inventory, it is best treated as a near-adjacent benchmarking source rather than a direct classroom or field study.

finding.finding_summary: Across 387 benchmark problems, LLM performance was strong on routine high-school mathematics but much weaker on Olympiad-level and some university-level topics. For example, GPT-4 Turbo scored 84.78% on high-school mathematics, 49.50% on university-level mathematics, and 10.14% on Olympiad-level mathematics; Llama-3-70B scored 52.17%, 21.78%, and 9.46% respectively. This indicates large performance variation by topic and difficulty rather than uniformly strong math reasoning.
finding.measure: Accuracy on MathOdyssey benchmark questions across Olympiad-level, high school, and university-level mathematics

paper_profiles.title: VNHSGE: VietNamese High School Graduation Examination Dataset for Large Language Models
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper introduces the VNHSGE dataset, a benchmark built from the Vietnamese National High School Graduation Examination and similar exams for evaluating large language models (LLMs). The dataset covers nine high-school subjects, including mathematics, literature, English, physics, chemistry, biology, history, geography, and civic education, and includes both multiple-choice questions and essay items, with Vietnamese and English versions.

The primary goal is not to test an educational intervention with students, but to create a broad evaluation resource for LLM capabilities on real exam content. The authors translate and structure the materials into Word and JSON formats, then use ChatGPT and BingChat to evaluate performance on subsets of the dataset and compare the models' responses with Vietnamese student score distributions. Their main conclusion is that the models can perform near human level in some humanities areas, but they still struggle more in mathematics and the natural sciences, especially on higher-order reasoning and multi-step problems.

Because this is a benchmark/dataset paper rather than a classroom implementation study, the evidence is indirect for K-12 learning outcomes. It does, however, provide descriptive findings about LLM performance on high-school mathematics items and shows that current models have limitations on more complex mathematics tasks.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that ChatGPT and BingChat handled knowledge and comprehension-level mathematics items reasonably well, but they struggled with complex calculations and multi-step deductive reasoning on higher-application problems. The math benchmark includes 2,500 multiple-choice questions drawn from Vietnamese high school exams, but the paper does not report a single overall math accuracy, effect size, or confidence interval for student learning outcomes.
finding.measure: Accuracy on Vietnamese high school mathematics multiple-choice questions and qualitative comparison to student score distributions

finding.finding_summary: The dataset includes literature essay and reading-comprehension items, and the authors state that ChatGPT and BingChat can respond to literary queries and generate essays at a comparatively strong level. However, the paper provides only descriptive claims in the excerpted text and does not report quantified effect sizes or formal learner outcomes for reading and writing performance.
finding.measure: Performance on literature essay, reading comprehension, and writing tasks

finding.finding_summary: The paper covers physics, chemistry, and biology items and reports that the models still have room to improve in these science subjects, especially on more complex, higher-application questions. The evidence is descriptive and benchmark-based rather than an intervention study, so no effect size or statistical uncertainty is reported.
finding.measure: Accuracy on physics, chemistry, and biology exam questions

finding.finding_summary: The authors frame the benchmark as testing reasoning, inference, and multi-step problem solving, especially for higher-application exam items across subjects. They conclude that current LLMs still struggle with advanced deductive reasoning in mathematics and other domains, but no direct student durable-skill outcomes are measured.
finding.measure: Reasoning and multi-step problem-solving performance on exam items

paper_profiles.title: FineMath: A Fine-Grained Mathematical Evaluation Benchmark for Chinese Large Language Models
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper introduces FineMath, a fine-grained benchmark for evaluating the mathematical reasoning abilities of Chinese large language models on elementary-school-level math word problems. The authors curate 1,584 Chinese problems from textbooks, workbooks, and the internet, categorize them into 17 math concept types, annotate difficulty by number of reasoning steps, and also convert items into multiple-choice format for evaluation purposes.

The paper is not an intervention study in K-12 classrooms; rather, it is an LLM evaluation benchmark paper. The authors test GPT-4, GPT-3.5-Turbo, and eight Chinese LLMs under zero-shot prompting, comparing performance across concepts, reasoning-step difficulty, prompts, and answer formats. They report that GPT-4 performs best overall, performance drops as reasoning steps increase, and both prompting and multiple-choice formatting can materially change measured accuracy. They also show that data contamination from Ape210K can inflate results for a contaminated model (MathGLM-10B) relative to a clean subset.

The main conclusion is that FineMath can provide a more diagnostic assessment of elementary math reasoning in Chinese LLMs than simple overall accuracy, but the benchmark paper does not present evidence of classroom or student learning impact. It mainly documents benchmark construction, contamination analysis, and evaluation-method sensitivity for generative AI models.

finding.finding_summary: The paper evaluates LLM performance on 1,584 Chinese elementary math word problems across 17 concept categories and three reasoning-step levels. GPT-4 achieved the best overall accuracy (0.73 under Prompt 0), while performance generally declined as reasoning steps increased; for GPT-4, accuracy was 0.83 on level-1 items, 0.77 on level-2, and 0.62 on level-3.
finding.measure: Accuracy on elementary-school math word problems (concept-level and reasoning-step-level benchmark accuracy)

paper_profiles.title: Generative AI as a lab partner: a case study
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This case study examines how high school students used ChatGPT during a physics laboratory activity and what that reveals about generative AI’s potential role in laboratory learning. The authors were interested in whether students would use ChatGPT as a lab partner for problem solving, conceptual support, and analysis, especially in a setting where the lab was intentionally designed to require students to seek outside help for some parts of the task.

The intervention was a structured high school physics lab on acoustic levitation and the speed of sound in air, carried out with seven small student groups (n=19) in Sweden. Students had access to the free version of ChatGPT (GPT-3.5) during the lab and were filmed, interviewed before and after the session, and analyzed through an inductive narrative approach supplemented by variation theory. The study does not test a learning product against a control condition; instead, it documents naturally occurring student-AI interactions, focusing on how students prompted ChatGPT, what kinds of answers they trusted, and how these interactions shaped their understanding of the lab.

The main conclusion is that ChatGPT can sometimes help students get unstuck by offering formulas, simple explanations, or approximate answers, but its usefulness depends heavily on students’ prior knowledge and ability to judge correctness. Students with more relevant physics knowledge were better able to detect errors or misleading explanations, while novices often accepted answers uncritically or were led toward incorrect interpretations. The authors conclude that generative AI may function as a lab-support tool, but only when students are given sufficient guidance and teachers remain central in framing the task and helping students evaluate AI-generated information.

finding.finding_summary: In a qualitative case study of 19 Swedish high school students working in seven lab groups, ChatGPT sometimes supported scientific reasoning by supplying relevant formulas, helping students compare models for the speed of sound, and prompting reflection on acoustic levitation. However, it also produced vague or incorrect explanations, and students with limited prior knowledge were unable to evaluate those claims well, sometimes adopting misleading interpretations.
finding.measure: Student reasoning during lab analysis and post-lab interviews about acoustic levitation and speed of sound

finding.finding_summary: The paper centers on how ChatGPT affected students’ problem-solving, metacognitive monitoring, and ability to evaluate information quality. Students with stronger prior knowledge and more probing interaction patterns used the tool more productively, while others relied on it uncritically or struggled to assess whether answers made sense.
finding.measure: Observed prompting, follow-up questioning, and students’ self-reports about evaluating ChatGPT responses

finding.finding_summary: Students generally reported skepticism about ChatGPT before and after the lab, but some found it motivating or useful for getting quick help and reducing frustration during difficult tasks. At the same time, over-reliance and misplaced trust were common, suggesting that any engagement benefit was conditional and accompanied by risks to critical engagement.
finding.measure: Pre- and post-lab interviews about trust, usefulness, and willingness to use ChatGPT

paper_profiles.title: Can Generative AI and ChatGPT Outperform Humans on Cognitive-Demanding Problem-Solving Tasks in Science?
paper_profiles.extended_summary: This paper asks whether generative AI systems, specifically ChatGPT and GPT-4, can outperform K-12 students on cognitively demanding problem-solving tasks. Rather than teaching an intervention, the study evaluates the models’ performance on 54 released 2019 NAEP science assessment items spanning grades 4, 8, and 12, then compares model performance to student item performance and item-level cognitive demand.

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT and GPT-4 generally outperformed the majority of students on the NAEP science items, with median percentages of students scoring below the models of 83% (ChatGPT) and 74% (GPT-4) at grade 4, 70% and 71% at grade 8, and 81% and 81% at grade 12. Across the final 47-item comparison set, both models showed strong item-level performance on science problem solving, but were less sensitive than students to increases in cognitive demand except at grade 4.
finding.measure: NAEP science item performance and item-level cognitive-demand coding
finding.study_size: n=47 items in final analysis (54 coded items initially); student samples reported by NAEP included n=30,400 (grade 4), n=31,400 (grade 8), and n=26,400 (grade 12)

paper_profiles.title: The Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence for Upper Secondary Mathematics Education Through the Lens of Technology Acceptance
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the 40th ACM/SIGAPP Symposium on Applied Computing (SAC '25)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how Finnish upper-secondary students perceive the use of generative AI in mathematics learning, using the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) as the main framework. Rather than testing learning gains, it focuses on whether students find GenAI useful, easy to use, enjoyable, and compatible with their prior experience, and how these perceptions shape their intention to use the tool.

The study was conducted in a Finnish general upper secondary school across four classroom teaching experiments during the 2023–2024 school year, involving 135 students in total and 102 respondents in the final survey sample. Students used Microsoft Copilot in advanced mathematics topics including equations and systems of equations, normal distribution, logic and programming, and congruence/Diophantine equations. The activities ranged from one 75-minute lesson to multi-lesson sequences with homework, and prompting was either teacher-prepared or student-directed depending on the session.

Using PLS-SEM and CB-SEM, the authors found that perceived usefulness was the strongest predictor of students’ intention to use GenAI, while perceived ease of use did not significantly predict intention. Perceived enjoyment strongly influenced usefulness and ease of use, and the added compatibility construct improved explanatory power, especially for perceived usefulness. The paper concludes that in this Finnish mathematics context, students’ adoption of GenAI is driven more by practical academic utility than by enjoyment alone, and that alignment with existing digital learning practices matters for acceptance.

finding.finding_summary: The paper is substantively about GenAI use in upper-secondary mathematics, but it does not measure math achievement or learning gains. Instead, it examines students’ acceptance-related beliefs about using Copilot in mathematics tasks across four experiments (final survey n=102; participation across activities n=135), with mathematics topics including equations, normal distribution, logic/programming, and congruence/Diophantine equations.
finding.measure: Technology acceptance constructs in mathematics learning context (perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use, perceived enjoyment, compatibility, intention to use)
finding.study_size: n=102 (survey sample); n=135 (participants across teaching experiments)

finding.finding_summary: Students’ perceived enjoyment was an important antecedent in the acceptance model. In the main model, perceived enjoyment strongly predicted perceived usefulness (β=0.652, p<.001, 95% CI [0.379, 0.877]) and perceived ease of use (β=0.715, p<.001, 95% CI [0.607, 0.806]), although it did not directly predict intention to use (β=0.126, p=.162).
finding.measure: Perceived enjoyment; intention to use GenAI

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly analyzes perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use, and compatibility as predictors of intention to use GenAI, which are closely tied to evaluative judgment and technology adoption rather than content mastery. Perceived usefulness was the strongest predictor of intention to use (β=0.737, p<.001, 95% CI [0.544, 0.868]), and compatibility significantly predicted usefulness (β=0.602, p<.001, 95% CI [0.335, 0.800]).
finding.measure: Technology acceptance / behavioral intention (intention to use GenAI)

finding.finding_summary: The study is centered on whether GenAI is seen as practically useful and easy to integrate into upper-secondary mathematics learning. Perceived usefulness was the strongest determinant of intention to use GenAI (β=0.737, p<.001), and compatibility also improved the model’s explanatory power for usefulness (R² for PU increased from 0.609 to 0.732 when compatibility was added).
finding.measure: Perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use, compatibility, intention to use
finding.effect_size: β=0.737; R² change for PU: 0.609 to 0.732

finding.finding_summary: The authors frame the findings as relevant for how GenAI can be integrated into Finnish upper-secondary mathematics education, especially because students are already accustomed to digital textbooks, computer-based assignments, and digital exams. However, the paper does not evaluate policy, governance, or institutional outcomes directly; its institutional implications are interpretive rather than measured.
finding.measure: Perceptions relevant to integration of GenAI into existing digital learning environments

paper_profiles.title: SCIBENCH: Evaluating College-Level Scientific Problem-Solving Abilities of Large Language Models
paper_profiles.venue: ICML (Proceedings of the 41st International Conference on Machine Learning)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper introduces SCIBENCH, a benchmark for evaluating large language models on college-level scientific problem solving. The benchmark includes 869 textbook problems from mathematics, physics, and chemistry, plus a closed set of 103 exam questions from college CS and math courses. A multimodal subset of 177 problems with figures/graphs is also included. The authors use the benchmark to compare a range of proprietary and open-source LLMs under zero-shot, few-shot, chain-of-thought, and tool-augmented prompting settings.

The central question is not whether an educational intervention improves student learning, but how well current LLMs can solve advanced scientific and mathematical problems. The study finds that performance remains limited even for strong models: GPT-4 with few-shot + Python achieves the best average score on the textbook set (43.22%), while multimodal performance is substantially lower (best reported 13.8%). The paper also analyzes error types via an LLM-based verifier and human annotation, concluding that different prompting strategies improve some skills while degrading others, with no universally effective prompting configuration.

Because this is a benchmark/evaluation study rather than a classroom implementation, it provides indirect evidence about generative AI capabilities in college-level STEM reasoning, not direct evidence about K-12 mathematics instruction or student outcomes. It is useful mainly as near-adjacent contrast for the requested K-12 generative AI mathematics inventory.

finding.finding_summary: The benchmark shows that LLMs can solve some college-level mathematics/scientific computation problems but remain far from reliable. Across the textbook dataset, the best average score was 43.22% for GPT-4 with few-shot prompting plus Python, while many open-source models scored near zero to low single digits on several subsets.
finding.measure: Accuracy on college-level math and science benchmark problems
finding.study_size: n=869 textbook problems; n=103 closed exam problems; math subset included calculus, statistics, probability, differential equations

finding.finding_summary: SCIBENCH was designed to assess scientific problem-solving across mathematics, physics, and chemistry, and it shows that current LLMs struggle with multi-step scientific reasoning, especially when problems require advanced equations, domain knowledge, and/or visual interpretation. The best reported score on the multimodal subset was 13.8%, indicating substantial limitations despite prompting and tool use.
finding.measure: Accuracy on scientific reasoning benchmark problems, including multimodal science questions
finding.study_size: n=869 textbook problems; n=177 multimodal subset; n=103 closed exam problems

paper_profiles.title: Mathematical Capabilities of ChatGPT
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper evaluates the mathematical capabilities of ChatGPT (two January 2023 versions) and GPT-4 on a newly created benchmark, GHOSTS, and a smaller subset, miniGHOSTS. The authors’ main question is not about education implementation, but about how well large language models can handle a broad range of advanced mathematical tasks, including factual recall, proof completion, symbolic integration, olympiad-style problem solving, and search-engine-like retrieval of mathematical definitions and theorems.

The study uses 709 prompts across six subdatasets, many curated by the authors from graduate-level textbooks, olympiad materials, math.stackexchange, and prior math datasets. Outputs were manually rated by experts using a 1–5 scale plus error and warning codes, and GPT-4 was evaluated on a 170-prompt subset. The paper finds that ChatGPT performs inconsistently and is generally below graduate-student level; it is strongest at factual lookup and weakest on proof-based and more advanced reasoning tasks. GPT-4 improves substantially over ChatGPT, especially on undergraduate-level material, but still falls short on graduate-level mathematics and remains error-prone.

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly evaluates mathematical reasoning across 709 prompts for ChatGPT and 170 prompts for GPT-4. ChatGPT’s 9-Jan version averaged 3.20/5 (SD=1.23) and the 30-Jan version averaged 3.29/5 (SD=1.28), while GPT-4 averaged 4.15/5 (SD=1.12) on the miniGHOSTS subset; however, both ChatGPT versions remained below a passing threshold on many subdatasets, especially proof-based and graduate-level tasks.
finding.measure: Human-rated mathematical task performance on the GHOSTS/miniGHOSTS benchmark (1–5 rating scale across proof, computation, integration, and retrieval tasks)

paper_profiles.title: Learning gain differences between ChatGPT and human tutor generated algebra hints
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether ChatGPT-generated algebra hints can support learning as effectively as human-authored hints inside an intelligent tutoring system. The authors frame the study as an initial learning-gain evaluation of generative AI for educational content production, motivated by the labor required to author high-quality hints for adaptive tutors.

The study compares ChatGPT-generated worked-solution hints against existing human tutor hints in Open Adaptive Tutor (OATutor). Participants were 77 Amazon Mechanical Turk workers, assigned randomly in a 2 x 2 design to either Elementary Algebra or Intermediate Algebra lessons and to either manual (human) hints or ChatGPT hints. Each condition included a three-item pre-test, a five-item acquisition phase, and a three-item post-test using the same items as the pre-test. ChatGPT hints were manually quality-checked before use; 30% of generated hints were rejected because they contained incorrect answers or incorrect solution steps.

Results showed that both conditions produced positive learning gains, but only the human-hint conditions showed statistically significant pre-post improvement. Human-authored hints produced substantially higher learning gains than ChatGPT hints in both algebra topics, with the between-condition differences reported as statistically significant (p = 0.038 in both lessons). The authors conclude that ChatGPT-generated hints are not yet competitive with human-authored hints in this setting and still require human supervision.

finding.finding_summary: In this randomized study with 77 Mechanical Turk participants, ChatGPT-generated algebra hints produced positive learning gains but significantly smaller gains than human-authored hints in both Elementary Algebra and Intermediate Algebra. The between-condition learning gains were reported as statistically significantly different (p = 0.038 in both topic areas), and only the human-hint conditions showed significant pre-post improvement.
finding.measure: Pre-test to post-test algebra score gains in OATutor lessons on equation solving

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT-generated help produces learning gains equivalent to human tutor-authored help on mathematics skills
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper evaluates whether generative AI can author effective mathematics tutoring hints. The authors test ChatGPT-generated worked-solution hints against human tutor-authored hints and a no-hint control in an online mathematics learning environment, focusing on whether ChatGPT can both produce usable instructional content and support learning as well as human-authored help.

The study uses a 3 x 4 randomized design with 274 Mechanical Turk participants, each assigned to one of three hint conditions (control, human tutor, ChatGPT) and one of four mathematics subject areas: Elementary Algebra, Intermediate Algebra, College Algebra, or Statistics. Learners completed a three-item pre-test, a five-problem acquisition phase, and a three-item post-test using OpenStax-derived problems in OATutor. The paper also separately evaluates hint quality, finding that 32% of ChatGPT-generated hints failed quality checks due to incorrect work or answers; self-consistency reduced errors substantially, especially in algebra.

For learning outcomes, ChatGPT hints produced a statistically significant overall gain relative to pre-test scores and outperformed the no-hint control, while human tutor hints also improved learning but were not statistically distinguishable from ChatGPT. Time-on-task was higher for both hint conditions than control, but ChatGPT and human hints did not differ significantly in time spent. The authors conclude that ChatGPT can generate mathematics help that is educationally comparable to human-authored help in this setting, but raw outputs still require quality control because of substantial error rates.

finding.finding_summary: In a randomized 3-condition study (N=274 analyzed), ChatGPT-generated worked-solution hints produced statistically significant learning gains on mathematics problems. Participants in the ChatGPT condition improved from 43.51% pre-test to 60.52% post-test (17.00% gain), outperforming the no-hint control (1.85% gain) and not differing significantly from human tutor-authored hints (11.62% gain).
finding.measure: Pre-test and repeated post-test scores on OpenStax-derived algebra and statistics problems delivered in OATutor

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly evaluates efficiency of generating instructional content with ChatGPT versus human tutor authoring. ChatGPT-produced hints were generated much faster than human-authored help, and the authors report that ChatGPT hints were produced in roughly 1/20th the time required for human tutor-authored hints; however, raw ChatGPT output also required substantial quality checking because 32% of hints failed the quality screen.
finding.measure: Hint generation time and manual quality-check time for instructional content creation

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT for Good? On Opportunities and Challenges of Large Language Models for Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a position paper that discusses the potential opportunities and challenges of large language models, especially ChatGPT and GPT-3, for education. It does not report a primary empirical study; instead, it synthesizes early examples and conceptual arguments about how LLMs might support learning, teaching, assessment, personalization, and educational content generation.

The paper covers use cases across educational levels, including primary, secondary, tertiary, and professional learning, but these are presented as illustrative possibilities rather than evaluated interventions. It highlights potential benefits such as personalized feedback, quiz generation, adaptive tutoring, and support for writing and problem solving, while also emphasizing risks including bias, privacy, plagiarism, overreliance, and difficulty distinguishing machine-generated from human-generated work.

For mathematics education specifically, the paper briefly notes that language models may be used to generate math word problems and other practice materials, but it does not present direct empirical evidence on K-12 mathematics learning, implementation, or outcomes. Its main conclusion is that LLMs are promising but require careful governance, human oversight, and further research before responsible educational integration.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that integrating large language models into education has both opportunities and serious institutional risks. It emphasizes the need for policies, human oversight, privacy protections, bias monitoring, and curriculum guidance, but reports no empirical institutional outcome data.
finding.measure: conceptual discussion of governance, policy, privacy, bias, and responsible deployment

finding.finding_summary: The authors suggest that LLMs could reduce teacher workload by helping with quiz generation, personalized feedback, lesson planning, and assessment, including semi-automated grading. However, these claims are speculative and not supported by direct empirical results in this paper.
finding.measure: conceptual discussion of teacher workload and productivity

finding.finding_summary: The paper discusses possible effects on critical thinking, problem solving, and fact-checking, arguing that LLMs may support these skills if used appropriately but may also weaken them through overreliance. No direct student outcome measures are reported.
finding.measure: conceptual discussion of critical thinking, problem-solving, and fact-checking

paper_profiles.title: Is ChatGPT a Good Teacher Coach? Measuring Zero-Shot Performance For Scoring and Providing Actionable Insights on Classroom Instruction
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the 18th Workshop on Innovative Use of NLP for Building Educational Applications (BEA 2023)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether ChatGPT can serve as an automated teacher coach by scoring classroom observations and generating feedback from elementary mathematics classroom transcripts. The authors define three zero-shot tasks for the model: predicting rubric scores from CLASS and MQI observation instruments, identifying highlights and missed opportunities in instruction, and giving actionable suggestions for eliciting more student mathematical reasoning.

The study uses the NCTE transcript dataset, which contains 1,660 video-derived 45–60 minute observations from 317 teachers across four school districts. For the main evaluations, the authors sample 10 transcripts for each quantitative scoring task family and 18 transcript segments for the qualitative feedback tasks, then compare ChatGPT’s outputs to expert human ratings and teacher judgments. The setting is U.S. elementary math classrooms, so the paper is directly relevant to K-12 math instruction, but it is not an intervention study with student learning outcomes.

Results show that ChatGPT performs poorly at rubric-based scoring: Spearman correlations with human ratings are low across CLASS and MQI items, and adding rubric descriptions or chain-of-thought-style reasoning does not improve performance. For qualitative feedback, human teachers judged many responses to be relevant or actionable, but often not insightful, and some responses were unfaithful to the transcript; for the suggestion task, 82% of suggestions were redundant, repeating what the teacher already did. Overall, the paper concludes that current generative AI has promise as a scalable coaching aid but is not yet reliable as an expert teacher coach.

finding.finding_summary: The paper evaluates whether ChatGPT can support scalable teacher coaching by automating classroom observation scoring and feedback generation. It finds that the model can sometimes produce relevant and actionable feedback, but it often fails to be insightful and frequently generates redundant suggestions (82% of suggestions repeated what the teacher already did), indicating only partial utility for reducing coaching workload.
finding.measure: Expert teacher ratings of model-generated scoring, highlights/missed opportunities, and actionable suggestions for instructional coaching
finding.study_size: quantitative scoring: n=100 transcript segments; qualitative Task B: 216 CLASS items and 288 MQI items; Task C: 36 suggestions

paper_profiles.title: Evaluating large language models in analysing classroom dialogue
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether a generative AI model, GPT-4, can accurately code classroom dialogue in a way that mirrors human expert annotation. The authors frame classroom dialogue analysis as an important but labor-intensive task for teaching diagnosis and instructional improvement, and test whether a customized GPT-4 system can reduce the time and effort required for qualitative coding.

The study uses transcript data from six mathematics lessons and six Chinese lessons taught in a Beijing middle school. Expert human coders and a customized GPT-4 system independently coded the dialogue using a 15-category classroom dialogue scheme, and the outputs were compared on agreement, Cohen’s kappa, and time required. The paper reports that GPT-4 substantially reduced coding time: one 41-minute math lesson took about 5 minutes with GPT-4 versus roughly 150 minutes manually, a ~30x speedup. Overall agreement between human and GPT-4 coding was high in most categories and around 90% at the dialogue-turn level, but several categories showed weaker performance, especially coordination-related codes, indicating that GPT-4 is promising for accelerating classroom discourse analysis but not uniformly reliable across all dialogue functions.

This is not an intervention study on student learning outcomes or a direct evaluation of mathematics instruction effects.
