Rather, it is a methodological validation study of generative AI for educational research and classroom analytics, with a small middle-school sample and subject-specific coding tasks. The main conclusion is that GPT-4 can approximate human coding well enough to support scalable analysis of classroom dialogue, while still requiring human oversight for nuanced categories and context-sensitive judgments.

finding.finding_summary: GPT-4 greatly reduced the time required to code classroom dialogue compared with manual annotation. For one 41-minute math lesson with 82 dialogue turns, automated coding took about 5 minutes versus about 150 minutes manually, implying roughly a 30x speedup; across the study, automated analysis of the six math lessons and six Chinese lessons reportedly took less than one hour total.
finding.measure: Time required to code classroom dialogue transcripts
finding.study_size: n=12 lessons (6 mathematics, 6 Chinese); detailed time comparison on 1 math lesson (82 turns, 41 min 29 s)

finding.finding_summary: The study found high agreement between human coders and GPT-4 on most classroom dialogue categories, suggesting that the model can support coding of discourse features related to reasoning, elaboration, coordination, and other talk moves. At the dialogue-turn level, agreement was reported as 90.37% for math lessons (576 turns) and 90.91% for Chinese lessons (348 turns), but some nuanced categories such as coordination and reasoned coordination showed weak or near-zero agreement, especially in math.
finding.measure: Inter-coder agreement and Cohen’s kappa for classroom dialogue codes capturing reasoning, elaboration, coordination, and related discourse moves
finding.study_size: n=12 lessons; math n=576 turns, Chinese n=348 turns

paper_profiles.title: MathChat: Converse to Tackle Challenging Math Problems with LLM Agents
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper presents MathChat, a conversational framework for solving difficult mathematics problems with large language models (LLMs) and a user-proxy agent that executes Python code, returns results, and prompts the model to continue or correct itself. The authors combine several prompting strategies—direct reasoning, program-of-thought prompting, and stepwise tool use—into a chat-based workflow designed for GPT-4.

The empirical evaluation is not a classroom or human-learning study; it is a benchmark test on level-5 problems from the MATH dataset. The main evaluation target is challenging high school competition mathematics, covering Algebra, Counting & Probability, Intermediate Algebra, Number Theory, Prealgebra, and Precalculus (Geometry was excluded). MathChat is compared against vanilla prompting, Program of Thoughts, and Program Synthesis on 1,192 problems, with additional 300-problem samples for prompt ablations.

Results show that MathChat improves accuracy over the other zero-shot baselines, reaching 44.71% overall on the full six-category test set versus 39.60% for Program Synthesis, 37.67% for Program of Thoughts, and 28.69% for vanilla prompting. The gains are strongest in Algebra and some computation-heavy categories, suggesting that conversational tool use and error correction can improve LLM math-solving performance. However, the study also emphasizes persistent failure modes and does not claim educational impact on students or classrooms.

finding.finding_summary: MathChat improved GPT-4’s accuracy on challenging high school math problems from the MATH dataset. On the full six-category level-5 test set (n=1,192), MathChat achieved 44.71% accuracy, compared with 39.60% for Program Synthesis, 37.67% for Program of Thoughts, and 28.69% for vanilla prompting. The biggest gains were in Algebra (59.93% vs. 43.32% PS, 42.67% PoT, 46.58% vanilla) and some computation-heavy categories.
finding.measure: Problem-solving accuracy on level-5 MATH benchmark problems

paper_profiles.title: Retrieval-augmented Generation to Improve Math Question-Answering: Trade-offs Between Groundedness and Human Preference
paper_profiles.venue: NeurIPS 2023 Workshop on Generative AI for Education (GAIED)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) can improve the quality of generative AI responses to middle-school math questions. The authors build a conceptual math question-answering system using GPT-3.5 and an OpenStax Prealgebra textbook as the retrieval corpus, then vary prompt guidance to see how grounded the generated answers are and how much humans prefer them.

The study is motivated by the need for scalable, conceptually oriented math tutoring in K-12 settings, especially for students who ask questions about algebra and geometry. The paper uses real student questions drawn from Math Nation discussion boards (51 answerable factual/conceptual questions from 554 posts) and evaluates three prompt conditions plus a retrieval-only baseline. The main experimental work is in three small studies: an automated groundedness comparison, a human preference survey with 9 educators and education-technology designers, and a relevance analysis of retrieved documents.

Results suggest that RAG can improve perceived answer quality, but only up to a point: low-guidance RAG responses were preferred over both no-guidance and high-guidance responses, while overly grounded responses were not preferred. Human ratings showed that high-guidance responses were more grounded in the textbook, but the trade-off is that too much grounding can reduce conversational usefulness. The paper does not measure student learning outcomes; instead, it focuses on response groundedness, human preference, and retrieval relevance as preliminary evidence for designing math QA systems for classroom use.

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests that a retrieval-augmented math QA system can improve the quality of generated responses for tutoring-like use, which may support scalable tutoring workflows, but it does not measure time savings or teacher workload directly. In the human preference study (n=9 raters over 51 queries), low-guidance RAG responses were preferred over no-guidance and high-guidance responses, indicating a potentially more usable system design for classroom-facing deployment.
finding.measure: Human preference rankings of generated QA responses

paper_profiles.title: LLaMA: Open and Efficient Foundation Language Models
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper presents LLaMA, a family of open foundation language models ranging from 7B to 65B parameters. The central problem is how to train competitive large language models using only publicly available data and relatively efficient architectures, while reducing the inference and deployment cost compared with much larger proprietary systems.

The study describes the pretraining corpus, architectural modifications (pre-normalization, SwiGLU, rotary embeddings), optimizer settings, and efficiency techniques used to train the models. It then evaluates model performance on a broad suite of natural language, reasoning, QA, code, bias, toxicity, and truthfulness benchmarks. The paper also includes a small instruction-finetuning experiment (LLaMA-I) showing improved MMLU performance after brief instruction tuning.

This is not an education intervention study and does not examine classroom use, learners, schools, or mathematics instruction in K-12 settings. The only mathematics-relevant evidence is benchmark evaluation on general mathematical reasoning tasks (MATH and GSM8k) for the language model itself, not an educational deployment. The main conclusion is that open models can be trained competitively on public data, with LLaMA-65B matching or exceeding several contemporaneous large language models on many benchmarks, while smaller variants offer substantially lower inference cost.

finding.finding_summary: LLaMA is evaluated on two math reasoning benchmarks, MATH (12K middle/high school math problems) and GSM8k (middle school math word problems), but this is model benchmark performance rather than an educational intervention. LLaMA-65B achieved 10.6 on MATH and 50.9 on MATH with majority voting (k=256), and 50.9 on GSM8k with majority voting 69.7, outperforming Minerva-62B on GSM8k despite not being fine-tuned on math data.
finding.measure: Benchmark accuracy on MATH and GSM8k (exact-match / problem-solving accuracy; majority-vote variants reported)

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT as a Math Questioner? Evaluating ChatGPT on Generating Pre-university Math Questions
paper_profiles.population: Elementary (PreK-5th), Middle School (6-8), High School, Undergraduate/Tertiary
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether ChatGPT can be used to generate pre-university mathematics questions. The authors frame the task in two settings: context-aware generation, where ChatGPT receives a math context and is asked to generate a question (with or without an expected answer), and context-unaware generation, where it is prompted to create questions from math curriculum topics and lesson definitions alone.

In the context-aware experiments, the paper evaluates ChatGPT on three established math question-generation benchmarks: SVAMP, GSM8K, and MATH. The authors compare ChatGPT against fine-tuned baselines such as GPT-2, BART, T5, MixQG, Flan-T5, and ProphetNet using automatic metrics and a human study. In the context-unaware setting, they build TopicMath/PRE-UMATH by crawling Khan Academy curricula across 121 topics and 428 lessons and then prompting ChatGPT to generate question-answer pairs for each lesson. Human educators rate the outputs on grammaticality, answerability, topic alignment, difficulty alignment, and usefulness.

The main conclusion is that ChatGPT can generate grammatically strong and context-relevant math questions, but its questions are often easier than intended, can repeat the input context, and may become trivial or nonsensical when asked to produce harder problems. The paper does not test educational outcomes for students; it is a question-generation and benchmarking study focused on model behavior and output quality. For the K-12 math evidence question, it is directly relevant as a generative AI implementation for math item generation, but it is not a classroom intervention study and provides no evidence on student learning gains.

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT generated pre-university math questions that were judged to be highly grammatical and generally useful for educational purposes, suggesting potential to reduce teacher effort in drafting questions. Human evaluators rated ChatGPT highly on grammaticality (e.g., Table 7 and Table 8 report means around 4.8-5.0/5 across settings), and the authors argue that this makes it a promising tool for question drafting and diversification rather than a direct student-facing learning intervention.
finding.measure: Human ratings of grammaticality, usefulness, topic relevance, and answerability for generated questions
finding.study_size: n=200 randomly selected cases per dataset in context-aware human evaluation; n=500 randomly selected samples in context-unaware human evaluation

paper_profiles.title: Mathematical Capabilities of ChatGPT
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper evaluates the mathematical capabilities of ChatGPT and GPT-4 on a newly constructed benchmark, GHOSTS, along with a smaller GPT-4 subset called miniGHOSTS. The authors designed prompts to probe multiple dimensions of mathematical reasoning, including fact recall, proof completion, symbolic integration, olympiad-style problem solving, and search-engine-like retrieval of mathematical definitions and theorem names.

The benchmark combines hand-crafted items with prompts drawn from existing mathematical datasets and textbooks, spanning elementary arithmetic through undergraduate, graduate, and olympiad-level mathematics. The study reports human-rated scores from 1 to 5 on 709 prompts for two ChatGPT versions and 170 prompts for GPT-4, with fine-grained error and warning codes used to characterize failure modes.

The main conclusion is that ChatGPT is useful mainly as a mathematical lookup assistant and performs inconsistently on advanced mathematics; GPT-4 improves substantially but still falls short of graduate-level performance. The authors find stronger performance on factual retrieval and some undergraduate-level tasks, but persistent weaknesses on proofs, complex symbolic reasoning, and olympiad problems. This is a benchmark/evaluation paper rather than a K-12 classroom intervention study, and it does not provide direct evidence about student learning in K-12 mathematics.

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly evaluates mathematical reasoning performance of ChatGPT (9-Jan and 30-Jan 2023) and GPT-4 on 709 GHOSTS prompts and 170 miniGHOSTS prompts. ChatGPT averaged rating 3.20 (SD=1.23) on the 9-Jan version and 3.29 (SD=1.28) on the 30-Jan version, while GPT-4 averaged 4.15 (SD=1.12) on miniGHOSTS; performance was strong on factual retrieval and some undergraduate tasks but weak on proof-based, olympiad, and graduate-level questions.
finding.measure: Human-rated benchmark scores (1-5) on mathematical prompts spanning factual recall, computation, proof completion, symbolic integration, and olympiad-style problem solving
finding.study_size: n=709 prompts for GHOSTS; n=170 prompts for miniGHOSTS
finding.std_deviation: SD=1.23 (9-Jan ChatGPT); SD=1.28 (30-Jan ChatGPT); SD=1.12 (GPT-4 miniGHOSTS)

paper_profiles.title: Students' Perceived Roles, Opportunities, and Challenges of a Generative AI-powered Teachable Agent: A Case of Middle School Math Class
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how middle school students perceive a generative AI-powered teachable agent (TA) when used in an authentic math classroom. The authors were interested in whether GenAI could extend the longstanding learning-by-teaching approach by making the TA more conversational, adaptive, and engaging, and in what students saw as the roles, benefits, and challenges of such a system.

The intervention was a classroom implementation of a GPT-4-Turbo-powered TA built for 6th-grade mathematics, specifically a rates-and-ratios unit. Students interacted with the TA across two class periods (about 47–50 minutes each) and completed eight AI-generated and human-reviewed math problems. The system used text chat, personalized topic and difficulty choices, gamification elements, and follow-up questions intended to elicit explanation and teaching behaviors from students.

The study used a qualitative, mixed-source design: classroom observation, open-ended surveys, and focus-group interviews with 14 selected students, drawn from a total of 108 sixth graders in six classes at a public laboratory middle school in the southeastern United States. Thematic analysis identified student-perceived roles for the TA (learning companion, facilitator, collaborative problem-solver), perceived opportunities (student-centered climate, autonomy, cognitive/social/emotional growth, improved math understanding, motivation, and positive attitudes toward AI), and barriers (weak problem presentation, superficial questions, mismatched learning styles, technical issues, limited multimodality, poor interoperability, and a need for more teacher facilitation). The paper concludes that GenAI may help realize learning-by-teaching in K-12 math, but only if the system is better designed for pedagogy, usability, and teacher support.

finding.finding_summary: Students reported that interacting with the GenAI-powered teachable agent helped them better understand rates and ratios, revise misconceptions, and apply math knowledge in new contexts. However, these were qualitative perceptions rather than measured achievement gains; the study did not report test scores or effect sizes for the full sample of 108 sixth graders.
finding.measure: Students' perceived understanding of rate and ratio, application of knowledge, and qualitative classroom observations

finding.finding_summary: Students described increased enjoyment of math, stronger self-efficacy, and higher intrinsic motivation while using the GenAI-powered TA. They also reported more engagement, enthusiasm, and willingness to continue working on problems, but these outcomes were based on thematic self-reports rather than standardized pre/post measures.
finding.measure: Perceived joy of math, self-efficacy, intrinsic motivation, and engagement from open-ended surveys, interviews, and observations

finding.finding_summary: Students perceived gains in cognitive, social, and emotional capacities, including elaboration, reasoning, perspective-taking, communication, and reflective thinking. They said the TA's prompts like 'Can you elaborate?' pushed them to explain their thinking more deeply and adapt explanations to the agent's perspective, but the paper did not include quantitative skill measures.
finding.measure: Perceived reasoning, elaboration, communication, perspective-taking, and reflective thinking

finding.finding_summary: The paper also found that students perceived interdisciplinary learning, especially noticing connections between computer science/AI and mathematics. This was a secondary theme rather than a primary outcome, and it was supported by qualitative comments about learning 'computer science and math at the same time.'
finding.measure: Perceived interdisciplinary learning and AI awareness

paper_profiles.title: Elementary Math Word Problem Generation using Large Language Models
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of automatically generating elementary-school math word problems (MWPs) with large language models (LLMs). The authors aim to create a system that can produce problems from scratch given only the desired grade, section/topic, and number of questions, reducing the time tutors spend manually authoring practice items. The work is explicitly framed as generative AI for educational content creation rather than student learning, and it focuses on K-6 math curriculum alignment, especially grades 1 through 6 under the Common Core Standards for Mathematics.

The intervention studied is a multi-stage LLM-based MWP generation pipeline. The authors compare open-source models (Llama-2, Mistral, Zephyr), prompt templates, decoding settings for diversity, fine-tuning with two created datasets, few-shot prompting, preference optimization (DPO, KTO, CPO), and a secondary LLM-based solvability filter. They also create and release two datasets: a 4K MWP corpus with grade and section labels, and a 1,005-item preference dataset for alignment methods. Human evaluation plus LLM-based evaluation is used to score generated problems across 12 error categories, including grade relevance, section relevance, solvability, realism, grammar, spelling, topic safety, and more.

The main conclusion is that LLMs can generate generally fluent and often solvable elementary MWPs, but they still struggle to reliably match the specified grade and topic/section requirements. Fine-tuning, few-shot prompting, preference optimization, and solvability filtering improve some measures, especially grade and section relevance, but performance remains imperfect. Because this is a system-building and evaluation paper focused on content generation quality rather than student outcomes, it provides indirect evidence for K-12 math instruction and does not test learning gains in classrooms.

finding.finding_summary: The paper shows that LLMs can generate elementary math word problems that are mostly solvable, mathematically coherent, and aligned with the intended format, but they often miss the exact grade and section requirements. In the best reported setup (few-shot + solvability filter), average evaluation reached 92.28% across error categories, with solvable problems at 84.17%, grade relevance at 74.52%, and section relevance at 78.76% (human/LLM-based evaluation; n=312 for the calibration subset and 8,561 questions reviewed overall).
finding.measure: Human and LLM-based evaluation of generated math word problems; error-category accuracy including solvability, grade relevance, and section relevance
finding.study_size: n=312 for calibration; 8,561 questions reviewed in total

finding.finding_summary: The system is intended to reduce the manual workload of tutors by automating math word problem creation. The paper does not report a time-saved effect size, but it presents the generation pipeline as a practical alternative to hand-authoring problems and reports that the generated questions can be produced in the desired format with high fluency and reasonable quality after fine-tuning and filtering.
finding.measure: Author-reported task automation for generating classroom practice problems; qualitative assessment of tutor workload reduction potential

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that diverse word problems can support students' logical thinking and problem-solving practice, and it evaluates diversity as a technical property of generated output. It reports improved diversity under the selected decoding setup, with lower Self-BLEU (0.003976) and Jaccard similarity (0.181161) for the best contrastive-search configuration, but this is an indirect proxy rather than a student-level learning measure.
finding.measure: Generated-question diversity measured by Self-BLEU and Jaccard similarity

paper_profiles.title: Evaluation Report on Large Language Models Solving High School Mathematics Questions
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This report evaluates how several large language models (LLMs) perform on high school mathematics exam questions. The paper asks whether current generative AI systems can answer mathematics problems accurately, quickly, and with reasonable logical reasoning and creative diversity, and it frames this as evidence for possible educational applications.

The study uses mathematics questions drawn from Chinese college entrance examinations from 2019 to 2023, organized by question type (multiple-choice, fill-in-the-blank, and comprehensive questions) and by difficulty. At least eight LLM APIs are tested, including GLM-4-Flash, ERNIE-Speed-128K, Spark-lite, Hunyuan-lite, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, gemma-2-9b-it, Meta-Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, and Yi-34B. The report compares model outputs using accuracy, response time, logical reasoning, guidance sensitivity, and multi-solution creativity metrics, with some expert re-review of a subset of answers.

Overall, the paper concludes that LLMs show promise for solving some high school mathematics questions, but performance is uneven across models and question types. Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and ERNIE-Speed-128K are presented as the strongest on accuracy, while Spark-lite and Hunyuan-lite are highlighted for some logic/guidance advantages and gemma-2-9b-it for speed. The report argues that current LLMs still need improvement in reasoning, creativity, and consistency, but it suggests they could be useful as educational tools and that further model optimization and prompt design may improve classroom utility.

finding.finding_summary: Across eight LLMs tested on high school mathematics exam questions, performance varied substantially by model, question type, and difficulty. The report reports single-solution accuracies ranging from 0.10 to 0.25 on item types and from 26.67% to 56.67% across difficulty bands, with multi-solution accuracy ranging from 0.35 to 0.64; Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and ERNIE-Speed-128K are described as the strongest overall on accuracy, while Spark-lite and Meta-Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct were weaker on some measures.
finding.measure: Accuracy on high school mathematics exam questions (multiple-choice, fill-in-the-blank, comprehensive; single-solution and multi-solution conditions)

finding.finding_summary: The report explicitly evaluates logical reasoning and guidance-related performance of the models, using chain-of-thought prompting, repeated guidance attempts, and success rate as indicators. Hunyuan-lite is described as strongest on guidance/logic, requiring an average of 3 attempts for successful guidance, while other models generally required 4-6 attempts; reported logic scores in the synthesis table ranged from 0.28 to 0.42.
finding.measure: Logic evaluation via guidance attempts, success rate, and chain-of-thought-based reasoning score

finding.finding_summary: The study directly measures response time for single-solution and multi-solution math problem solving. In single-solution tasks, reported average times ranged from 0.32 s to 4.50 s for multiple-choice items and from 0.34 s to 16.01 s for comprehensive items; in multi-solution tasks, Spark-lite was fastest at 688 s and GLM-4-Flash slowest at 7400 s. The paper concludes that gemma-2-9b-it and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct were among the fastest on several single-solution categories, while Spark-lite had the clearest efficiency advantage in multi-solution generation.
finding.measure: Model response time / processing time for solving mathematics questions

finding.finding_summary: The report argues that LLMs have potential educational applications and may support future personalized learning, prompt design, and instructional use in high school mathematics, but these conclusions are inferential rather than direct institutional evidence. The paper does not measure school-level outcomes, policy effects, or implementation outcomes in real classrooms, so the finding is best characterized as speculative/implicational rather than demonstrated institutional impact.
finding.measure: Author interpretation of educational applicability and implications

paper_profiles.title: AMO-Bench: Large Language Models Still Struggle in High School Math Competitions
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper introduces AMO-Bench, a new benchmark of 50 original, human-crafted advanced mathematics problems intended to evaluate large language models (LLMs) on Olympiad-level or harder math reasoning. The authors argue that existing high-school math competition benchmarks such as AIME and HMMT are becoming saturated for top-tier models and may also be vulnerable to contamination or memorization effects.

AMO-Bench is constructed through a multi-stage human review process: problems are created by mathematics experts, checked for quality by multiple reviewers, screened for originality via web and dataset comparisons, and filtered for difficulty using preliminary testing with several advanced LLMs. Each item requires only a final answer, allowing parser-based grading for most items and LLM-based grading for descriptive items. The benchmark’s category mix includes algebra, functions/sequences, geometry, number theory, and combinatorics.

The empirical portion evaluates 26 LLMs on the benchmark using 32 samples per model and reports AVG@32 accuracy. Performance is generally low: the best model, GPT-5-Thinking (High), reaches 52.4% accuracy, while most models score below 40%. The paper also reports that higher reasoning effort / longer outputs are associated with better performance and that pass@k continues to improve as k increases, suggesting room for gains from more test-time compute. This is a benchmark paper rather than a study of K-12 student learning or classroom implementation.

finding.finding_summary: The paper evaluates 26 LLMs on 50 Olympiad-level mathematics problems in AMO-Bench. The best-performing model, GPT-5-Thinking (High), achieved 52.4% accuracy (AVG@32), while most models scored below 40%, indicating that current models still struggle substantially with advanced mathematical reasoning. The benchmark is not an intervention study with students; it is a model-evaluation study on high-difficulty math problem solving.
finding.measure: Accuracy on AMO-Bench math benchmark (AVG@32)

paper_profiles.title: Elementary School Students’ and Teachers’ Perceptions Towards Creative Mathematical Writing with Generative AI
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how elementary school students and teachers perceived a generative AI–supported activity for creative mathematical writing. The authors focus on whether a GenAI-powered platform can help children generate, revise, and represent math stories, and what benefits and challenges users perceive in classroom use.

The study was implemented in six 5th-grade classrooms across two U.S. schools with 79 students and six teachers. The instructional sequence included an Ask step (analyze a math story), a Represent step (use visual tools to model ideas), and a Transform step (provide prompts so GPT-4 and DALL·E 3 could draft and illustrate a math story). After four class periods, the researchers conducted focus-group interviews with 10 students and individual interviews with all six teachers, triangulated with open-ended survey responses and classroom observations. The analysis was thematic and produced six themes: four benefit themes (creativity, mathematical understanding, AI literacy, and affective engagement) and two challenge themes (student-related and AI-related barriers).

The paper concludes that GenAI can support creative mathematical writing by helping students generate ideas, understand math problems, and build interest and ownership, but it also creates risks such as overreliance, weak critical evaluation, insufficient feedback, reduced autonomy, limited social interaction, and accessibility issues. The authors argue that GenAI should be designed as a pedagogical collaborator rather than a perfect content generator, with stronger supports for feedback, adaptation, and inclusive communication.

finding.finding_summary: Students and teachers reported that GenAI-supported creative mathematical writing helped students understand math problems, represent mathematical ideas, and surface misconceptions. However, the paper does not report quantitative achievement gains; the evidence is based on thematic analysis of perceptions from 79 5th-grade students and 6 teachers, with 10 student interviews and classroom observations.
finding.measure: Perceived mathematical understanding, mathematical knowledge representation, and misconception detection during creative mathematical writing
finding.study_size: n=79 students; n=6 teachers; n=10 student interviewees

finding.finding_summary: Participants perceived the GenAI-supported activity as increasing interest, enjoyment, curiosity, and ownership of learning. These outcomes were identified through interviews, open-ended survey responses, and observations rather than standardized affective measures.
finding.measure: Perceived interest, curiosity, enjoyment, and ownership in math learning

finding.finding_summary: The study reports perceived gains in creativity, flexible/divergent thinking, and AI literacy, especially prompt engineering and evaluating AI strengths and weaknesses. These were emergent themes from qualitative analysis, not direct performance outcomes, but they were central to the paper's claims about student learning.
finding.measure: Perceived creative thinking, flexible thinking, and AI literacy/prompt engineering

finding.finding_summary: The paper centers on creative mathematical writing, and participants described improved writing originality, story development, and revising AI-generated drafts. The evidence is qualitative and specific to math-story writing, with no standardized writing assessment reported.
finding.measure: Perceived quality of creative mathematical writing and story drafting/revision
finding.study_size: n=79 students; n=6 teachers; n=10 student interviewees

paper_profiles.title: Can ChatGPT pass the Vietnamese National High School Graduation Examination?
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether ChatGPT can pass the Vietnamese National High School Graduation Examination (VNHSGE). The authors evaluate ChatGPT in zero-shot mode on an evaluation set derived from VNHSGE and related exam questions, using a fixed prompt format and binary grading against human-provided ground truth answers.

The paper examines multiple subjects in the exam, including mathematics, literature, English, physics, chemistry, biology, history, geography, and civic education, and compares ChatGPT’s scores with Vietnamese student score distributions from prior years. The authors report that ChatGPT achieves roughly passing-level combined scores and is stronger in language-heavy subjects such as English and literature than in some science subjects, though performance varies by subject and year.

The study is not an intervention study with K-12 students; it is a benchmark-style evaluation of a large language model on high-school exam items. Its main conclusion is that ChatGPT can sometimes reach passing-level performance on this exam, but the model remains inconsistent and needs improvement, especially on more complex or non-textual tasks such as some geography and civic-education items.

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT achieved math scores ranging from 5.2 to 6.6 on a 10-point scale across 2019-2023, with an average of 5.88. The authors report that these scores were sufficient for the model to contribute to passing-level combined scores, but they were generally below the majority of Vietnamese students in the comparison charts.
finding.measure: VNHSGE mathematics exam score (10-point scale)

finding.finding_summary: In literature, ChatGPT scored between 5.63 and 7.5, with an average of 6.8 on a 10-point scale. The paper reports that the model often outperformed the majority of Vietnamese students in literature, although in 2022 it was slightly lower than the student benchmark.
finding.measure: VNHSGE literature exam score (10-point scale)

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT performed strongest in English, with scores from 7.6 to 8.6 and an average of 7.92 across 2019-2023. The authors state that ChatGPT consistently outperformed the majority of Vietnamese students in English language proficiency on the exam.
finding.measure: VNHSGE English exam score (10-point scale)

finding.finding_summary: Performance varied across science subjects. Physics scores ranged from 5.75 to 6.5 (avg. 6.1) and biology from 5.25 to 6.0 (avg. 5.8), with the paper describing these as generally lower than the majority of Vietnamese students; chemistry was the weakest subject, ranging from 4.0 to 6.25 (avg. 4.8). The authors also note that ChatGPT’s performance was inconsistent across years and subject complexity.
finding.measure: VNHSGE physics, chemistry, and biology exam scores (10-point scale)

finding.finding_summary: Across history, geography, and civic education, ChatGPT showed uneven performance. History scores ranged from 4.25 to 7.75 (avg. 5.65), geography from 5.0 to 7.5 (avg. 6.15), and civic education from 6.0 to 8.25 (avg. 7.05); the paper reports that geography and civic education were often below the majority of Vietnamese students, while history was sometimes above them.
finding.measure: VNHSGE history, geography, and civic education exam scores (10-point scale)

finding.finding_summary: Using the Ministry of Education and Training’s graduation scoring formula, the authors report that ChatGPT’s combined natural and social science scores were sufficient to pass the exam in all years analyzed. The reported combined scores ranged from 6.30 to 6.94, indicating pass-level performance at the level of the exam system rather than individual student outcomes.
finding.measure: Computed graduation combination score (GAS) using VNHSGE subject scores

paper_profiles.title: VNHSGE: VietNamese High School Graduation Examination Dataset for Large Language Models
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper introduces VNHSGE, a Vietnamese High School Graduation Examination dataset created to benchmark large language models (LLMs). The dataset aggregates official and practice exam questions from 2019–2023 across nine subjects, including mathematics, literature, English, physics, chemistry, biology, history, geography, and civic education. It provides both Vietnamese and English versions, includes images for multimodal evaluation, and standardizes questions, answers, and explanations for LLM assessment.

The paper’s primary purpose is not to study a teaching intervention, but to evaluate how current LLMs perform on high-school exam content. The authors test ChatGPT and BingChat against selected items from the dataset and compare model performance to Vietnamese students’ exam score distributions. They report that the models reach human-level performance in some humanities areas, but still have room to improve in mathematics and the natural sciences, where multi-step reasoning and computational accuracy are harder.

For mathematics specifically, the dataset is positioned as a benchmark for complex high-school math reasoning, covering topics such as geometry, sequences, probability, derivatives, logarithms, integrals, complex numbers, and spatial calculus. However, the paper does not report a controlled educational study, instructional deployment, or learner outcome change from using generative AI in classrooms. Its evidence is descriptive and benchmark-oriented rather than intervention-based.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that ChatGPT and BingChat still have room to improve in mathematics and struggle with complex calculations and multi-step deductive reasoning. In the authors’ qualitative comparison against Vietnamese high school exam items, the models handled knowledge/comprehension-level math questions better than application/high-application items, but no numerical effect size or formal statistical test is reported.
finding.measure: Performance on Vietnamese high school mathematics exam questions (accuracy/qualitative correctness across difficulty levels)

finding.finding_summary: The paper indicates that LLMs have difficulty with advanced mathematical reasoning and multi-step deduction, implying limited performance on reasoning-intensive tasks. This is based on benchmark evaluation of ChatGPT and BingChat on high-school exam questions, but the paper does not provide a formal measure of critical thinking or metacognitive skill gains, nor any effect size.
finding.measure: Reasoning complexity in math exam items; qualitative assessment of multi-step deductive reasoning

paper_profiles.title: U-MATH: A University-Level Benchmark for Evaluating Mathematical Skills in Large Language Models
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper introduces U-MATH, a new benchmark for evaluating large language models (LLMs) on university-level mathematics, and µ-MATH, a meta-evaluation benchmark for judging the quality of LLM-generated solution verification. The authors argue that existing math benchmarks are too school-focused, too small, too multiple-choice oriented, or too narrowly competition-based, and therefore do not adequately capture the practical mathematical reasoning needed for university coursework.

U-MATH contains 1,100 previously unpublished problems sourced from real US university coursework across six subjects: algebra, differential calculus, integral calculus, multivariable calculus, precalculus, and sequences and series. About 20% of the problems include visual elements. The paper evaluates a broad set of open and proprietary LLMs on these problems, using accuracy as the main metric, and finds that reasoning models outperform standard models, text-only performance is substantially higher than visual performance, and open-weight models lag proprietary multimodal systems on visual tasks.

The paper also introduces µ-MATH, which uses a subset of U-MATH problems paired with LLM-generated solutions to test whether LLM judges can correctly verify mathematical solutions. The authors find that evaluation/judgment is a distinct and non-trivial capability, with the best models reaching an F1 score of 90.1% but still showing systematic biases and instability. Overall, the paper is a benchmark-and-evaluation study of LLM mathematical reasoning rather than a study of student learning, classroom intervention, or K-12 instruction. It provides no direct evidence on generative AI for K-12 mathematics.

finding.finding_summary: This paper does not test an educational intervention on learners; instead it benchmarks LLMs on university-level math problem solving. The main results are descriptive performance scores, with the best reasoning model reaching 93.1% accuracy on text-only U-MATH and 58.5% on visual U-MATH, and the best judge reaching 90.1% macro-F1 on µ-MATH.
finding.measure: LLM accuracy on U-MATH; macro-F1 on µ-MATH
finding.study_size: n=1,100 U-MATH problems; n=1,084 µ-MATH samples

paper_profiles.title: Short-term AI literacy intervention does not reduce over-reliance on incorrect ChatGPT recommendations
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether a brief AI literacy intervention can reduce high school students’ tendency to over-rely on incorrect ChatGPT recommendations while solving math puzzles. The authors note that, although generative AI is increasingly discussed for education, there is limited direct experimental evidence on whether teaching students about AI’s limitations changes reliance behavior in the context of large language models.

The study randomly assigned 36 12th-grade Estonian students to either an intervention text or a control text. The intervention text explained how ChatGPT works, its limitations and risks, and tips for using it wisely; the control text included only general introductory information about ChatGPT. After reading the text, students solved eight Kangaroo-style math puzzles with ChatGPT recommendations, four correct and four incorrect, and decided whether to adopt each recommendation. The primary outcome was over-reliance on incorrect ChatGPT advice; secondary outcomes included under-reliance on correct advice, confidence, and decision time.

Results showed substantial over-reliance overall: students accepted incorrect ChatGPT recommendations in 52.1% of cases. The intervention did not significantly reduce over-reliance (48.68% vs 55.88% in control; Welch’s t(28.78) = -0.73, p = .236, d = -0.25), but it did significantly increase under-reliance on correct recommendations (36.84% vs 19.12%; t(34) = 2.35, p = .025, d = 0.78). The authors conclude that a short AI literacy text is insufficient to reduce over-reliance on ChatGPT and may inadvertently encourage students to ignore correct AI advice.

finding.finding_summary: Students used ChatGPT while solving eight math puzzles, but the intervention did not improve math-task decision accuracy in the intended direction. Over-reliance on incorrect recommendations was 48.68% in the intervention group versus 55.88% in control, a non-significant difference (Welch’s t(28.78) = -0.73, p = .236, d = -0.25).
finding.measure: Acceptance/rejection of ChatGPT recommendations on Kangaroo math puzzles; over-reliance rate and task correctness

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly studied reliance-related critical thinking and metacognitive behavior when students evaluated ChatGPT outputs. The intervention did not reduce over-reliance, but it increased under-reliance and was associated with decision time: longer initial decision times correlated with lower over-reliance (rs = -0.41, p = .013) and higher under-reliance on correct answers (rs = 0.35, p = .038).
finding.measure: Over-reliance, under-reliance, and initial decision time while judging ChatGPT recommendations

finding.finding_summary: The intervention increased self-reported knowledge in some AI literacy dimensions, but it did not reduce confidence in using ChatGPT recommendations in a statistically significant way. Confidence was slightly lower in the intervention group (M = 3.58) than in control (M = 3.67), but the difference was not significant (U = 188.50, p = .400).
finding.measure: Self-reported confidence in previous puzzle answers; self-reported perceived AI literacy improvement

paper_profiles.title: SCIBENCH: Evaluating College-Level Scientific Problem-Solving Abilities of Large Language Models
paper_profiles.venue: ICML (Proceedings of the 41st International Conference on Machine Learning)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper introduces SCIBENCH, a benchmark for evaluating large language models (LLMs) on college-level scientific problem solving. The dataset includes 869 textbook problems from college mathematics, chemistry, and physics, plus a closed exam subset of 103 questions from college computer science and math courses. The benchmark is designed to be harder than existing science and math benchmarks because it emphasizes free-response, multi-step reasoning, advanced computation, and, in some cases, visual context.

The study evaluates several unimodal and multimodal LLMs, including GPT-4, GPT-3.5, Claude2, LLaMA-2, Mistral, and multimodal systems such as LLaVA, Qwen-VL-Plus, and InternLM-XComposer2. Models are tested under zero-shot, few-shot, chain-of-thought, and tool-augmented prompting, including Python and Wolfram Language. The paper reports that even the strongest configuration remains far from perfect: GPT-4 with few-shot Python prompting reaches the best reported average on the textbook set (43.22%), while multimodal performance is lower and tool use can sometimes hurt other skills.

The work is not an intervention study in K-12 classrooms; it is a benchmark/evaluation paper for undergraduate-level scientific reasoning. It concludes that current LLMs still struggle with advanced scientific problem solving, especially when tasks require accurate calculation, code conversion, and integration of textual and visual information. The paper also proposes an error-analysis framework that attributes mistakes to missing skills such as logical decomposition, assumption identification, and calculation.

finding.finding_summary: SCIBENCH directly evaluates mathematics problem solving on a college-level math subset (calculus, statistics, differential equations) and reports wide variation across models and prompting strategies. The best overall configuration on the textbook dataset was GPT-4 with few-shot Python prompting, reaching 43.22% average accuracy, but performance remained far from mastery and some tool-augmented settings reduced performance on certain models.
finding.measure: Accuracy on college-level mathematics problems (calculus, statistics, differential equations) in SCIBENCH
finding.study_size: n=369 math problems in the textbook dataset (161 calculus, 93 statistics, 55 differential equations; plus exam math subset not separately counted here)

finding.finding_summary: The central aim is to assess scientific problem-solving across mathematics, physics, and chemistry using complex free-response items that require domain knowledge, reasoning, and numerical computation. Across the full textbook dataset, even the strongest configuration achieved only 43.22% average accuracy, and the multimodal subset performance was lower (GPT-4 PoT at 13.8%), indicating substantial remaining limitations in scientific reasoning.
finding.measure: Accuracy on scientific problem-solving benchmark items across math, physics, and chemistry; also multimodal scientific problem solving
finding.study_size: n=869 textbook problems plus n=177 multimodal subset and n=103 closed exam problems

finding.finding_summary: The paper explicitly analyzes broader problem-solving skills such as logical decomposition, assumption identification, abstract reasoning, logical reasoning, and code conversion. CoT improved calculation-related errors in some settings, but also increased errors in other skills; for example, zero-shot CoT reduced calculation-error attribution to 13.6% from 29.0%, while raising some other error categories.
finding.measure: Error profiles / skill-attribution categories derived from incorrect LLM solutions
finding.study_size: n=112 human-annotated errors used to define the skill taxonomy; then applied to benchmark errors

finding.finding_summary: The study examines whether external tools such as Python and Wolfram Language improve the efficiency and effectiveness of solving scientific problems. Tool use sometimes improved numerical accuracy for some models, but Wolfram Language often did not help and could reduce performance, suggesting that the overhead of code conversion and syntax errors can offset gains in efficiency.
finding.measure: Model accuracy under tool-augmented prompting (Python, Wolfram Language) compared with prompting-only baselines

paper_profiles.title: CMM-Math: A Chinese Multimodal Math Dataset To Evaluate and Enhance the Mathematics Reasoning of Large Multimodal Models
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper introduces CMM-Math, a new Chinese multimodal mathematics benchmark and training dataset for evaluating and improving large multimodal models (LMMs) on math reasoning. The authors emphasize that prior multimodal math datasets were largely in English and often focused on evaluation only; in contrast, CMM-Math includes both benchmark and training splits and covers 12 grade levels from primary school through high school.

The dataset was constructed from more than 10,000 real Chinese exam papers, then cleaned and annotated into 28,069 problems with images, text, detailed solutions, and labels for grade level, subject, and question type. The paper evaluates several open-source and closed-source LMMs on the benchmark and also trains a new model, Math-LMM, in a three-stage pipeline: foundational pre-training, foundational fine-tuning, and mathematical fine-tuning.

The main empirical contribution is benchmark evaluation rather than a classroom intervention. Results show that current LMMs struggle on the more difficult multimodal math items, especially at higher grade levels and in geometry-related subjects. Math-LMM improves performance relative to several open-source baselines on CMM-Math and also transfers reasonably to English multimodal math benchmarks (MathVista and MATH-V), but the paper does not study student learning outcomes, teacher use, or classroom implementation.

finding.finding_summary: The paper evaluates mathematical reasoning performance of large multimodal models on CMM-Math (28,069 problems; 5,821 evaluation items). Across all evaluated models, mean accuracy was 35.66%, with performance generally higher on lower grade levels and arithmetic/statistics, and substantially lower on geometry-related subjects and higher grade levels. Math-LMM improved over many open-source baselines, reaching 48.57% accuracy (72B) and outperforming other open-source LMMs on several difficult levels, but the study is about model benchmark performance rather than student achievement.
finding.measure: Accuracy on Chinese multimodal math benchmark items; GPT-4o-graded scores for open-ended responses

paper_profiles.title: CMATH: Can Your Language Model Pass Chinese Elementary School Math Test?
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether current large language models (LLMs) can solve Chinese elementary-school math word problems at a grade-appropriate level. To address that question, the authors introduce CMATH, a benchmark of 1.7k elementary-level math word problems collected from real Chinese workbooks and exams, with annotations for grade, answer, number of reasoning steps, and number of digits.

The study evaluates several commercial and open-source LLMs in a zero-shot setting, including GPT-4, ChatGPT, and multiple Chinese-language models. Performance is reported by grade level and by problem complexity. GPT-4 is the only model that reaches at least 60% accuracy across all six grades; ChatGPT performs well through grade 4 but drops in grades 5–6, and the other models fail across most or all grades.

The paper also includes a small robustness experiment using a manually created distractor set of 60 problems, each augmented with irrelevant numeric information. GPT-4 remains comparatively robust, while the other models—especially ChatGPT—are more easily misled by distractors. Overall, the paper is a benchmark/evaluation study rather than an educational intervention, and it concludes that current general-purpose LLMs still struggle with elementary math reasoning outside the strongest model available at the time.

finding.finding_summary: The paper evaluates math word-problem solving accuracy on CMATH (n=1,700 problems; plus a distractor set of n=60 problems). GPT-4 is the only model to achieve success (accuracy ≥60%) across all six elementary grades, while ChatGPT succeeds through grades 1–4 and other models largely fail. Performance declines as grade level, reasoning steps, and number of digits increase; on the distractor set, GPT-4 remains comparatively robust whereas ChatGPT and other models deteriorate as irrelevant information is added.
finding.measure: Accuracy on elementary-school math word problems by grade; accuracy under distractor augmentation

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT for Good? On Opportunities and Challenges of Large Language Models for Education
paper_profiles.population: Not reported; broad education contexts spanning elementary, secondary, tertiary, and professional development
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This position paper examines the opportunities, challenges, and ethical considerations of large language models such as ChatGPT in education. Rather than testing a specific intervention, it synthesizes emerging examples and prior work to discuss how LLMs may support learning, teaching, assessment, content generation, feedback, and educational access across age groups and settings.

The paper is not an empirical study of K-12 mathematics outcomes. Its main contribution is a conceptual and literature-based discussion of potential educational uses, including generating quizzes, explanations, feedback, and math word problems, alongside risks such as bias, privacy, overreliance, plagiarism, and difficulty distinguishing AI-generated from student-generated work. The authors conclude that LLMs may be useful educational tools if integrated carefully with human oversight, critical thinking, and strong governance, but they do not report direct evidence of durable learning gains, posttest retention, or transfer in mathematics or any other subject.

Because the article is a position paper, it does not present original experimental data or independent assessments of student learning. Any claims about benefits are framed as possibilities or as summaries of prior studies, not as direct empirical findings from this paper.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that LLMs can reduce teacher workload by automating or assisting with quiz generation, feedback, grading support, lesson planning, and content creation. These are presented as anticipated efficiencies and literature-based examples rather than results from a direct experiment in this paper; no effect size, sample size, or independent outcome measure is reported.
finding.measure: Teacher workload / grading effort / content-generation efficiency

finding.finding_summary: The paper discusses potential support for critical thinking, problem-solving, and fact-checking, but also warns that overreliance on LLMs may weaken these skills. No direct empirical test of durable skill gains is reported in this position paper, and no independent posttest or transfer assessment is presented.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, problem-solving, fact-checking, and related 21st-century skills

finding.finding_summary: Mathematics is mentioned only as a potential application area, including generating practice problems and math word problems, but the paper reports no direct empirical evidence of improved math performance. There are no independent posttests, delayed posttests, transfer tests, or other assessments demonstrating math gains in this paper.
finding.measure: Mathematics learning/performance

paper_profiles.title: Embracing the future of Artificial Intelligence in the classroom: the relevance of AI literacy, prompt engineering, and critical thinking in modern education
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This article is a conceptual discussion of how AI, especially generative AI such as ChatGPT, should be integrated into educational practice. It addresses concerns about students over-relying on AI, the risks of hallucinations and plagiarism, and the need for schools to help learners use AI responsibly rather than banning it outright.

The paper proposes three core competencies for AI-era education: AI literacy, prompt engineering, and critical thinking. Its main evidence base is a case study from Kalaidos University of Applied Sciences in Zurich, plus a narrative literature review and informal discussions with students and staff. The author describes institutional AI guidelines and offers recommendations such as workshops, mandatory AI courses, documentation of AI use, and classroom activities that position AI as a sparring partner rather than a ghostwriter.

The paper is aimed primarily at higher education and adult learners, though it suggests the ideas may also be useful for younger students. It does not report an intervention trial or outcome data on achievement; instead, it argues that better education about AI tools and their limits is needed to support ethical use, critical evaluation, and informed classroom integration.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports a case study of institutional AI policy formation at Kalaidos University of Applied Sciences, including the creation of internal AI guidelines effective July 1, 2023. The discussion argues that a middle-ground policy allowing AI use with documentation and critical review is preferable to outright bans or unrestricted use, but no outcome data on implementation effectiveness are reported.
finding.measure: Institutional AI guidelines, policy approach, and qualitative observations from university discussions

finding.finding_summary: The article argues that AI literacy, prompt engineering, and critical thinking are essential skills and cites prior literature suggesting these capacities can be fostered through instruction and practice. However, the paper itself does not present direct empirical evidence that these skills improved, nor does it report independent, delayed, or transfer assessments.
finding.measure: Not directly measured in this paper; discussed as skills to be cultivated through AI literacy and prompting practices

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests that AI can support teachers by helping with curricula, case study creation, and classroom activities, and it frames AI as potentially increasing efficiency in academic work. These claims are descriptive and not backed by direct performance data, effect sizes, or comparative trials in the paper.
finding.measure: Perceived usefulness for curriculum creation, case study construction, and classroom support

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT in higher education: Considerations for academic integrity and student learning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how ChatGPT was being discussed in mainstream news coverage in relation to higher education, with particular attention to academic integrity concerns and claims that the tool might support student learning. The authors ask what themes dominate public discourse and whether ChatGPT is being framed more as a cheating threat or as a learning aid.

The study is not an experiment on student learning outcomes. Instead, it is a content analysis of 100 English-language news articles from Australia, New Zealand, the United States, and the United Kingdom published between 2020 and February 2023. Articles were coded for themes such as university responses, academic dishonesty, AI detection, assessment redesign, institutional policy, and potential learning benefits. The corpus was dominated by integrity concerns and calls to redesign assessment to avoid AI misuse, while fewer articles discussed ChatGPT as a learning support tool.

The main conclusion is that public and institutional discussion of ChatGPT in higher education was mixed but tilted heavily toward cheating and assessment security, with comparatively less attention to learning benefits, equity, or student voice. The paper argues that universities should move toward clearer policy guidance and more constructive assessment design, while also exploring how generative AI might be used ethically to support learning. It does not provide direct empirical evidence about learning gains, persistence of gains, or performance on independent or delayed posttests.

finding.finding_summary: The paper found that mainstream news coverage and university responses to ChatGPT were dominated by academic integrity concerns, assessment redesign, and policy uncertainty rather than clear institutional consensus. In the coded corpus of 100 news articles, academic integrity was the most common theme (n=88), while universities were more often described as undecided (n=22) or banning ChatGPT (n=18) than explicitly allowing it (n=10).
finding.measure: Content analysis of news articles coded for themes related to university responses and policy positions

paper_profiles.title: War of the chatbots: Bard, Bing Chat, ChatGPT, Ernie and beyond. The new AI gold rush and its impact on higher education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This article reviews the rapid emergence of generative AI chatbots, especially ChatGPT, Bing Chat, Bard, and Ernie, and discusses their implications for higher education. It is primarily a critical narrative review rather than an empirical study: the authors summarize chatbot background, tech-industry dynamics, and the scholarly literature on assessment, learning, teaching, and academic integrity.

A central part of the paper is a comparative, hands-on test of selected chatbots on tasks relevant to higher education, with emphasis on whether these tools can support or threaten assignments and examinations. The paper reports that the models perform unevenly: GPT-4 and GPT-3.5 do best, while Bing Chat and Bard perform poorly in the authors’ test. The discussion highlights concerns about hallucinations, unreliable reasoning, and the possibility that apparent performance gains may be limited to immediate, tool-assisted responses rather than durable learning.

The paper does not study K-12 mathematics interventions or student learning outcomes directly. Its empirical content is focused on higher-education chatbot benchmarking and literature synthesis, with recommendations for assessment redesign and institutional responses. As such, it provides contextual evidence about chatbot capabilities and educational implications, but not evidence of persistent learning gains on independent posttests or delayed transfer assessments.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that generative AI is already forcing higher education institutions to rethink assessment, academic integrity policies, and teaching practices. It does not report an outcome effect size because it is not an intervention study; instead, it synthesizes concerns and recommendations based on the authors’ review and chatbot comparisons.
finding.measure: policy and assessment implications discussed in narrative review

finding.finding_summary: The paper repeatedly notes that chatbots can speed up drafting, summarizing, coding, and other knowledge-work tasks, and cites examples where GPT-4 generated usable outputs within minutes. However, these efficiency claims are descriptive and demonstration-based rather than measured in a controlled study, so no effect size or sample size is reported.
finding.measure: tool-mediated task completion speed / productivity in demonstration examples

finding.finding_summary: The paper discusses critical thinking, reasoning, and transfer mostly as concerns and as goals for redesigning assessment, not as directly measured outcomes. Its discussion suggests that chatbot gains are limited to immediate assisted performance and do not establish durable understanding or independent transfer, but no direct learning-test evidence is reported.
finding.measure: reasoning / transfer / critical evaluation discussed in narrative review

paper_profiles.title: The effect of ChatGPT on students’ learning performance, learning perception, and higher-order thinking: insights from a meta-analysis
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether ChatGPT improves students’ learning outcomes, learning perceptions, and higher-order thinking, and whether those effects vary by course type, learning model, duration, role of ChatGPT, and application area. The authors meta-analyzed 51 quasi-experimental and experimental studies published from November 2022 to February 2025, extracting 72 independent effect sizes and using Hedges’s g as the effect-size metric.

Across the full sample, ChatGPT showed a large positive effect on learning performance (g=0.867, 95% CI [0.683, 1.052]), and moderate positive effects on learning perception (g=0.456, 95% CI [0.287, 0.625]) and higher-order thinking (g=0.457, 95% CI [0.255, 0.650]). The study found statistically significant moderation by course type, learning model, and duration for learning performance, and by duration for learning perception; no significant moderators were found for most other factors. The authors argue that effects are stronger in problem-based learning and in 4–8 week interventions, suggesting that continuous use and appropriate pedagogical scaffolding help produce more stable gains.

For the research question about durability, the paper does not report independent posttests, delayed posttests, or transfer tests in a way that allows a separate extraction of durable learning effects versus immediate assisted performance. The meta-analysis aggregates general post-test/experiment outcomes from the primary studies and therefore supports only indirect inference that benefits may be stronger with sustained use; it does not provide direct evidence that gains persist on independent assessments beyond tool-supported practice.

finding.finding_summary: Across 44 independent studies, ChatGPT improved learning performance with a large overall effect (Hedges’s g=0.867, 95% CI [0.683, 1.052]). The meta-analysis used post-test data from experimental/control groups (or pre-post data where needed), so this reflects overall course performance on study-specific assessments rather than an independent delayed or transfer test.
finding.measure: Learning performance (tests/exams and study-specific achievement measures)
finding.study_size: k=44 independent studies; primary studies included 72 effect sizes across 51 articles

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT also improved learning perception across 19 independent studies, with a moderate effect (g=0.456, 95% CI [0.287, 0.625]). The paper reports that longer use, especially interventions lasting more than 8 weeks, produced stronger perception gains (g=1.054), suggesting benefits that accumulate with continued exposure.
finding.measure: Learning perception (questionnaires/scales)

finding.finding_summary: For higher-order thinking, ChatGPT produced a moderate positive effect across 9 independent studies (g=0.457, 95% CI [0.255, 0.650]). The authors report stronger effects when ChatGPT was used as an intelligent tutor and in STEM-related courses, but the evidence is still based on immediate study outcomes rather than separate independent posttests or delayed transfer measures.
finding.measure: Higher-order thinking (e.g., critical thinking, creative thinking questionnaires/scales)

paper_profiles.title: Promises and challenges of generative artificial intelligence for human learning
paper_profiles.population: Not applicable (conceptual perspective; no human participants studied)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This perspective paper examines how generative AI (GenAI), especially large language models and diffusion models, may reshape human learning across support, content creation, feedback, and assessment. The paper asks what GenAI can contribute to learning, and what risks accompany its use, with attention to educational validity, ethics, transparency, privacy, and the possibility that AI assistance may create an illusion of learning rather than durable understanding.

Rather than reporting a new empirical study, the authors synthesize prior research and illustrative examples from K-12 and higher education, including AI tutors, AI-generated learning resources, AI feedback systems, and AI-enabled assessment tools. A central argument is that GenAI can improve immediate task performance and engagement, but the field lacks robust evidence that these gains persist on independent or delayed assessments. The paper repeatedly emphasizes that apparent benefits may be limited to tool-mediated performance, and it calls for longitudinal, randomized, and methodologically rigorous studies to test whether learning transfers beyond the AI-supported context.

The paper’s main conclusion is that GenAI should be used as a human-centered learning tool, not as a replacement for meaningful instruction or assessment. The authors argue that future research must distinguish assisted performance from genuine learning, and that AI literacy, ethical safeguards, and stronger evidence standards are needed before strong claims can be made about educational impact.

paper_profiles.title: Is ChatGPT a General-Purpose Natural Language Processing Task Solver?
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the 2023 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (EMNLP 2023)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether ChatGPT functions as a general-purpose zero-shot NLP task solver. The authors evaluate ChatGPT (gpt-3.5-turbo) and GPT-3.5 (text-davinci-003) on 20 benchmark datasets spanning arithmetic reasoning, commonsense reasoning, symbolic and logical reasoning, natural language inference, question answering, dialogue, summarization, named entity recognition, and sentiment analysis.

The study is not an intervention or educational trial; it is a benchmark comparison of model outputs under standardized prompts. For the mathematics-relevant portion of the paper, the authors test arithmetic word-problem datasets such as MultiArith, GSM8K, AddSub, AQUA-RAT, SingleEq, and SVAMP, primarily using zero-shot prompting and zero-shot chain-of-thought prompting. ChatGPT often outperforms GPT-3.5 on arithmetic reasoning, especially with chain-of-thought, but the evaluation is entirely on immediate benchmark test accuracy rather than on instruction, tutoring, or classroom learning.

Across the broader benchmark suite, ChatGPT is strongest on tasks that reward reasoning and dialogue, but it underperforms fine-tuned models on many tasks and struggles with sequence tagging and summarization length control. The paper’s main conclusion is that ChatGPT is a capable but not fully general zero-shot task solver. For the sub-question about durable learning in K-12 mathematics, the paper provides no evidence about independent posttests, delayed posttests, transfer tests, or learning persistence; it only reports direct performance on benchmark math problems, including assisted performance under chain-of-thought prompting.

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT outperformed GPT-3.5 on arithmetic reasoning benchmarks, especially when zero-shot chain-of-thought prompting was used. On six arithmetic datasets, ChatGPT’s zero-shot accuracies were 79.8 on MultiArith, 95.8 on GSM8K, 23.8 on AddSub, 78.9 on AQUA-RAT, 88.6 on SingleEq, and 83.5 on SVAMP; with chain-of-thought, performance improved to 95.8, 78.9, 88.6, 53.5, 91.5, and 77.5 respectively. These are immediate benchmark results on tool-mediated problem solving, not independent posttests or delayed assessments.
finding.measure: Accuracy on arithmetic reasoning datasets (MultiArith, GSM8K, AddSub, AQUA-RAT, SingleEq, SVAMP)

paper_profiles.title: Detecting hallucinations in large language models using semantic entropy
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of hallucinations in large language models (LLMs): cases where models generate fluent but incorrect or unsupported answers. The authors propose semantic entropy, an uncertainty-estimation method that clusters multiple sampled model outputs by meaning rather than by surface form, and then measures entropy over meaning-clusters to identify likely confabulations.

The method is evaluated on question answering datasets (TriviaQA, SQuAD 1.1, BioASQ, NQ-Open) and a mathematical word-problem dataset (SVAMP), using several open-weight LLMs (LLaMA 2 Chat, Falcon Instruct, Mistral Instruct) and GPT-4 for a biography-generation task. Across these settings, semantic entropy generally outperforms naive entropy, a P(True) baseline, and an embedding-regression baseline for detecting incorrect answers and for improving rejection-based accuracy. The paper also includes a small mathematics-related evaluation on SVAMP, where semantic entropy predicts confabulations in elementary-school math word problems, but it does not study instruction, tutoring, or learning gains for students.

finding.finding_summary: The paper includes a mathematical word-problem benchmark (SVAMP) as one of several test domains, but the outcome studied is model confabulation detection, not student learning or math achievement. The reported result is that semantic entropy can detect incorrect model answers in elementary-school math word problems, with overall performance summarized across datasets and models by AUROC averaging 0.790 across 30 task-model combinations; no independent posttest, delayed posttest, or transfer assessment of learner gains is reported.
finding.measure: Confabulation detection performance on SVAMP using AUROC / AURAC
finding.study_size: n=400 train and n=400 test examples sampled for each dataset; SVAMP is one of 5 datasets

paper_profiles.title: Should There be a Teacher In-the-Loop? A Study of Generative AI Personalized Tasks
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether a teacher should remain in the loop when using generative AI to personalize middle school mathematics problems to students’ interests. The study focuses on seven 7th-grade math teachers who used ChatGPT/GPT-4o to modify Illustrative Mathematics problems in Units 4 and 6, and on the responses of 521 students who completed the personalized assignments in ASSISTments.

The researchers analyzed teacher prompt logs, teacher speech during the task-authoring sessions, student open-ended comments, and student 1-5 ratings of how interesting and personally relevant the problems were. Teachers typically asked the model to adapt broad or specific popular-culture contexts, but they also spent substantial effort fixing realism, numerical plausibility, readability, and other issues. The study found that teachers did not become more time efficient over time; in fact, Unit 6 personalization took more prompts and more time than Unit 4. Student ratings were higher in Unit 6 than Unit 4, and ratings were best when teachers used about 3-5 prompts per problem, but the study did not measure student learning or independent math performance outcomes. The authors conclude that teacher-in-the-loop personalization can support student interest but remains time-consuming and tends to operate at a relatively broad grain size, making fine-grained personalization difficult.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers did not become more efficient over time. Personalizing 143 problems took an average of 246 seconds per problem (SD=165.7), and Unit 6 took longer than Unit 4: 286 seconds versus 204 seconds per problem (B=70.4, SE=29.6, t=2.38, p=0.0189). Teachers also used more prompts in Unit 6 than Unit 4, 4.6 versus 3.2 prompts per problem (B=1.26, SE=0.41, t=3.08, p=0.0025), indicating increasing effort rather than time savings.
finding.measure: Teacher time per problem (seconds) and number of ChatGPT prompts per problem
finding.std_deviation: SD=165.7 seconds for time; SD=2.6 prompts per problem

finding.finding_summary: Student ratings of the personalized problems were modestly positive but below the midpoint of the scale overall, with average interestingness = 2.46 and closeness-to-interests = 2.53 on 1-5 scales. Ratings were significantly higher in Unit 6 than Unit 4 (interestingness 2.56 vs 2.27; closeness 2.66 vs 2.28; combined model B=0.33, SE=0.095, t=3.49, p=0.0012), suggesting that the revised second-round problems were better received by students.
finding.measure: Student 1-5 ratings of interestingness and closeness to interests
finding.study_size: n=52 problems with ratings; 521 students assigned the tasks
finding.std_deviation: Unit 4 interestingness SD=1.17; Unit 6 interestingness SD=1.26; Unit 4 closeness SD=1.20; Unit 6 closeness SD=1.29

finding.finding_summary: The paper did not measure independent math achievement, so there is no direct evidence of durable learning gains on posttests, delayed tests, or transfer tasks. The only math-related quantitative evidence is that teachers often had to revise numerical realism and problem structure, and that using 3-5 prompts per problem was associated with higher student ratings of the problem (about 0.24 points on a 5-point scale; B=0.240, SE=0.085, t=2.84, p=0.0073), but this is a perception outcome rather than an achievement outcome.
finding.measure: Problem-level personalization quality as reflected in student ratings; no direct math achievement measure reported

paper_profiles.title: Elementary School Students’ and Teachers’ Perceptions Towards Creative Mathematical Writing with Generative AI
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how elementary school students and their teachers perceive a GenAI-powered learning environment for creative mathematical writing. The authors are interested in whether AI can support elementary students in composing math stories, understanding math ideas, and engaging more deeply with mathematics, while also identifying the challenges and design limitations of such systems.

The intervention was a classroom implementation of a GenAI-powered platform that supported a three-step routine: Ask, Represent, and Transform. Students in six fifth-grade classrooms across two U.S. schools used GPT-4 and DALL·E 3 to draft, revise, and illustrate culturally relevant math stories over multiple class periods, and the researchers collected focus group interviews, teacher interviews, open-ended surveys, and observation notes.

The study is qualitative and reports thematic findings rather than achievement outcomes. Students and teachers perceived benefits in creativity, mathematical understanding, AI literacy, and affective engagement such as interest, curiosity, and ownership. Reported challenges included weak critical evaluation of AI output, insufficient feedback and adaptability, reduced opportunities for autonomy and social connection, and accessibility concerns. Because the paper does not measure independent posttests, delayed posttests, transfer tests, or other direct learning outcomes, it provides no empirical evidence about whether gains persist beyond immediate tool-supported activity.

finding.finding_summary: No direct achievement effect was measured. The paper reports students' and teachers' perceptions that the GenAI-supported math story activity helped students understand problems, represent mathematical ideas, and notice misconceptions, but these are qualitative perceptions from interviews and observations rather than independent posttest results. No sample-level learning gains, effect sizes, or durable/transfer outcomes were reported.
