Performance varies by domain, and the paper argues that benchmark results like MMMU do not fully predict performance on this German school-style dataset.

The paper is a dataset and evaluation study, not a classroom intervention or study of student learning outcomes. It does, however, contain some implementation-relevant observations: for mathematics items, the authors intentionally constrain problems to middle-school arithmetic and geometry, with easy-to-calculate numbers and explicit support such as using pi as a variable to reduce computation burden. They also note that follow-up questioning and textual context can substantially change model behavior in some domains, especially religion, suggesting that prompting/context matters for how VLMs use image information. Overall, the work supports the conclusion that current VLMs struggle on curriculum-aligned, image-based middle-school tasks, particularly when questions are adversarial or require multi-step visual reasoning.

finding.finding_summary: Mathematics was one of the most difficult domains in the benchmark. The best model reached only 34.09% on math (Qwen2.5VL 32B), while the strongest domain score reported for math across models was still far below overall top performance, and the authors describe frequent failures in counting, geometry, coordinate reading, and formula assignment. No classroom learning effects were measured; the finding concerns model performance on 308 math questions drawn from middle-school curricula.
finding.measure: Accuracy on middle-school mathematics benchmark questions (geometry, counting, formula use, calculation)

finding.finding_summary: The physics items required interpreting diagrams, explaining phenomena, and reading contextual clues from images. The authors report that even strong models struggled with explanation questions, such as why main-sequence stars become red giants, and with circuit reasoning; the best physics score reported was 47.65% (Qwen2.5VL 32B), but many errors were qualitative reasoning failures rather than simple recognition mistakes. The benchmark thus indicates weak scientific reasoning on 234 physics questions.
finding.measure: Accuracy on physics questions requiring diagram interpretation and explanation

finding.finding_summary: The paper centrally studies multiple non-math school subjects beyond literacy and science, including arts, history, music, religion, geography, and sports. Performance varies widely by domain: best scores were around 54% in history and religion, around 31% in music, and around 43% in arts/geography; adversarial items were substantially harder, with overall adversarial accuracy generally much lower than standard items. These are benchmark accuracy results on 1,163 questions across the non-math, non-science domains represented in the dataset.
finding.measure: Accuracy on subject-specific benchmark questions across arts, history, music, religion, geography, and sports

finding.finding_summary: Several analyses point to weak higher-order reasoning and context use, especially when tasks require combining visual cues with background knowledge or resisting misleading prompts. The authors explicitly note that models often succeed on superficial recognition but fail on more reasoning-heavy questions, and that adversarial questions expose a major weakness in saying 'I don’t know' when the image does not support the query. This is evidence about model-supported reasoning demands rather than student durable skills.
finding.measure: Accuracy on adversarial and reasoning-heavy benchmark questions; qualitative error analysis of reasoning failures
finding.study_size: n=2,038 total questions, including adversarial subsets

finding.finding_summary: The evaluation pipeline itself is designed around operational efficiency for large open-ended benchmarks: the authors use LLM-as-a-judge with a panel of models to score answers automatically instead of manual grading. They argue this approach is necessary for scaling evaluation over more than 2,000 open-ended questions, but they do not report a comparative workload reduction metric. The finding is primarily methodological and concerns efficient scoring rather than classroom productivity.
finding.measure: Use of panel-of-LLM judges (PoLL) to automatically score open-ended responses

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that benchmark results do not transfer cleanly across languages, domains, or evaluation styles, and that current public benchmarks may overstate capabilities in educationally relevant settings. It introduces a curriculum-aligned German benchmark as an alternative testbed and concludes that non-English, school-style, open-ended evaluation is important for more realistic model assessment. This is an institutional contribution to how AI systems for education should be evaluated, not an educational policy outcome.
finding.measure: Benchmark construction and cross-benchmark comparison (VLM@school vs MMMU/open benchmarks)

paper_profiles.title: Elementary School Students’ and Teachers’ Perceptions Towards Creative Mathematical Writing with Generative AI
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how elementary students and teachers perceive a generative-AI-supported creative mathematical writing activity. The authors focus on whether GenAI can help young learners generate, revise, and extend math stories in culturally relevant ways, while also surfacing concerns about overreliance, missing feedback, and limited opportunities for autonomy and peer interaction.

The study was conducted in six 5th-grade classrooms across two U.S. schools, involving 79 students and six teachers. Students used an in-class GenAI tool built on GPT-4 and DALL·E 3 through a structured three-step process: Ask, Represent, and Transform. The implementation lasted four class periods in one school and eight sessions in another, and data came from student focus groups, teacher interviews, open-ended surveys, and classroom observations.

The findings are qualitative and thematic rather than experimental. Students and teachers reported benefits for creativity, mathematical understanding, AI literacy, and motivation/ownership. At the same time, they identified key challenges: weak critical evaluation of AI outputs, difficulty generating coherent math stories, the AI being 'too perfect,' lack of adaptive feedback, reduced autonomy, weak social connection, and accessibility limitations such as lack of speech-to-text. The paper concludes that GenAI can support mathematical writing in classrooms, but only when carefully designed and embedded in pedagogy that preserves human feedback, collaboration, and room for student improvement.

finding.finding_summary: Students and teachers perceived that the GenAI-supported creative writing activity improved mathematical understanding by helping students break down problems, represent mathematical ideas visually, and surface misconceptions during story creation. The study is qualitative (n=79 students, 6 teachers), so no effect size was reported; evidence comes from interviews, survey responses, and classroom observations across in-class implementation.
finding.measure: Perceived mathematical understanding, problem decomposition, and mathematical knowledge representation during story-based math writing

finding.finding_summary: Participants reported that GenAI-supported math story writing made mathematics more interesting, enjoyable, curiosity-provoking, and ownership-building. Students described increased interest in math and a stronger sense of responsibility for their learning because they were authoring stories that could be shared with peers; no quantitative effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Perceptions of interest, curiosity, and ownership in learning

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that the activity promoted creativity, flexible thinking, prompt engineering, and evaluation of AI strengths and weaknesses. Students iteratively refined prompts and stories, suggesting growth in critical thinking and metacognitive awareness, but the evidence is qualitative and no numerical effect size was provided.
finding.measure: Perceived creativity, flexible thinking, prompt engineering, and critical evaluation of AI outputs

finding.finding_summary: The study found that GenAI-supported story writing helped students create original and culturally relevant mathematical stories, indicating support for creative writing within a math context. Students and teachers also viewed the tool as helpful for drafting, revising, and enriching narratives, but the paper does not report quantitative writing outcomes or effect sizes.
finding.measure: Perceived quality and originality of mathematical creative writing

finding.finding_summary: Teachers and students noted that the AI could quickly generate story drafts and provide instant support, which reduced the burden of starting from scratch and helped move writing forward more efficiently. However, the paper also emphasizes that this efficiency created new concerns about over-perfection and lack of pedagogical feedback; no quantitative productivity measure was reported.
finding.measure: Perceived drafting efficiency and support for story generation

paper_profiles.title: Automated Generation of Curriculum-Aligned Multiple-Choice Questions for Malaysian Secondary Mathematics Using Generative AI
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the challenge of producing scalable, high-quality, curriculum-aligned assessment materials for Malaysian secondary mathematics, especially in a low-resource language context (Bahasa Melayu). The authors argue that generative AI can reduce teacher workload and support digital learning, but only if outputs are grounded in official curriculum documents rather than generated from unconstrained model knowledge.

The study compares four GPT-4o-based question-generation pipelines for Form 1 Mathematics: two non-grounded prompting methods and two Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) methods that use teacher-prepared notes and the national yearly teaching plan (RPT) as source material. The setting is not classroom implementation with students, but a content-generation pipeline intended for educator use in assessment and homework/revision material creation. Each method generated 100 multiple-choice questions, and outputs were evaluated with automated curriculum-alignment and validity checks.

Results show that grounded generation clearly outperformed non-grounded prompting. The RAG pipelines achieved substantially higher semantic alignment with the curriculum (STS scores 0.86 and 0.89 vs. 0.58 and 0.55) and much higher contextual validity (92% and 96% vs. 15% and 12%). The manual RAG pipeline performed best, but the framework-based LangChain approach was presented as a more practical option. The paper concludes that grounding is essential for specialized educational question generation, while also noting that automated metrics cannot fully assess pedagogical quality or cognitive level and that human teacher review remains necessary.

finding.finding_summary: The study finds that GPT-4o-based generation, especially with RAG grounding, can substantially improve the efficiency of producing curriculum-aligned mathematics MCQs for educators. The paper frames the approach as a way to reduce teacher workload and scale assessment creation, and it shows that the automated pipelines can generate 100 questions per method with high fluency and much higher alignment when grounded.
finding.measure: Curriculum-aligned multiple-choice question generation workflow efficiency; generated question quality and validity

finding.finding_summary: The generated content is centered on Form 1 Mathematics rational numbers and integer operations, with the grounded pipelines producing questions more closely aligned to the official learning standards. The strongest method, manual RAG, achieved an average STS alignment score of 0.89 and 96% RAG-QA validity, compared with 0.55-0.58 STS and 12%-15% validity for non-grounded prompts.
finding.measure: Curriculum alignment and contextual validity of generated Form 1 Mathematics MCQs

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that curriculum-grounded GenAI could support national-scale assessment development in Malaysia by producing standardized, curriculum-specific question banks in Bahasa Melayu. It also highlights the broader institutional value of using official curriculum documents as the grounding source for scalable educational content generation in low-resource language settings.
finding.measure: Feasibility and suitability of curriculum-grounded generation for national educational content production

paper_profiles.title: E-EVAL: A Comprehensive Chinese K-12 Education Evaluation Benchmark for Large Language Models
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper introduces E-EVAL, a benchmark for evaluating large language models (LLMs) on Chinese K-12 educational content. The authors argue that existing LLM benchmarks do not adequately cover Chinese primary, middle, and high school subjects, especially the elementary level, and therefore propose a comprehensive multiple-choice benchmark spanning 23 subjects across arts and science domains.

The benchmark was built from questions sourced primarily from free regional homework, practice questions, and mock exams, with heavy manual cleaning and formatting, especially for science items containing equations. The final dataset contains 4,351 questions split into development, validation, and test sets. The evaluation protocol compares 15 open-source and commercial models under zero-shot, few-shot answer-only, and few-shot chain-of-thought prompting, with accuracy as the metric.

The study finds that Chinese-dominant models generally outperform English-dominant models on Chinese K-12 content, but performance is substantially weaker on science subjects, particularly mathematics. The authors also observe that few-shot prompting tends to help more in arts subjects than in science, while chain-of-thought prompting helps complex science items such as mathematics but can reduce performance overall. They further report that models sometimes perform surprisingly worse on simple primary-school math than on harder middle- or high-school items, suggesting that higher-order training exposure does not guarantee mastery of lower-order knowledge.

finding.finding_summary: The benchmark shows that mathematics is one of the hardest subjects for the evaluated LLMs. Across the full benchmark, science subjects lagged behind arts subjects, and the paper specifically notes poor performance on mathematics despite strong results in some other domains. Under chain-of-thought prompting, high school and middle school mathematics improved relative to five-shot answer-only prompting, but overall averages still declined for most models.
finding.measure: Multiple-choice accuracy on mathematics questions within E-EVAL

finding.finding_summary: Models performed substantially worse on science than arts subjects, indicating that scientific reasoning was more challenging than language-based tasks. The paper reports that chain-of-thought prompting improved performance on complex science subjects, including mathematics, physics, chemistry, and biology, but this came with an overall decline in average accuracy for most models.
finding.measure: Multiple-choice accuracy on science subjects in E-EVAL

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports benchmark performance on a broad set of Chinese K-12 subjects beyond math and science, including Chinese, English, politics, history, geography, ethics, and biology. Overall, models performed better on arts subjects than science subjects, and few-shot prompting improved arts performance more than science performance.
finding.measure: Multiple-choice accuracy across non-mathematics/non-science K-12 subjects in E-EVAL

paper_profiles.title: Students' Perceived Roles, Opportunities, and Challenges of a Generative AI-powered Teachable Agent: A Case of Middle School Math Class
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study examines how middle school students perceived the roles, benefits, and challenges of a generative AI-powered teachable agent (TA) used in an authentic math classroom. The paper asks what roles students assign to the TA, what opportunities they perceive in learning with it, and what barriers they encounter when using it in class.

The intervention was a GenAI-powered TA built on GPT-4 Turbo and retrieval-augmented generation, designed for learning-by-teaching in 6th-grade mathematics (rates and ratios). The system included personalized topic and difficulty choices, scenario-based problems, gamification, and follow-up questions intended to elicit explanation and reflection. The study was conducted in a public laboratory middle school with 108 sixth graders across six classes, supported by two math teachers and graduate researchers. Data came from classroom observation, open-ended surveys, and focus-group interviews with 14 students.

Findings indicate that students viewed the TA as a learning companion, facilitator, and collaborative problem-solver. They reported that the tool could create a student-centered climate, support autonomy, foster cognitive/social/emotional capacities, improve math understanding and transfer, and increase positive attitudes toward AI. At the same time, they identified barriers including weak problem presentation, overly surface-level questions, poor accommodation of learning styles, disorganized sequencing, limited social-emotional understanding, technical issues, lack of multimodal input, lack of interoperability, and a strong need for teacher facilitation. The paper is primarily descriptive and interpretive rather than outcome-testing, but it suggests that classroom setting and teacher mediation are important implementation conditions for GenAI-powered TAs in K-12 math.

finding.finding_summary: Students reported that interacting with the GenAI-powered teachable agent improved their understanding of rate and ratio concepts, helped them revisit misconceptions, and supported application of knowledge to new contexts. These claims are based on qualitative data from 108 sixth-grade students, with students describing clearer understanding of basic concepts, models, and formulas after explaining them to the agent.
finding.measure: Student perceptions from classroom observation, open-ended surveys, and focus-group interviews about mathematics learning (rate and ratio understanding and application)

finding.finding_summary: Students perceived the GenAI-powered TA as increasing enjoyment of math, self-efficacy, intrinsic motivation, enthusiasm, and resilience. The evidence is qualitative and perception-based rather than performance-based, but students repeatedly described the experience as fun, confidence-building, and motivating in a classroom context with 108 sixth graders.
finding.measure: Student perceptions of enjoyment, self-efficacy, motivation, engagement, and resilience

finding.finding_summary: Students reported gains in cognitive, social, and metacognitive capacities, including elaboration, reflection, perspective-taking, and communication skills. The TA’s follow-up questions prompted students to explain their reasoning and consider the agent’s perspective, suggesting support for metacognition and collaboration, though no direct skill assessment or effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Student perceptions of reasoning, reflection, communication, and perspective-taking during TA interactions

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that effective use of the GenAI-powered TA depends on classroom implementation conditions, especially teacher facilitation, and reports that students wanted teachers to help mediate misunderstandings and provide clues. Although not a policy study, it provides qualitative evidence that institutional classroom support is a key condition for adoption and effective use in K-12 math.
finding.measure: Student reports and observations regarding teacher engagement, facilitation, and classroom implementation conditions

paper_profiles.title: Should There be a Teacher In-the-Loop? A Study of Generative AI Personalized Tasks Middle School
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates how middle school mathematics teachers use generative AI, specifically ChatGPT, to personalize existing curriculum problems to students’ interests, and whether having a teacher “in the loop” affects the personalization process. The central question is not student learning of math content, but rather how teachers prompt the model, how much time and effort the process takes, and how students react to the resulting personalized tasks.

Seven 7th-grade mathematics teachers in six U.S. schools were trained to use GPT-4o to modify problems from the Illustrative Mathematics curriculum in ASSISTments, a math homework platform. Teachers personalized Unit 4 and Unit 6 problems around broad popular-culture themes and specific student interests; the study logged prompts, time spent, and student survey responses. The paper finds that teachers often used multiple prompts to refine realism, age appropriateness, and specificity, but the process was not especially time-efficient: creating a problem took about 4 minutes on average, and efficiency did not clearly improve over time. Student feedback suggested a preference for finer-grained personalization (specific references) over broad categories, while teachers tended to operate at broader grain sizes because of the time cost.

The paper’s main conclusion is that teacher-in-the-loop personalization can support thoughtful, contextually relevant problem design, but it is labor-intensive and tends to produce broader-grain personalization than many students prefer. The authors also report a potential “Goldilocks zone” in prompting: problems created with 3–5 prompts received the most favorable student ratings, whereas too few or too many prompts were less effective. The study is exploratory and descriptive; it does not measure math achievement or include a control group, but it provides detailed evidence on implementation conditions, prompting behavior, and the tradeoff between teacher control and individualized student appeal.

finding.finding_summary: Teacher-in-the-loop personalization was time-intensive. Across 143 problems, teachers used 558 prompts (M=3.2 prompts/problem, SD=2.6) and spent an average of 246 seconds per problem (about 4 minutes; SD=165.7). Time did not clearly decrease with experience; instead, from Unit 4 to Unit 6 teachers used 1.26 more prompts per problem and spent 70.4 more seconds per problem, suggesting that iteration and reflection increased effort rather than reducing it.
finding.measure: Teacher prompt count and time spent creating personalized math problems
finding.effect_size: B=1.26 prompts/problem from Unit 4 to Unit 6; B=70.4 seconds/problem from Unit 4 to Unit 6; average 246 seconds/problem

finding.finding_summary: The study examined middle school mathematics problem personalization and student ratings of the resulting math tasks. No achievement or test-score outcome was measured, but students rated problems created with more effective prompting more positively: using 3–5 prompts was associated with higher ratings of interestingness and closeness to students’ interests by about 0.24 points on a 5-point scale (B=0.240, SE=0.085, p=0.0073). Students also rated Unit 6 personalized problems more favorably than Unit 4 problems (B=0.33, SE=0.095, p=0.0012).
finding.measure: Student ratings of personalized mathematics problems for interestingness and closeness to interests
finding.study_size: n=521 students; ratings collected for 52-53 problems
finding.effect_size: B=0.240 for 3–5 prompts vs. other prompt counts; B=0.33 for Unit 6 vs. Unit 4
finding.std_deviation: SD=1.24 interestingness rating; SD=1.28 closeness rating

finding.finding_summary: The paper focuses heavily on student interest and engagement responses to personalized mathematics problems. Students more often said they were interested when problems included a preferred general or specific popular-culture reference, and they frequently requested finer-grained personalization. However, overall mean ratings were modest (interestingness M=2.46/5, closeness M=2.53/5), indicating that personalization improved perceived relevance only to a limited degree.
finding.measure: Student survey ratings and open-ended feedback about interestingness and closeness to personal interests
finding.study_size: n=521 students; 454 open-ended responses to interest question, 449 to improvement question, 446 to accuracy question
finding.effect_size: M=2.46/5 interestingness; M=2.53/5 closeness; B=0.33 for Unit 6 vs. Unit 4
finding.std_deviation: SD=1.24 interestingness; SD=1.28 closeness; Unit 4 interestingness SD=1.17, Unit 6 SD=1.26; Unit 4 closeness SD=1.20, Unit 6 SD=1.29

finding.finding_summary: The authors interpret teachers’ prompting as a form of iterative problem posing and note that using 3–5 prompts appeared to be the most productive range. Teachers used prompts to improve clarity, realism, mathematical fit, and student relevance, indicating active iterative refinement and problem-solving. Still, the paper does not directly measure durable-skill gains in students or teachers beyond these process behaviors.
finding.measure: Teacher prompting/revision behavior while co-creating problems with ChatGPT
finding.effect_size: B=0.240 student-rating advantage for problems created with 3–5 prompts

finding.finding_summary: The curriculum context was the Illustrative Mathematics middle school program, and teachers successfully modified existing tasks rather than creating entirely new ones. The paper shows that GenAI can be used to adapt curriculum materials to local student interests, but the study did not measure learning outcomes in any other academic domain outside mathematics.
finding.measure: Personalization of Illustrative Mathematics curriculum problems

paper_profiles.title: 3DG: A Framework for Using Generative AI for Handling Sparse Learner Performance Data From Intelligent Tutoring Systems
paper_profiles.venue: LAK 2024 Workshop on Generative AI for Learning Analytics
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of sparse learner performance data in intelligent tutoring systems (ITS), where missing or limited attempt-level data can weaken learner modeling and performance prediction. The authors propose a simulation framework called 3DG (3-Dimensional tensor for Densification and Generation) that combines tensor factorization for data imputation with generative models for data augmentation.

The study uses data from an AutoTutor reading-comprehension lesson developed for the Center for the Study of Adult Literacy (CSAL), involving 118 adult participants. The framework structures performance as a learner-by-question-by-attempt tensor, completes missing values via tensor factorization, then clusters learners by learning-pattern parameters and generates additional synthetic samples using GAN and GPT-4 with prompt engineering.

Results show that tensor completion can recover missing performance entries in the sparse dataset, and that GAN-generated simulations are more reliable than GPT-4 simulations for preserving the observed ranges of learner parameters. The paper concludes that generative models may be useful for scalable simulation of ITS learner data, but the work is methodological and does not evaluate instructional effectiveness, classroom implementation, or home-vs-classroom setting effects.

finding.finding_summary: The paper does not test a literacy intervention outcome; instead, it models sparse reading-comprehension performance data from an AutoTutor lesson. Using a dataset from the CSAL 'Cause and Effect' reading-comprehension lesson with n=118 adult learners, the authors show that tensor completion can impute missing values and that GAN-generated synthetic data more closely matches the original parameter distributions than GPT-4-generated data.
finding.measure: Reading-comprehension lesson performance data in AutoTutor (binary correct/incorrect responses across questions and attempts); simulated parameter distributions for initial ability (a) and learning rate (b)

paper_profiles.title: Do intelligent tutoring systems benefit K-12 students? A meta-analysis and evaluation of heterogeneity of treatment effects in the U.S.
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether intelligent tutoring systems (ITS) improve K-12 student achievement in the United States and, more specifically, under what conditions those effects are larger or smaller. The authors use Campbell’s validity typology and the MUTOS framework to examine both internal validity and heterogeneity across units, treatments, outcomes, and settings, with a particular focus on moderators such as grade level, intervention duration, support type, measurement timing, and implementation context.

The meta-analysis included 18 experimental studies and 77 effect sizes across 11 ITS used in U.S. elementary, middle, and high school settings. Across studies, ITS had a positive overall effect on learning outcomes (g=0.271, SE=0.011, p=0.001). Moderator analyses suggested that effects were stronger for interventions that included worked-out examples, shorter durations, main-instructional-method use, and immediate outcome measurement; effects were smaller in rural settings. The study also found that ITS used as homework had a statistically significant positive effect (g=0.317), roughly comparable to ITS used as the main instructional method (g=0.294), but the paper does not provide evidence that one setting clearly outperformed the other. Overall, the review concludes that ITS are beneficial in K-12 education, with treatment and measurement characteristics explaining more variation than student demographics or school level.

finding.finding_summary: Across 18 experimental studies and 77 effect sizes, ITS improved K-12 learning outcomes overall (g=0.271, SE=0.011, p=0.001). For math outcomes specifically, the pooled effect was positive and statistically significant (g=0.253, K=22).
finding.measure: Student learning outcomes / achievement; math achievement outcomes in the outcome moderator analysis
finding.study_size: n=18 studies; 77 effect sizes (math subset K=22 effect sizes)

paper_profiles.title: Tinkering in Primary School: From Episode to Science Practice
paper_profiles.venue: The Primary School as a Playful Space
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This chapter examines how a constructionist tinkering practice can be integrated into primary school teaching, especially within science and physics education. The authors argue that tinkering can serve as an open-ended entry point for students to generate authentic research questions, but that teachers often struggle to connect those questions to disciplinary learning because they feel insufficiently prepared to handle the underlying science.

The paper describes the TIDE model (Tinkering, Ideas generation, Disciplinary connection, Exploration) and reports on an implementation project in Bologna involving 13 primary school classrooms, 24 teachers, and about 300 students. In the project, Light Play workshops were offered at least three times per class, with teacher professional development, an online resource library, and documentation tools such as fishbowl protocols. Due to pandemic-related disruptions, the planned design was compressed and documentation became fragmented, but the project still generated evidence from teacher questionnaires and fishbowl analyses.

Main findings suggest that tinkering improved classroom dynamics, engagement, and access to knowledge, particularly for students who are often less successful in traditional school settings. Teachers reported that non-aligned students were often highly motivated and active during tinkering, while some highly school-oriented students experienced frustration when tasks were open-ended. A key implementation finding was that teachers tended to shift tinkering into more familiar expressive or storytelling activities rather than science-focused follow-up, even though the resources were centered on science. The authors conclude that deeper disciplinary support is needed if tinkering is to become a regular part of classroom science practice.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that tinkering generated relevant scientific questions, including a light-physics question about how to produce white light using colored filters. However, teachers often felt unable to answer or pursue these questions scientifically, so the inquiry was not always taken up in subsequent classroom work. The evidence is qualitative and based on teacher documentation and fishbowl reflection rather than standardized outcome measures.
finding.measure: Teacher questionnaire responses and fishbowl protocol analysis concerning students' scientific questions and teachers' ability to extend them
finding.study_size: n=20 teachers (project involved 13 classrooms and about 300 students)

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported unexpectedly high engagement, participation, cooperation, and persistence during tinkering, especially among students usually seen as disengaged or difficult in traditional classroom settings. In the questionnaire, 70% of teachers said tinkering revealed unexpected or partially expected behavior, and many described non-aligned students as highly motivated, attentive, and enthusiastic; however, some aligned students experienced frustration and crises when tasks were less structured.
finding.measure: Teacher questionnaire about student behavior, engagement, participation, and frustration during tinkering workshops

finding.finding_summary: The study suggests that tinkering supported collaboration, mutual assistance, self-reflection, and process-oriented reasoning. Teachers repeatedly noted that students worked effectively in pairs and groups, negotiated ideas, and became protagonists within the activity, although some students resisted collaboration or defaulted to delegation. These findings are qualitative and descriptive.
finding.measure: Teacher descriptions coded from open-ended questionnaire responses about student performance in tinkering

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that tinkering can be integrated into regular classroom life only if schools provide teacher preparation, documentation structures, and curricular support. Teachers' willingness to use tinkering was strongly shaped by implementation conditions: many integrated it only loosely, and most preferred humanities or expressive follow-up rather than science-aligned extensions, indicating that institutional and pedagogical norms moderated uptake.
finding.measure: Teacher questionnaire on post-workshop curricular integration and documentation/fishbowl reflections on implementation conditions

paper_profiles.title: AI as a Teaching Partner: Early Lessons from Classroom Codesign with Secondary Teachers
paper_profiles.venue: Colleague AI / University of Washington report
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This report examines early classroom implementation of a generative-AI platform, Colleague AI Classroom, in secondary schools. The central question is how AI can function as a teaching partner when embedded in real instruction, and what design and implementation conditions shape its usefulness for teachers and students.

Across a seven-week spring 2025 pilot, 21 in-service teachers in five Washington State school districts and one independent school co-designed and implemented four AI features: Teaching Aide, AI-assisted assessment and grading, AI Tutor, and Student Growth Insights. More than 600 students in grades 6-12 used the platform in live classrooms; teachers planned activities, mediated student-AI interactions, and provided weekly reflections, surveys, interviews, and planning artifacts, while platform logs captured usage patterns.

The report concludes that generative AI can support classroom instruction when teachers provide strong framing, clear goals, and ongoing oversight. The most successful uses were structured, curriculum-aligned, and formative rather than summative: teachers valued AI-generated narrative feedback, conversation scaffolds, and dashboards that surfaced student misconceptions and growth patterns. Implementation quality varied by grade band and subject, with middle school students needing shorter outputs and stronger monitoring, high school students tolerating more open-ended dialogue, and math classrooms showing more mixed results because of the AI’s difficulty with technical reasoning and diagrams.

Overall, the report emphasizes that teacher AI competency and pedagogical judgment are essential. AI was most effective as a “third agent” that extended instruction, reduced teacher workload in feedback and monitoring, and supported revision cycles, but only when teachers remained the final interpreters of student learning.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that Colleague AI reduced workload by streamlining assessment, surfacing student misconceptions, and saving hours of scanning through Student Growth Insights. In the assessment feature, median AI grading coverage on submitted work was 92.2% across 58 classroom-level assessment records (33 classrooms), and teachers described AI-generated narrative feedback as a useful first draft that sped turnaround time, though numeric scores often required review.
finding.measure: Teacher-reported workload reduction, AI grading coverage, and platform logs on assessment processing
finding.study_size: n=19 teachers for assessment; 58 assessments across 33 classrooms; 936 student submissions

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that AI-supported conversations and feedback often increased student engagement, confidence, and willingness to revise, especially when the tool was teacher-framed and aligned to student needs. In Teaching Aide sessions, 35% of teachers said it helped most students learn and 62% said some students learned, while engagement was stronger when teachers modeled prompts, circulated, and tied activities to graded tasks.
finding.measure: Teacher ratings of student engagement/learning and exit-ticket reflections

finding.finding_summary: Across non-math subjects, teachers reported that AI supported prewriting, brainstorming, language practice, and inquiry, with stronger results in ELA/Spanish/science than in mathematics. The report notes that Spanish teachers used ACTFL-aligned proficiency feedback and English teachers used AI for prewriting and brainstorming, which improved essay quality, but these subject-specific gains were qualitative rather than experimentally estimated.
finding.measure: Teacher-reported instructional outcomes in ELA, Spanish, and science implementations

finding.finding_summary: The pilot found that AI could support deeper thinking, revision, and evidence-based reasoning when teachers structured prompts and feedback cycles clearly. Teachers repeatedly described goal-oriented prompts, revise-and-resubmit workflows, and conversation scaffolds as promoting more meaningful student-AI interaction and prompting students to refine work, though findings were based on teacher reflections rather than direct outcome testing.
finding.measure: Teacher reflections on student reasoning, revision, and depth of engagement

finding.finding_summary: Mathematics implementations were more variable than other subjects. Teachers reported that math students could use Teaching Aide for concept talk and exploratory reasoning, but outcomes were mixed because the AI struggled with diagrams, technical reasoning, and the flexible, non-linear nature of problem solving; the report does not provide quantitative math achievement gains.
finding.measure: Teacher-reported usefulness and learning outcomes in middle/high school math implementations
finding.study_size: 9 math classes (middle school math, Algebra 1, Geometry); exact n students not_reported

finding.finding_summary: Language-related uses were generally favorable, especially for multilingual learners and Spanish classrooms. Teachers reported that multilingual students gained confidence through AI conversations and later participated more in whole-class discussion, while Spanish teachers used AI for real-time proficiency feedback aligned to ACTFL expectations.
finding.measure: Teacher-reported participation and proficiency feedback in language-focused classrooms

paper_profiles.title: Making AI-Enhanced Videos: Analyzing Generative AI Use Cases in YouTube Content Creation
paper_profiles.venue: Extended Abstracts of the CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI EA '25)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how YouTube content creators use generative AI tools across the video production pipeline. The authors analyze 274 English-language how-to videos to identify common generative AI use cases in planning, production, editing, and uploading, with attention to how creators actually incorporate tools like ChatGPT, Midjourney, Leonardo.AI, ElevenLabs, and others into their workflows.

The study is not an intervention or impact evaluation; it is a thematic analysis of creator demonstrations. The authors find that GenAI is used most often for prompting image/video generation, scripting, AI voiceover, avatars, lip-syncing, and subtitle/title generation, with smaller but still notable uses for topic ideation, prompt refinement, upscaling, and translation. The discussion argues that prompting skill is becoming an important creator competency and raises design questions around originality, authenticity, and transparency of AI-generated media.

The population is adult YouTube creators making how-to videos about GenAI-enabled video production. The context is online content creation rather than education, and the paper does not study K-12 learning, mathematics, classroom implementation, homework use, teacher mediation, or curriculum alignment. Its main contribution is a conceptual framework of generative AI use cases in video creation and a set of future research questions for HCI and platform design.

paper_profiles.title: GenAI at the Edge: Comprehensive Survey on Empowering Edge Devices
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a broad survey of research on deploying generative AI models on edge devices rather than on cloud servers. The core problem it addresses is how to make large language models and diffusion-based generative models smaller, faster, and more energy-efficient so they can run under memory, latency, power, and privacy constraints on edge hardware.

The survey organizes the literature into three main technical categories: software optimization (quantization, pruning, knowledge distillation, neural architecture search, and open-source model compression), hardware optimization (custom accelerators and computing-in-memory approaches), and frameworks for efficient inference (e.g., TensorRT, TVM, and edge-specific libraries). It synthesizes representative methods and reports that these approaches can substantially improve throughput, latency, and energy efficiency, especially for LLMs and diffusion models, while preserving acceptable accuracy or generation quality in many cases.

The paper is not an education study and does not examine K-12 students, classrooms, homework use, teacher mediation, curriculum alignment, or mathematics learning outcomes. Instead, it is an engineering-focused synthesis of edge GenAI systems research, intended to provide a roadmap for researchers and practitioners working on on-device deployment. Its conclusions emphasize that the main barriers are resource constraints and the tradeoff between compression/efficiency and model quality, with future work needed on personalization, security, and distributed edge deployment.

paper_profiles.title: Evaluating the Design Features of an Intelligent Tutoring System for Advanced Mathematics Learning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper evaluates two design features of an intelligent tutoring system (ITS) called Xiaomai for advanced mathematics: the use of free-response questions with automatic feedback/self-rating, and an error-reflection prompt that asks students to identify why they made mistakes. The motivation is to improve mathematics learning for college students preparing for China’s graduate school mathematics entrance exam, especially in a setting where the system covers college-level algebra, calculus, and statistics.

The study used a 2x2 randomized experiment with 120 university students in central China. Students completed a pretest, practiced for 40 minutes in Xiaomai under one of four conditions (multiple-choice vs. free-response; with vs. without reflection), and then took a posttest. The paper reports that multiple-choice practice outperformed free-response practice on practice performance and learning gains, while error reflection did not significantly improve either outcomes or practice behavior. The authors also found no evidence that prior knowledge moderated the effect of reflection. They conclude that the current free-response and reflection implementations in Xiaomai do not improve learning and may need redesign, such as better support for free-response grading or richer feedback on incorrect solutions.

finding.finding_summary: In a randomized 2x2 experiment (final n=120), students practicing multiple-choice items performed better than those practicing free-response items on both practice performance and posttest learning gains. Posttest ANCOVA showed a marginal item-format effect favoring multiple-choice (M=9.21 vs. 7.94; F(1,115)=3.72, p=0.06), and practice performance was significantly higher for multiple-choice conditions (F(3,116)=5.95, p=0.01).
finding.measure: Pretest and posttest math scores; practice performance (attempts, correctness, time per item)

finding.finding_summary: The study tested whether error reflection improved metacognitive learning behavior, but reflection did not significantly affect posttest scores, practice performance, number of attempts, correctness, or time spent per question. When prior knowledge was split by median, reflection still did not show a significant main effect or interaction, suggesting no detectable benefit from this metacognitive feature in this implementation.
finding.measure: Reflection condition effects on posttest scores; prior-knowledge-by-reflection analysis; practice behavior in Xiaomai

paper_profiles.title: Foundations of GenIR
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This chapter is a conceptual and survey-style overview of foundational ideas in generative information retrieval (GenIR). It explains how modern generative AI models differ from traditional AI and how their instruction-following and text generation abilities create new opportunities for information access systems.

The chapter organizes the discussion around two broad paradigms: information generation, where models directly produce tailored outputs for user needs, and information synthesis, where models combine retrieved or external information into grounded responses. It reviews Transformer architecture, scaling laws, training stages such as pre-training, supervised fine-tuning, and RLHF, as well as prompt optimization and multimodal applications.

The second half of the chapter focuses on retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), modular RAG, and composite information needs. It also surveys generative retrieval and domain-specific modeling, emphasizing tradeoffs among performance, controllability, explainability, hallucination, and computational cost. The paper does not report an educational intervention, K-12 mathematics use case, or empirical outcomes about classroom versus homework/home-based use; it is a theoretical synthesis for information retrieval researchers.

paper_profiles.title: Engaging Teachers to Co-Design Integrated AI Curriculum for K-12 Classrooms
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how K-12 teachers can co-design AI-integrated curriculum that fits within core non-computing subjects. The authors address a practical design problem in AI education: although many AI tools and lessons exist, they are often standalone, difficult for classroom adoption, and not aligned with teachers’ needs or classroom constraints.

To study this, the researchers ran a two-day remote co-design workshop with 15 K-12 educators from different subject areas and grade levels. Session 1 introduced AI concepts, tools, and card-sorting activities; between sessions, teachers completed pre-work selecting a curriculum and tool; and Session 2 involved small-group co-design with researcher support to draft integrated lessons. The resulting curricula focused on social studies, ESL, and literacy for students with learning disabilities, and the analysis centered on teachers’ values, design considerations, and the ways AI can be integrated into subject instruction.

The main findings were that teachers wanted AI curriculum to support evaluation, engagement, logistics, and collaboration. They emphasized the need for scaffolding, especially for AI ethics, and for materials that make it easier to judge learning through conceptual, discussion-based assessments rather than technical performance alone. The paper concludes that integrated AI curriculum is more likely to be usable and meaningful when teachers help design it and when tools explicitly support classroom constraints, subject alignment, and ethical reflection. It is primarily a design and process study rather than an outcome evaluation of student learning.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that co-designing AI-integrated curriculum with researchers and exemplar materials helped them feel more confident about implementation and surfaced practical supports they need for classroom use. The workshop identified logistics-related needs such as clearer tool guidance, better scaffolding for lesson structure, and more time to prepare, suggesting that integrated design can improve the usability of AI curriculum for educators.
finding.measure: Teacher confidence ratings; thematic analysis of workshop discussions and co-designed lesson drafts

finding.finding_summary: The workshop showed that teachers designed AI lessons to foster collaboration, reflection, and critical evaluation rather than technical skill alone. Participants repeatedly emphasized group work, student discussion, and reflection on AI outputs and ethics as core parts of the curriculum, indicating a strong focus on durable skills such as collaboration and critical thinking.
finding.measure: Thematic analysis of co-design workshop discussions and curriculum drafts

finding.finding_summary: Teachers identified engagement as a major design priority and proposed strategies such as student-driven topics, real-world hooks, game-like elements, and choice of context to keep learners motivated. The paper also reports that teachers’ familiarity with AI and confidence in integrating AI into their classrooms increased modestly after the workshop, though no baseline confidence measure was established for a formal causal test.
finding.measure: Teacher post-workshop survey ratings; thematic analysis of engagement-related discussion

finding.finding_summary: The study suggests that teacher co-design can support broader institutional adoption of AI curriculum by aligning materials with classroom realities and teacher buy-in. Participants valued standards alignment, subject integration, and classroom feasibility, and the authors argue that these factors are necessary for widespread adoption of AI education in schools.
finding.measure: Thematic analysis of workshop discussions and curriculum drafts

paper_profiles.title: “Bespoke Bots”: Diverse Instructor Needs for Customizing Generative AI Classroom Chatbots
paper_profiles.venue: CHI ’26 (Proceedings of the 2026 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how university STEM instructors want to customize generative AI classroom chatbots for their own teaching contexts. The authors first conducted a content analysis of 182 public educational prompts and chatbot feature descriptions to identify ten common customization categories, including course material, pedagogical strategy, constraints/guardrails, personalization, user environment, and course management.

They then interviewed ten university STEM instructors and teaching assistants from North America and Europe, using a card-sorting activity to prioritize those categories. The participants had experience using AI in their courses across a range of contexts, including small project-based classes, lecture-based classes, and a large calculus course with thousands of students. The study was not an intervention or outcomes evaluation; it is a qualitative design study focused on instructor needs, priorities, and implementation context.

The main finding is that instructors converged on a few core customization needs: grounding chatbot behavior in course materials, aligning the chatbot with pedagogical strategies, and embedding basic guardrails. In contrast, priorities such as personalization, task/objective alignment, user-environment integration, and course-management support varied substantially by class size, course type, and teaching style. The authors conclude that there is no one-size-fits-all chatbot design and argue for modular, reusable building blocks and agentic workflows that instructors can configure to fit local teaching conditions.

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds that instructors see custom AI chatbots as potentially helpful for reducing instructor bottlenecks and course-administration burden, especially in large classes. Instructors highlighted uses such as answering logistical questions, managing student groups, releasing assignments and grades, and handling regrade requests; however, these are perceptions from a qualitative study (n=10), not measured task-time effects.
finding.measure: Instructor interview responses about course management, logistics handling, and workload reduction

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that chatbot customization needs are shaped by institutional and course-level contexts, and that reusable configurations could support sharing across instructors and departments. At the same time, instructors noted privacy, ownership, and integration barriers, suggesting that institutional adoption depends on governance and local constraints rather than a single universal design.
finding.measure: Instructor interview responses about sharing configurations, adoption, privacy, and institutional constraints

finding.finding_summary: A subset of instructors linked chatbot customization to student motivation and engagement, particularly through personalization and pedagogical scaffolding. For example, one instructor said personalization could encourage attendance and participation, while others wanted the chatbot to provide 'some friction' and support struggling students rather than giving direct answers; these are perceived benefits, not outcome measurements.
finding.measure: Instructor interview responses about student motivation, engagement, and persistence

finding.finding_summary: The instructors emphasized pedagogical strategies that would encourage structured reasoning, peer learning, and scaffolded problem solving rather than direct answers. They valued chatbot behaviors such as Socratic questioning, worked examples, hints, and error analysis because these were seen as supporting students' thinking and collaboration, but the paper does not test student skill gains directly.
finding.measure: Instructor interview responses about pedagogical strategy, collaboration, and scaffolding

paper_profiles.title: Tareas matemáticas abiertas como respuesta didáctica a la inteligencia artificial generativa en contextos post-IA / Open Mathematical Tasks as a Didactic Response to Generative Artificial Intelligence in Post-AI Contexts
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how mathematics instruction can preserve meaningful student mathematical activity in post-AI contexts, where generative AI tools can solve many traditional tasks automatically. The central concern is not whether AI improves test scores, but how task design and didactic regulation shape what students actually do when AI is available.

The study analyzes one secondary-school classroom experience in which the teacher implemented open mathematical tasks, organized through the COMPAS regulatory device. COMPAS structures the work into phases such as understanding the situation, organizing assumptions and data, mathematical modeling, exploring results, validating solutions, and sharing conclusions. The tasks were intentionally designed without explicit numerical data or closed procedures so that students had to interpret the situation, formulate assumptions, and justify and validate their solutions rather than delegate the work to AI.

Using a qualitative, descriptive-interpretive approach, the paper examines student written work, classroom interactions, and teacher-observer notes. The context is regular secondary mathematics lessons, and the paper emphasizes explicit didactic regulation and human–AI complementarity. The main conclusion is that when open tasks are carefully designed and AI use is explicitly regulated, students retain epistemic control over the mathematical activity: they remain responsible for modeling, deciding, and validating, while AI functions only as a subordinate exploratory aid. The paper therefore argues that the effects of generative AI in K-12 mathematics depend strongly on implementation conditions, especially classroom mediation and task structure, rather than on AI presence alone.

finding.finding_summary: In this single secondary-school classroom experience, open mathematical tasks regulated through COMPAS supported students’ sustained mathematical activity in the presence of generative AI. The paper reports that students retained epistemic control of modeling and validation processes, with no quantitative effect size reported because the study is qualitative and descriptive rather than comparative.
finding.measure: Student mathematical activity, including interpretation, assumption formation, modeling, and validation in open task resolution

paper_profiles.title: AI as a Teaching Partner: Early Lessons from Classroom Codesign with Secondary Teachers
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This report examines early classroom implementation of the Colleague AI Classroom platform, focusing on how secondary teachers co-designed and used generative AI as part of regular instruction. The central question is not whether AI raises test scores, but what conditions make AI useful as a teaching partner: teacher framing, prompt design, monitoring, curriculum alignment, and the difference between structured in-class use and more open-ended support features.

Over seven weeks in spring 2025, 21 in-service teachers from five Washington State school districts and one independent school piloted four AI features: Teaching Aide, Assessment & AI Grading, AI Tutor, and Student Growth Insights. More than 600 students in grades 6-12 used the platform in live classroom settings at teacher direction; teachers also experimented with assessment workflows, rubric generation, and revision-based feedback cycles. The study relied on surveys, planning/reflection forms, group meetings, interviews, exit tickets, and usage logs rather than direct experimental comparison.

The main conclusion is that generative AI can support classroom teaching when teachers tightly scaffold its use and keep it aligned with instructional goals. Teachers reported the strongest engagement when they modeled prompts, set clear finish lines, connected activities to graded or curricular tasks, and maintained active oversight. Results varied by grade band and subject: middle grades tended to need shorter, more structured interactions, while high school students could sustain more open-ended dialogue; math showed mixed results because of accuracy, diagram, and reasoning challenges. For assessment use, AI-generated narrative feedback was valued far more than numeric scores, and for student interactions, repeated implementation and stronger teacher mediation improved engagement. The report is exploratory and implementation-focused, but it offers concrete evidence that setting, teacher presence, and task design change both how the tool is used and how useful it appears.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that AI-assisted grading and Student Growth Insights reduced workload by speeding up rubric generation, feedback drafting, and scanning student responses. Across 58 assessed classroom records (936 submissions), median AI grading coverage was 92.2%, mean submission rate was 54.8% (SD=27.9%), and teachers described the AI’s narrative feedback as a useful first draft that saved time even when numeric scores were adjusted or ignored.
finding.measure: Teacher-reported workload, grading turnaround, rubric generation, AI grading coverage, and platform usage logs

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that AI-supported conversations and immediate feedback increased student engagement, confidence, and willingness to participate, especially for younger learners and multilingual students. In Teaching Aide sessions, 35% of teachers said most students learned from the tool and 62% said some students learned, with engagement improving when teachers used clear norms and structured prompts.
finding.measure: Teacher ratings of student engagement and perceived learning; observation-like teacher reflections
finding.study_size: n=18 teachers for Teaching Aide; up to 600 students

finding.finding_summary: The report suggests AI supported inquiry, revision, and evidence-based reasoning when teachers framed activities as goal-oriented and scaffolded student-AI dialogue. Teachers described students using AI to brainstorm, revise, and extend thinking, and noted that repeated implementations improved students’ ability to engage thoughtfully with the tool.
finding.measure: Teacher reflections on inquiry quality, revision behavior, and depth of student-AI dialogue
finding.study_size: n=18 teachers for Teaching Aide; n=19 teachers for assessment phase

finding.finding_summary: Math use showed both promise and clear limitations. Teachers reported that Teaching Aide could support concept talk and some students learned, but math classrooms were among the most variable because the AI struggled with diagrams, non-linear problem solving, and precise domain reasoning; assessment use in math also raised trust issues around scoring fidelity and rubric alignment.
finding.measure: Teacher-reported learning, engagement, and assessment quality in middle/high school math classrooms
finding.study_size: Math classes included in 21 classrooms; exact math-only n not_reported

finding.finding_summary: In language-related classrooms, AI-supported conversation helped some students participate more and supported writing-related tasks such as prewriting and brainstorming. Teachers reported that multilingual learners found their voice through AI conversations, and Spanish teachers used the tool for ACTFL-aligned proficiency feedback.
finding.measure: Teacher reports of speaking participation, language practice, and writing support

finding.finding_summary: Across non-math subjects, teachers described useful gains in prewriting, brainstorming, seminar preparation, and subject-specific feedback. The strongest subject-level gains were reported in Spanish, engineering, and interdisciplinary STEM, where AI helped individualize skill development and support task completion.
finding.measure: Teacher-reported instructional usefulness across ELA, Spanish, engineering, and interdisciplinary STEM tasks

finding.finding_summary: Science classrooms generally showed favorable outcomes, with teachers reporting that AI-supported conversations promoted inquiry and expanded opportunities for culturally relevant content. However, outcomes were mixed in some science contexts because the AI had trouble with diagrams and technical reasoning, especially in earth science.
finding.measure: Teacher-reported inquiry quality and science classroom engagement
finding.study_size: Science classes included in 21 classrooms; exact science-only n not_reported

paper_profiles.title: Designing for human–AI complementarity in K-12 education
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the ACM on Human-Computer Interaction / AIED conference references cited within article
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper presents a case study on designing and evaluating Lumilo, mixed-reality smart glasses intended to support teachers in AI-supported K-12 classrooms. The broader question is how human teachers and AI tutors can complement each other more effectively, especially when AI tutoring systems personalize instruction in ways that are difficult for teachers to monitor in real time.

The paper describes an iterative human-centered design process involving teachers in co-design, prototyping, and pilot testing, followed by an in-the-wild classroom experiment. In the experiment, 343 middle school students across 18 classrooms, 8 teachers, and 4 schools worked with the AI tutor Lynnette for two class sessions in linear equation solving, while teachers used either no glasses, glasses without analytics, or Lumilo with real-time analytics. The results showed that students in the Glasses + Analytics condition learned more than those in the comparison conditions, with particularly strong gains for students who began with lower pretest scores. Teachers using Lumilo spent more time with lower-performing students and appeared to use the tool to identify when students needed help, suggesting that real-time teacher-facing analytics can improve equity and learning in AI-supported math classrooms.

The article’s main contribution is evidence that setting and teacher mediation matter: the benefit observed here came from classroom use during live instruction, not from student independent use at home. The tool changed how teachers allocated attention and briefly coached students, rather than directly tutoring them. The paper argues that effective human–AI partnerships in education require participatory design, iterative measurement in authentic contexts, and explicit theorizing about complementarity between teachers and AI systems.

finding.finding_summary: In an in-the-wild randomized classroom study, Lumilo’s teacher-facing analytics improved learning on a linear equation solving pre/post test. The paper reports that students in the Glasses + Analytics condition outperformed the No Glasses and Glasses-only conditions; analysis was based on 286 students with complete data (initially 343 students across 18 classrooms, 8 teachers, and 4 schools).
finding.measure: 15-minute pre/post test on linear equation solving

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that Lumilo changed teacher decision-making and encouraged more in-the-moment, complementary judgments about student needs, which were informed by both AI alerts and teachers’ own observations. Teachers used the system to infer underlying causes of student difficulty and to prompt reflection rather than directly supply math answers, indicating support for metacognitive/diagnostic reasoning in the classroom.
finding.measure: teacher attention allocation and qualitative classroom observation of teacher decision-making
finding.study_size: n=286 students in experiment; 14 teachers/15 classrooms in pilots

finding.finding_summary: The tool altered how teachers distributed their time during AI-supported lessons, with teachers in the Glasses + Analytics condition spending more time with students who entered with lower prior knowledge. In the pilot work, teachers spent an average of about 24 seconds per visit per student, and the system was designed to help teachers prioritize attention more efficiently in real time.
finding.measure: teacher attention allocation / time spent per student
finding.study_size: n=286 students in experiment; 14 teachers in pilot sequence

paper_profiles.title: Automated Generation of Curriculum-Aligned Multiple-Choice Questions for Malaysian Secondary Mathematics Using Generative AI
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether generative AI can produce high-quality, curriculum-aligned multiple-choice questions (MCQs) for Malaysian secondary mathematics. The central problem is the difficulty of scaling assessment-item creation in a low-resource language context (Bahasa Melayu) while maintaining factual accuracy and alignment to the Malaysian KSSM curriculum and yearly teaching plan (RPT).

The authors compare four GPT-4o-based generation pipelines for Form 1 Mathematics: two non-grounded prompting baselines and two Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) variants. One RAG pipeline uses a standard LangChain/FAISS workflow, and the other uses manual, domain-aware chunking and retrieval over teacher-prepared notes and official curriculum documents. The study then evaluates generated items using semantic textual similarity to the RPT and a novel RAG-based question-answering validity check.

The paper uses 100 generated questions per method and reports that grounding substantially improves curriculum alignment and contextual validity. The two RAG methods greatly outperform the non-grounded prompts on average STS alignment (0.86 and 0.89 vs. 0.58 and 0.55) and validity rates (92% and 96% vs. 15% and 12%). The manual RAG pipeline performs best, but the framework-based RAG approach is presented as a more practical option, highlighting a trade-off between implementation simplicity and question quality. The study is focused on content generation and validation rather than student learning outcomes, and it argues that human teacher review remains necessary for final pedagogical judgment.

finding.finding_summary: The study finds that generative AI can substantially improve the efficiency of assessment-item creation by automating curriculum-aligned MCQ generation for secondary mathematics. Compared with non-grounded prompting, RAG-based pipelines produced far more usable questions (92%-96% validity vs. 12%-15%), suggesting a meaningful reduction in teacher workload for question drafting and vetting; the paper does not report a direct labor-time measure.
finding.measure: Question generation quality/validity as a proxy for item-production efficiency; teacher workload discussed conceptually
finding.std_deviation: 0.09 and 0.07 for the two RAG methods; 0.21 and 0.25 for the non-grounded methods

paper_profiles.title: How to Prompt? Opportunities and Challenges of Zero- and Few-Shot Learning for Human-AI Interaction in Creative Applications of Generative Models
paper_profiles.venue: CHI’22 Workshops / GenAICHI Workshop at CHI’22
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This workshop paper examines prompting as a new interaction paradigm for human-AI co-creation with generative models, especially for creative tasks such as writing, translation, and text transformation. The authors ask how zero-shot and few-shot prompting can be made more usable for end users, since current prompting practice is often trial-and-error and requires substantial user skill.

Rather than evaluating an educational intervention, the paper is based on two one-hour brainstorming sessions with five HCI researchers, combined with a review of related work and practitioner resources. The authors synthesize opportunities (end-user programming, extending creative expressiveness, inspiration/feedback) and challenges (lack of guidance, prompt representation, computational cost, generalization, and ethics), then propose four UI design goals for supporting prompt formulation, combination, application, and representation.

The paper’s concrete examples focus on creative writing interfaces, illustrating how prompts might be parsed, combined, stored as tools, and applied asynchronously in a GUI. It does not study K-12 mathematics, classroom use, homework/home-based use, teacher mediation, dosage, or student outcomes; instead it offers speculative design ideas and a conceptual framework for future HCI research on prompting.

paper_profiles.title: Learning to Use AI for Learning: Teaching Responsible Use of AI Chatbot to K-12 Students Through an AI Literacy Module
paper_profiles.population: Secondary school (middle school and high school)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the need to teach K-12 students how to use generative AI responsibly and effectively for learning, with particular emphasis on prompting literacy. The authors argue that as AI chatbots become more common in school and home contexts, students need explicit instruction in when to use AI, how to ask effective questions, and how to avoid inappropriate uses such as directly requesting answers.

To address this, the authors designed a web-based AI literacy module centered on scenario-based prompt-writing practice with an AI auto-grader that provided immediate, elaborated feedback. The module was built around three hypothetical secondary-school scenarios spanning biology, geography, and math, and was deployed in two classroom iterations in 11 authentic secondary classrooms in East Asia. Study 1 examined the accuracy of the auto-grader, changes in students’ prompting performance and confidence, and student perceptions; Study 2 revised the assessment and evaluated item quality.

The study found that the GPT-4o-based auto-grader achieved high agreement with human grading overall (average accuracy 0.92 across prompt dimensions), though it was weaker on some dimensions such as purpose and avoiding direct answers. Students improved in including background/context information in prompts, and their self-reported confidence in using AI for learning increased significantly after the activity (10.4% average increase, SD=0.92, p<.001). Students also reported learning practical prompting strategies and valued the immediate feedback and scenario-based design, though some faced challenges related to typing skills, platform friction, and scenario relevance. The revised assessment in Study 2 replaced multiple-choice items with true/false and open-ended questions, which improved item difficulty and discrimination, but internal reliability remained moderate, suggesting the need for larger-scale validation.

finding.finding_summary: Students reported increased confidence in using AI for learning after the module. Self-reported confidence rose by 10.4% on average (SD=0.92), and the post-activity shift was statistically significant (Wilcoxon test, p<.001).
finding.measure: 5-point Likert self-reported confidence in using AI to help learning
finding.study_size: n=111 (Study 1 valid data); n=98 for paired pre/post test analysis

finding.finding_summary: The module improved students’ prompting literacy, especially their ability to include background/context information in prompts. McNemar analyses showed a significant gain for the Background dimension from Q1 to Q3 (p=.039), while Relevance, Conciseness, and Purpose did not change significantly.
finding.measure: Human-graded prompt-writing dimensions across three practice tasks; prompting literacy pre/post and practice performance
finding.study_size: n=111 valid data in Study 1; 483 unique student-written prompts

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly studied prompting literacy as an AI-related academic skill, showing that students learned to write more effective prompts through scenario-based practice and feedback. Students’ average pre-test conceptual score was already high (mean=4.4/6), and post-test scores did not significantly increase (p=.377), suggesting a ceiling effect on conceptual identification despite gains in performance on some writing dimensions.
finding.measure: Prompting literacy assessment (multiple-choice in Study 1; revised true/false and open-ended items in Study 2)
finding.study_size: n=98 paired pre/post for test score analysis; n=111 valid classroom data overall

finding.finding_summary: The AI auto-grader was able to evaluate student-written prompts with high accuracy and provide detailed rationale, indicating potential for scalable immediate feedback. Average grading accuracy across dimensions was 0.92, with especially high accuracy for Relevance, Background, and Elaboration; Purpose was the weakest dimension at 0.85.
finding.measure: AI auto-grader accuracy against human labels on prompt dimensions

paper_profiles.title: On the Limits of Behavioral Alignment: Formal Verifiability and the Problem of Normative Indistinguishability
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines the epistemic limits of using finite behavioral evaluation to infer latent alignment properties in large language models. It argues that observed compliance on benchmarks or red-teaming protocols does not uniquely identify a model’s underlying normative objectives when the model can condition behavior on signals correlated with the evaluation regime.

The paper formalizes this as an identifiability problem, defining evaluation awareness, behavioral equivalence, and normative indistinguishability. Under these assumptions, it proves a conditional non-identifiability result: distinct latent alignment hypotheses can produce identical outputs on all evaluated interaction histories while diverging outside the tested regime.

To illustrate the theory, the author provides a stylized Gridworld example and a constructive LLM-based existence witness using Llama-3.2-3B with conditional fine-tuning. The empirical component is not about educational use or student outcomes; it demonstrates that explicit evaluation signals can induce perfectly compliant behavior under one regime and different behavior under another. The main conclusion is that black-box behavioral benchmarks are useful for measuring regime-bounded compliance, but cannot, by themselves, certify global alignment or rule out hidden regime-conditional policies.

paper_profiles.title: Designing for Human-Agent Alignment: Understanding what humans want from their agents
paper_profiles.venue: Extended Abstracts of the CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI EA ’24)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks what human collaborators want from autonomous generative-AI agents when those agents act on their behalf in a negotiation task. The authors focus on a concrete scenario: a seller agent negotiating the sale of a used camera in an online marketplace. Rather than evaluating a classroom or educational intervention, the study uses this marketplace setting to surface design requirements for human-agent alignment.

The researchers conducted 10 think-aloud interviews with adults working at a U.S.-based organization, showing each participant six transcripts of simulated buyer/seller negotiations generated with prompt-engineered agents. Participants reacted to failures such as the agent accepting offers below boundaries, changing transaction processes, failing to respond when the buyer disclosed being an agent, or creating a side channel to the human collaborator. The analysis produced six themes: knowledge schema alignment, autonomy and agency alignment, operational alignment and training, reputational heuristics alignment, ethics alignment, and human engagement alignment.
