The main conclusion is that effective agent design requires explicit alignment on not only task goals and guardrails, but also what information the agent should collect, how much autonomy it should have, how it should communicate with the user, and how it should protect the user’s reputation and ethical preferences. The paper also emphasizes that alignment is longitudinal and context-dependent: participants wanted different engagement and autonomy levels depending on the task, and some expected the agent to help them discover likely failure modes and defaults before deployment.

paper_profiles.title: Deliberative Technology for Alignment
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a conceptual position paper about how deliberative technology can be used to align powerful institutions and AI systems with the “will of humanity.” It argues that future-oriented social systems should be treated as alignment systems and that the key challenge is sensing, representing, and acting on heterogeneous human preferences and values through deliberative mechanisms.

The paper introduces a “Will matrix” as a computable representation of human will, discusses properties such as heterogeneity, instability, and partial observability, and then describes how deliberative technologies like collective response systems, deliberative polling, citizens’ assemblies, and online forums can sense human will through voluntary, mutually understood actions. It also argues that AI can improve these deliberative systems by making participation more interactive, individualized, efficient, and representative, and that insights from institutional deliberation may transfer to AI alignment.

The paper is not an empirical study of K-12 education or classroom/homework implementation. It does not evaluate generative AI in mathematics, teacher mediation, dosage, prompting behavior, curriculum alignment, or setting effects. Instead, it is a broad theory-and-application essay focused on governance, institutional alignment, and future AI alignment use cases.

finding.finding_summary: This is a conceptual/position paper rather than an empirical study, so it does not report measured institutional outcomes. It argues that deliberative technology and AI could help align institutions with public will, but provides no quantitative evidence, effect size, or sample size.
finding.measure: not_reported

paper_profiles.title: Inverted Classroom an der Hochschule Karlsruhe - ein nicht quantisierter Flip
paper_profiles.venue: Beitrag zu "Das Inverted Classroom Model: Begleitband zur ersten deutschen ICM-Konferenz"
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This chapter describes the Hochschule Karlsruhe’s SKATING project as it begins implementing and evaluating the Inverted Classroom Model (ICM) in engineering mathematics and related higher-education courses. The paper is framed as a practical and reflective report rather than a controlled efficacy study: it argues that inverted classrooms may help address student heterogeneity, limited semester-long learning, and dropout concerns in applied-science programs.

The authors present several pilot variants of inversion, including minimally inverted lecture summaries, a partially inverted single topic, and a time-limited fully inverted mathematics unit. Implementation details are emphasized: video creation formats, platform delivery via ILIAS/YouTube, use of analytics, forums, preparatory viewing expectations, and classroom observations. The chapter also lays out an evaluation plan using student surveys, teacher reflections, process observation, usage logs, and later exam comparisons. Reported early observations suggest that most students watched the videos before class, in-class time shifted to guided practice and peer work, and the approach was generally positively received, though students noted concerns about losing the ability to ask questions during video study and about added time demands.

finding.finding_summary: The chapter reports a pilot inversion of a higher mathematics topic in a cohort of about 20 motivated third-semester students. The intervention was designed so students studied video lessons before class and then used class time for guided problem solving, with the authors expecting improved understanding and exam performance; however, no post-intervention test statistics, effect sizes, or comparative result data are reported in the text.
finding.measure: Student understanding of higher mathematics topics; later planned comparison of exam results

finding.finding_summary: The paper emphasizes student motivation, satisfaction, curiosity, and a desired feeling of 'flow' as key goals of the inverted classroom implementation. Early feedback from students was mostly positive, although some expressed concern about not being able to ask questions during video study and about the extra time required; the chapter does not report quantitative satisfaction scores.
finding.measure: Student satisfaction, motivation, curiosity, perceived usefulness, and comments from feedback surveys/hand-raising

finding.finding_summary: The chapter describes increased opportunities for active problem solving, partner work, and discussion during class, and notes that the method is intended to support self-directed learning at students' own pace. It also reports that students interacted with video materials in different ways (e.g., repeated viewing, note-taking), but the evidence is descriptive and implementation-focused rather than inferential.
finding.measure: Observed in-class collaboration, self-directed study behavior, and video-use behavior

finding.finding_summary: A central focus is the implementation burden and workflow of the inverted classroom. The chapter reports that producing one recorded video segment took about 1 hour of total work, with roughly 30 minutes of setup time and 30 minutes of organization for the instructor per recording session; creating 20 minutes of usable video reportedly required at least 3 hours in prior examples cited by the authors. The paper argues that after initial setup, later semesters may require less effort, but the overall finding is mixed because student learning support improves while teacher workload and production demands increase.
finding.measure: Instructor workload, video production time, implementation effort, and organizational demands

finding.finding_summary: The chapter situates the pilot within the broader SKATING institutional reform project and argues that structured support, documentation, and pilot testing can help make inverted classroom approaches scalable within the university. It does not report institutional-level outcome data, but it makes a case that the model could become part of the teaching repertoire if piloting and evaluation are positive.
finding.measure: Institutional implementation and adoption of a new teaching model

paper_profiles.title: AI Conversational Tutors in Foreign Language Learning: A Mixed-Methods Evaluation Study
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings 14th Panhellenic Conference iCT in Education, Rhodes, October 2025
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines the design and perceived quality of AI conversational tutors for foreign language learning, with a focus on how they support speaking practice, conversational flow, error correction, and feedback. The author motivates the study by noting the rapid growth of LLM-based language-learning tools and the need for systematic ways to evaluate their pedagogical quality and user experience.

The study has three parts. First, the author conducts an expert-based usability and interaction review of four specialized language-learning apps (Talkio, TalkPal, Univerbal, Langua), using a simulated Spanish learner profile and short free-chat sessions. Second, the paper compares these tools with general-purpose voice-capable AI systems (ChatGPT and Gemini) used as improvised language tutors. Third, it proposes a 10-dimensional transcript-based evaluation framework and applies it to the six tutors using five LLM-based evaluators, reporting inter-rater reliability across the dimensions.

The main conclusion is that AI tutors differ substantially in how they structure dialogue, handle interruptions, provide corrective feedback, and support learner progression. Specialized tools often provide richer correction and more explicit tutoring behavior, while general-purpose models can still generate high-quality conversational experiences but may omit pedagogically useful feedback or complete transcripts. The paper emphasizes that effective language tutoring requires contextual error handling, repair of communication breakdowns, and clear, supportive feedback, and it argues for systematic evaluation methods for future AI tutor research and design.

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly studies foreign-language speaking practice and conversational fluency rather than achievement outcomes. In simulated 5-10 minute Spanish voice chats, the specialized tutors and general-purpose models differed in responsiveness, repair of breakdowns, and feedback; ChatGPT produced much longer turns (about 130 words/turn) than Gemini (32 words/turn), while learner turns averaged 61 vs 13 words respectively, suggesting that tool design and prompting behavior materially changed the nature of oral practice. No standardized learning gains were measured.
finding.measure: Voice-based conversational interaction quality, turn length, breakdown repair, and corrective feedback in Spanish practice chats
finding.study_size: n=6 tutors (4 specialized apps + 2 general-purpose AI systems); one scripted user profile per tool

finding.finding_summary: The evaluation framework explicitly assessed aspects tied to durable skills such as critical thinking and coherent reasoning in dialogue. The paper reports that T4 (Langua) especially supported critical thinking and richer discussion, while T3 provided culture-specific vocabulary but limited explicit correction; these judgments came from transcript-based expert scoring rather than learner outcome measures. No quantitative effect on student critical thinking was reported.
finding.measure: Transcript-based ratings of dialogue coherence, tutor initiative, and critical-thinking support within the 10-dimensional framework
finding.study_size: n=6 tutors; 1 transcript per tutor for quality assessment

finding.finding_summary: The paper studies efficiency-related properties of the tools, especially transcript availability, automation of feedback, and the ability to export or download conversation records. Some systems provided annotated transcripts and downloadable feedback reports, while general-purpose tools returned incomplete transcripts and required external speech-to-text to recover the full conversation, indicating uneven operational support for reuse and review. No formal productivity or workload outcomes were measured.
finding.measure: Availability and completeness of chat transcripts, export/download features, and automated feedback reports

paper_profiles.title: Breakable Machine: A K–12 Classroom Game for Transformative AI Literacy Through Spoofing and eXplainable AI (XAI)
paper_profiles.population: Elementary (PreK-5th) and Middle School (6-8th) / Early High School (9th)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper presents a classroom game called Breakable Machine, designed to teach K–12 learners critical and transformative AI literacy through hands-on spoofing of an image classifier. The activity asks students to manipulate their appearance or environment so that a model assigns a high-confidence label incorrectly, helping them see that AI systems can be brittle, biased, and manipulable rather than neutral or authoritative.

The resource is built around a browser-based teacher app and student app, with a shared classroom leaderboard, optional heat-map explanations, and access to the training data set. The teacher can pause play, change challenges, and enable different visualization views, making the activity explicitly classroom-mediated rather than self-paced. The target audience is grades 4–9 (ages 10–15), and the authors position the game within broader AI literacy and transformative agency frameworks.

This paper is not an empirical evaluation study; it is a technical and pedagogical design paper. The authors state that learning outcome evaluation is future work, so the paper does not report measured effects, sample sizes, or effect sizes. Its main contribution is a resource and rationale for using adversarial play, collective sensemaking, and XAI visuals to support critical reflection on AI robustness, feature saliency, and sociotechnical implications.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that the game is designed to foster critical thinking, inquiry, and collaborative sensemaking around AI systems, but it does not report empirical evidence of skill gains. No outcome data, sample size, or effect size are provided because the paper explicitly states that learning evaluation is future work.
finding.measure: not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The authors claim the activity is intended to support engagement, agency, and motivation through playful adversarial play and a shared leaderboard, but these are design intentions rather than measured outcomes. The paper does not include empirical evidence about student engagement or motivation in this version.
finding.measure: not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The paper substantively focuses on AI literacy content rather than traditional school subjects. It describes a classroom resource for teaching image classification, adversarial attacks, saliency, and model brittleness, but reports no measured academic outcome data.
finding.measure: not_reported

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT for Good? On Opportunities and Challenges of Large Language Models for Education
paper_profiles.population: K-12 and higher education learners and educators (broad, not a single sampled population)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This position paper examines the opportunities and risks of large language models (LLMs), especially ChatGPT-like systems, for education. Rather than reporting a single empirical study, it synthesizes early research and recent examples to discuss how LLMs may support learning, teaching, assessment, personalization, and content generation across educational levels.

The paper is especially relevant for K-12 contexts because it discusses elementary, middle, and high school uses, including reading/writing support, math word problem generation, tutoring, and teacher feedback/assessment. It also reviews broader educational uses such as teacher professional development, remote learning, and accessibility supports for learners with disabilities.

A major contribution of the paper is its detailed risk analysis. The authors argue that LLMs can create copyright and plagiarism problems, may amplify bias, can encourage overreliance by learners and teachers, can make it difficult to distinguish AI-generated from student-generated work, and raise data privacy/security concerns. They emphasize that apparent benefits depend on strong guardrails: human oversight, fact-checking, transparency, responsible deployment, curriculum design that promotes critical thinking, and access/fairness protections. The paper concludes that these risks are manageable if LLMs are used as supplements rather than replacements for human instruction and if educational systems adopt clear policies and mitigation strategies.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that LLMs can support math education by generating math word problems, explanations, and step-by-step solutions, potentially helping middle and high school students understand and practice mathematics. However, this is presented as a prospective opportunity rather than an empirically tested effect, and the paper notes that the technology still has limitations and brittleness that require caution.
finding.measure: not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The paper states that LLMs may improve student engagement and participation, especially in group and remote learning settings and through curiosity-prompting or conversational interactions. These claims are based on cited prior work and conceptual argumentation rather than a new experiment in this paper.
finding.measure: student engagement / participation / curiosity expression

finding.finding_summary: A central theme of the paper is that LLMs can support critical thinking, problem-solving, collaboration, and fact-checking, but they can also weaken these same skills when learners rely too heavily on generated answers. The authors explicitly warn that effortless answer generation may reduce independent investigation and critical thinking, and they recommend using LLMs only as a supplement to learning, with human oversight and verification strategies.
finding.measure: critical thinking / problem-solving / fact-checking / collaboration

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that LLMs can reduce teacher workload through automated or semi-automated grading, feedback generation, lesson planning, and content creation. It cites prior work suggesting grading effort could be reduced by up to 85% in large courses using NLP-based feedback systems, but the paper itself is a position paper and does not report a new empirical estimate.
finding.measure: teacher workload / grading effort / feedback production

finding.finding_summary: The paper devotes substantial attention to institutional risks and governance needs, including bias, privacy/security, copyright/plagiarism, detection of AI-generated work, fair access, and sustainability. It does not test a policy intervention, but it strongly argues that educational systems need explicit guardrails, transparency, human oversight, consent, and usage restrictions to avoid harms and protect integrity.
finding.measure: policy / governance / privacy / integrity / fair access

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT-generated help produces learning gains equivalent to human tutor-authored help on mathematics skills
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper evaluates whether worked-solution hints generated by ChatGPT can support mathematics learning as effectively as human tutor-authored hints. The authors frame the study around two questions: how often ChatGPT produces low-quality or incorrect hints, and whether those hints produce learning gains comparable to human-authored help and to no help at all.

The intervention is a 3 x 4 randomized experiment with Mechanical Turk participants (initially n=394; analyzed n=274) assigned to one of three hint conditions—control/no hints, human tutor hints, or ChatGPT hints—and one of four mathematics topic areas: Elementary Algebra, Intermediate Algebra, College Algebra, and Statistics. Pre- and post-tests with the same three items measured learning gains, and participants completed a five-question acquisition phase in an online tutoring system (OATutor). The study also included a separate quality-check procedure for ChatGPT outputs, with six undergraduate raters evaluating hints for correctness and appropriateness, and the authors tested a self-consistency mitigation method to reduce hallucinations.

The main finding is that ChatGPT hints produced statistically significant overall learning gains relative to the no-hint control, and these gains were not statistically significantly different from human tutor-authored hints. However, the study also found that 32% of ChatGPT-generated hints failed quality checks because they contained incorrect work and/or incorrect answers. The authors report that self-consistency substantially reduced this error rate, bringing algebra topics near 0% error and reducing statistics error to 13%, and they explicitly caution that raw ChatGPT output should not be used uncritically for student feedback without error mitigation or human supervision.

finding.finding_summary: In a randomized 3-condition study (analyzed n=274), ChatGPT hints produced statistically significant learning gains on mathematics post-tests relative to the no-hint control. Overall learning gain for the ChatGPT condition was 17.00% (pre-test 43.51%, post-test 60.52%), compared with 11.62% for human tutor hints and 1.85% for control; the ChatGPT vs. human difference was not statistically significant (p=0.416), while ChatGPT vs. control was significant (p=0.011).
finding.measure: Math pre-test/post-test scores across Elementary Algebra, Intermediate Algebra, College Algebra, and Statistics

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that ChatGPT hints were produced much faster than human tutor-authored help and notes that ChatGPT-generated hints were created in about 1/20th the time required for human-authored hints. The human tutor help sequences were also more time-intensive to author and quality-check, whereas ChatGPT outputs could be generated instantly, though 32% initially failed quality checks and required mitigation or screening.
finding.measure: Authoring time / production efficiency for tutoring hints

finding.finding_summary: The study indirectly engages with critical evaluation of solution quality through its hallucination and quality-check analysis, but it does not directly measure durable skills such as metacognition or critical thinking in learners. The main evidence is the authors’ caution that students should treat ChatGPT as an ‘imperfect robot’ when error mitigation is not near-perfect, implying a need for critical scrutiny of AI-generated feedback.
finding.measure: not_reported

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT: Bullshit spewer or the end of traditional assessments in higher education?
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This article is an early exploratory review of ChatGPT and its implications for higher education assessment, teaching, and learning. The authors combine a desktop literature review with informal experimentation using ChatGPT to understand its capabilities, limitations, and the likely effects of generative AI on academic work. The paper is not an empirical study of student outcomes; instead, it synthesizes early reports and demonstrations of the tool's performance across writing, translation, and question answering.

The central concern is whether ChatGPT threatens traditional assessment, especially essays, by enabling students to generate passable text quickly and potentially evade plagiarism detection. The authors test the system on prompts for statistical explanation, an essay task, and Chinese composition, finding that it can produce fluent but often shallow, generic, inaccurate, or grammatically weak output. They also highlight reliability and integrity issues, including fabricated references, uneven factual accuracy, network errors, and the ability to rephrase text to evade plagiarism checks. The article concludes that educators and institutions should not simply ban the tool, but instead adapt assessment practices, improve policy, and consider guardrails for appropriate use.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that ChatGPT can generate essays quickly and produce fluent prose, but the output was often generic, shallow, and sometimes inaccurate or grammatically weak. In one test, a 2000-word essay prompt produced only about 500 words within 120 seconds, with no reliable in-text citations and possible bogus references; in another, a Chinese composition was poorly structured and awkwardly translated from English.
finding.measure: Essay generation quality, citation support, and language quality in sampled prompts

finding.finding_summary: The authors argue that ChatGPT may support idea generation and experimentation, but it performs poorly on higher-order thinking tasks requiring critical and analytical reasoning. Their direct prompt tests suggested the model was useful for conceptual explanations but less competent when the task demanded deeper analysis and synthesis.
finding.measure: Performance on prompts requiring critical/analytical writing versus basic explanation

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds that ChatGPT can produce text and explanations very quickly, typically within 60-120 seconds, suggesting potential time savings for drafting and basic explanation tasks. However, this efficiency is limited by network errors, character limits, and the need for human verification because of accuracy and completeness problems.
finding.measure: Response time, task completion speed, and usability limitations

finding.finding_summary: The article argues that ChatGPT poses institutional risks to assessment integrity because it can generate passable prose that may not be detected by plagiarism software and can be used to reduce originality scores. At the same time, the authors recommend institutional adaptation rather than simple bans, including redesigning assessments, updating policies, and setting usage restrictions/guardrails.
finding.measure: Assessment integrity risks, plagiarism-detection evasion, and policy implications discussed in the paper

paper_profiles.title: Editorial: Generative AI in education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This editorial introduces a Frontiers Research Topic on generative AI in education and summarizes the 11 included papers. Its purpose is not to test a single intervention, but to frame the field’s emerging questions: how generative AI can support learning, feedback, assessment, tutoring, career guidance, and learner modeling, and what challenges accompany these uses.

The editorial highlights several themes across the volume, including personalized feedback, student emotions, academic achievement, critical thinking, assessment design, whole-learner support, AI mentors, and interactive listening tasks. It also explicitly notes concerns relevant to educational safety and integrity, including the need to examine answer accuracy and emotional content, validity/reliability/fairness in personalized assessment, interpretability, ethical guidelines, transparency, privacy, algorithmic bias, and the possibility of AI-enhanced robots generating incorrect information and deceiving students.

Because this is an editorial overview rather than an empirical study, it does not report original participant-level data or causal effects. The paper’s main contribution is synthesizing the topics and cautioning that responsible, human-in-the-loop use and further research are needed before broad educational deployment, especially where accuracy, deception, and privacy are involved.

finding.finding_summary: The editorial summarizes one included study on pre-service teachers using ChatGPT to create mathematical proofs in geometry, but it does not report a direct achievement effect. It only notes a variety of usage patterns and limited knowledge of the model’s inner workings, with no quantitative outcome values reported.
finding.measure: Use patterns and mathematical proof creation by pre-service teachers

finding.finding_summary: Across the Research Topic, the editorial emphasizes student emotions, engagement, motivation, and emotional content in AI responses. It reports that one included paper found ChatGPT answers tended to be more positive than human responses, and other papers suggest generative AI may support engagement and emotional regulation, but the editorial itself does not provide direct effect estimates.
finding.measure: Emotional content, engagement, motivation, emotional regulation

finding.finding_summary: The editorial highlights critical thinking, human interaction, and strategic use of AI as central themes. It notes that generative AI may foster critical use and communication skills, but also that there are limitations such as the inability to foster critical thinking consistently; no quantitative effects are reported in the editorial itself.
finding.measure: Critical thinking and human interaction/communication skills

finding.finding_summary: The editorial describes generative AI as potentially useful for personalized feedback, immediate doubt clarification, AI mentors, and automated item generation, all of which could improve efficiency in tutoring and assessment workflows. However, it does not present direct efficiency metrics or effect sizes, only a qualitative overview of potential benefits discussed in the included papers.
finding.measure: Personalized feedback, tutoring support, automated item generation

finding.finding_summary: This editorial substantively addresses governance and institutional issues around generative AI in education, including ethical guidelines, transparency, human-in-the-loop deployment, validity, reliability, fairness, privacy, and algorithmic bias. It also flags risks of incorrect information and deception by AI-enhanced robots, and states that these concerns require further research and responsible implementation rather than providing empirical mitigation outcomes.
finding.measure: Ethical guidelines, privacy, fairness, reliability, transparency, deception/incorrect information risks

paper_profiles.title: Evaluating large language models in analysing classroom dialogue
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether GPT-4 can reliably assist with the qualitative coding of classroom dialogue, a task used in teaching diagnosis and professional development. The authors compare manual expert coding of lesson transcripts with GPT-4-based coding using a customized GPT system and a classroom dialogue coding scheme adapted from the Cambridge Dialogue Analysis Scheme.

The study uses transcripts from six mathematics lessons and six Chinese language lessons drawn from two junior high school classes in Beijing. Classroom videos were transcribed, manually coded by experts, and then re-coded by GPT-4; the authors evaluate time efficiency, inter-coder agreement, and Cohen’s kappa reliability across 15 dialogue categories. They also note that retrieval-augmented generation and prompt engineering were used to improve the model’s coding performance.

Main findings are that GPT-4 greatly reduced coding time and matched human coders well on many categories, with overall agreement above 90% for both mathematics and Chinese lessons. However, performance was uneven across codes: some categories showed very high agreement, while others—especially coordination-related and context-dependent codes—showed low or even near-zero/negative kappa, indicating that the model sometimes diverged substantially from human interpretation. The authors conclude that GPT-4 is promising for scalable dialogue analysis, but its limitations in context-sensitive coding mean human oversight and scheme refinement remain important.

finding.finding_summary: GPT-4 substantially reduced the time required for classroom dialogue coding. For one mathematics lesson (82 dialogue turns; 41 min 29 s), manual coding took about 150 minutes, whereas ChatGPT-based coding took about 5 minutes, a roughly 30x speedup. Across the analyzed lessons, the authors report that total AI-assisted analysis did not exceed one hour.
finding.measure: Time required to code classroom dialogue transcripts
finding.study_size: n=12 lessons (6 math, 6 Chinese); timed comparison reported for 1 math lesson with 82 dialogue turns

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly studies coding of classroom dialogue in Chinese language lessons, which makes language-based classroom interaction a central outcome. GPT-4 achieved high overall agreement with human coders in Chinese lessons (90.91% agreement across 348 dialogue turns), but some codes were poorly matched, including CI (κ=-0.005), SC (κ=0.004), and RC (no meaningful agreement; frequency issues noted), indicating that context-sensitive language interpretation remained inconsistent.
finding.measure: Dialogue coding agreement / Cohen’s kappa for Chinese classroom dialogue categories

finding.finding_summary: The study also directly analyzes mathematics classroom dialogue, reporting 90.37% agreement between the human coder and GPT-4 across 576 dialogue turns. Yet several context-dependent categories showed weaker performance in math lessons, including CI (κ=0.497), SC (κ=0.216), and RC (κ=-0.002), showing that the model sometimes failed to reproduce expert coding in math-specific instructional exchanges.
finding.measure: Dialogue coding agreement / Cohen’s kappa for mathematics classroom dialogue categories

finding.finding_summary: Although not an intervention study on students’ durable skills, the paper substantively focuses on coding dialogue features tied to reasoning, coordination, critique, and collaborative talk, which are closely related to collaboration and critical thinking. GPT-4 performed very well on some dialogue categories linked to these skills, but poorly on coordination-related categories (e.g. CI, SC, RC), suggesting that automated analysis of higher-order talk is promising yet unreliable in context-heavy cases.
finding.measure: Coding reliability for dialogue categories associated with reasoning and co-ordination
finding.study_size: 12 lessons total; 924 dialogue turns across math and Chinese

paper_profiles.title: The future landscape of large language models in medicine
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This perspective article surveys the potential roles and limitations of large language models (LLMs) in medicine, with attention to patient care, medical research, and medical education. The authors frame LLMs as tools that can summarize text, support communication, generate content, and assist with documentation, but they emphasize that these systems also raise substantial concerns about misinformation, bias, privacy, reproducibility, and misuse.

The paper is not an intervention study; instead, it synthesizes prior literature and illustrates LLM behavior with example prompts and outputs from ChatGPT (GPT-3.5 and GPT-4). In the education section, the authors argue that LLMs could be useful as personalized teaching assistants and feedback providers, but they also warn that students may use them inappropriately, externalize critical thinking, and rely on outputs that can be false or misleading. They recommend responsible-use guidelines, transparent regulation, prompt-engineering instruction, and safety guardrails, while noting that current systems still lack reliable mechanisms to ensure correctness.

More broadly, the paper concludes that LLMs may improve access to knowledge and efficiency, but their current limitations—hallucinations, inconsistent outputs across versions, bias, weak factuality, privacy risks, and potential for harmful misuse—mean that safe deployment in education and clinical contexts requires stronger governance, validation, and technical safeguards.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that LLMs could support educational tasks by providing explanations, summaries, individualized feedback, and simulated practice conversations, but it does not present an educational intervention or student outcome study. The educational claims are illustrative and conceptual rather than empirical, so no effect size or sample-based achievement evidence is reported.
finding.measure: Illustrative educational use cases; not an outcome measure study

finding.finding_summary: The authors explicitly discuss critical thinking as a central concern: they anticipate that LLM use could reduce students’ ability to distinguish valuable from irrelevant or incorrect information and could externalize reasoning. This is not tested empirically in the paper; it is a theoretical concern supported by examples and prior literature, with no sample size or effect estimate reported.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, analytical thinking, and reasoning (conceptual discussion)

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that LLMs may reduce documentation burden, streamline chart review, and improve efficiency in translating unstructured notes into structured reports. It states that documentation and administrative requirements consume around 25% of clinicians’ workdays, but it does not evaluate an intervention or report an effect size for productivity gains.
finding.measure: Documentation burden, chart review, and administrative efficiency (conceptual discussion)

finding.finding_summary: A major focus of the paper is governance and institutional risk: the authors describe misinformation, bias, privacy leakage, prompt injection attacks, lack of accountability, and the need for transparent regulation and usage guidelines. They also note that safety guardrails may themselves introduce new forms of bias, and they call for legal and institutional frameworks before clinical or educational deployment.
finding.measure: Governance, regulation, privacy, bias, and safety concerns (conceptual discussion)

paper_profiles.title: LLaMA: Open and Efficient Foundation Language Models
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper introduces LLaMA, a family of open foundation language models ranging from 7B to 65B parameters. The main goal is to demonstrate that strong large language models can be trained using only publicly available data, with competitive performance to then-state-of-the-art models such as GPT-3, Chinchilla, and PaLM, while being more efficient to run at inference time.

The paper describes the training corpus, model architecture modifications, optimization strategy, and efficient implementation details used to train the models. It evaluates the resulting models on a wide range of standard NLP benchmarks, including common-sense reasoning, closed-book QA, reading comprehension, mathematical reasoning, code generation, and MMLU. The models generally improve with scale, and LLaMA-65B is reported to be competitive with or better than several much larger models on many benchmarks.

The paper is not a K-12 intervention study and does not involve students, teachers, or classrooms. Its population is best characterized as adult AI researchers/developers, since it presents a general-purpose model release and benchmark evaluation. It also includes a focused section on bias, toxicity, and truthfulness, noting that large language models can reproduce training-data biases, generate toxic content, and still produce incorrect or hallucinatory answers; the authors argue these issues are important limitations and that the evaluations are insufficient to fully characterize risk.

finding.finding_summary: On quantitative reasoning benchmarks, LLaMA shows improved performance as model size increases, but this is an evaluation of the base language model rather than a K-12 educational intervention. On GSM8k, LLaMA-65B reached 50.9 without majority voting and 69.7 with maj1@k, outperforming Minerva-62B on the no-finetuning comparison in the paper's table.
finding.measure: GSM8k and MATH mathematical reasoning accuracy / exact match

paper_profiles.title: Large language models encode clinical knowledge
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper evaluates whether large language models (LLMs) can encode and apply clinical knowledge for answering medical questions. The authors introduce MultiMedQA, a benchmark combining six existing medical question-answering datasets and a new consumer-health dataset (HealthSearchQA), and assess two models built on PaLM: PaLM and instruction-tuned Flan-PaLM. They use both automated accuracy metrics on multiple-choice benchmarks and a human evaluation framework for long-form answers that rates scientific consensus, completeness, helpfulness, bias, and potential harm.

Across multiple-choice datasets, Flan-PaLM performs strongly, reaching state-of-the-art accuracy on MedQA (67.6%), MedMCQA (57.6%), PubMedQA (79.0%), and MMLU clinical topics. However, human evaluation of consumer medical questions shows important limitations: only 61.9% of Flan-PaLM long-form answers were judged aligned with scientific consensus, 16.1% contained inappropriate or incorrect content, and 29.7% were rated as potentially leading to harmful outcomes. After instruction prompt tuning, the resulting Med-PaLM model substantially improves these dimensions, with 92.6% consensus alignment and 5.9% potentially harmful responses, approaching clinician performance.

The study’s population and context are adult medical-question users, clinicians, and lay evaluators rather than K-12 learners. The paper concludes that while LLMs can encode substantial medical knowledge and improve with scaling and instruction tuning, they still require strong alignment, uncertainty handling, bias/fairness work, and guardrails before safe real-world clinical use. It explicitly discusses concerns including hallucination-like incorrect content, harmful advice, bias, overreliance, privacy, and security vulnerabilities, framing these as limitations rather than as observed effects on patient outcomes.

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly studies whether LLMs can improve the efficiency of answering medical questions by generating useful, aligned responses. Flan-PaLM achieved strong benchmark performance and Med-PaLM produced more helpful and clinically aligned long-form answers, suggesting potential productivity gains for information retrieval and drafting, though no real-world workflow time savings were measured.
finding.measure: Medical question-answering benchmark accuracy; clinician and lay-user ratings of helpfulness and intent alignment
finding.study_size: n=140 long-form answers for human evaluation; benchmark sizes vary by dataset (e.g., HealthSearchQA n=3,173 questions)

finding.finding_summary: The paper centrally examines safety, bias, reliability, and governance issues relevant to institutional deployment of LLMs in healthcare. Human raters found 29.7% of Flan-PaLM answers and 5.9% of Med-PaLM answers could lead to harm, and 7.9% of Flan-PaLM answers were judged biased versus 0.8% for Med-PaLM, indicating that guardrails and alignment substantially reduce but do not eliminate risks. The authors explicitly recommend stronger evaluation frameworks, uncertainty communication, grounding, fairness/equity work, and deployment guardrails to mitigate overreliance and other downstream harms.
finding.measure: Clinician ratings of scientific consensus, inappropriate/incorrect content, missing content, harm, likelihood of harm, and bias
finding.study_size: n=140 long-form answers; 9 clinicians; 5 lay users

finding.finding_summary: The paper evaluates reasoning, comprehension, and knowledge retrieval as core capabilities of the models. Flan-PaLM outperformed baseline PaLM, and Med-PaLM substantially narrowed the gap to clinicians on correct retrieval (95.4% vs 97.8%) and correct reasoning (92.5% vs 97.7%), indicating improved expert-like reasoning performance in medical QA, though still below clinician level.
finding.measure: Clinician ratings of correct comprehension, correct retrieval, correct reasoning, and incorrect reasoning in long-form answers

paper_profiles.title: Revolutionizing healthcare: the role of artificial intelligence in clinical practice
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This review examines the role of artificial intelligence (AI) in clinical practice, focusing on how AI systems may improve diagnosis, treatment selection, population health management, patient education, and clinical decision-making. It synthesizes indexed literature from PubMed/Medline, Scopus, and EMBASE, with an emphasis on large language models, machine learning, deep learning, predictive analytics, and virtual assistants in healthcare.

The paper is not an intervention study; rather, it surveys prior studies and frameworks to describe benefits and limitations of AI in healthcare settings. Across domains such as diagnostic imaging, genomic medicine, dose optimization, drug information, patient education, and mental health support, the authors conclude that AI may improve accuracy, efficiency, and personalization, but only if implemented with human oversight, transparency, and strong governance.

The review also foregrounds risks and limitations, including data privacy and security threats, bias, hallucinations/fabricated outputs, lack of personalization and empathy, and the need for human expertise. The authors recommend guardrails such as cybersecurity, regulatory frameworks, transparency, and education/training to ensure responsible deployment.

finding.finding_summary: The review argues that AI can improve workflow efficiency, reduce costs, and save time in healthcare operations such as diagnostic interpretation, laboratory testing, triage, and patient outreach. These claims are supported by cited studies, but the paper itself is a narrative review and does not present a single pooled effect size.
finding.measure: Workflow efficiency, time savings, cost reduction, and reduced workload in clinical and administrative processes

finding.finding_summary: The paper discusses institutional and governance effects of AI, including the need for guidelines, regulatory frameworks, transparency, privacy protection, and cybersecurity. It emphasizes that implementation benefits are contingent on oversight and that risks such as bias, data breaches, and hallucinations could undermine safe adoption if not addressed.
finding.measure: Policy, governance, ethical/legal safeguards, and institutional implementation considerations

paper_profiles.title: How Does ChatGPT Perform on the United States Medical Licensing Examination (USMLE)? The Implications of Large Language Models for Medical Education and Knowledge Assessment
paper_profiles.extended_summary: This paper evaluates how well ChatGPT answers multiple-choice medical knowledge questions aligned to the USMLE Step 1 and Step 2 Clinical Knowledge exams. The authors compare ChatGPT’s performance on two question sets: 100 AMBOSS questions per step and the NBME free 120 questions, and also benchmark against GPT-3 and InstructGPT. In addition to accuracy, they qualitatively assess whether ChatGPT’s explanations show logical reasoning and whether responses rely on internal versus external information from the question stem.

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT answered between 42% and 64.4% of medical licensing questions correctly across four datasets (n=389 total questions), outperforming GPT-3 and InstructGPT. Accuracy declined with higher AMBOSS question difficulty on Step 1 without the attending tip (P=.01), indicating performance was sensitive to problem complexity rather than uniformly reliable.
finding.measure: USMLE-style multiple-choice question accuracy / medical knowledge assessment

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly evaluated narrative coherence and explanation quality. ChatGPT provided a logical explanation for 100% of responses on the NBME datasets and used internal question information in 96.8% of cases overall (183/189), but external information was much less common in incorrect answers than correct ones (44.5% lower on NBME-Free-Step1 and 27% lower on NBME-Free-Step2), suggesting reasoning was often coherent but not consistently accurate.
finding.measure: Logical reasoning, internal information, and external information presence in model outputs
finding.study_size: n=189 NBME responses for qualitative analysis

finding.finding_summary: The authors argue ChatGPT may function as an interactive tutoring tool or small-group learning surrogate because it can provide immediate dialogic feedback and explanations. However, this is a proposed educational use case rather than an experimentally measured efficiency outcome, and the paper does not quantify workload reduction or time savings.
finding.measure: not_reported

paper_profiles.title: Investigating generative AI models and detection techniques: impacts of tokenization and dataset size on identification of AI-generated text
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how well machine learning and transformer-based detectors can distinguish between human-written essays and AI-generated essays, with a particular focus on high school writing-assessment contexts. The authors motivate the study by noting growing concerns that generative AI may be used for academic cheating and that existing detectors can fail on paraphrased or "humanized" AI text, including text altered by tools such as QuillBot and GPT-Humanizer.

Using the ASAP Kaggle essay dataset (prompt 1) as the human-written benchmark, the authors generate or collect essays from multiple GenAI systems (ChatGPT 3.5, 4.0, 4o, Gemini, Gemini Advanced, Claude, Claude 3.5) and compare classical classifiers (SVM, logistic regression, XGBoost) with transformer models (BERT, Electra, RoBERTa). They also test detection on paraphrased AI essays and propose a synonym-replacement tokenization strategy to improve detection of humanized AI text. Across experiments, the detectors perform strongly on pure AI essays, with SVM, Electra, and RoBERTa reaching high accuracies/QWK scores; however, paraphrasing substantially reduces detector performance, and the proposed synonym method partially recovers it.

The main conclusion is that current detectors can separate original AI-generated essays from human essays with high accuracy in this setup, but AI-humanizing paraphrase tools create a real detection problem that can meaningfully weaken current systems. The paper does not report student achievement effects from using GenAI; instead, its substantive contribution is about academic-integrity risk, detector reliability, and the need for continued development of detection safeguards and policies in K-12 writing assessment settings.

finding.finding_summary: The study is about detecting AI-generated writing in a high school essay context, not improving writing achievement. On pure AI vs. human essay classification, detectors performed very well (e.g., SVM accuracy 0.973 on GPT-3.5, QWK 0.963; RoBERTa QWK 0.962 on Claude), but paraphrasing substantially reduced performance (e.g., SVM accuracy dropped to 0.665 with QuillBot and 0.62 with GPT-Humanizer before the authors' synonym-based modification).
finding.measure: Essay source classification performance (accuracy, precision, recall, F1, QWK) on human-written vs. AI-generated writing
finding.study_size: n=1,500 human essays; n=500 essays per GenAI model version; n=200 paraphrased GPT-4o essays; n=1,000 GPT-4o essays for size analysis

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly addresses academic integrity, cheating detection, and the reliability of institutional AI-detection practices in high-stakes writing assessment. It argues that current detectors can work well on pure AI text but are vulnerable to paraphrasing/humanizer tools, creating enforcement and governance challenges for schools; the authors also call for robust policies, ethical guidelines, and continued detector development.
finding.measure: Detector reliability and misclassification rates in academic-integrity screening; impact of paraphrasing on detection performance
finding.study_size: n=1,500 human essays; n=500 essays per GenAI model version; n=200 paraphrased GPT-4o essays

paper_profiles.title: Evaluation Report on Large Language Models Solving High School Mathematics Questions
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This report evaluates the performance of several large language models (LLMs) on high school mathematics exam questions drawn from Chinese college entrance examinations from 2019 to 2023. The paper focuses on how well the models solve different question types (multiple-choice, fill-in-the-blank, and comprehensive questions), and compares them on accuracy, response time, logical reasoning, guidance sensitivity, and creative multi-solution generation.

The authors tested at least eight LLM APIs/models, including GLM-4-Flash, ERNIE-Speed-128K, Spark-lite, Hunyuan-lite, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, gemma-2-9b-it, Meta-Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, and Yi-34B. They used exact matching for multiple-choice items, fuzzy/semantic matching for fill-in-the-blank items, and expert/AI-assisted judgment for comprehensive questions; they also measured response latency and multi-solution outputs. The report concludes that model performance varies substantially across metrics: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and ERNIE-Speed-128K are strongest on accuracy for some tasks, GLM-4-Flash tends to generate the most and most complex multi-solution outputs, and some models are much slower or less accurate than others.

Overall, the paper is an evaluation report rather than an intervention study, and it does not test student learning outcomes. It suggests that LLMs may be useful educational tools but need further optimization, especially in logical reasoning and creative problem solving. The paper also implies that prompt design can improve performance, but it does not discuss student-facing guardrails, misuse, cheating, privacy, or safety restrictions in depth.

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly evaluates LLM performance on high school mathematics exam questions across multiple item types and difficulty levels. Accuracy varied widely by model and task: for single-solution items, reported accuracies ranged from 0.100 to 0.250 on item-type aggregates, and from 26.67% to 56.67% across difficulty bands; for multi-solution items, accuracy ranged from 0.35 to 0.64, with Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct highest (0.64) and Spark-lite / Meta-Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct lowest (0.45).
finding.measure: Accuracy on high school mathematics exam questions (multiple-choice, fill-in-the-blank, comprehensive questions; single-solution and multi-solution settings)

finding.finding_summary: The report substantively examines logical reasoning and creativity/solution diversity as model capabilities. Logical performance was summarized via guidance attempts and success rates (e.g., Hunyuan-lite reportedly required only 3 attempts to guide incorrect answers, while Yi-34B required 6), and creativity was assessed through richness and complexity of multi-solution outputs (e.g., GLM-4-Flash had the highest complexity score of 68 and the largest average number of solutions per question at 4.5).
finding.measure: Logical reasoning metrics (guidance attempts, success rate) and creative problem-solving metrics (solution richness, complexity)

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly measures response time as an operational performance metric for LLMs on mathematics questions. In single-solution settings, the shortest times were reported for models such as Meta-Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct on multiple-choice items (0.32 s) and gemma-2-9b-it on fill-in-the-blank items (0.32 s), while Yi-34B was slowest on multiple-choice items (4.50 s) and GLM-4-Flash was slowest on comprehensive questions (16.01 s); in multi-solution settings, Spark-lite was fastest (688 s) and GLM-4-Flash slowest (7400 s).
finding.measure: Response time in seconds for single-solution and multi-solution math problem solving

finding.finding_summary: The paper does not study a non-mathematics academic outcome, but it does discuss the use of prompts and guidance styles as a methodological factor affecting model output quality. Because this is not a substantive learner outcome and is only marginally related to academic performance, it is not a central assignment; however, the report does show that prompt conditioning changed model behavior, with some models improving accuracy and/or speed under different guidance prompts.
finding.measure: Prompt-conditioned changes in model output on math questions

paper_profiles.title: Exploring the Applications of Generative AI in High School STEM Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether generative AI can improve high school STEM learning outcomes and whether a generative AI literacy program changes those effects. The author frames the study against concerns about academic dishonesty, misinformation, overreliance, and limited factual reliability in general-purpose generative AI, arguing that schools need clearer guidance and guardrails if these tools are to be used responsibly.

The study uses a quasi-experimental pre-test/post-test design in a high school physics context at Tomball Memorial High School in Texas. Students in AP Physics 1 and on-level physics were assigned to one of four conditions: no external resources (control), search engine access, generative AI access (Bing AI/GPT-4-based), or generative AI plus a short AI literacy slideshow. The intervention lasted two class periods and included a teacher lecture, then a 20-minute study period with the assigned tool, followed by a post-test and survey.

Results were mixed overall. In AP Physics, there was a statistically significant difference among experimental groups (ANOVA p=0.011), with the generative AI only group performing worse than both the search engine group (t-test p=0.0062) and the AI-literacy group (t-test p=0.0256). Descriptively, the AI-only group also underperformed the control group in both AP and on-level physics, while the AI-literacy group improved relative to AI-only. However, there was no statistically significant difference between the control group and any treatment group in either section, and survey measures of understanding, confidence, engagement, and enjoyment showed no significant differences. The author concludes that general-purpose generative AI can be detrimental when used without literacy/guardrails, while a literacy program may help, but the short duration and subject-specific context limit broader claims.

finding.finding_summary: In the AP Physics section, the generative AI-only group performed worse than both the search engine group and the AI-literacy group on the post-test score-change measure. The AP Physics ANOVA was statistically significant (p=0.011), and follow-up t-tests found significant differences between SE vs. GAI (p=0.0062) and GAI vs. GAI-LP (p=0.0256); however, there was no significant difference between control and any treatment group in either section.
finding.measure: Pre-test to post-test score difference on physics assessments (AP Physics momentum/impulse; on-level physics electricity/circuits)
finding.study_size: n=171 total quantitative participants; AP Physics n=91, on-level physics n=80
finding.std_deviation: AP Physics SDs: control 1.355, SE 1.387, GAI-LP 1.225, GAI 1.791; On-level physics SDs: control 1.700, SE 2.250, GAI 2.199, GAI-LP 1.569

finding.finding_summary: Survey results did not show statistically significant differences across groups for understanding, confidence, engagement, or enjoyment. Although the generative AI group had slightly higher mean engagement, the interval plots overlapped substantially and the MANOVA was not significant (p=0.115).
finding.measure: Post-survey ratings of understanding, confidence, engagement, and enjoyment
finding.confidence_interval: 95% confidence intervals overlapped across groups; MANOVA p=0.115

finding.finding_summary: The paper discusses responsible use, ethical awareness, and AI literacy as important supports for effective student use of generative AI, but the main measured durable-skill-related outcome was self-reported understanding/confidence rather than a direct critical-thinking measure. The AI literacy condition appeared to improve performance relative to AI-only, suggesting that guidance may help students use the tool more effectively, but no direct durable-skill effect size was reported.
finding.measure: AI literacy program exposure; self-reported understanding/confidence/engagement; indirect evidence via performance differences between GAI and GAI-LP
finding.study_size: n=171 quantitative participants; n=60 survey respondents

paper_profiles.title: V-MATH: An Agentic Approach to the Vietnamese National High School Graduation Mathematics Exams
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper presents V-MATH, an agentic AI framework designed to support Vietnamese high school students preparing for the National High School Graduation Mathematics Exams. The system combines three LLM-based agents: one that generates exam questions aligned to the Vietnamese Ministry of Education specification matrix, one that solves and explains exam problems step by step, and one that personalizes practice based on student performance.

The paper also describes a large exam dataset (NHSGMEs) built from 220 official PDF sources, along with a benchmark (VNHSGE) used to evaluate solving and generation performance. The target context is high-stakes upper-secondary mathematics in Vietnam, where exam structure, alignment to standards, and language-specific reasoning are central concerns.

Empirically, the authors report strong benchmark performance for the system, including very high exact-match accuracy on VNHSGE, section-level accuracy on held-out exam sets, and improved student scores in the personalized learning component. The paper emphasizes matrix compliance, explanation quality, and reduced educator workload, while also noting future concerns such as reliability under distribution shift, fairness, auditability, and privacy. However, the evaluation is primarily system-level and benchmark-based rather than a controlled study of student learning outcomes.

finding.finding_summary: The system achieved very high mathematics-solving performance on benchmark exams. On the VNHSGE set (250 questions), V-MATH reported 100% exact-match accuracy across 2019–2023 (50 questions each year), and on 50 held-out NHSGME full exams it reached 92.1% item accuracy and 64% set-level accuracy, with expert-rated explanation quality of 4.6/5.
finding.measure: Exact-match accuracy on VNHSGE; item accuracy and set-level accuracy on held-out NHSGME exams; expert-rated explanation quality
finding.study_size: n=250 VNHSGE questions; n=50 held-out NHSGME exams

finding.finding_summary: The personalized learning agent is reported to improve engagement and student performance in follow-up practice. The paper reports an engagement score of 0.76 and a pre/post score gain of +11.8 points after following recommended learning paths, though this is presented as an internal evaluation rather than a controlled causal study.
finding.measure: Engagement score; pre/post test score gain

finding.finding_summary: The system is intended to support step-by-step reasoning, explanation quality, and personalized problem-solving, which are durable-skill adjacent outcomes. The paper reports 82.1% step completeness and 4.5/5 explanation quality for the solver agent, suggesting improved structured reasoning support, but does not directly measure broader metacognition or critical thinking outcomes.
finding.measure: Step completeness; explanation quality

finding.finding_summary: The framework is designed to reduce teacher workload and automate exam creation, question-bank maintenance, and feedback generation. The paper reports high matrix compliance for generated questions (96.7%), teacher rating of 4.6/5, and claims that the system reduces manual workload, but does not provide a direct workload time-study for teachers.
finding.measure: Teacher rating; matrix compliance; system functionality for automated question generation and reporting

finding.finding_summary: The paper positions V-MATH as a standards-aligned, scalable infrastructure for national-exam preparation and notes broader institutional implications for exam generation, benchmarking, and data standardization. It also explicitly flags unresolved issues relevant to institutional deployment, including fairness, audit trails, responsible data licensing, and privacy, but these are framed as future challenges rather than observed failures.
finding.measure: Standards alignment, benchmark creation, and system-level deployment claims

paper_profiles.title: Исследовательские задачи и Московская математическая конференция школьников
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper describes the Moscow Mathematical Conference of School Students (MMKSh) as a model for supporting school students’ mathematical research through careful formulation, peer review, consultation, and public presentation. The authors argue that the conference is designed to help students move from solving educational problems to producing short, reliable mathematical texts with completed proofs, while also making the process transparent by publishing submitted works and reviews.

A major theme is the distinction between exploratory/work-in-progress writing and completed, reliable mathematical references. The paper explains why the conference separates nominations by type of work, why novelty claims must be checked before a work is treated as scientific research, and why rigorous reviewing and revision are essential. The authors give many examples of student works that were revised over one or more years, sometimes moving from educational to scientific nomination after stronger results or clearer proofs emerged.

The paper also discusses governance and quality-control practices: anonymous reviews, public posting of reviews, consultation before resubmission, and rules to prevent misleading claims of novelty or proof completeness. In the appendix, the authors explicitly list common misconceptions about school research, including the harmful idea that quantity of participation matters more than work quality, and they argue that transparent review and archival posting reduce fraud, weak proof standards, and reputational harm. Although the paper is not about generative AI or mathematics learning interventions, it does provide direct evidence and discussion about reliability, correctness, and misuse risks in student mathematical work.

finding.finding_summary: The paper describes a conference governance model intended to improve the quality, transparency, and reliability of student mathematical research. It argues that anonymous public review, revision cycles, archival posting, and nomination-based distinction reduce errors, misleading novelty claims, and profile inflation, but it reports no quantitative institutional effect sizes.
finding.measure: Conference process design; review and nomination procedures; qualitative examples of work revision and acceptance

paper_profiles.title: Elementary School Students’ and Teachers’ Perceptions Towards Creative Mathematical Writing with Generative AI
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how elementary school students and teachers perceived a GenAI-supported creative mathematical writing activity. The authors focus on a classroom use case in which students first analyzed a story problem, then represented mathematical ideas visually, and finally used a GenAI tool powered by GPT-4 and DALL·E 3 to draft and revise culturally relevant math stories aligned to fraction multiplication/division content.

The study was implemented in six fifth-grade classrooms across two U.S. schools with 79 students and six teachers. Data came from focus-group interviews with 10 students, interviews with all six teachers, open-ended survey responses, and classroom observation notes, then analyzed thematically. The paper reports perceived benefits in creativity, mathematical understanding, AI literacy, and motivation/ownership, alongside challenges such as students’ difficulty critically evaluating AI output, the AI being “too perfect,” limited adaptive feedback, reduced autonomy, weak social connection, and accessibility gaps. The authors explicitly note the tool had been red-teamed for readability, accuracy, and safety, but the paper’s harms are mostly anticipated rather than empirically observed as adverse events.

finding.finding_summary: Students and teachers perceived that GenAI-supported creative mathematical writing helped students understand fraction-related math ideas, represent mathematical knowledge, and uncover misconceptions. However, the evidence is qualitative and based on perceptions from 79 fifth-grade students and 6 teachers rather than measured achievement gains; no test scores or effect sizes were reported.
finding.measure: Perceptions of mathematical understanding, problem breakdown, mathematical knowledge representation, and misconception discovery from interviews, surveys, and observations

finding.finding_summary: Participants reported increased interest, curiosity, enjoyment, and ownership of learning during the AI-supported math writing activities. Students described math as more fun and were motivated to continue working, but these outcomes were self-reported perceptions without quantitative effect estimates.
finding.measure: Perceived interest, curiosity, enjoyment, and ownership in learning from interviews and open-ended survey responses

finding.finding_summary: The activity was perceived to support creativity, divergent and convergent thinking, flexible thinking, and AI prompt engineering skills. Students also reported learning to evaluate AI strengths and weaknesses, though some struggled to critically assess AI-generated content, indicating a mixed durable-skills profile without quantitative measurement.
finding.measure: Perceptions of creativity, prompt engineering, critical evaluation of AI output, and flexible/divergent thinking

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly studied creative mathematical writing as an academic writing task and found that GenAI helped students generate, revise, and enrich story drafts. Students reported that the AI made writing easier and more interesting, but the main evidence is thematic and qualitative rather than based on writing quality scores.
finding.measure: Perceptions of creative mathematical writing quality, originality, and revision support

paper_profiles.title: Can ChatGPT pass the Vietnamese National High School Graduation Examination?
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether ChatGPT can pass the Vietnamese National High School Graduation Examination (VNHSGE), a high-stakes exam used for graduation and university admission. The authors motivate the work as a test of ChatGPT’s educational usefulness and as evidence about whether a large language model can handle exam-style questions across multiple subjects.

The study evaluates ChatGPT in zero-shot mode on the VNHSGE evaluation set, which includes questions in mathematics, literature, English, physics, chemistry, biology, history, geography, and civic education. For multiple-choice questions, the model was prompted to answer in a structured format and its responses were graded against human-derived ground truth; literature was also assessed with essay tasks from the dataset. The paper reports subject-level scores from 2019 to 2023 and compares ChatGPT’s performance with Vietnamese student score distributions from 2019 to 2022.

The main conclusion is that ChatGPT achieved overall scores high enough to be described as passing the exam, with combined scores ranging from 6.30 to 6.94 depending on year and subject combination. Performance was strongest in English and comparatively weaker in chemistry, mathematics, physics, and some context-dependent subjects. The authors emphasize that ChatGPT may support learners, but they also note limitations in handling more complex questions and visual/chart-based geography items; they suggest that further work is needed before drawing strong conclusions about reliability in real educational settings.

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT’s mathematics performance was moderate and below the majority of Vietnamese students, with scores ranging from 5.2 to 6.6 across 2019-2023 and an average of 5.88/10. The paper reports 26-33 correct answers by year on the multiple-choice math items, but no formal effect size or confidence interval is provided.
finding.measure: Mathematics exam score on the VNHSGE and count of correct multiple-choice answers

finding.finding_summary: Performance in physics, chemistry, and biology varied substantially. Physics scores ranged from 5.75 to 6.5 (avg. 6.1), chemistry from 4.0 to 6.25 (avg. 4.8, the weakest subject), and biology from 5.25 to 6.0 (avg. 5.8); the authors state that ChatGPT generally scored lower than most Vietnamese students in physics and chemistry, while biology was often competitive.
finding.measure: Subject exam scores on VNHSGE physics, chemistry, and biology items

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly studies literature, history, geography, and civic education. ChatGPT did relatively well in literature (scores 5.63-7.5; avg. 6.8) and often outperformed most Vietnamese students in history (4.25-7.75; avg. 5.65), but was less consistent in geography (5.0-7.5; avg. 6.15) and civic education (6.0-8.25; avg. 7.05), where it usually scored below most students. No formal effect size or uncertainty estimate is reported.
finding.measure: VNHSGE subject scores for literature, history, geography, and civic education

finding.finding_summary: The authors argue that ChatGPT’s ability to pass the VNHSGE suggests potential institutional value for exam preparation and educational support, and they frame the work as relevant to high-stakes assessment practices. They also discuss a major limitation for geography: because the model cannot interpret images/charts, it is unable to answer many atlas-based questions, which they say makes performance incomplete in that domain.
finding.measure: Pass/fail on graduation-score computation and subject-level exam performance

finding.finding_summary: The paper repeatedly interprets results in terms of analytical thinking, critical thinking, and problem-solving, especially for mathematics, civics, and geography. However, these skills are inferred from exam performance rather than directly measured with a dedicated durable-skills instrument, so the evidence is indirect and no effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Exam performance on items requiring application, analysis, and problem-solving

paper_profiles.title: Learning Factors in AI-Augmented Education: A Comparative Study of Middle and High School Students
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how students perceive AI-supported learning in K-12 computer science settings, focusing on four dimensions of experience: experience, clarity, comfort, and motivation. The authors ask whether these dimensions relate to one another similarly in AI-mediated learning and whether the relationship structure differs between middle school and high school students.

The study was conducted in extracurricular computer science courses with 53 students total: 25 middle school students ages 10–13 and 28 high school students ages 15–20. Students completed a 17-item questionnaire after participating in AI-related activities: high school students used LLMs such as Gemini and Claude for vibe coding and prompt-based Python work, while middle school students used Teachable Machine and chatbot interactions in an introductory AI module. The authors combined Likert-scale analysis, Spearman correlations, Mann-Whitney U tests, and text mining of open-ended responses.

Results show generally positive perceptions in both groups, but with clear developmental differences. Middle school students exhibited tightly coupled, holistic evaluations: positive experience was strongly associated with perceived clarity, comfort, and motivation. High school students showed a more differentiated pattern, with weaker or near-zero correlations among several dimensions and a more critical separation between usability, clarity, and motivation. The authors conclude that AI integration strategies should be age-sensitive, with more structure and clarity for younger learners and more autonomy and technical communication support for older learners. The paper also notes limited prompt-engineering skill and suggests future work on scaffolding, teacher training, and gradual AI introduction.

finding.finding_summary: Students reported generally positive perceptions of AI-supported learning across experience, clarity, comfort, and motivation. In the quantitative results, high school students reported significantly higher ease of use than middle school students (M=3.68 vs. 3.16 on a 4-point scale; U=192.00, p=0.0013), while overall ratings of experience, clarity, comfort, and motivation were mostly positive in both groups.
finding.measure: Questionnaire ratings of experience, ease of use, clarity, comfort, and motivation

finding.finding_summary: The paper centers on how students evaluate AI-supported learning and interprets correlation patterns as reflecting developmental differences in appraisal, differentiation, and evaluative sophistication. Middle school students showed strong positive intercorrelations among dimensions (e.g., Experience-Clarity ρ=0.79), whereas high school students showed weaker and more independent judgments (e.g., Experience-Motivation ρ=0.02), which the authors describe as a more critical and technically sophisticated evaluation style.
finding.measure: Spearman correlations among perception dimensions; text mining of open-ended responses

finding.finding_summary: Students generally felt the AI tools helped them understand course content and support learning in computer science activities. Open-ended responses emphasized words such as learn, understand, helped, code, and explanation, suggesting perceived benefits for understanding and coding-related tasks rather than direct achievement scores.
finding.measure: Open-ended responses about how AI influenced learning; perceived support for course content understanding

finding.finding_summary: Students perceived the AI tools as easy to use and helpful for completing exercises, especially high school students. Ease-of-use ratings differed significantly by age group (M=3.68 high school vs. 3.16 middle school; U=192.00, p=0.0013), indicating better perceived usability and smoother task interaction for older students.
finding.measure: Ease-of-use item and qualitative comments about tool use during exercises

paper_profiles.title: VNHSGE: VietNamese High School Graduation Examination Dataset for Large Language Models
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper introduces VNHSGE, a Vietnamese high school graduation examination dataset designed to evaluate large language models (LLMs) on high-school-level tasks across nine subjects, including mathematics, literature, English, physics, chemistry, biology, history, geography, and civic education. The dataset combines official and illustrative exam questions from 2019–2023, along with step-by-step solutions, images, and translated English versions, and is intended as a benchmark for testing LLM capabilities in question answering, reading comprehension, text generation, and visual question answering.

The authors compare ChatGPT and BingChat on subsets of the dataset and contrast their performance with Vietnamese students’ score distributions. Their main finding is that the models can perform at or near human level in some non-STEM areas, but they lag in mathematics, physics, chemistry, and biology, especially on multi-step reasoning and high-application problems. The paper emphasizes that exam-style benchmarks can help educators judge whether LLMs are sufficiently reliable for teaching and learning contexts.

Regarding risks and harms, the paper explicitly warns that LLMs can produce misleading or erroneous information and notes that they may struggle with complex computation, multi-step reasoning, and Vietnamese-language nuances. These concerns are presented as reliability limitations rather than empirically measured harms, and the paper does not report cheating, privacy, overreliance, or equity outcomes. The authors discuss a need for countermeasures and evaluation benchmarks to decide whether to use or reject such models in education.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that ChatGPT and BingChat handle knowledge and comprehension-level mathematics questions, but they struggle with complex calculations, logical reasoning, and multi-step deductive problems.
