No formal effect size is reported; the evidence is based on accuracy comparisons against Vietnamese student performance on exam items (n not reported for the model evaluation subset, though the dataset contains 2,500 math questions).
finding.measure: Accuracy on Vietnamese high school mathematics exam questions (knowledge, comprehension, application, and high-application levels)

finding.finding_summary: The models are described as weaker on physics, chemistry, and biology, particularly on higher-difficulty and applied questions that require scientific reasoning and multi-step inference. The paper reports qualitative performance comparisons rather than a statistical effect estimate; no effect size or confidence interval is provided.
finding.measure: Accuracy/performance on high school physics, chemistry, and biology exam questions

finding.finding_summary: The authors state that ChatGPT and BingChat perform at a human level in literature and English, which are the paper’s literacy-related domains. This conclusion is based on comparison to Vietnamese student score distributions and model responses on exam questions, but the paper does not provide a formal effect size or confidence interval.
finding.measure: Performance/accuracy on literature and English exam questions, including reading comprehension and essay-type tasks

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports human-level performance in history, geography, and civics education, indicating that the models can answer a substantial share of non-STEM high-school exam questions in these subjects. The finding is descriptive and benchmark-based, with no reported effect size or inferential statistics.
finding.measure: Accuracy on history, geography, and civic education exam questions

paper_profiles.title: An Experience of Introducing Primary School Children to Programming using Ozobots (Practical Report)
paper_profiles.venue: WiPSCE '21 (The 16th Workshop in Primary and Secondary Computing Education)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This practical report describes an outreach project that introduced primary school children to programming concepts using Ozobot Evo robots. The authors aimed to support early computational thinking instruction in primary schools, where teachers and schools may lack equipment or training, and to make the transition from unplugged activities to more concrete programming experiences easier.

The intervention consisted of two-hour workshops delivered at eight primary schools in Germany and Austria to children in grades 3–5, typically in pairs and guided by 2–4 project participants. The workshop sequence moved from discovering the robot’s capabilities, to line-following with pen-and-paper worksheets, to inserting and reasoning about color-code commands, to exploring randomness, and finally to block-based programming in OzoBlockly on tablets, including debugging an intentionally incorrect program.

The paper is descriptive rather than experimental, and its main contribution is a set of design recommendations and lessons learned from implementation. The authors report that children were generally enthusiastic, that the pen-and-paper mode worked especially well as an entry point, and that step-by-step activities reduced difficulty and supported successful completion of tasks. They also document practical limitations and challenges such as battery drain when using Bluetooth, update/connectivity issues, occasional unexpected robot behavior, language limitations in the software, and the need for explicit guidance when students misused the remote-control feature or misunderstood the repeatable nature of programs. Overall, the report concludes that Ozobots are well suited for introductory primary-school programming, while noting that further work is needed to extend learning to more advanced concepts.

finding.finding_summary: The workshop supported introductory programming and computational thinking in primary school children through a progression from unplugged/pen-and-paper tasks to block-based coding. The authors report that every pair of children successfully programmed a functioning dance, and that the sequence concept could be transferred to BeeBots in later sessions, indicating learning of basic programming concepts rather than a measured academic test gain.
finding.measure: Successful completion of workshop programming tasks and observed transfer of the sequence concept
finding.study_size: n=8 schools; approximately 20–25 students per workshop

finding.finding_summary: The authors describe strong student enthusiasm, enjoyment, and positive attitudes toward programming and robots. They report that all children stated they had enjoyed programming with the Ozobot, and that girls and boys were motivated by positive feedback during the activities.
finding.measure: Observed enthusiasm and post-activity student statements of enjoyment
finding.study_size: n=8 schools; approximately 20–25 students per workshop

finding.finding_summary: The workshops were designed to develop basic sequencing, testing, and debugging practices, and the authors note that children learned to reason about program order and to correct erroneous implementations. They also report that the use-modify-create progression helped children move from following given examples to making their own programs, suggesting growth in early problem-solving and metacognitive programming skills.
finding.measure: Observed ability to sequence commands, debug incorrect programs, and create original paths/programs
finding.study_size: n=8 schools; approximately 20–25 students per workshop

finding.finding_summary: The report identifies several efficiency issues affecting implementation, including rapid battery drain when using Bluetooth, time-consuming manual preparation of incorrect programs on each tablet, and occasional update/connectivity problems that prevented some robots from being used with tablets. At the same time, the authors note that naming robots and using step-by-step worksheets made classroom management easier and reduced some practical friction.
finding.measure: Observed workshop logistics, battery life, pairing/update issues, and preparation time
finding.study_size: n=8 schools; approximately 20–25 students per workshop

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that Ozobots can help schools introduce programming even where primary curricula do not yet include computational thinking, and it offers recommendations for workshop design and resource preparation. The contribution is institutional in the sense of supporting adoption and implementation in schools, but it does not evaluate policy change or school-wide outcomes empirically.
finding.measure: Implementation lessons and recommendations for school outreach and classroom adoption

paper_profiles.title: VLM@school – Evaluation of AI image understanding on German middle school knowledge
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper presents VLM@school, a new benchmark for evaluating vision-language models (VLMs) on German middle-school curriculum content. The authors argue that existing multimodal benchmarks are often English-only, heavily multiple-choice, and poorly aligned with real classroom or textbook-style reasoning, so they build a dataset of 486 images and 2,038 open-ended questions spanning nine school subjects including mathematics, science-related physics and biology, geography, history, arts, music, religion, and sports.

The evaluation tests 13 open-weight VLMs on these tasks using automated LLM-based judging. The central finding is that even the strongest models remain weak on this benchmark: the best model reaches under 45% overall accuracy, with especially poor performance on math, music, and adversarial questions designed to be unanswerable from the image. The paper also shows that scores on public benchmarks such as MMMU do not reliably predict performance on this more curriculum-grounded dataset, suggesting that benchmark gains may not transfer to real-world multimodal understanding in school-like settings.

Although the paper is not an intervention study, it does document reliability and misuse-related issues relevant to educational deployment of generative AI. The authors report frequent wrong answers, hallucinated explanations, and failure to say when a question is unanswerable, especially on adversarial items; they also note that models sometimes give wild guesses or misleading follow-up answers. In the conclusion, they suggest that chain-of-thought/reasoning approaches might improve performance, and they emphasize the need for more rigorous evaluation and carefully designed prompts/benchmarks, but they do not propose classroom guardrails or usage restrictions for learners directly.

finding.finding_summary: The benchmark includes 308 math questions, and all tested VLMs performed weakly on this domain. The best model reached about 34.09% on math (Qwen2.5VL 32B), while smaller models were much lower (e.g. Ovis2 4B at 9.09%), indicating substantial reliability problems for middle-school mathematical reasoning tasks that require reading diagrams, counting, or basic geometry.
finding.measure: Open-ended middle-school math questions from textbook-style images (area, circumference, angles, counting, coordinate reading)

finding.finding_summary: The paper’s physics and biology sections show that models often failed on diagram interpretation and explanation-based reasoning. In physics, the best models reached only about 47.65% (Qwen2.5VL 32B) and 47.65% on physics in Table 4, while the discussion reports systematic errors in explaining phenomena such as why main-sequence stars become red giants and in interpreting circuits; in biology, models also struggled to map labels, colors, and numbers to anatomical parts.
finding.measure: Open-ended physics and biology questions grounded in images/diagrams
finding.study_size: n=234 physics questions; n=169 biology questions

finding.finding_summary: Across the non-math school subjects, performance was mixed but often poor, with substantial weaknesses in history, geography, music, religion, arts, and sports. For example, the best models reached about 54.36% in history, 49.13% in arts, 31.03% in music, 52.92% in religion, and 43.84% in sports, with many category-specific failures such as reverse map lookup, legend reading, and identifying artistic styles or sports situations.
finding.measure: Open-ended curriculum questions in arts, geography, history, music, religion, and sports
finding.study_size: arts n=286; geography n=251; history n=264; music n=166; religion n=206; sports n=154

finding.finding_summary: The benchmark is explicitly used to test whether models can integrate visual clues with background knowledge, make inferences from diagrams/maps, and avoid overconfident guessing. The authors repeatedly report failures in multi-step reasoning, reverse lookup, and choosing not to answer when information is missing, suggesting limited metacognitive reliability rather than robust reasoning skill.
finding.measure: Open-ended multi-step visual reasoning and unanswerable/adversarial question performance
finding.study_size: n=2038 questions total; adversarial subset included across domains

finding.finding_summary: The paper does not directly study student motivation or engagement, but it does evaluate a key affective-adjacent capability: whether models can appropriately abstain and acknowledge uncertainty. The authors report that models often fail to say ‘I don’t know’ and instead hallucinate or guess, which is framed as a practical trust and safety concern for educational use.
finding.measure: Accuracy on adversarial questions requiring refusal/abstention

paper_profiles.title: On Perception of Prevalence of Cheating and Usage of Generative AI
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how university teaching staff perceive the prevalence of student cheating and the impact of generative AI on academic integrity. The author combines an anonymous survey of 32 teachers in the Department of Information Technology at Uppsala University with institutional statistics on cheating investigations from 2004 to 2023.

The survey asked teachers to rate how common cheating is, whether it is increasing, whether the use of generative AI for writing tasks counts as cheating, and how widespread student use of generative AI is. The paper does not evaluate an AI intervention or student achievement; instead, it focuses on perceptions of dishonesty and the relationship between those perceptions and recorded cheating investigations. Teachers generally believed cheating is not highly prevalent, but that it is increasing, and they were split to mildly permissive on whether AI use constitutes cheating.

The main conclusion is that teachers perceive generative AI as a growing factor in academic dishonesty and believe many students use it, while not necessarily labeling all AI use as cheating. The author reports that these perceptions broadly align with institutional cheating-trend data, including a peak during the COVID-19 pandemic years. The paper also includes qualitative comments suggesting guardrails such as assignment redesign, explicit AI-use policies, and tasks that require explanation or higher-level reasoning, but it does not empirically test those safeguards.

finding.finding_summary: In a survey of 32 teachers, respondents perceived cheating as not highly prevalent but increasing over time, and they believed generative AI use by students was widespread. The paper compares these perceptions with university cheating-investigation statistics from 2004 to 2023 and reports that the perceived trend broadly aligns with the institutional record, including a COVID-19-era peak; no effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Teacher perceptions of cheating prevalence/trend and generative AI use; annual institutional cheating-investigation counts

paper_profiles.title: Tareas matemáticas abiertas como respuesta didáctica a la inteligencia artificial generativa en contextos post-IA
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a didactic problem arising from the widespread availability of generative AI in school mathematics: many traditional tasks can now be solved automatically, reducing students’ need to interpret situations, make decisions, or validate answers mathematically. The author frames this as a “post-AI” context in which task design and classroom regulation must assume the presence of generative AI rather than simply banning it.

The study examines one secondary-school classroom experience in which open mathematical tasks were implemented alongside a regulatory teaching device called COMPAS. COMPAS structures work through phases such as understanding the situation, organizing assumptions and data, mathematical modeling, producing and exploring results, analysis and validation, and socialization/synthesis. The paper is qualitative and descriptive-interpretive, relying on student written work, classroom interaction records, and teacher-researcher observations.

The main conclusion is that, when open tasks are carefully designed and AI use is explicitly regulated, students can retain epistemic control over mathematical activity even while using generative AI. The paper argues that AI should function as a subordinate resource for exploration or checking rather than as a source of definitive answers, and that the key didactic safeguard is to require interpretation, assumptions, modeling, and validation before any technological assistance is used. The observed tensions between student models and AI-generated answers are presented as productive rather than harmful, because they stimulate discussion and critical validation.

finding.finding_summary: The paper does not report achievement test gains, but it provides qualitative evidence that students engaged in mathematical modeling and validation when working on open tasks in the presence of generative AI. Under explicit didactic regulation, students retained epistemic control and treated AI outputs as objects for checking rather than as final answers; however, no effect size or quantitative achievement outcome is reported.
finding.measure: student task productions, classroom interactions, observed modeling and validation practices

finding.finding_summary: The study reports qualitative evidence of students exercising decision-making, justification, critical evaluation, and discussion while solving open mathematical tasks. These behaviors were especially visible when students compared their own models with AI-generated responses and revised assumptions, suggesting support for metacognitive and critical-thinking processes, though no quantitative measure was used.
finding.measure: observed agency, justification, critical discussion, and validation practices

finding.finding_summary: The paper qualitatively suggests that open tasks supported active participation and engagement in classroom mathematics, with students taking an involved role in constructing and revising models. The evidence is descriptive rather than measured, so no effect size or standardized engagement outcome is reported.
finding.measure: observed participation and engagement in classroom problem solving

paper_profiles.title: Designing AI Peers for Collaborative Mathematical Problem Solving with Middle School Students: A Participatory Design Study
paper_profiles.venue: CHI '26 (Proceedings of the 2026 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems)
paper_profiles.extended_summary: This paper asks how middle school students want generative AI to function as a peer in collaborative mathematical problem solving (CPS), rather than as a tutor. The authors argue that most AI-in-education work has focused on one-to-one instructional roles, while CPS in mathematics requires shared reasoning, turn-taking, and social coordination that may be poorly served by tutor-like AI. To study this, the team ran a five-day participatory design summer camp with 24 rising grades 6–8 students.

finding.finding_summary: The study does not evaluate learning gains, but it does provide direct evidence about how an AI peer affected students' mathematical problem-solving experience. Students reported that AI peers reduced temporal demand during CPS (NASA-TLX temporal demand: M=5.67, SD=4.38 vs. 9.62, SD=4.13 in human-only CPS; p=0.002, d=1.15), but they also felt the AI's rigid, teacher-like procedures could be distracting and sometimes gave different or overly direct answers that did not support their desired reasoning process. Students preferred hints, checks, and concept refreshers over full solutions.
finding.measure: NASA-TLX temporal demand during collaborative math problem solving; qualitative reports about math help, hints, and direct answers
finding.study_size: n=22 for paired quantitative comparisons; n=24 enrolled

finding.finding_summary: Students reported that AI peers lowered time pressure but also reduced social warmth and affective engagement. On the GEQ, Attractions to Group-Social was lower with AI peers (M=5.21, SD=1.81) than in human-only CPS (M=6.50, SD=2.05; p=0.029, d=0.94), and students described AI behavior as rude, mean, or not listening when it repeated itself or failed to respond to their emotional state. Several students said the system's lack of encouragement or empathy led them to feel frustrated or blame themselves when they got stuck.
finding.measure: GEQ group-social cohesion; interview and reflection reports of frustration, trust, and emotional support
finding.study_size: n=22 for paired quantitative comparisons; interviews n=18; whole-class reflections across 5 sessions

finding.finding_summary: The paper centrally examines collaboration, co-agency, and coordination in group problem solving. Students said the AI should work with them rather than do the work for them, and they disliked repeated or divergent turns that disrupted shared sense-making. Quantitatively, perceived group integration-task was lower with AI peers (M=4.76, SD=1.58) than in human-only CPS (M=5.54, SD=1.52; p=0.047, d=0.81), indicating weaker coordination even though the AI reduced time pressure.
finding.measure: GEQ Group Integration-Task; qualitative reports on co-agency, turn-taking, and coordination
finding.study_size: n=22 for paired quantitative comparisons; n=24 enrolled

finding.finding_summary: AI peers improved perceived efficiency by reducing students' sense of time pressure during collaborative math work, but this came with higher physical/operational burden from typing and managing the text-based interface. NASA-TLX physical demand was higher with AI peers (M=8.48, SD=4.65) than in human-only CPS (M=4.90, SD=2.41; p=0.014, d=1.14), suggesting the system was faster in one sense but more cumbersome to use.
finding.measure: NASA-TLX temporal demand and physical demand during CPS
finding.effect_size: d=1.15 (temporal demand reduction); d=1.14 (physical demand increase)
finding.std_deviation: SD=4.38 vs. 4.13 (temporal demand); SD=4.65 vs. 2.41 (physical demand)

finding.finding_summary: The paper includes some educational design discussion around prompt selection, school norms, and grade-aligned tasks, but it does not substantively measure a non-mathematics academic outcome. Any mention of instruction is in service of designing the AI peer and not an assessed academic domain, so there is no empirical achievement result for this category.
finding.measure: not_reported

paper_profiles.title: Integration of AI in STEM Education – Addressing Ethical Challenges in K-12 Settings
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a critical conceptual review of AI integration in K-12 STEM education, focused on the ethical risks and implementation challenges of using AI-powered tools in classrooms. Rather than testing a specific generative AI intervention, the authors synthesize recent scholarship on intelligent tutoring systems, automated assessments, predictive analytics, and surveillance technologies, with attention to bias, privacy, equity, and pedagogical integrity.

The paper argues that AI can support personalized learning, feedback, and operational efficiency, but only if schools address serious risks such as algorithmic bias, black-box decision-making, student surveillance, and uneven access across districts. It proposes a three-phased implementation roadmap and a four-phase professional development framework grounded in TPACK and critical algorithmic literacy. The framework includes bias audits, low-resource adaptations, ethics instruction, and student data governance to reduce harm and support equitable adoption.

The population of interest is K-12 students and educators in STEM settings, especially schools considering AI-enabled instruction, assessment, or monitoring. The paper does not report new empirical data; its conclusions are based on literature synthesis and policy-oriented recommendations. Its main contribution is a responsible-integration framework emphasizing safeguards, human oversight, and equity-centered design rather than achievement effects from a tested intervention.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that AI tools can reduce teacher workload and increase scalability through automated assessment, personalized feedback, and 24/7 tutoring access. It does not present new data, but cites prior work suggesting these tools can free educators for higher-order instruction and support efficient intervention delivery.
finding.measure: teacher workload, scalability, and instructional efficiency

finding.finding_summary: The paper centers on institutional implications of AI adoption, emphasizing both benefits and harms: policy alignment, governance, ethical audits, and data governance are presented as necessary to avoid privacy violations, inequity, and biased decision-making. No original effect sizes are reported; the argument is conceptual and based on synthesized literature rather than new empirical measurement.
finding.measure: policy readiness, governance practices, equity audits, and student data governance

finding.finding_summary: The paper discusses student engagement and agency as potential benefits of AI integration, while warning that surveillance, bias, and over-reliance may undermine motivation and learning engagement. In its implementation scenario, success is evaluated with student engagement surveys, but no numerical results are reported.
finding.measure: student engagement surveys; engagement and agency

finding.finding_summary: The paper claims AI can support critical thinking through ethics-oriented activities, but also warns that over-dependence on ITS and automated assessments may constrain creative problem-solving, reduce critical thinking, weaken debugging ability, and suppress scientific curiosity. These concerns are presented as literature-based harms rather than newly measured outcomes.
finding.measure: critical thinking, creative problem-solving, debugging ability, and scientific curiosity

finding.finding_summary: The paper discusses AI use in science/STEM contexts, noting potential benefits such as adaptive feedback and improved mastery of complex scientific material, alongside risks that AI systems may misread inputs, limit nuanced reasoning, or narrow higher-order scientific inquiry. No primary empirical findings are reported in the paper itself.
finding.measure: mastery of STEM/science material, scientific argument refinement, and misconception detection

paper_profiles.title: Elementary School Students’ and Teachers’ Perceptions Towards Creative Mathematical Writing with Generative AI
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates how elementary school students and teachers perceive a generative AI-supported environment for creative mathematical writing. The authors are motivated by two related questions: what educational benefits students and teachers perceive, and what challenges or barriers emerge when GenAI is used to help children create math stories.

The study was conducted in six fifth-grade classrooms across two U.S. schools with 79 students and six teachers. Students used a custom GenAI-powered platform built with GPT-4 and DALL·E 3 to complete a three-step activity—Ask, Represent, and Transform—where they first analyzed a math story, then represented their thinking visually, and finally co-created or revised a math story with AI. Data came from student focus groups, teacher interviews, open-ended survey responses, and classroom observations, and were analyzed through mixed inductive/deductive thematic analysis.

The paper reports perceived benefits in creativity, mathematical understanding, AI literacy, and affective engagement such as interest, curiosity, and ownership. At the same time, it identifies several challenges: students sometimes failed to critically evaluate AI-generated content, struggled to formulate effective prompts, found the AI output too perfect, and desired more adaptive feedback, autonomy, social interaction, and accessibility features. The authors also note that the platform was red-teamed and designed with a checklist for reviewing AI output, reflecting an explicit attempt to mitigate safety and quality concerns. Overall, the paper is a qualitative classroom study about perceptions and design implications rather than an achievement-effect study.

finding.finding_summary: Students and teachers perceived that GenAI-supported creative mathematical writing improved mathematical understanding, including breaking down word problems, representing ideas, and uncovering misconceptions. The study is qualitative and does not report test-score gains; evidence comes from interviews and observations with 79 fifth-grade students and 6 teachers rather than quantitative outcome measures.
finding.measure: Perceived mathematical understanding, problem decomposition, mathematical knowledge representation, and misconception identification from interviews, open-ended surveys, and classroom observations

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly studies creative mathematical writing, a writing-centered academic task, and reports that GenAI helped students generate, revise, and elaborate math stories. Participants described gains in originality, divergent/convergent thinking during writing, and making their stories more interesting and unique, though no standardized writing scores were reported.
finding.measure: Perceived creative writing quality and originality in mathematical story writing

finding.finding_summary: Students and teachers perceived that working with GenAI made math more enjoyable, increased interest and curiosity, and strengthened ownership of learning. These are reported as lived-experience themes from interviews and survey comments, not as quantitative motivation or engagement scales.
finding.measure: Perceived interest, curiosity, enjoyment, and ownership of learning

finding.finding_summary: The study reports that GenAI-supported story writing promoted prompt engineering, evaluation of AI strengths and weaknesses, and flexible thinking, but also revealed students’ difficulty critically evaluating AI outputs and generating coherent stories. These durable-skill effects are based on qualitative perceptions rather than performance assessments.
finding.measure: Perceived prompt engineering, critical evaluation of AI content, flexible/divergent thinking, and story formulation skills

finding.finding_summary: Participants perceived that the AI could quickly generate story drafts and reduce the time/effort needed to start creative writing, suggesting efficiency benefits in drafting and idea generation. However, this was not measured as a productivity outcome and no timing or workload metrics were reported.
finding.measure: Perceived time/effort savings in drafting and revising math stories

paper_profiles.title: Learning Factors in AI-Augmented Education: A Comparative Study of Middle and High School Students
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how key learning-perception factors relate to one another in AI-mediated education, and whether those relationships differ between middle school and high school students. The authors focus on four dimensions drawn from educational psychology and learning analytics: experience, clarity, comfort, and motivation. They are especially interested in whether AI changes the structure of these perceptions compared with traditional learning environments.

The study was conducted in extracurricular computer science contexts with authentic classroom activities. A total of 53 students participated: 25 middle school students (ages 10–13) and 28 high school students (ages 15–20). High school students used LLMs such as Gemini and Claude for vibe coding and prompt-based Python work, while middle school students used Teachable Machine for introductory AI activities and chatbot interaction. Data came from a 17-item questionnaire with Likert-scale and open-ended items, analyzed using Spearman correlations, Mann-Whitney U tests, and text mining.

The main conclusion is that students generally reported positive experiences with AI tools, but the perception structure differed by age. Middle school students showed tightly linked, holistic evaluations: positive impressions of one dimension tended to generalize to the others. High school students showed weaker and more differentiated associations, suggesting a more critical appraisal of clarity, usability, comfort, and motivation. The paper argues that AI integration strategies should be developmentally responsive, with younger learners benefiting from more structured introductions and clearer scaffolding, and older learners benefiting from more technically sophisticated and autonomy-supporting designs. The paper also notes difficulties in students formulating effective prompts and recommends explicit prompt-engineering instruction and gradual AI introduction.

finding.finding_summary: Students generally reported positive experiences with the AI tools, including comfort, motivation, and willingness to use AI again. In the quantitative results, middle school students averaged 3.04/4 on motivation (Q14) and 3.40/4 on comfort (Q8), while high school students averaged 2.96/4 on motivation and 3.75/4 on comfort; open-ended responses also emphasized that the AI helped them learn and understand better. The authors interpret these perceptions as evidence that AI-supported activities were experienced positively overall, though motivation and comfort were more differentiated among high school students.
finding.measure: Questionnaire ratings of comfort and motivation (Q8, Q14), plus open-ended reflections on learning experience

finding.finding_summary: The paper centrally studies how students evaluate AI-supported learning across experience, clarity, comfort, and motivation, which are treated as interrelated perception factors. Correlations were strong and positive for middle school students (e.g., Experience-Clarity ρ=0.79; Clarity-Motivation ρ=0.60), but substantially weaker and more selective for high school students (e.g., Experience-Clarity ρ=0.51; Experience-Motivation ρ=0.02; Experience-Comfort ρ=0.16), indicating a developmental shift from holistic to more differentiated evaluation. The authors argue this reflects more sophisticated appraisal and metacognitive differentiation in older students.
finding.measure: Spearman correlations among aggregated perception dimensions (Experience, Clarity, Comfort, Motivation) and item-level questionnaire responses

finding.finding_summary: The AI activities were embedded in computer science/programming learning, and students reported that the tool helped them understand course content and support coding tasks. For example, Q6 (helped understand course content) had means of 2.80/4 for middle school and 3.04/4 for high school, and open-ended responses frequently included terms such as learn, understand, helped, code, and explanation. The authors conclude that students perceived AI as beneficial for learning and coding support in this CS context.
finding.measure: Questionnaire item on understanding course content (Q6) and open-ended reflections on learning/coding support

paper_profiles.title: Engaging Teachers to Co-Design Integrated AI Curriculum for K-12 Classrooms
paper_profiles.venue: ACM [conference/workshop venue not specified in provided text]
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how K-12 teachers think about and design AI-integrated lessons when AI is embedded into existing core subjects rather than taught as a standalone computing topic. The authors ask how to address teachers’ values and design considerations, and how AI can be integrated into core curriculum in ways that are feasible and accessible for diverse learners.

To investigate this, the researchers ran a two-day remote co-design workshop with 15 K-12 educators from multiple subjects and countries. Teachers participated in presentations about AI, card-sorting, pre-work, group co-design, and an ethics-focused discussion, then created draft AI-integrated curricula for social studies, ESL, and literacy for students with learning disabilities. The workshop data included audio recordings, questionnaires, and participant artifacts, which were thematically analyzed.

The main findings are that teachers valued evaluation, engagement, logistics, and collaboration when designing AI lessons, and that they repeatedly needed scaffolding to define AI learning goals and to implement ethics and diversity discussions. The co-designed lessons integrated AI through data, reflection, and ethics, suggesting that AI can be meaningfully embedded into non-CS subjects. The paper concludes that teacher co-design can help make AI education more accessible, but that further scaffolding and implementation support are needed for classroom use.

finding.finding_summary: The study found that co-designing AI curriculum with 15 K-12 educators helped surface practical needs for classroom adoption, including evaluation, engagement, logistics, and collaboration. Teachers produced three draft integrated curricula and reported increased familiarity with AI (mean 4.8/7 to 5.8/7) and confidence in integrating AI (mean 5.6/7), suggesting promise for broader institutional uptake of AI curriculum when teacher expertise is included.
finding.measure: Teacher familiarity with AI, confidence integrating AI, and co-designed curriculum artifacts

finding.finding_summary: A central result was that teachers intentionally built in reflection, collaboration, and ethics discussion as part of AI-integrated lessons. The paper reports that these curricular designs were meant to support students’ critical thinking about data, bias, and real-world implications rather than only technical AI skills.
finding.measure: Co-designed lesson plans and teacher discussion themes

finding.finding_summary: Teachers emphasized student engagement as a key design goal and proposed anchors such as real-world questions, student-driven topics, and gamification to keep learners motivated. The study does not test student outcomes directly, but it documents strong educator consensus that engagement supports are necessary for AI-integrated K-12 lessons.
finding.measure: Teacher design discussions and workshop artifacts

finding.finding_summary: One of the three co-designed curricula targeted ESL and centered on AI-supported pronunciation practice, with students recording correct and incorrect pronunciations to train a classification model. The paper presents this as an integrated lesson design, not as an outcome evaluation, so no student learning effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Co-designed ESL pronunciation curriculum

finding.finding_summary: Another co-designed curriculum targeted literacy for students with learning disabilities, using vocabulary words and associated images to train a classification model. The paper reports the design of this curriculum and teachers’ reasoning about evaluation and ethics, but it does not measure literacy gains.
finding.measure: Co-designed literacy curriculum for students with learning disabilities

finding.finding_summary: The paper includes an exemplar physics curriculum in which students build paper airplanes and use resulting data to train a model predicting flight effectiveness. This is presented as a curriculum design demonstrating how AI can be embedded in non-computing subjects, not as a measured learning intervention.
finding.measure: Co-designed physics curriculum using paper-airplane data and ML prediction

paper_profiles.title: Using Transformers to Provide Teachers with Personalized Feedback on their Classroom Discourse: The TalkMoves Application
paper_profiles.population: K-12 mathematics teachers and their students
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper presents TalkMoves, an automated system that analyzes K-12 mathematics classroom recordings and gives teachers personalized feedback on their use of accountable talk moves. The paper addresses the challenge of scaling expert classroom-observation feedback, which is normally time-consuming and requires trained human coders. The authors frame the system as a way to help teachers reflect on and improve discourse practices that support student engagement and mathematical reasoning.

The approach combines automated speech recognition with transformer-based natural language processing models to classify teacher utterances into six talk-move categories (plus none) using sentence pairs that include prior student context. The study uses 501 transcribed K-12 math lessons from multiple sources, with expert human annotation serving as ground truth. The best-performing model is RoBERTa-Large, reaching F1 = 79.33% and MCC = 0.7779 on the test set; a smaller DistilRoBERTa model is deployed in the application for efficiency.

The context is a pilot deployment with 21 teachers in two Midwestern U.S. school districts during the 2019-2020 school year. Teachers used the application, viewed feedback, completed surveys, and participated in interviews. The main conclusion is that the system can produce feedback that is generally on par with domain experts in reliability, but the authors emphasize technical challenges in noisy classroom speech data and note that automatic speech recognition underestimates student talk, which can affect downstream classification and feedback quality. The paper is primarily a model/system development paper rather than an outcome study of student learning.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that TalkMoves can automate and scale teacher feedback that would otherwise require highly trained human observers to hand-code transcripts. The system is intended to reduce time and expertise demands in classroom observation workflows, and the best model achieved F1 = 79.33% (MCC = 0.7779) on classifying talk moves for feedback generation.
finding.measure: Model performance for automated talk-move classification; intended reduction in human coding/feedback workload
finding.study_size: n=501 transcripts; pilot deployment with n=21 teachers

finding.finding_summary: The paper presents TalkMoves as an end-to-end instructional support system intended to scale professional learning across teachers and districts. The authors report a pilot deployment with 21 teachers in two Midwestern school districts and position the tool as an institutional infrastructure for scalable feedback on classroom discourse.
finding.measure: Pilot implementation in schools and feasibility of scaled feedback infrastructure

paper_profiles.title: Why Avoid Generative Legal AI Systems? Hallucination, Overreliance, and their Impact on Explainability
paper_profiles.venue: FORVM- Acta Juridica et Politica Special Issue planned for 2026
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper argues against routine use of generative AI systems in legal practice, focusing on the risks of hallucination, overreliance, and weakened explainability. It frames generative legal AI (GLAI) as a set of legal-domain tools used for document drafting, legal research, decision support, and public-facing legal assistance, and situates the discussion within European AI governance (GDPR and the EU AI Act).

The paper is primarily conceptual and argumentative rather than empirical. It synthesizes legal and technical literature, international reports, and illustrative incidents to show how hallucinated outputs, persuasive fluent text, and automation bias can cause professionals to trust inaccurate AI outputs. It also discusses possible mitigations, especially explainability and human oversight, but concludes that these measures are insufficient unless hallucination and overreliance are effectively solved.

Although the article is not about K-12 education or mathematics, it is relevant to the requested sub-question because it directly documents misuse and harm patterns associated with generative AI: fabricated citations, inaccurate reasoning, overreliance, professional error, privacy concerns, and high-stakes decision risk. The author’s core conclusion is that generative AI should not be used routinely in legally consequential settings without strong restrictions and meaningful human scrutiny.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that hallucinations and overreliance in generative legal AI undermine explainability, human oversight, judicial independence, and protection of fundamental rights. It cites illustrative real-world incidents such as withdrawn court opinions containing fabricated citations and a Turkish enforcement-office case in which AI output was prioritized over documentary evidence, but it does not report a controlled empirical effect estimate.
finding.measure: Legal decision integrity, explainability, human oversight, and institutional risk in legal workflows

finding.finding_summary: The paper states that generative AI can improve efficiency in legal research, drafting, and document processing, but argues that these gains are offset by the time burden of verifying hallucinated outputs and the risk that checking AI-generated work may require more effort than doing the work manually. No original quantitative productivity study is presented.
finding.measure: Professional workflow efficiency and verification burden

finding.finding_summary: The article contends that overreliance on fluent generative AI output can erode critical thinking, professional skepticism, and legal reasoning. It presents this as a conceptual and practice-based harm supported by examples of users deferring to AI recommendations, but it does not provide a direct measured effect size or experimental outcome.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, professional skepticism, and reasoning quality

finding.finding_summary: The paper discusses automation bias, anthropomorphic trust, and emotional simulation as drivers of uncritical reliance on AI outputs. It argues that these mechanisms can weaken user caution and increase dependence on the system, but the article itself does not measure motivation, engagement, or self-regulation empirically.
finding.measure: Trust, reliance, and automation bias in users

paper_profiles.title: Competing Visions of Ethical AI: A Case Study of OpenAI
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how OpenAI has publicly framed “ethics,” “safety,” “alignment,” and related concepts over time in its own communications. The authors ask whether OpenAI’s discourse reflects substantive ethical engagement or instead a narrower rhetorical emphasis on safety and risk.

Using a longitudinal mixed-methods case study, the authors build a corpus of 454 OpenAI-authored or co-authored documents from December 2015 through July 2025, including 424 website articles and 30 publications. They combine keyword frequency analysis, topic modeling, and qualitative content analysis of documents that mention ethics-related terms, with attention to differences between public web articles and academic-style publications.

The main conclusion is that OpenAI’s public discourse overwhelmingly foregrounds safety, risk, and alignment while using ethics language sparsely and often superficially. The authors argue that this pattern is consistent with ethics-washing: ethics is more visible in academic or collaborative publications than in public-facing communications, and even there it is often peripheral rather than central. They conclude that OpenAI’s framing shifts governance toward technical safety and compliance registers, while sidelining broader justice-oriented ethical concerns.

finding.finding_summary: The study finds a strong discursive shift at OpenAI toward safety, risk, alignment, and compliance, while explicit ethics language remains rare in public-facing communications. Across 424 web articles, only 16 (3.8%) contained any ethics-related term; in 180 publications, 31 (17.2%) did so, but usually only briefly and in peripheral contexts. The authors interpret this as evidence of ethics-washing and a narrowing of governance discourse, not as a measured causal effect on educational or product outcomes.
finding.measure: Longitudinal content analysis of OpenAI public communications, including keyword frequencies, topic clustering, and qualitative coding of ethics-related usage
finding.study_size: n=454 documents (424 web articles; 30 publications in final corpus; 180 publications reviewed in broader screening)

paper_profiles.title: Mathematical Capabilities of ChatGPT
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper evaluates the mathematical capabilities of two versions of ChatGPT (9-January-2023 and 30-January-2023) and GPT-4 using a newly created benchmark suite, GHOSTS, plus a smaller miniGHOSTS subset. The authors designed prompts spanning advanced mathematics, including proof completion, theorem-style questions, olympiad-style problem solving, symbolic integration, and definition/retrieval tasks intended to mimic how a mathematician might use a language model as an assistant.

The study is not an intervention in a K-12 setting; rather, it is a benchmark evaluation of model outputs on graduate-level and undergraduate-level mathematics problems. The authors manually rated 709 prompts (1636 ratings total) and found that ChatGPT was most useful as a facts/retrieval assistant, while both ChatGPT versions performed poorly on graduate-level proof and computation tasks. GPT-4 improved substantially, but still failed on graduate-level difficulty and was not consistently reliable.

The paper’s main conclusion is that these models are inconsistent mathematical tools: they can produce occasionally insightful answers, but overall performance is below a graduate student level. The authors explicitly note that the models frequently give wrong answers without expressing uncertainty, and that GPT-4 can still make mistakes in seemingly simple calculations. They frame the system as potentially useful only when the user is sufficiently expert to detect errors, functioning more like a search engine or knowledge base than a dependable solver.

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly evaluates mathematical problem solving across 709 prompts (1636 human ratings) and finds mixed performance: ChatGPT averaged 3.20 (SD=1.23) on the 9-Jan version and 3.29 (SD=1.28) on the 30-Jan version, while GPT-4 averaged 4.15 (SD=1.12) on the miniGHOSTS subset. Performance was strong on fact retrieval and some undergraduate-level tasks, but poor on graduate-level proof-based questions, olympiad-style problems, and more complicated symbolic calculations.
finding.measure: Human-rated correctness/quality score on mathematics prompts (rating scale 1-5) across GHOSTS and miniGHOSTS; subtask-specific ratings
finding.study_size: n=709 prompts (1636 ratings); GPT-4 on n=170 prompts
finding.confidence_interval: 95% CI reported graphically for subdataset means; exact values not_reported

paper_profiles.title: Should There be a Teacher In-the-Loop? A Study of Generative AI Personalized Tasks Middle School
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether teachers should remain in the loop when using generative AI to personalize middle school mathematics tasks. The authors focus on context personalization in math word problems, using GPT-4o/ChatGPT to adapt Illustrative Mathematics problems to students’ interests and then examining both teacher prompting behavior and student reactions.

Seven 7th-grade mathematics teachers from six U.S. schools participated. They were trained on personalization, then used ChatGPT to modify 143 problems for 521 students across two units (proportional relationships/percentages and expressions/equations/inequalities). The study combines log analysis of teacher-LLM interactions, video/transcript coding, and student survey feedback about interest, closeness to interests, and whether anything in the problem was inaccurate.

The main findings are that teachers frequently had to revise ChatGPT outputs for realism, numerical appropriateness, readability, and occasional inappropriate content, and that the process was not especially time efficient. Teachers averaged about 3.2 prompts and roughly 4 minutes per problem, with no clear evidence that efficiency improved over time; in fact, Unit 6 took more prompts and more time than Unit 4. Students generally preferred more specific popular-culture references, but they often cared more about surface-level interest than realism, and overall ratings of interestingness and closeness were modest. The authors conclude that teacher-in-the-loop personalization can support professional learning and quality control, but it is constrained by time costs and by the mismatch between broad teacher-selected personalization and students’ desire for finer-grained customization. They also note that AI can produce unrealistic or occasionally inappropriate content, making teacher oversight important.

finding.finding_summary: The study did not measure student achievement directly, but it did examine students’ ratings of personalized mathematics problems as a proxy for task relevance. For 52-53 problems, students rated interestingness and closeness to interests on 1-5 scales; problems created with 3-5 teacher prompts received higher ratings by about 0.24 points on average (B=0.240, SE=0.085, p=0.0073).
finding.measure: Student ratings of problem interestingness and closeness to interests for personalized math tasks
finding.study_size: n=521 students; 143 problems; ratings available for 52-53 problems
finding.std_deviation: SD=1.24 (interestingness), SD=1.28 (closeness); problem creation time SD=165.7 seconds; prompts SD=2.6

finding.finding_summary: Students generally responded more positively when problems matched their interests, especially when the task used a specific popular-culture reference rather than a broad topic. In the closed-ended ratings, Unit 6 problems were rated higher than Unit 4 on interestingness (2.56 vs. 2.27) and closeness (2.66 vs. 2.28), with the increase statistically significant (B=0.33, SE=0.095, p=0.0012).
finding.measure: Student self-reported interestingness and closeness-to-interests ratings; open-ended feedback about interest
finding.study_size: n=521 students; 446-454 open-ended responses; 52-53 rated problems
finding.std_deviation: SD=1.17 to 1.29 depending on unit and measure

finding.finding_summary: Teacher-facing personalization with ChatGPT was time-consuming and did not become clearly more efficient with experience. paper_profiles.title: The mathematics in middle-aged Arab caliphate and it application to contemporary teaching in high schools
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a historical обзор of major mathematical contributions associated with the medieval Arab caliphate, written with an explicit educational aim: to stimulate interest and support teaching in high schools. The authors summarize selected Arabic mathematicians and present classic arithmetic and algebraic puzzles, then discuss how these examples can be used in contemporary mathematics instruction.

The paper does not test an intervention or collect data from students. Instead, it surveys historical developments such as place-value numeration, algebra, number theory, the Chinese remainder theorem, and geometric work by scholars including al-Khwarizmi, Thabit ibn Qurra, al-Haytham, al-Karaji, and others. Its main conclusion is that medieval Arabic mathematics made substantial contributions to the development of modern mathematics and that these historical examples may enrich high-school teaching and student interest.

No empirical study of learners, achievement, engagement, or classroom implementation is reported. The article is best characterized as a descriptive historical and pedagogical essay rather than an outcomes study.

finding.finding_summary: The paper does not evaluate an instructional treatment or report student outcomes; it only describes historical mathematical content and suggests it could be used in high school teaching. No achievement data, sample, or effect estimate are reported.
finding.measure: not_reported

paper_profiles.title: Short-term AI literacy intervention does not reduce over-reliance on incorrect ChatGPT recommendations
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether a brief AI literacy intervention can reduce high school students’ tendency to rely on incorrect ChatGPT recommendations while solving math puzzles. The authors frame the problem as over-reliance on generative AI, especially the risk that students may accept incorrect or hallucinated outputs without verification.

In the experiment, 36 Estonian 12th-grade students were randomly assigned to read either a short control text about ChatGPT or a longer intervention text that explained ChatGPT’s working mechanism, limitations, hallucinations, biases, and tips for wise use. After reading, students solved eight Kangaroo-style math puzzles with ChatGPT suggestions; four suggestions were correct and four were intentionally incorrect. Over-reliance was defined as accepting an incorrect ChatGPT recommendation, and under-reliance as rejecting a correct recommendation.

Results showed widespread over-reliance: students accepted incorrect recommendations 52.1% of the time overall, and 94.4% of participants accepted at least one incorrect suggestion. The intervention did not significantly reduce over-reliance (intervention M=48.68% vs. control M=55.88%, Welch’s t(28.78)=-0.73, p=.236, d=-0.25), but it did significantly increase under-reliance (M=36.84% vs. 19.12%, t(34)=2.35, p=.025, d=0.78), meaning students were more likely to ignore correct ChatGPT answers after the literacy text. The authors conclude that short AI literacy texts may not be enough to prevent over-reliance and caution schools about adopting LLMs in secondary education without stronger guardrails.

finding.finding_summary: The study directly measured student performance on eight Kangaroo math puzzles with ChatGPT assistance (n=36). The intervention did not significantly reduce over-reliance on incorrect recommendations (48.68% vs. 55.88%, Welch’s t(28.78)=-0.73, p=.236, d=-0.25), but it did significantly increase under-reliance on correct recommendations (36.84% vs. 19.12%, t(34)=2.35, p=.025, d=0.78).
finding.measure: Reliance on ChatGPT recommendations while solving math puzzles; over-reliance and under-reliance rates
finding.effect_size: d=-0.25 for over-reliance; d=0.78 for under-reliance
finding.std_deviation: SD=24.26 (intervention over-reliance), SD=33.69 (control over-reliance), SD=24.11 (intervention under-reliance), SD=20.78 (control under-reliance)

finding.finding_summary: The paper substantively examines critical evaluation and slow/analytical thinking as mechanisms related to reliance on AI advice. Longer initial decision times were associated with less over-reliance on incorrect recommendations (Spearman rs=-0.41, p=.013) and more under-reliance on correct recommendations (rs=0.35, p=.038), suggesting that deliberate thinking reduced blind acceptance but also increased rejection of correct AI advice.
finding.measure: Initial decision time and reliance behavior; self-reported AI literacy understanding
finding.effect_size: rs=-0.41 for over-reliance vs. time; rs=0.35 for under-reliance vs. time
finding.std_deviation: SD=0.77 minutes (intervention total decision time), SD=1.12 minutes (control total decision time)

finding.finding_summary: The authors explicitly caution schools and countries planning to integrate LLMs into secondary education, arguing that widespread over-reliance could harm critical thinking in the long term. This is not an achievement outcome per se, but a system-level concern based on the observed 52.1% over-reliance rate and the failure of the short intervention to reduce it.
finding.measure: Observed over-reliance rate and authors’ policy/implementation implications
